Basic Concept

Worked Example Principles of Antimicrobial Therapy Ch 43 — Principles of Antimicrobial Therapy · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept
Principles of Antimicrobial Therapy
Review Module Chapter
Ch 43 — Principles of Antimicrobial Therapy

Related Content

  • Perform hand hygiene before and after each client contact to prevent the spread of infection.
  • Recognize invasive procedures that increase the risk of infection (indwelling urinary catheter, IV catheter, cardiac catheterization).
  • Encourage prevention by having clients maintain an up-to-date immunization status.
  • Instruct clients to take the full course of antimicrobials the provider prescribes to prevent medication resistance and recurrence of infection.
  • Use infection-control procedures to prevent transmission of resistant micro-organisms.

Underlying Principles

  • Selective toxicity: kill or inhibit the microbe without harming host cells (exploits microbial-specific structures: cell wall, ribosomes, folate synthesis)
  • Empiric vs definitive therapy:
    • Empiric: best-guess antibiotic based on likely organisms before culture results
    • Definitive: narrowed agent based on culture and sensitivity (C&S)
  • Spectrum: narrow (one or few organisms) preferred over broad-spectrum when possible (↓ resistance, ↓ disrupting normal flora)
  • Bacteriostatic vs bactericidal: bactericidal needed for serious infections, endocarditis, immunocompromised clients
  • Resistance mechanisms: enzymatic inactivation (β-lactamases), altered targets, ↓ permeability, efflux pumps
  • Antibiotic stewardship principles:
    • Confirm bacterial (not viral) infection before prescribing
    • Use the narrowest effective agent
    • Shortest effective duration
    • Correct dose for organism, site of infection, renal/hepatic function
    • De-escalate when culture results allow
  • Combination therapy indications: synergy (e.g., β-lactam + aminoglycoside for enterococcal endocarditis), polymicrobial infections, prevent resistance (TB), empiric coverage in life-threatening sepsis
  • Concentration-dependent (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones) vs time-dependent (β-lactams, vancomycin) killing — informs dosing strategies
  • Pharmacokinetic factors: tissue penetration (CSF for meningitis, lung for pneumonia, urine for UTI), protein binding, half-life
  • Superinfection risk: antibiotic-associated diarrhea (C. difficile), Candida overgrowth

Nursing Interventions

  • Perform hand hygiene before and after each client contact to prevent the spread of infection.
  • Recognize invasive procedures that increase the risk of infection (indwelling urinary catheter, IV catheter, cardiac catheterization).
  • Encourage prevention by having clients maintain an up-to-date immunization status.
  • Instruct clients to take the full course of antimicrobials the provider prescribes to prevent medication resistance and recurrence of infection.
  • Use infection-control procedures to prevent transmission of resistant micro-organisms.
  • Evaluate the effectiveness of treatment.
Worked Example Antibiotic Resistance & Superinfection Ch 43 — Principles of Antimicrobial Therapy · Resistance section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Antibiotic Resistance & Superinfection

Defining Characteristics

Antibiotic resistance is the ability of microorganisms to survive exposure to antimicrobials that previously killed them or inhibited their growth, reducing treatment effectiveness.

Superinfection is a new infection that develops during antimicrobial treatment, when normal protective flora are killed, allowing overgrowth of resistant organisms or fungi.

  • Resistance is a major global public health threat
  • Examples: MRSA, VRE, multidrug-resistant gram-negatives, C. difficile
  • Promoted by overuse and misuse of antibiotics

Antecedents

  • Overuse/misuse of antibiotics (viral illnesses, unnecessary prescriptions)
  • Incomplete antibiotic courses (not finishing prescription)
  • Broad-spectrum antibiotic use
  • Antibiotics in agriculture
  • Prolonged or repeated antibiotic exposure
  • Immunocompromise, hospitalization, invasive devices
  • Poor infection control

Negative Consequences

  • Treatment failure — infections that no longer respond to standard antibiotics
  • Need for more toxic, expensive, last-line antibiotics
  • Superinfections: C. difficile colitis (severe diarrhea), oral/vaginal candidiasis (yeast)
  • Increased morbidity, mortality, length of stay
  • Spread of resistant organisms (outbreaks)
  • Untreatable infections (worst case)

Related Concepts

Antimicrobial stewardship, MRSA/VRE, C. difficile, broad- vs narrow-spectrum, normal flora, culture and sensitivity, de-escalation, infection control, candidiasis, prophylactic vs therapeutic use.

Exemplars

  • Antimicrobial stewardship: use the right drug, dose, duration; narrow spectrum when culture allows (de-escalation); avoid antibiotics for viral infections.
  • Complete the full course: stopping early leaves surviving resistant organisms → recurrence and resistance. Key patient teaching.
  • C. difficile superinfection: watch for new watery diarrhea during/after antibiotics (especially clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, broad-spectrum); use contact precautions; soap and water (not just alcohol gel) for hand hygiene (spores); treat with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin.
  • Candidiasis superinfection: oral thrush or vaginal yeast during antibiotics — treat with antifungals; teach to report.
  • Culture before antibiotics: obtain cultures before the first dose so the causative organism and sensitivities guide therapy.
  • Infection control: hand hygiene, isolation precautions for resistant organisms (MRSA/VRE contact precautions).
  • Patient teaching: take all doses, do not share/save antibiotics, do not demand antibiotics for colds, report new diarrhea or yeast symptoms.
Worked Example Culture & Sensitivity / Antibiotic Selection Ch 43 — Principles of Antimicrobial Therapy · Selection section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Culture & Sensitivity / Antibiotic Selection

Defining Characteristics

Culture and sensitivity (C&S) testing identifies the causative organism and determines which antibiotics will be effective, guiding rational antibiotic selection.

  • Culture: grows and identifies the organism
  • Sensitivity: tests the organism against various antibiotics (susceptible / intermediate / resistant)
  • Empiric therapy: broad-spectrum started before results (based on likely organisms)
  • Definitive/targeted therapy: narrowed once C&S returns (de-escalation)

Antecedents

  • Suspected bacterial infection requiring treatment
  • Need to identify the pathogen and effective drug
  • Severe infection/sepsis (empiric broad-spectrum started promptly)
  • Treatment failure or resistant organism suspected
  • Host factors influencing choice (allergies, renal/hepatic function, pregnancy, age, site of infection)

Negative Consequences

  • If cultures NOT obtained before antibiotics: organism may not grow → cannot target therapy
  • Wrong/ineffective antibiotic → treatment failure, worsening infection
  • Unnecessary broad-spectrum use → resistance, superinfection
  • Toxicity if drug inappropriate for host (renal/hepatic, allergy)
  • Subtherapeutic or toxic levels without monitoring (e.g., vancomycin, aminoglycosides)

Related Concepts

Empiric vs definitive therapy, broad- vs narrow-spectrum, de-escalation, minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), trough/peak levels, therapeutic drug monitoring, host factors, sepsis bundles, antimicrobial stewardship.

Exemplars

  • KEY PRINCIPLE: obtain cultures BEFORE the first antibiotic dose — antibiotics can prevent organism growth and obscure results. (In sepsis, draw blood cultures then give antibiotics promptly — do not excessively delay.)
  • Empiric → definitive: start broad-spectrum empirically for serious infection → narrow to the specific effective agent when sensitivities return (de-escalation reduces resistance).
  • Host factors in selection: allergies (penicillin), renal function (dose-adjust/avoid nephrotoxic), hepatic function, pregnancy (avoid tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones), age (avoid certain drugs in children), site of infection (drug penetration, e.g., CNS).
  • Therapeutic drug monitoring: for narrow-index antibiotics (vancomycin, aminoglycosides), monitor trough (just before next dose — efficacy/toxicity) and sometimes peak; adjust to renal function.
  • Timing of doses around cultures: draw the trough before the dose; collect specimens correctly (clean technique).
  • Nursing role: ensure cultures collected before first dose, administer antibiotics on time to maintain levels, monitor effectiveness (fever, WBC, symptoms) and toxicity, advocate de-escalation per stewardship.
  • Patient teaching: why cultures matter, importance of completing the course, reporting lack of improvement.
Worked Example Antimicrobial Hypersensitivity / Allergy Ch 43 — Principles of Antimicrobial Therapy · Resistance section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Antimicrobial Hypersensitivity / Allergy

Defining Characteristics

Antimicrobial hypersensitivity is an immune-mediated adverse reaction to an antibiotic, ranging from mild rash to life-threatening anaphylaxis. Penicillins are the most common cause of drug allergy.

  • Immediate (IgE-mediated): within minutes-hours — urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, anaphylaxis
  • Delayed: hours-days — maculopapular rash, and severe reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, DRESS)
  • Distinguish true allergy from intolerance (e.g., GI upset is NOT an allergy)

Antecedents

  • Prior exposure and sensitization to the antibiotic or related class
  • Documented or reported drug allergy
  • Genetic predisposition (atopy; HLA types for severe reactions)
  • Higher risk drugs: penicillins, cephalosporins, sulfonamides, vancomycin
  • Repeated or high-dose courses
  • Cross-reactivity between related drug classes

Negative Consequences

  • Anaphylaxis — airway compromise, shock, death (medical emergency)
  • Severe cutaneous reactions: Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS
  • Need to avoid effective antibiotics (mislabeled allergies limit options → broader/less ideal drugs → resistance)
  • Serum sickness, organ involvement
  • Treatment delays

Related Concepts

Anaphylaxis, epinephrine, IgE-mediated reaction, cross-reactivity, penicillin allergy, cephalosporin cross-sensitivity, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, red man syndrome (vancomycin), allergy verification, drug intolerance vs allergy.

Exemplars

  • Always assess allergy history BEFORE administering any antibiotic; clarify the reaction (true allergy vs intolerance/side effect).
  • Anaphylaxis recognition/response: hives, swelling, wheezing, hypotension within minutes → stop drug, call for help, epinephrine IM, airway/oxygen, IV fluids, antihistamines/corticosteroids adjunctively; monitor closely.
  • Penicillin–cephalosporin cross-reactivity: historically overestimated; low (~1–2%) with modern cephalosporins, but caution/clarify the penicillin reaction severity before giving a cephalosporin.
  • Vancomycin “red man syndrome”: flushing/rash from rapid infusion (histamine release) — NOT a true allergy; slow the infusion and premedicate (antihistamine).
  • Sulfonamide allergy: can be significant (rash, SJS); document and avoid.
  • Severe delayed reactions (SJS/TEN, DRESS): discontinue drug immediately, supportive care, dermatology; never rechallenge.
  • Documentation: record the specific drug, reaction type, and severity; flag the chart/allergy band; avoid mislabeling intolerances as allergies (preserves treatment options).
  • Monitoring after first dose: observe for early reaction; have emergency equipment available.

Worked Example Therapeutic Drug Monitoring (Peak & Trough) Ch 44/45 — Antibiotics · Drug-level monitoring · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Diagnostic Procedure
Therapeutic Drug Monitoring (Peak & Trough Levels)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 44/45 — Antibiotics & Narrow-Index Drugs

Description of Procedure

Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) is the measurement of serum drug concentrations to keep a narrow-therapeutic-index medication within its effective, non-toxic range and to guide dosing.

  • Trough level: the LOWEST concentration — drawn just before the next dose; reflects clearance/safety
  • Peak level: the HIGHEST concentration — drawn a set time after administration (e.g., ~30 min after an IV aminoglycoside finishes); reflects efficacy
  • Common TDM drugs: vancomycin, aminoglycosides (gentamicin), digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, theophylline

Indications

  • Drugs with a narrow therapeutic index (small gap between effective and toxic)
  • Confirming therapeutic levels / dose adjustment
  • Suspected toxicity or treatment failure
  • Renal or hepatic impairment (altered clearance)
  • Drug interactions affecting levels
  • Adherence assessment

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre:

  • Verify the correct timing order (peak vs trough) and the exact time the last dose was given/finished
  • Coordinate with pharmacy/lab; label tubes with draw time
  • Confirm which medication and target range

Intra (draw):

  • Trough: draw immediately before the next scheduled dose — do NOT give the dose until the trough is drawn
  • Peak: draw at the protocol-specified time after the dose (timing is critical — a mistimed level is uninterpretable)
  • Draw from a site away from the infusing line (avoid contamination/falsely high results)
  • Document exact draw time and last-dose time

Post:

  • Report results promptly; hold/adjust dose per provider if trough is elevated (toxicity risk) or peak is sub/supratherapeutic
  • Monitor for drug-specific toxicity (e.g., nephro/ototoxicity, digoxin toxicity, lithium toxicity)
  • Document interventions and dosing changes

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Drug level within therapeutic range
  • Effective treatment without toxicity
  • Correctly timed draws (interpretable results)
  • Appropriate dose adjustments made
  • No signs of drug toxicity

Potential Complications

  • Mistimed draw → uninterpretable level → wrong dosing decision
  • Drawing from the infusing line → falsely elevated level
  • Giving the dose before the trough is drawn → lost trough
  • Toxicity if elevated trough not acted on (e.g., vancomycin/aminoglycoside nephro/ototoxicity, digoxin/lithium toxicity)
  • Treatment failure if subtherapeutic levels missed
  • Specimen hemolysis affecting results
Worked Example Culture & Sensitivity Specimen Collection Ch 43 — Principles of Antimicrobial Therapy · Selection section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Diagnostic Procedure
Culture & Sensitivity Specimen Collection
Review Module Chapter
Ch 43 — Principles of Antimicrobial Therapy

Description of Procedure

Culture and sensitivity (C&S) specimen collection obtains a sample (blood, urine, sputum, wound, etc.) to identify the causative organism and determine which antimicrobials are effective.

  • Culture: grows/identifies the organism
  • Sensitivity: tests the organism against antibiotics (susceptible/intermediate/resistant)
  • Cardinal rule: obtain cultures BEFORE the first antibiotic dose whenever possible

Indications

  • Suspected bacterial infection requiring targeted therapy
  • Sepsis (blood cultures before antibiotics)
  • Treatment failure or suspected resistance
  • Need to de-escalate from empiric broad-spectrum therapy
  • Recurrent or complicated infections

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre:

  • Collect the specimen BEFORE administering the first antibiotic dose (antibiotics suppress growth → false negatives)
  • Gather correct container/medium; verify orders and site
  • Hand hygiene; appropriate PPE

Intra (collection):

  • Use aseptic/sterile technique to avoid contamination with normal flora
  • Blood cultures: disinfect site; collect from 2 different sites (and label); adequate volume
  • Urine: clean-catch midstream or sterile catheter specimen
  • Sputum: deep cough (not saliva), ideally early morning
  • Wound: from the wound bed after cleaning, not surface exudate
  • Label accurately (site, time); avoid contaminating the lid/interior

Post:

  • Transport to lab promptly (delays alter results)
  • After collection, the ordered empiric antibiotic can be started (do not delay in sepsis)
  • Monitor for results; anticipate de-escalation/targeting once sensitivities return
  • Document collection time, site, and antibiotic timing

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Uncontaminated specimen yielding accurate organism identification
  • Sensitivities guide effective, targeted therapy
  • Cultures obtained before antibiotics (interpretable)
  • Appropriate de-escalation from broad-spectrum therapy
  • Infection resolved with the correct agent

Potential Complications

  • Antibiotics given before collection → organism may not grow → cannot target therapy
  • Contamination with normal flora → false-positive / misleading results → unnecessary/wrong antibiotics
  • Delayed transport → organism overgrowth or death → inaccurate results
  • Inadequate volume (blood cultures) → reduced sensitivity
  • Wrong specimen type (e.g., saliva instead of sputum)
Worked Example Tuberculin Skin Testing (Mantoux/PPD) Ch 47 — Mycobacterial, Fungal, and Parasitic Infections · TB section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Diagnostic Procedure
Tuberculin Skin Test (Mantoux/PPD)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 47 — Mycobacterial, Fungal, and Parasitic Infections

Description of Procedure

The Mantoux tuberculin skin test (TST/PPD) screens for TB infection by injecting purified protein derivative intradermally and measuring the delayed hypersensitivity reaction.

  • 0.1 mL PPD injected intradermally (forearm) → raised wheal/bleb
  • Read at 48–72 hours by measuring the induration (firm raised area), NOT redness, in millimeters
  • A positive result indicates TB infection/exposure, not necessarily active disease

Indications

  • Screening high-risk groups (healthcare workers, immunocompromised, close contacts, recent immigrants from high-prevalence areas, incarcerated, homeless)
  • Suspected TB exposure
  • Pre-employment / pre-enrollment screening
  • Baseline before immunosuppressive therapy

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre:

  • Assess for prior positive TST (do not repeat — risk of severe reaction), prior BCG vaccine (may cause false-positive), recent live vaccine
  • Select intradermal site (volar forearm)

Intra (administration):

  • Inject 0.1 mL intradermally at a 5–15° angle, bevel up, producing a wheal
  • Do NOT aspirate or massage; do not cover tightly
  • Circle/mark site; document time, site, lot number

Post (reading):

  • Return in 48–72 hours for reading
  • Measure induration in mm (palpate the firm area) — do not measure redness/erythema
  • Interpret per risk category (≥ 5 mm, ≥ 10 mm, or ≥ 15 mm cutoffs depending on risk)
  • Positive result → follow-up chest X-ray and sputum (rule out active disease)
  • Document measurement and interpretation

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Correct intradermal placement (wheal formed)
  • Read within the 48–72 hr window
  • Induration measured accurately in mm
  • Appropriate interpretation and follow-up for positives
  • TB infection identified for treatment/prophylaxis

Potential Complications

  • Measuring redness instead of induration → misinterpretation
  • Missing the 48–72 hr reading window → invalid result (must repeat)
  • Subcutaneous (not intradermal) injection → invalid test
  • False-positive (prior BCG); false-negative (immunocompromise, anergy, very recent infection)
  • Rarely, severe local reaction/blistering (especially repeat testing of a known positive)
  • A positive TST alone does not distinguish latent from active TB

Worked Example Pediatric Pharmacology Considerations Ch 6 — Individual Considerations of Medication Administration · Pediatric section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Growth and Development
Pediatric Pharmacology Considerations

Defining Characteristics

Children are NOT small adults — pediatric pharmacology requires understanding age-specific changes in absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) that affect drug action.

Key age-related differences:

  • Neonates/infants: immature liver (reduced CYP450) → slower metabolism; higher body water (~75%) → larger volume of distribution for water-soluble drugs; immature renal function → slower clearance; immature BBB → greater CNS effects
  • Toddlers/preschoolers: CYP450 actually higher than adults (per kg) → may need proportionally higher doses for some drugs
  • School-age/adolescents: approach adult kinetics; puberty alters metabolism

Antecedents

  • Current age and weight (use weight in kg, not pounds)
  • Developmental stage affecting cooperation, swallowing ability, comprehension
  • Renal and hepatic maturity (neonate vs older child)
  • Drug formulation availability (liquid, chewable, crushable)
  • Caregiver health literacy and willingness to administer at home
  • Drug reference with pediatric-specific dosing (Lexicomp, Harriet Lane)

Negative Consequences

  • 10-fold dosing errors — classic peds error from decimal misplacement
  • Underdosing when adult doses extrapolated without weight-based calculation
  • Overdose toxicity — especially acetaminophen (hepatotoxicity), opioids (respiratory depression)
  • Drug-induced developmental damage — tetracycline tooth staining, fluoroquinolone tendon/cartilage damage
  • Aspiration with poorly designed liquid administration
  • Reye syndrome from aspirin during viral illness

Related Concepts

Weight-based dosing, safe dose range verification, body surface area (BSA) dosing, oral syringe technique, Reye syndrome, drugs contraindicated in children, atomoxetine in ADHD, family-centered care, vaccination schedules.

Exemplars

  • Drugs to AVOID in children: aspirin (Reye syndrome with viral illness); tetracyclines < 8 yo (tooth discoloration); fluoroquinolones (cartilage damage); codeine (variable CYP2D6 metabolism → respiratory depression in ultra-rapid metabolizers); promethazine < 2 yo (respiratory depression)
  • Acetaminophen: safe in all ages including neonates; weight-based 10–15 mg/kg/dose
  • Ibuprofen: approved > 6 months; weight-based 5–10 mg/kg/dose
  • Vaccines: follow CDC schedule precisely; live vaccines (MMR, varicella) at 12–15 months
  • Administration tips: use oral syringes; place liquid in cheek pouch (not back of throat — aspiration); offer favorite drink as chaser (NOT essential medication); never bribe with “candy”
  • Family involvement: teach parents about medication safety storage, accurate measurement, completing antibiotic courses
Worked Example Geriatric Pharmacology & Beers Criteria Ch 6 — Individual Considerations of Medication Administration · Geriatric section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Growth and Development
Geriatric Pharmacology & Beers Criteria

Defining Characteristics

Older adults (≥ 65 years) experience physiologic changes that affect drug pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, increasing the risk of adverse drug events.

Major changes:

  • Decreased gastric acid, slower GI motility → altered absorption
  • Decreased lean body mass, increased fat → lipid-soluble drugs (benzodiazepines, opioids) have longer duration
  • Decreased albumin → more free (active) drug for protein-bound drugs (warfarin, phenytoin)
  • Decreased liver size and blood flow, reduced CYP450 → slower metabolism
  • Decreased renal function (eGFR drops ~1 mL/min/year after 30) → slower clearance of renally cleared drugs
  • Increased receptor sensitivity to many CNS drugs

The Beers Criteria (AGS-updated 2023) is the standard list of potentially inappropriate medications (PIMs) in older adults.

Antecedents

  • Age ≥ 65 years (especially ≥ 75)
  • Polypharmacy (≥ 5 medications) — very common in this population
  • Multiple comorbidities
  • Cognitive impairment affecting adherence and self-monitoring
  • Functional limitations (vision, dexterity, swallowing)
  • Multiple prescribers contributing to medication list
  • Renal or hepatic impairment
  • Falls risk, frailty

Negative Consequences

  • Falls and fractures — from benzodiazepines, opioids, antihypertensives, anticholinergics
  • Delirium — especially from anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, opioids
  • Bleeding — warfarin, NSAIDs, antiplatelets
  • Adverse drug events are 4× more common than in younger adults
  • Hospitalization and mortality — ADEs are a leading cause of preventable harm in older adults
  • Prescribing cascade — new symptom from drug A treated with drug B, leading to drug C, etc.

Related Concepts

Polypharmacy, Beers Criteria, STOPP/START criteria, deprescribing, anticholinergic burden, fall risk assessment, medication reconciliation, brown bag review, prescribing cascade, frailty.

Exemplars

  • Beers list — AVOID in older adults:
  • First-gen antihistamines (diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine) — anticholinergic burden
  • Benzodiazepines (lorazepam, alprazolam, diazepam) — falls, sedation, cognitive impairment
  • Z-drugs (zolpidem) — falls, complex sleep behaviors
  • TCAs (amitriptyline) — anticholinergic, orthostatic
  • Anticholinergics (oxybutynin) — cognitive impairment, urinary retention
  • Skeletal muscle relaxants (cyclobenzaprine) — sedation, anticholinergic
  • NSAIDs — GI bleeding, kidney injury
  • Long-acting sulfonylureas (glyburide) — prolonged hypoglycemia
  • Safer alternatives: Tylenol over NSAIDs; melatonin/CBT-I over zolpidem; SNRIs over TCAs; loratadine over diphenhydramine
  • Deprescribing strategy: annual brown bag review; STOP medications without ongoing indication; taper carefully (especially CNS-active drugs)
Worked Example Medications in Pregnancy and Lactation Ch 6 — Individual Considerations of Medication Administration · Pregnancy section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Growth and Development
Medications in Pregnancy and Lactation

Defining Characteristics

Medications administered during pregnancy or lactation can affect the developing fetus or breastfed infant. Risk-benefit analysis is required: untreated maternal disease may be MORE dangerous than the medication.

The FDA replaced the old Pregnancy Categories (A, B, C, D, X) with the Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling Rule (PLLR) in 2015, which uses narrative descriptions rather than letter categories. Many older references still use the legacy A–X system.

Key principle: most drugs cross the placenta via passive diffusion (especially lipid-soluble, low molecular weight). Lactation similarly depends on lipid solubility, protein binding, and molecular size.

Antecedents

  • Pregnancy status (verify with hCG before prescribing teratogens)
  • Gestational age (organogenesis weeks 4–10 — most vulnerable to teratogenesis)
  • Breastfeeding status
  • Maternal condition (untreated illness may pose greater risk than medication)
  • Drug class and known reproductive safety data
  • Availability of safer alternatives
  • Family planning intentions

Negative Consequences

  • Teratogenesis — congenital malformations from drug exposure during organogenesis
  • Fetal toxicity — later in pregnancy (e.g., ACE inhibitors → renal damage; NSAIDs → premature ductus closure)
  • Neonatal withdrawal — opioids, SSRIs, benzodiazepines
  • Lactation transfer — drug effect in infant (lithium, methimazole, chemotherapy contraindicated)
  • Withholding necessary treatment — untreated depression, epilepsy, infection can harm mother and fetus
  • Spontaneous abortion or stillbirth from certain medications

Related Concepts

Teratogens, FDA Pregnancy Categories (legacy A/B/C/D/X), PLLR (Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling Rule), organogenesis, placental transfer, neonatal abstinence syndrome, drug excretion in breast milk, LactMed database, methyldopa (preferred HTN in pregnancy), Tdap timing.

Exemplars

  • Known teratogens (Category X equivalents): isotretinoin, thalidomide, warfarin (replace with heparin/LMWH), methotrexate, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, statins, finasteride, lithium (avoid 1st trimester), valproate (neural tube defects), phenytoin (cleft palate), tetracyclines (teeth/bone)
  • Safer choices in pregnancy: acetaminophen (preferred analgesic), labetalol/methyldopa/nifedipine (HTN), heparin/LMWH (anticoagulation), insulin (diabetes), penicillins/cephalosporins (most infections)
  • Avoided in 3rd trimester: NSAIDs (premature ductus closure), aspirin (bleeding)
  • Lactation contraindications: lithium, methotrexate, ergot alkaloids, chemotherapy, radioactive iodine, illicit drugs
  • Lactation generally safe: most antibiotics, acetaminophen, ibuprofen, most antihypertensives, SSRIs (preferred: sertraline, paroxetine)
  • Tdap in pregnancy: recommended every pregnancy 27–36 weeks (maternal antibody transfer protects newborn)
  • Folic acid: 400–800 mcg/day BEFORE conception and through 1st trimester (prevents neural tube defects)

Worked Example Gentamicin Ch 5 — Adverse Effects, Interactions, and Contraindications · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Gentamicin
Review Module Chapter
Ch 5 — Adverse Effects, Interactions, and Contraindications
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Gentamicin is a bactericidal aminoglycoside antibiotic that binds irreversibly to the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit, blocking protein synthesis and causing mRNA misreading.

  • Active against aerobic gram-negative bacilli: E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Proteus, Serratia, Enterobacter
  • Limited gram-positive activity — often combined with cell-wall agents (penicillins, vancomycin) for synergy against enterococci and staphylococci
  • Concentration-dependent killing with prolonged post-antibiotic effect

Therapeutic Use

  • Gentamicin is a narrow-spectrum aminoglycoside antibiotic prescribed to treat serious infections caused by aerobic bacilli.

Complications

  • Gentamicin can injure cells of the proximal renal tubules (nephrotoxicity).
  • Gentamicin is ototoxic — can cause permanent hearing loss and vestibular damage.
  • Naproxen and other NSAIDs can independently cause renal insufficiency.
  • The glomerular filtration rate of the kidneys decreases with advanced age, ↑ risk for nephrotoxicity.
  • Combining gentamicin with naproxen significantly increases the risk of acute kidney injury.

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to aminoglycosides
  • Pre-existing renal impairment — requires dose adjustment
  • Pre-existing hearing or vestibular impairment
  • Myasthenia gravis — can worsen neuromuscular weakness
  • Pregnancy Category D — fetal ototoxicity reported
  • Caution in elderly (age-related ↓ renal function) and dehydrated clients
  • Avoid concurrent nephrotoxic or ototoxic drugs when possible

Interactions

  • Loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide) → ↑ ototoxicity
  • Nephrotoxic drugs (vancomycin, NSAIDs, amphotericin B, cisplatin) → ↑ nephrotoxicity
  • Neuromuscular blockers (succinylcholine, vecuronium) → potentiated blockade → respiratory paralysis risk
  • Cephalosporins → additive nephrotoxicity
  • IV magnesium → ↑ neuromuscular blockade
  • Penicillins — NEVER mix in same syringe/IV line (mutual inactivation); space doses 1 hr apart

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ fever, ↓ WBC count toward normal
  • Negative blood, urine, or wound cultures post-therapy
  • Resolution of infection-specific signs (↓ purulent drainage, ↓ pain at infection site, improved oxygenation in pneumonia)
  • Therapeutic drug levels:
    • Peak 5-10 mcg/mL
    • Trough < 2 mcg/mL
  • No nephrotoxicity: BUN/creatinine stable, urine output > 30 mL/hr
  • No ototoxicity: hearing and balance intact, no tinnitus or vertigo

Medication Administration

  • Routes: IV (most common), IM, topical, ophthalmic
  • Adult IV dose:
    • Traditional: 1-2 mg/kg q8h
    • Extended-interval ("once-daily"): 5-7 mg/kg q24h
  • Pediatric dose: 2-2.5 mg/kg q8h (weight-based)
  • Infuse IV over 30-60 minutes — NEVER IV push (neuromuscular blockade)
  • Dose-adjust based on CrCl in renal impairment
  • Obtain peak (1 hr post-infusion) and trough (just before next dose) levels at steady state (3rd-4th dose)
  • Therapeutic range: peak 5-10 mcg/mL, trough < 2 mcg/mL

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor intake and output; report urine output < 30 mL/hr
  • Daily weights to track fluid status
  • Encourage adequate fluid intake (unless contraindicated)
  • Hold naproxen if possible during gentamicin therapy; collaborate with provider
  • Educate client to report hearing changes, tinnitus, dizziness, decreased urine output

Client Education

  • Report immediately: hearing changes, ringing in ears (tinnitus), dizziness, balance problems, ↓ urine output, swelling
  • Increase fluid intake (≥ 2 L/day unless contraindicated) to support renal clearance
  • Complete the full prescribed course even if symptoms resolve
  • Avoid NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin) without provider approval
  • Inform all providers of gentamicin therapy before any new prescription
  • Keep all lab appointments — BUN, creatinine, and drug levels are essential
  • Notify provider if pregnant or planning pregnancy (fetal risk)
  • Report new or unusual symptoms during therapy
Worked Example Warfarin Ch 5 — Adverse Effects, Interactions, and Contraindications · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Warfarin
Review Module Chapter
Ch 5 — Adverse Effects, Interactions, and Contraindications
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Warfarin is an oral anticoagulant that inhibits vitamin K-dependent synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X (and proteins C and S) in the liver.

  • Onset is delayed (3-5 days) — bridge with heparin if rapid anticoagulation needed
  • Therapeutic range monitored by INR:
    • Most indications: 2.0-3.0
    • Mechanical heart valves: 2.5-3.5
  • Reverses with vitamin K (slow, hours-days) or fresh frozen plasma / prothrombin complex concentrate (rapid, emergency)

Therapeutic Use

  • Atrial fibrillation — stroke prevention (CHA2DS2-VASc ≥ 2)
  • Mechanical heart valves (target INR 2.5-3.5)
  • Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) treatment and prevention
  • Pulmonary embolism (PE) treatment and prevention
  • Post-MI for left ventricular thrombus or severe LV dysfunction
  • Antiphospholipid syndrome
  • Hypercoagulable states (Factor V Leiden, protein C/S deficiency)

Complications

  • Bleeding — most common; ranges from minor (gum, nose, bruising) to major (GI, intracranial, retroperitoneal)
  • Warfarin-induced skin necrosis — rare; days into therapy, often in protein C-deficient clients
  • Purple toe syndrome — cholesterol microembolization
  • Hair loss (alopecia)
  • Hypersensitivity reactions
  • Hepatic injury (rare)
  • Teratogenicity (Category X) — fetal warfarin syndrome, fetal bleeding

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Pregnancy Category X — teratogenic (fetal warfarin syndrome)
  • Active bleeding or recent major surgery
  • Severe hypertension or thrombocytopenia
  • Hemorrhagic stroke, peptic ulcer disease, esophageal varices
  • Vitamin K deficiency
  • Caution with falls risk (elderly), alcohol abuse, hepatic disease

Interactions

  • St. John's wort is a CYP450 inducer (CYP3A4 and others)
  • It will ↓ warfarin levels → ↓ anticoagulation effect → ↑ risk of thrombosis/stroke
  • St. John's wort also interacts with: OCPs, antiretrovirals, digoxin, antidepressants (serotonin syndrome)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • INR within therapeutic range (2.0-3.0 standard; 2.5-3.5 mechanical valves)
  • No new thrombotic events (stroke, DVT, PE, MI)
  • Resolution of existing clot (per imaging or clinical findings)
  • No bleeding complications: stable Hgb/Hct, no bruising or unexplained bleeding

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (also IV form for emergencies)
  • Adult starting dose: 2-5 mg/day, then titrate to INR
  • Take at the same time each day (usually evening)
  • Do NOT double-up missed doses — skip if > 12 hours late and resume normal schedule
  • INR monitoring: initially weekly, then monthly when stable
  • Bridge with heparin or LMWH initially until INR therapeutic for 2 consecutive days

Nursing Interventions

  • Notify the provider of the supplement use
  • Educate client to discontinue St. John's wort or monitor INR closely
  • Document the interaction
  • Recheck INR within 1 week of stopping the supplement (may need warfarin dose adjustment)

Client Education

  • Always inform providers about ALL supplements, including "natural" and herbal products
  • "Natural" does NOT mean "safe" — supplements have real drug interactions
  • Read labels; bring all supplements to medication reconciliation visits
Worked Example Anaphylaxis Recognition and Treatment Ch 5 — Adverse Effects, Interactions, and Contraindications · Anaphylaxis section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure
Anaphylaxis Recognition and Treatment
Review Module Chapter
Ch 5 — Adverse Effects, Interactions, and Contraindications

Description of Procedure

Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening, IgE-mediated systemic hypersensitivity reaction. Onset is typically within minutes of exposure (may be delayed up to 30–60 min).

Classic presentation involves at least 2 of:

  • Skin/mucosa: urticaria (hives), pruritus, flushing, angioedema (lips, tongue, throat swelling)
  • Respiratory: wheezing, stridor, dyspnea, hypoxia, throat tightness
  • Cardiovascular: hypotension, tachycardia, syncope, shock
  • GI: abdominal cramps, vomiting, diarrhea

Epinephrine IM is FIRST-LINE. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are ADJUNCTS, not substitutes.

Indications

  • Any client with known severe allergy receiving a triggering medication (penicillins, sulfa, contrast dye, NSAIDs)
  • First-time IV antibiotics — especially penicillins, cephalosporins, vancomycin
  • Latex exposure in sensitized clients (banana, kiwi, avocado cross-reactivity)
  • Bee/wasp stings, food allergies (peanuts, shellfish, tree nuts)
  • ALL clinical settings — any nurse may encounter anaphylaxis

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre (prevention):

  • Document allergies thoroughly — type of reaction (rash vs anaphylaxis), severity, antidote used
  • Verify allergies before EVERY medication administration
  • For first IV doses of high-risk drugs: stay with client first 15 min; have emergency equipment ready
  • Skin test before penicillin if remote history of severe reaction

Intra (active anaphylaxis — act fast):

  1. STOP the offending agent immediately (clamp IV, remove patch, etc.)
  2. Call for help / activate rapid response
  3. Epinephrine 0.3–0.5 mg IM (1 mg/mL strength, 0.3–0.5 mL) in lateral thigh — repeat every 5–15 min as needed
  4. Position: supine with legs elevated (Trendelenburg) unless respiratory distress — then high Fowler’s
  5. Establish airway — prepare for intubation if stridor/swelling
  6. High-flow oxygen 100% via non-rebreather
  7. Large-bore IV access; IV fluid bolus 1–2 L 0.9% NS
  8. Adjuncts (after epinephrine): diphenhydramine 25–50 mg IV, methylprednisolone IV (delayed onset; prevents biphasic reaction)
  9. For bronchospasm: albuterol nebulizer
  10. If unresponsive to IM epinephrine: IV epinephrine drip (ICU)

Post:

  • Continuous monitoring (cardiac, oxygen sat, BP) for at least 4–6 hours (biphasic reaction risk)
  • Document the reaction in detail (time, signs, treatments, response)
  • Add the allergen to allergy list with severity
  • Discharge teaching: epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen) use; medical alert ID; allergist referral

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Stabilization of airway, breathing, circulation
  • Resolution of urticaria, angioedema, hypotension within 30–60 min
  • No biphasic reaction in the observation window
  • Client and family demonstrate correct use of epinephrine auto-injector
  • Allergy properly documented to prevent future re-exposure

Potential Complications

  • Death — respiratory or cardiovascular collapse if treatment delayed
  • Biphasic reaction — second episode 1–72 hr (most within 8 hr) after apparent resolution; observation required
  • Cerebral hypoxia — prolonged hypoxia or hypotension
  • Cardiac arrhythmias from epinephrine in clients with CAD
  • Adverse effects of epinephrine: tachycardia, hypertension, anxiety, tremor
  • Recurrence on re-exposure if allergy not documented
Worked Example CYP450 Drug Interactions Ch 5 — Adverse Effects, Interactions, and Contraindications · Interactions section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
CYP450 Drug Interactions

Defining Characteristics

The cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzyme system is the body’s primary mechanism for metabolizing drugs, mostly in the liver. CYP3A4 handles ~50% of all drugs; other major isoforms include CYP2D6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP1A2.

Drug interactions occur when one drug induces (speeds up) or inhibits (slows down) a CYP enzyme, changing the level of another drug that is metabolized by that same enzyme.

  • Inducer → faster metabolism → lower drug levels → therapeutic failure
  • Inhibitor → slower metabolism → higher drug levels → toxicity

Antecedents

  • Polypharmacy — the more drugs, the higher the interaction risk (especially in older adults)
  • Use of known CYP450 inducers or inhibitors (rifampin, phenytoin, ketoconazole, erythromycin, ritonavir)
  • Foods/supplements that affect CYP enzymes (grapefruit juice = CYP3A4 inhibitor; St. John’s wort = CYP3A4 inducer)
  • Genetic variations — CYP2D6 poor metabolizers vs ultra-rapid metabolizers
  • Lack of medication reconciliation across providers

Negative Consequences

  • Treatment failure — rifampin reduces effectiveness of oral contraceptives, warfarin, methadone, HIV antiretrovirals
  • Drug toxicity — erythromycin/clarithromycin raise statin levels → rhabdomyolysis; ketoconazole raises warfarin INR → bleeding
  • Unintended pregnancy when OCPs lose efficacy due to inducers
  • Serotonin syndrome from accumulation of serotonergic drugs when metabolism is inhibited
  • Cardiotoxicity from QT-prolonging drugs (e.g., azoles + amiodarone)
  • Hospital admissions and death from preventable interactions

Related Concepts

First-pass effect, pharmacogenomics, polypharmacy, medication reconciliation, narrow therapeutic index, prodrugs (codeine via CYP2D6), drug-food interactions, grapefruit effect, St. John’s wort, drug-induced QT prolongation.

Exemplars

  • Potent CYP3A4 inhibitors (raise drug levels): grapefruit juice, erythromycin, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, fluconazole, ritonavir, diltiazem, verapamil
  • Potent CYP3A4 inducers (lower drug levels): rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, St. John’s wort, dexamethasone
  • Classic warfarin interactions: amiodarone, fluconazole, metronidazole, SSRIs increase INR (bleeding risk); rifampin decreases INR (clot risk)
  • Statin-grapefruit: grapefruit + simvastatin or atorvastatin → rhabdomyolysis; switch to pravastatin or rosuvastatin (not CYP3A4)
  • Prodrug failure: codeine requires CYP2D6 to become morphine; poor metabolizers get no pain relief, ultra-rapid metabolizers risk overdose
  • Rifampin + OCPs: contraceptive failure; use barrier method during and 4 weeks after rifampin
Worked Example Black Box Warnings (FDA) Ch 5 — Adverse Effects, Interactions, and Contraindications · Special section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Black Box Warnings (FDA)

Defining Characteristics

A Black Box Warning (BBW) — officially “Boxed Warning” — is the strongest warning the FDA can require on a drug’s prescribing information. It indicates serious or life-threatening risks that the prescriber and patient must understand.

The warning is enclosed in a literal black box at the top of the package insert, distinguishing it from routine warnings. It does NOT prohibit use — it requires informed risk-benefit weighing.

Categories include: increased mortality risk, life-threatening adverse effects, REMS (Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy) drugs, specific populations to avoid (pregnancy, pediatrics, older adults), and serious drug-drug interactions.

Antecedents

  • Post-marketing surveillance data showing serious adverse events (often unrecognized in pre-approval trials)
  • FDA review of MedWatch reports and clinical trials
  • Specific high-risk populations identified (e.g., young adults with antidepressants → suicidality)
  • Drug class effects (e.g., all atypical antipsychotics → increased mortality in dementia)
  • Regulatory action to ensure prescribers and patients are informed

Negative Consequences

  • Catastrophic adverse events when warning is overlooked (e.g., fluoroquinolone tendon rupture in older adults on steroids)
  • Increased mortality in specific populations (atypical antipsychotics in dementia clients)
  • Inadequate informed consent and risk discussion with patients
  • Legal liability for prescribers and institutions
  • Possible underuse of beneficial medications due to overcaution

Related Concepts

REMS programs, post-marketing surveillance, MedWatch reporting, informed consent, FDA pregnancy categories (legacy), high-alert medications, pharmacovigilance, drug labeling, off-label use.

Exemplars

  • SSRIs/SNRIs in adolescents/young adults: increased suicidality in < 25 yo; close monitoring first weeks
  • Antipsychotics in older adults with dementia-related psychosis: increased mortality (cardiovascular and infectious)
  • LABAs (salmeterol) as asthma monotherapy: increased asthma-related death; must be combined with ICS
  • Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin): tendon rupture (especially Achilles), peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects, aortic aneurysm risk — reserve for when no alternative
  • Metformin: lactic acidosis (rare but fatal) in renal impairment or with IV contrast
  • Warfarin: major bleeding risk; requires INR monitoring
  • NSAIDs: cardiovascular and GI bleeding risk
  • Methotrexate: fatal toxicity with daily dosing (must be WEEKLY for rheumatoid arthritis)
  • Bupropion in adolescents: suicidality warning
  • Carbamazepine in Asians: Stevens-Johnson syndrome with HLA-B*1502; screen before prescribing
Worked Example Paroxetine Ch 7 — Anxiety and Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Medication
Review Module Chapter
Ch 7 — Anxiety and Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI)
  • Increases serotonin availability in the synaptic cleft
  • Used for: generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, social anxiety, PTSD, OCD, depression

Therapeutic Use

  • Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)
  • Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD)
  • Panic Disorder
  • Social Anxiety Disorder
  • Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)
  • Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)
  • Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD)
  • Vasomotor symptoms of menopause (low-dose Brisdelle)

Complications

  • GI: nausea (most common), diarrhea, dry mouth, weight gain (more than other SSRIs)
  • Sexual dysfunction: ↓ libido, erectile dysfunction, anorgasmia (very common, often persistent)
  • Suicidal ideation (FDA boxed warning, especially age < 25)
  • Hyponatremia / SIADH (especially elderly)
  • Bleeding (antiplatelet effect)
  • Discontinuation syndrome — worst of all SSRIs (flu-like, dizziness, "brain zaps")
  • Serotonin syndrome (with other serotonergic agents)
  • Activation of mania in bipolar clients
  • Insomnia or drowsiness, headache, dizziness, sweating, tremor

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to paroxetine or other SSRIs
  • Concurrent MAOIs or within 14 days of stopping MAOI (serotonin syndrome risk)
  • Concurrent thioridazine, pimozide (QT prolongation)
  • Pregnancy Category D (cardiac defects in first trimester) — strongest concern of SSRIs
  • Caution: bipolar disorder (can trigger mania), suicidal ideation (esp. age < 25), bleeding disorders, hyponatremia/SIADH, seizure disorder, hepatic/renal impairment
  • Caution: elderly (↑ falls, hyponatremia risk)

Interactions

  • MAOIs, linezolid, methylene blue → serotonin syndrome (life-threatening)
  • Other serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, triptans, tramadol, St. John's wort) → ↑ serotonin syndrome risk
  • Warfarin, NSAIDs, aspirin, antiplatelets → ↑ bleeding risk
  • Tamoxifen → paroxetine inhibits CYP2D6 → ↓ tamoxifen efficacy (avoid combo)
  • Phenytoin, carbamazepine → ↓ paroxetine levels
  • Alcohol → additive CNS depression

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ anxiety symptoms (worry, restlessness, irritability, muscle tension)
  • ↓ panic attack frequency and severity
  • ↓ PTSD symptoms (flashbacks, hypervigilance, avoidance)
  • ↓ OCD symptoms (intrusive thoughts, compulsions)
  • Improved daily functioning, sleep, concentration, social engagement
  • No suicidal ideation (esp. monitor in first 4-12 weeks and when changing dose)
  • No serotonin syndrome signs

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral
  • Adult dose: start 10-20 mg PO daily, titrate to 20-50 mg/day
  • Take in the morning (may cause insomnia) or evening (may cause drowsiness) — assess individual response
  • Take with or without food
  • Do NOT crush or split CR tablets
  • Onset of therapeutic effect: 4-6 weeks — set realistic expectations
  • Discontinuation: taper gradually over weeks (paroxetine has the worst SSRI withdrawal — flu-like, dizziness, irritability)

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess baseline mental status, suicide risk, and target symptoms
  • Monitor for suicidal ideation, especially in clients < 25 yr, during initial weeks and after dose changes (FDA black box warning)
  • Watch for serotonin syndrome: hyperthermia, agitation, tremor, myoclonus, hyperreflexia, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, GI upset (medical emergency)
  • Monitor for activation of mania in clients with bipolar disorder
  • Monitor sodium levels (SIADH risk, especially in elderly)
  • Reinforce 4-6 week onset; encourage adherence during initial period
  • Assess for sexual side effects (common cause of nonadherence)

Client Education

  • Takes 4–6 weeks for full effect — must continue even if not feeling immediate benefit
  • Take at the same time daily
  • Do NOT abruptly discontinue — paroxetine has worst withdrawal of SSRIs (flu-like, dizziness, irritability); taper over weeks
  • AVOID alcohol, MAOIs, St. John's wort, triptans (serotonin syndrome)
  • Report: worsening depression, suicidal thoughts, unusual bleeding, signs of serotonin syndrome
  • Sexual side effects: discuss with provider — may switch agent
  • Avoid in pregnancy (Category D — cardiac defects); use sertraline if needed
Worked Example Sertraline Ch 8 — Depressive Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Medication
Review Module Chapter
Ch 8 — Depressive Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Sertraline is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI):

  • Selectively blocks serotonin reuptake at presynaptic neurons → ↑ serotonin in synaptic cleft
  • Onset of mood improvement: 2-4 weeks for partial response; 6-8 weeks for full effect
  • Minimal effect on norepinephrine, dopamine, or histamine receptors → fewer anticholinergic and cardiac side effects than older antidepressants
  • First-line for major depressive disorder due to favorable side-effect profile

Therapeutic Use

  • Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)
  • Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)
  • Panic disorder
  • Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
  • Social anxiety disorder
  • Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD)

Complications

  • GI: nausea (very common), diarrhea, dyspepsia, dry mouth
  • Sexual dysfunction: ↓ libido, ejaculatory dysfunction, anorgasmia
  • Suicidal ideation (FDA boxed warning, especially age < 25)
  • Hyponatremia / SIADH (especially elderly)
  • Bleeding risk (antiplatelet effect, GI bleeding with NSAIDs)
  • Insomnia or somnolence, headache, dizziness, tremor, sweating
  • Weight changes (less than paroxetine)
  • Serotonin syndrome (with other serotonergic agents)
  • Activation of mania in bipolar clients
  • Discontinuation syndrome (less severe than paroxetine)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to sertraline or other SSRIs
  • Concurrent MAOIs or within 14 days of stopping MAOI (serotonin syndrome)
  • Concurrent pimozide (QT prolongation)
  • Pregnancy Category C (preferred SSRI in pregnancy after risk-benefit; less risk than paroxetine)
  • Caution: bipolar disorder (can trigger mania), suicidal ideation (esp. age < 25), bleeding disorders, hyponatremia, seizure disorder, hepatic impairment
  • Caution: elderly (↑ falls, hyponatremia)

Interactions

  • MAOIs, linezolid, methylene blue → serotonin syndrome (life-threatening)
  • Other serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, triptans, tramadol, St. John's wort, ondansetron) → ↑ serotonin syndrome
  • Warfarin, NSAIDs, aspirin → ↑ bleeding risk
  • Pimozide → QT prolongation
  • Alcohol → additive CNS depression (avoid)
  • Highly protein-bound — may displace other protein-bound drugs (warfarin, digoxin)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ depressive symptoms: ↓ sadness, hopelessness, anhedonia
  • ↑ energy, ↑ interest in activities
  • Improved sleep, appetite, concentration
  • Restored social and occupational functioning
  • No suicidal ideation (especially monitor in first 4-12 weeks and during dose changes)
  • No serotonin syndrome

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral
  • Adult dose: start 25-50 mg PO daily, titrate weekly to 50-200 mg/day
  • Take in the morning to reduce insomnia
  • Take with food (improves absorption and GI tolerance)
  • Onset: 2-4 weeks for initial response; 6-8 weeks for full effect
  • If discontinuing: taper gradually over 2-4 weeks to prevent discontinuation syndrome (flu-like, dizziness, electric-shock sensations)

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess baseline mood, suicide risk, and target depressive symptoms
  • Monitor for suicidal ideation closely in age < 25, during first 4-12 weeks, and after dose changes (FDA black box warning)
  • Assess for serotonin syndrome: hyperthermia, agitation, tremor, hyperreflexia, diaphoresis, tachycardia, GI upset
  • Monitor for activation of mania in clients with undiagnosed bipolar disorder
  • Monitor sodium levels (SIADH risk in elderly)
  • Monitor for sexual side effects (common; affects adherence)
  • Reinforce that mood improvement takes weeks; encourage adherence during initial period
  • Assess for weight changes, GI symptoms (nausea, diarrhea common initially)

Client Education

  • Report immediately: suicidal thoughts, worsening depression or mood changes, signs of serotonin syndrome (high fever, agitation, tremor, fast heart rate, sweating, confusion)
  • Takes 2-4 weeks for initial benefit, up to 6-8 weeks for full effect — keep taking as prescribed
  • Take in the morning with food
  • Do NOT abruptly stop — taper gradually under provider supervision
  • Avoid alcohol
  • Tell ALL providers about sertraline before starting any new medication
  • Avoid St. John's wort, other herbal supplements without provider approval
  • Use caution driving until you know how the medication affects you
  • Discuss any sexual side effects with provider (often manageable, do not stop on your own)
  • Continue therapy/counseling as recommended
Worked Example Risperidone Ch 11 — Medications for Children and Adolescents Who Have Mental Health Issues · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Risperidone
Review Module Chapter
Ch 11 — Medications for Children and Adolescents Who Have Mental Health Issues
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Risperidone is a second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic:

  • Blocks D2 dopamine receptors (similar to first-generation) → ↓ positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions)
  • Blocks 5-HT2A serotonin receptors → improves negative symptoms and ↓ extrapyramidal side effects (EPS) compared to first-generation
  • Also blocks α1-adrenergic and H1 receptors → orthostatic hypotension and sedation
  • Available as oral or long-acting IM injection (every 2 weeks)

Therapeutic Use

  • Schizophrenia (acute and maintenance therapy)
  • Bipolar I disorder (acute manic and mixed episodes)
  • Irritability associated with autism spectrum disorder (age 5-17)
  • Tourette syndrome (off-label)
  • Aggression/behavioral disturbances in dementia (used with caution — FDA boxed warning for ↑ mortality in elderly with dementia)

Complications

  • New onset of diabetes mellitus or loss of glucose control in clients who have diabetes
  • Weight gain
  • Hypercholesterolemia
  • Orthostatic hypotension
  • Anticholinergic effects (urinary hesitancy or retention, dry mouth)
  • Agitation
  • Dizziness
  • Sedation
  • Sleep disruption
  • Tremors
  • Agranulocytosis, neutropenia
  • Hyperprolactinemia

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to risperidone
  • Boxed warning: elderly clients with dementia-related psychosis — ↑ mortality risk
  • Caution: cardiovascular disease, cerebrovascular disease, seizure disorder
  • Caution: Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies (extreme sensitivity)
  • Caution: diabetes mellitus (atypicals ↑ glucose, lipids, weight)
  • Caution: hyperprolactinemia, breast cancer history
  • Pregnancy Cat C; possible neonatal extrapyramidal/withdrawal symptoms in 3rd trimester

Interactions

  • CNS depressants (alcohol, benzodiazepines, opioids) → additive sedation
  • Antihypertensives → additive hypotension
  • Levodopa, dopamine agonists → antagonized by risperidone (avoid in Parkinson)
  • Carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampin → ↓ risperidone levels
  • Fluoxetine, paroxetine → ↑ risperidone levels
  • QT-prolonging drugs (amiodarone, methadone) → ↑ arrhythmia risk

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ positive symptoms: ↓ hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thinking
  • ↓ negative symptoms: ↑ motivation, ↑ emotional expression, ↑ social engagement
  • ↓ agitation and aggression
  • Improved functioning and quality of life
  • No extrapyramidal symptoms (rigidity, tremor, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia)
  • No neuroleptic malignant syndrome
  • Stable weight, glucose, lipids

Medication Administration

  • Routes: oral (tablet, ODT, oral solution), long-acting IM injection
  • Adult oral: 1-2 mg/day initially, titrate to 4-8 mg/day; max 16 mg/day
  • Long-acting IM (Consta): 25-50 mg every 2 weeks (deep gluteal/deltoid)
  • Take with or without food
  • Rise slowly to ↓ orthostatic hypotension
  • Continue oral form for ≥ 3 weeks after first IM injection (slow onset of LAI)
  • Monitor: weight, BMI, fasting glucose, lipid panel at baseline, 12 weeks, then annually

Nursing Interventions

  • Obtain the client's fasting blood glucose prior to and periodically throughout treatment.
  • Instruct the client to report indications of diabetes mellitus including increased thirst, urination, and appetite.
  • Advise clients to follow a healthy, low-caloric diet.
  • Recommend regular exercise.
  • Monitor weight throughout treatment.
  • Monitor cholesterol and triglycerides, especially if weight gain is more than 30 lb.
  • Monitor blood pressure with first dose and instruct client to change positions slowly.
  • Encourage the client to sip fluids throughout the day.
  • Monitor and report manifestations of an infection (a sore throat).
  • Monitor and report gyneocomastia and amenorrhea.

Client Education

  • Report immediately: high fever with muscle rigidity (NMS), uncontrollable movements (especially of face/tongue), severe dizziness, fainting, chest pain, signs of infection
  • Takes several weeks for full effect; continue as prescribed
  • Rise slowly to prevent dizziness/falls
  • Take with or without food
  • Do NOT abruptly stop — taper under provider supervision
  • Avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants
  • Avoid driving until you know how the medication affects you
  • Monitor weight; eat balanced diet; report rapid weight gain
  • Keep all lab and follow-up appointments (metabolic monitoring)
  • Use sunscreen and protective clothing (photosensitivity)
Worked Example Methylphenidate (Ritalin / Concerta) Ch 11 — Medications for Children and Adolescents · Stimulants section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Methylphenidate (Ritalin, Concerta, Daytrana)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 11 — Medications for Children and Adolescents
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • CNS stimulant — inhibits reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine in synaptic clefts
  • Increases focus, attention, and behavioral control
  • Schedule II controlled substance (high abuse potential)

Therapeutic Use

  • Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) — in children ≥ 6 yr, adolescents, adults — FIRST-LINE
  • Narcolepsy
  • Off-label: treatment-resistant depression, cognitive impairment in MS

Complications

  • Cardiovascular (BLACK BOX): increased BP/HR; sudden death in children with structural heart disease; avoid in known cardiac problems
  • Growth suppression — modest height/weight slowing; monitor growth charts; consider drug holidays
  • Appetite suppression, weight loss — common
  • Insomnia — especially with afternoon doses
  • Anxiety, irritability, dysphoria
  • New-onset or worsening psychiatric symptoms (mania, psychosis, tics)
  • Dependence and abuse potential (Schedule II)
  • Priapism (rare but emergency)
  • Peripheral vasculopathy (cold/discolored fingers, toes — Raynaud-like)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Structural cardiac disease, cardiomyopathy, serious heart rhythm abnormalities
  • Glaucoma, hyperthyroidism, severe hypertension
  • History of substance abuse (caution; abuse risk)
  • Concurrent MAOI use (within 14 days) — hypertensive crisis
  • Tic disorders (may worsen)
  • Children < 6 yr (not approved)
  • Psychotic disorders (may worsen)

Interactions

  • MAOIs — CONTRAINDICATED (hypertensive crisis)
  • SSRIs/SNRIs — risk of serotonin syndrome (caution)
  • Warfarin, anticonvulsants, TCAs — methylphenidate can increase their levels
  • Antihypertensives — reduced effect
  • Caffeine, decongestants — additive stimulant effects
  • Alcohol — worsens dysphoria; interacts with extended-release formulations

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Improved attention, focus, on-task behavior
  • Reduced impulsivity and hyperactivity
  • Improved school/work performance
  • Parent/teacher rating scales (Vanderbilt, Conners) show improvement
  • Stable height/weight on growth chart
  • Stable BP and HR
  • Tolerable side effects

Medication Administration

  • Routes: oral (IR, ER, sustained-release, OROS); transdermal patch (Daytrana)
  • Start low; titrate; immediate-release 2–3 times daily; ER once daily morning
  • Last dose before 4 PM to minimize insomnia
  • Take with breakfast and/or lunch (helps appetite suppression)
  • Concerta: do NOT crush or chew (osmotic shell)
  • Daytrana patch: apply morning, remove 9 hr later
  • Schedule II — no refills; new prescription monthly; secure storage

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline: BP, HR, EKG (if cardiac history), height/weight, family cardiac history
  • Monitor growth quarterly; document on growth chart
  • Monitor BP, HR, mood at every visit
  • Assess for tics, anxiety, mood changes
  • Educate about Schedule II requirements (no sharing, secure storage)
  • Consider drug holidays (weekends, summer) to allow growth catch-up
  • Substance use screening for adolescents
  • Coordinate with school nurse for in-school doses

Client Education

  • Take exactly as prescribed; do not share with others (illegal — Schedule II)
  • Take with food in the morning to reduce appetite suppression
  • Last dose by 4 PM to avoid insomnia
  • Report: rapid heartbeat, chest pain, dizziness, fainting (cardiac signs)
  • Report: new mood changes, hallucinations, severe anxiety, tics
  • Maintain regular sleep, balanced meals, regular exercise
  • Adolescents: avoid alcohol and other substances; do not use to enhance studying
  • Store securely away from siblings/visitors
  • Do not stop abruptly (withdrawal symptoms can occur with high doses)
  • Keep follow-up appointments for growth and BP monitoring
Worked Example ADHD in Children and Adolescents Ch 11 — Medications for Children and Adolescents · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 11 — Medications for Children and Adolescents

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) — neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent patterns of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interfere with functioning across multiple settings (school, home, work).

  • DSM-5 requires: ≥ 6 symptoms in children (≥ 5 in adolescents/adults) of inattention OR hyperactivity-impulsivity, present < 12 yr, in ≥ 2 settings, for > 6 months
  • Three presentations: predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, combined
  • Prevalence ~5–10% in children; persists into adulthood in ~50–65%
  • Boys diagnosed more often; girls often missed (more inattentive presentation)
  • Common comorbidities: learning disabilities, anxiety, depression, ODD, conduct disorder, tic disorders

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Dopamine and norepinephrine dysregulation in prefrontal cortex and basal ganglia — impaired executive function
  • Underactivation of prefrontal cortex → poor attention regulation, working memory, impulse control
  • Altered reward processing → preference for immediate over delayed rewards
  • Genetic component — heritability 70–80%
  • Environmental contributors: prenatal alcohol/tobacco/lead exposure, prematurity, low birth weight, head injury
  • NOT caused by: bad parenting, too much sugar, video games, or food dyes (myths)

Expected Findings

Inattention symptoms:

  • Difficulty sustaining attention; easily distracted
  • Careless mistakes; trouble following instructions
  • Difficulty organizing tasks; loses things; avoids tasks requiring sustained effort
  • Forgetfulness in daily activities

Hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms:

  • Fidgeting, leaving seat, running/climbing inappropriately
  • Unable to play quietly; “driven by a motor”; excessive talking
  • Blurts out answers; difficulty waiting turn; interrupts others

Assessment tools:

  • Vanderbilt ADHD Rating Scale (parents and teachers)
  • Conners Rating Scales
  • NICHQ assessment
  • School observation, academic records, family history

Nursing Care

Treatment plan: multimodal — pharmacotherapy + behavioral interventions + school accommodations

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Stimulants (first-line): methylphenidate, amphetamines — 70–80% response rate
  • Non-stimulants: atomoxetine (SNRI), guanfacine ER, clonidine ER — for those who don’t tolerate stimulants or have tic disorder/substance abuse concerns
  • Bupropion (off-label) — especially for comorbid depression

Behavioral interventions:

  • Parent training in behavior management
  • Behavior modification at home and school
  • Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (older children, adolescents)
  • Structured routines, consistent expectations

School accommodations:

  • 504 plan or IEP
  • Preferred seating, extended time, frequent breaks
  • Written instructions, organizational support

Client Education

  • ADHD is a medical condition — not laziness or poor parenting
  • Medication helps regulate brain function but is not a cure; behavioral strategies remain important
  • Stimulants: report cardiovascular symptoms, mood changes, growth concerns; take in the morning; balanced meals important
  • Non-stimulants: longer onset (weeks); monitor for suicidal ideation in atomoxetine
  • Set up routines: consistent sleep/wake times, balanced meals, exercise
  • Use planners, alarms, checklists, organizers
  • Collaborate with school: share rating scale results, accommodations
  • Address co-occurring conditions (anxiety, learning disabilities)
  • Adolescents: avoid stimulant diversion/misuse; substance abuse risk is real
  • Long-term outlook: many do well with treatment; ADHD often persists but symptoms can be managed
Worked Example Antidepressant Black Box Warning in Adolescents Ch 11 — Medications for Children and Adolescents · Antidepressants section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Antidepressant Black Box Warning in Adolescents

Defining Characteristics

The FDA Black Box Warning on all antidepressants states there is increased risk of suicidal ideation and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults (< 25 years) taking these medications, particularly during initial treatment and dose changes.

Critical clarification: The warning describes increased ideation, not completed suicide. Untreated depression itself carries significant suicide risk. The treatment decision involves balancing risks of treatment vs untreated illness, with close monitoring as the safety measure.

Of the SSRIs, only fluoxetine is FDA-approved for pediatric depression (≥ 8 yr); escitalopram approved for ≥ 12 yr for depression. Sertraline approved for OCD (≥ 6 yr).

Antecedents

  • Age < 25 years (especially during initial treatment)
  • Recently started antidepressant or had recent dose change (first 1–3 months highest risk)
  • Pre-existing depression severity
  • Comorbid anxiety, substance use, or trauma history
  • Family history of suicide
  • Pediatric-specific factors: developmental cognitive changes, social pressures, identity formation
  • Inadequate monitoring or follow-up plan

Negative Consequences

  • Increased suicidal ideation/attempts in vulnerable young patients
  • Undertreatment of pediatric depression if providers overly avoid effective therapy due to BBW
  • Continued untreated depression has its own significant morbidity and mortality
  • Family distress and reduced trust in medical care
  • Activation of mania in undiagnosed bipolar disorder
  • Discontinuation of medication without appropriate planning

Related Concepts

Pediatric depression, suicide risk assessment, safety planning, lethal-means counseling (general, not method-specific), informed consent in minors, parental involvement, FDA Black Box Warnings, REMS programs, CBT, family therapy, 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

Exemplars

  • Informed consent discussion: “The medication can help your child’s depression but during the first weeks, some young people have new or worsening thoughts of suicide. We’ll monitor closely. Untreated depression also carries serious risk. Together we’re choosing the safer path with careful monitoring.”
  • Monitoring schedule: Weekly visits for first 4 weeks, then every 2 weeks for 4 weeks, then monthly — this is the FDA recommendation for new SSRI in < 18 yr.
  • What to monitor: changes in mood, behavior, suicidal thoughts, irritability, agitation, aggression, sleep, appetite, impulsivity, withdrawal from family/friends, talk of death.
  • Family education: Parents should know to call provider if child shows new agitation, panic, severe irritability, talking about suicide, or any sudden changes. Maintain open communication.
  • Safety planning: collaborate with child and family on a written plan including recognizing warning signs, coping strategies, support contacts, and general restriction of access to potentially harmful items in the home (never name methods).
  • Provider responsibilities: document informed consent, monitor adherence, assess for mania (especially if family history of bipolar), continue treatment plan as long as benefit outweighs risk.
  • 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline — available 24/7. Crisis Text Line: text HOME to 741741.
Worked Example Varenicline Ch 12 — Substance Use Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Varenicline
Review Module Chapter
Ch 12 — Substance Use Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Varenicline is a nicotinic receptor agonist that promotes the release of dopamine to simulate the pleasurable effects of nicotine.

Therapeutic Use

Varenicline is indicated to reduce nicotine cravings and block the desired effects of nicotine in clients who have tobacco use disorder.

Complications

  • New-onset hypertension
  • Loss of glycemic control in clients who have diabetes mellitus
  • Nausea
  • Vomiting
  • Insomnia
  • New-onset depression
  • Suicidal thoughts

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to varenicline
  • Severe renal impairment (CrCl < 30) — dose adjust
  • End-stage renal disease on dialysis — reduce dose
  • Caution: history of psychiatric illness (depression, suicidal ideation, bipolar) — although FDA removed boxed warning in 2016, monitor closely
  • Caution: cardiovascular disease (slight ↑ MI risk vs placebo in trials)
  • Caution: seizure disorder
  • Pregnancy Cat C; breastfeeding

Interactions

  • Nicotine replacement therapy (patch, gum) → ↑ adverse effects (nausea, dizziness); not recommended together
  • Cimetidine → ↑ varenicline levels (only with severe renal impairment)
  • Alcohol → ↑ neuropsychiatric effects, intoxication
  • Few other clinically significant drug interactions (renal excretion, not metabolized by CYP enzymes)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • The client will maintain smoking cessation.
  • The client will report reduced cravings for nicotine.

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral
  • Start 1 week BEFORE quit date OR start and quit within 8-35 days
  • Titration:
    • Days 1-3: 0.5 mg PO daily
    • Days 4-7: 0.5 mg PO BID
    • Day 8 onward: 1 mg PO BID
  • Take with food and a full glass of water to reduce nausea
  • Treatment duration: 12 weeks (additional 12 weeks can be considered for continued abstinence)
  • Renal dose-adjust if CrCl < 30

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess smoking history, motivation, and prior cessation attempts
  • Set a quit date with the client (typically 1 week after starting medication)
  • Assess baseline mental health: depression, suicidal ideation, prior psychiatric history
  • Monitor for neuropsychiatric symptoms: depression, mood changes, agitation, suicidal ideation (post-marketing reports)
  • Assess for nausea (very common); reinforce taking with food and water
  • Provide cessation counseling and support resources (telephone quit lines, behavioral therapy)
  • Reinforce 12-week course; consider extended duration for high relapse risk

Client Education

  • Clients who are commercial truck or bus drivers, airplane pilots, or air traffic controllers should not take varenicline.
  • Take medication after a meal.
  • Titrate as prescribed to minimize adverse effects.
  • Notify the provider if adverse effects occur.
Worked Example Phenytoin Ch 13 — Chronic Neurologic Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Phenytoin
Review Module Chapter
Ch 13 — Chronic Neurologic Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Phenytoin is a first-generation anticonvulsant (hydantoin):

  • Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in neurons → stabilizes neuronal membranes → suppresses sustained repetitive neuron firing → ↓ seizure spread
  • Effective against most seizure types EXCEPT absence seizures and infantile spasms
  • Narrow therapeutic window: 10-20 mcg/mL (free phenytoin: 1-2 mcg/mL)
  • Non-linear (zero-order) kinetics at therapeutic doses — small dose changes can cause large level changes

Therapeutic Use

Phenytoin is a hydantoin medication that suppresses partial seizure and primary generalized seizure activity in the affected neurons.

Complications

  • CNS effects
  • Gingival hyperplasia
  • Teratogenic birth defects
  • Decreases effectiveness of oral contraceptives, warfarin, and glucocorticoids
  • Causes stimulation of hepatic medication-metabolizing enzymes
  • Alcohol (acute use), diazepam, cimetidine, and valproic acid increase phenytoin levels.
  • Carbamazepine, phenobarbital, and chronic alcohol use decrease phenytoin levels.
  • Additive CNS depressant effects can occur with concurrent use of CNS depressants.

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to phenytoin or other hydantoins
  • Sinus bradycardia, second/third-degree heart block, Adams-Stokes syndrome (IV use)
  • Pregnancy Category D — fetal hydantoin syndrome (cleft lip/palate, cardiac defects, growth deficiency)
  • Caution: hepatic impairment, hypoalbuminemia (↑ free drug)
  • Caution: diabetes (↑ glucose), porphyria, suicidal ideation
  • Caution: Asian ancestry with HLA-B*1502 allele (↑ Stevens-Johnson syndrome risk)

Interactions

  • Phenytoin is a potent CYP enzyme inducer → ↓ levels of many drugs:
    • Warfarin (effect variable: initially ↑ INR, then ↓ — close monitoring)
    • Oral contraceptives → contraceptive failure
    • Carbamazepine, valproate (variable)
    • Corticosteroids, theophylline, doxycycline, quinidine, digoxin
  • Drugs that ↑ phenytoin levels (toxicity): cimetidine, fluconazole, isoniazid, amiodarone, omeprazole
  • Drugs that ↓ phenytoin levels: rifampin, chronic alcohol, antacids, sucralfate, enteral feeds (hold feed 1 hr before/after)
  • Alcohol (acute) → ↑ levels; alcohol (chronic) → ↓ levels

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ seizure frequency and severity
  • Therapeutic drug level: 10-20 mcg/mL (total)
  • No status epilepticus episodes
  • Improved quality of life and functioning
  • No signs of toxicity: nystagmus (lateral gaze first), ataxia, slurred speech, confusion, drowsiness
  • No serious adverse effects (rash, blood dyscrasias)

Medication Administration

  • Routes: oral, IV (use fosphenytoin for IV in most cases)
  • Adult oral: 100 mg PO TID or 300-400 mg ER once daily
  • Loading dose (status epilepticus): 15-20 mg/kg IV (fosphenytoin), max rate 150 mg PE/min
  • Phenytoin IV: max rate 50 mg/min in adults (hypotension, dysrhythmias if too fast); NEVER mix with dextrose (precipitates)
  • Use NS only; flush before and after
  • Use in-line filter for IV phenytoin
  • Take oral with food to ↓ GI upset
  • Shake suspension well; use oral syringe for accuracy
  • Hold tube feeds 1 hr before and after dose (↓ absorption)
  • Monitor drug levels: total 10-20 mcg/mL, free 1-2 mcg/mL

Nursing Interventions

  • Instruct the client to refrain from alcohol and other medications that cause CNS depression, such as barbiturates.
  • Encourage the client to use dental floss and massage gums daily.
  • Instruct the client to avoid pregnancy and use an alternate form of contraception.
  • Monitor INR if on warfarin and blood glucose levels if taking a glucocorticoid.
  • Monitor therapeutic effects of warfarin and glucocorticoids.
  • Never abruptly discontinue antiepileptic medications.
  • Advise clients to avoid use of alcohol and other CNS depressants
  • Monitor blood phenytoin levels

Client Education

  • Report immediately: rash (any new rash — call before next dose), bruising/bleeding, sore throat/fever, yellowing of skin or eyes, severe drowsiness or confusion, suicidal thoughts
  • Meticulous oral hygiene — brush gently 2x/day, floss daily, see dentist every 6 months (gingival hyperplasia common)
  • Take with food to reduce GI upset
  • Shake suspension well before each dose; use oral syringe for accuracy
  • Do NOT abruptly stop — sudden discontinuation can trigger status epilepticus
  • Hold tube feeds 1 hr before and after dose if applicable
  • Wear medical alert ID
  • Avoid alcohol
  • Use backup contraception — phenytoin reduces effectiveness of oral contraceptives
  • Notify provider if pregnant or planning pregnancy (teratogenic)
  • Tell ALL providers about phenytoin (many drug interactions)
