  • Keep all lab appointments (drug levels, CBC)
Worked Example Ciprofloxacin/hydrocortisone Ch 14 — Eye and Ear Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Ciprofloxacin/hydrocortisone
Review Module Chapter
Ch 14 — Eye and Ear Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Combination otic suspension for ear infections:

  • Ciprofloxacin — fluoroquinolone antibiotic that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV → bactericidal against gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria in the ear canal
  • Hydrocortisone — corticosteroid that reduces inflammation, edema, and pain via inhibition of inflammatory mediators
  • Topical formulation minimizes systemic absorption

Therapeutic Use

The bactericidal effects of ciprofloxacin and the anti-inflammatory effect of hydrocortisone decreases pain, edema, and erythema in the ear.

Complications

  • Rash
  • Dizziness, lightheadedness, tremors, restlessness, and convulsions

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Perforated tympanic membrane (caution; use products approved for this)
  • Hypersensitivity to fluoroquinolones or corticosteroids
  • Viral or fungal ear infections (steroid may worsen)
  • Caution in pregnancy and breastfeeding (limited topical absorption)

Interactions

  • Minimal systemic interactions due to topical use
  • If used concurrently with systemic fluoroquinolones, consider total exposure
  • Other topical ear drops — space administration if multiple are prescribed

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ ear pain
  • ↓ ear drainage and discharge
  • ↓ swelling and erythema of ear canal
  • Hearing returns to baseline (was muffled due to inflammation/exudate)
  • No new symptoms suggesting otitis media or spread

Medication Administration

  • Route: otic (ear) drops only
  • Adult: 3 drops in affected ear BID × 7 days
  • Pediatric (≥ 6 mo): same dose
  • Warm bottle in hand for 1-2 min before use (cold drops cause dizziness)
  • Have client lie with affected ear up
  • Adult: pull pinna up and back; child < 3 yr: pull down and back
  • Instill drops, then have client maintain position for 60 seconds
  • Massage tragus gently to work drops in
  • Do not touch dropper to ear
  • Complete full 7-day course even if symptoms resolve

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess ear for drainage, pain, erythema, edema
  • Verify tympanic membrane status (intact vs perforated)
  • Teach proper instillation technique with return demonstration
  • Demonstrate warming the bottle (not in microwave!) — warm in hands
  • Reinforce age-appropriate pinna technique (up and back vs. down and back)
  • Monitor for hypersensitivity reactions (rash, itching, swelling)

Client Education

  • Keep foreign bodies out of ear canal.
  • Avoid manual measures to remove cerumen.
  • Dry ear canal after bathing or swimming using a towel.
  • Avoid use of ear plugs except for swimming.
Worked Example Latanoprost (Xalatan) Ch 14 — Eye and Ear Disorders · Glaucoma meds section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Latanoprost (Xalatan)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 14 — Eye and Ear Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Prostaglandin F2-alpha analog — increases uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humor → decreases intraocular pressure (IOP) by 25–33%
  • Most effective IOP-lowering eye drop class
  • Convenient once-daily dosing

Therapeutic Use

  • Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) — FIRST-LINE
  • Ocular hypertension
  • Some forms of secondary glaucoma
  • Generally NOT used for angle-closure glaucoma (acute treatment requires different approach)

Complications

  • Iris pigmentation darkening — gradual brown discoloration of light-colored irises; often permanent
  • Eyelash growth / darkening — longer, thicker, darker lashes (cosmetic; sometimes desired)
  • Periorbital skin darkening
  • Ocular irritation, stinging, burning at instillation
  • Conjunctival hyperemia (red eye)
  • Macular edema (rare but possible)
  • Reactivation of herpes simplex keratitis
  • Minimal systemic absorption → few systemic effects

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to latanoprost or benzalkonium chloride (preservative)
  • Active intraocular inflammation (iritis, uveitis)
  • History of macular edema
  • Active herpes simplex keratitis
  • Caution in pregnancy and lactation (limited data)
  • Aphakic eyes (no lens) — increased macular edema risk

Interactions

  • Other ophthalmic drops — separate by at least 5 minutes
  • Thimerosal-containing eye drops — can precipitate latanoprost (avoid combination or separate widely)
  • NSAIDs (eye drops) — may reduce latanoprost effect
  • Minimal systemic drug interactions (very low absorption)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • IOP reduction — goal < 21 mmHg or specific target based on baseline (often 25–33% reduction)
  • Stable visual fields on perimetry testing
  • No progression of optic nerve cupping on exam
  • Tolerable side effects; adherence to once-daily regimen

Medication Administration

  • Route: ophthalmic (eye drop)
  • Dose: 1 drop in affected eye(s) ONCE DAILY in the evening
  • Evening dosing more effective (works through the night)
  • Refrigerate unopened bottles; once opened, can store at room temp for 6 weeks
  • Do NOT exceed once daily dosing — reduces effectiveness
  • If a dose missed: continue with next scheduled dose (don’t double up)

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline: IOP measurement, eye exam, document baseline iris color, visual fields
  • Verify dosing schedule (once daily evening)
  • Teach proper instillation: punctal occlusion (press inner corner) for 1–2 min to minimize systemic absorption and maximize ocular effect
  • If multiple eye drops: space by ≥ 5 minutes
  • Remove contact lenses before instillation; wait 15 min before reinserting
  • Monitor IOP at 4–8 weeks after starting; then per provider routine (typically every 3–6 months)
  • Document iris color changes
  • Assess for adherence (forgetting is common — consider phone alarms)

Client Education

  • Take ONCE daily in the evening — consistency is essential
  • Do not exceed once daily — more isn’t better (paradoxically less effective)
  • Wash hands; tilt head back; pull down lower lid; instill 1 drop into pocket; close eye gently
  • Press inner corner of eye for 1–2 minutes (punctal occlusion) — reduces systemic absorption and improves effect
  • Wait 5 minutes before instilling other eye drops
  • Possible iris darkening (permanent), eyelash growth, periorbital skin darkening — cosmetic effects
  • Glaucoma is a lifelong condition; medication is required indefinitely
  • Schedule regular eye exams to monitor IOP and progression
  • Notify provider of new redness, pain, vision changes, or any infection
  • Do not stop without provider approval (vision loss can occur)
Worked Example Glaucoma Ch 14 — Eye and Ear Disorders · Glaucoma meds section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Glaucoma
Review Module Chapter
Ch 14 — Eye and Ear Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Glaucoma — a group of progressive eye diseases characterized by optic nerve damage, typically associated with elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), leading to irreversible vision loss starting peripheral and progressing centrally.

Two main types:

  • Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (POAG) — most common (90%); painless, gradual peripheral vision loss; often asymptomatic until late; bilateral
  • Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma — medical emergency; sudden severe eye pain, headache, nausea, halos around lights, fixed mid-dilated pupil; can cause blindness within hours if untreated

Normal IOP: 10–21 mmHg. Glaucoma diagnosis based on optic nerve appearance, visual field testing, and IOP — not IOP alone (normal-tension glaucoma exists).

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • POAG: resistance to aqueous humor outflow through trabecular meshwork → gradual IOP elevation → optic nerve damage
  • Angle-closure: peripheral iris blocks trabecular meshwork (narrow anterior chamber angle) → sudden, severe IOP rise
  • Elevated IOP compresses optic nerve fibers and blood vessels → ischemia → cell death
  • Optic disc cupping develops; nerve fibers lost progressively
  • Risk factors: age > 60, African or Asian ancestry, family history, diabetes, high myopia, prolonged corticosteroid use, eye trauma

Expected Findings

POAG (chronic):

  • Often asymptomatic in early stages
  • Gradual loss of peripheral vision (“tunnel vision” in late stage)
  • Mild eye discomfort, frequent prescription changes
  • IOP > 21 mmHg (often)
  • Optic disc cupping on fundoscopy
  • Visual field defects on perimetry

Angle-closure (acute — emergency):

  • Sudden severe eye pain, headache
  • Nausea, vomiting
  • Blurred vision, halos around lights
  • Fixed mid-dilated pupil; eye feels hard on palpation
  • Conjunctival injection (red eye)
  • IOP often > 40 mmHg

Nursing Care

POAG treatment:

  • Prostaglandin analogs (latanoprost, bimatoprost) — FIRST-LINE
  • Beta blockers (timolol) — second-line; systemic absorption can cause bradycardia, bronchospasm
  • Alpha agonists (brimonidine), carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (dorzolamide), miotics (pilocarpine)
  • Laser trabeculoplasty if drops insufficient
  • Surgical: trabeculectomy, drainage devices

Angle-closure (EMERGENCY):

  • Immediate ophthalmology consult
  • IV mannitol (osmotic), IV acetazolamide (CAI) to rapidly lower IOP
  • Topical miotics (pilocarpine) once IOP lowered
  • Topical beta blocker, alpha agonist
  • Definitive: laser peripheral iridotomy

Nursing care:

  • Routine eye exams for at-risk populations (annual after age 40, more frequent if positive family history)
  • Teach eye drop technique and adherence
  • Avoid medications that can trigger angle-closure (anticholinergics, some antihistamines, sympathomimetics) in susceptible clients
  • Falls prevention for peripheral vision loss

Client Education

  • Vision loss from glaucoma is permanent — goal is to PREVENT further loss
  • Medications must be taken EXACTLY as prescribed, lifelong
  • Do not stop drops even if vision feels normal (asymptomatic disease)
  • Schedule regular eye exams: IOP measurement, visual fields, optic nerve imaging
  • Learn proper instillation technique with punctal occlusion
  • Multiple drops: space by ≥ 5 minutes
  • Family members should be screened (genetic component)
  • Seek immediate care for sudden eye pain, vision changes, halos, severe headache, nausea (signs of angle-closure)
  • Avoid activities that increase IOP excessively: heavy lifting, prolonged head-down position; specific activity restrictions depend on type and severity
  • Inform all providers of glaucoma diagnosis (drug list checks)
  • Vision aids and home modifications for safety
Worked Example Eye Drop Administration Technique Ch 14 — Eye and Ear Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill
Ophthalmic Medication Administration
Review Module Chapter
Ch 14 — Eye and Ear Disorders

Description of Skill

Proper administration of ophthalmic medications (eye drops and ointments) ensures therapeutic effect, minimizes systemic absorption, prevents contamination, and avoids ocular injury.

Eye drops achieve immediate effect; ointments have longer contact time but blur vision (typically used at bedtime). Key techniques: punctal occlusion (reduces systemic absorption), spacing multiple drops (≥ 5 min), and avoiding tip contact with the eye (contamination).

Indications

  • Glaucoma management (chronic IOP control)
  • Eye infections (bacterial conjunctivitis, keratitis)
  • Ocular inflammation (allergic conjunctivitis, uveitis)
  • Pre- and post-operative eye care (cataract, retinal surgery)
  • Diagnostic procedures (mydriatics, anesthetics)
  • Dry eye / lubrication

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre:

  • Verify order: medication name, concentration, eye (OD = right, OS = left, OU = both), dose, frequency
  • Two patient identifiers, check allergies
  • Gather supplies: bottle/tube, tissues, gloves
  • Assess eyes: discharge, redness, swelling, vision; cleanse with sterile saline if discharge present (inner-to-outer canthus, separate gauze each eye)
  • Position client supine or seated with head tilted back

Intra (administration):

  1. Hand hygiene; don gloves
  2. Have client look upward
  3. Gently pull down lower lid to create conjunctival sac (“pocket”)
  4. Hold dropper 1–2 cm above the eye (do NOT touch eye or eyelid — contamination)
  5. Instill the prescribed number of drops into the conjunctival sac (NOT directly on cornea)
  6. Have client close eye gently (do not squeeze tight); blot excess with tissue
  7. Apply punctal occlusion (press inner canthus) for 1–2 min — reduces systemic absorption and prolongs ocular contact
  8. For ointment: same lower-lid technique; squeeze ribbon 1/4–1/2 inch into sac, twist tube to detach; instruct gentle blinking
  9. Multiple drops: wait ≥ 5 minutes between
  10. Drops before ointments (ointments hold contact time)

Post:

  • Document medication, dose, eye, time, response
  • Assess for adverse effects: stinging, redness, blurred vision (expected initially), systemic effects
  • Reinforce client/family education

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Medication reaches target eye without contamination of dropper tip
  • Client tolerates instillation without injury
  • Therapeutic effect achieved (e.g., IOP reduction, infection resolution, allergic symptom relief)
  • Minimal systemic side effects (punctal occlusion effective)
  • Client/family demonstrate correct technique for home use

Potential Complications

  • Contamination of dropper tip → ocular infection (touching eye/eyelid)
  • Systemic absorption → significant effects (especially beta blockers → bradycardia, bronchospasm; if punctal occlusion not used)
  • Corneal abrasion from improper technique (touching eye with dropper)
  • Sub-therapeutic dose if drop missed eye, wiped immediately, or eye blinked excessively
  • Drug interaction if multiple drops too close together (washout effect)
  • Adverse drug reactions: hypersensitivity, stinging, burning, blurred vision
  • Cross-contamination between eyes if dropper used on both without cleaning
Worked Example Succinylcholine Ch 15 — Miscellaneous Central Nervous System Medications · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Medication
Review Module Chapter
Ch 15 — Miscellaneous Central Nervous System Medications
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Succinylcholine is a depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent:

  • Binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at neuromuscular junction → depolarizes muscle
  • Initially causes brief muscle fasciculations (visible twitching), then sustained paralysis
  • Cannot be reversed pharmacologically — wait for plasma cholinesterase to metabolize drug
  • Ultra-short duration: onset 30-60 sec; total duration 5-10 min
  • Used ONLY when rapid, brief paralysis is needed
  • Hydrolyzed by plasma pseudocholinesterase

Therapeutic Use

  • Endotracheal intubation
  • Electroconvulsive therapy
  • Endoscopy
  • Adjunct to mechanical ventilation
  • Muscle relaxation during surgery

Complications

  • Malignant hyperthermia — life-threatening; severe hyperthermia, muscle rigidity (esp. masseter), tachycardia, hypercarbia, metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia, rhabdomyolysis, dark urine; treat with dantrolene
  • Hyperkalemia — normally mild; MASSIVE and fatal in burns, crush injuries, denervation, prolonged immobility
  • Prolonged apnea in pseudocholinesterase deficiency
  • Bradycardia (vagal stimulation, esp. with repeated doses, especially in children)
  • Cardiac arrest (esp. children with undiagnosed muscular dystrophy)
  • ↑ intraocular pressure (avoid in open eye injury)
  • ↑ intragastric pressure → aspiration risk
  • ↑ ICP (caution in head injury)
  • Muscle pain post-procedure (myalgia from fasciculations)
  • Hypersensitivity reactions

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Personal or family history of malignant hyperthermia — life-threatening reaction
  • Severe burns, crush injuries, denervation injuries (24-72 hr post-injury) — massive K+ release → fatal hyperkalemia
  • Skeletal muscle myopathies (Duchenne muscular dystrophy, etc.)
  • Acute narrow-angle glaucoma, penetrating eye injuries (↑ intraocular pressure)
  • Pseudocholinesterase deficiency (genetic or acquired) — prolonged paralysis
  • Pre-existing hyperkalemia
  • Major nerve damage, paraplegia (chronic) — hyperkalemia risk
  • Caution: children (rare cardiac arrest reported), pregnancy Cat C

Interactions

  • Anesthetics (halothane, sevoflurane, isoflurane) → ↑ malignant hyperthermia risk
  • Aminoglycosides, polymyxins, clindamycin → potentiate neuromuscular blockade
  • Magnesium → enhanced and prolonged blockade
  • Lithium → prolonged blockade
  • Calcium channel blockers → enhanced blockade
  • Anticholinesterases (neostigmine) → DO NOT REVERSE succinylcholine (different mechanism); may prolong
  • Cyclosporine, oral contraceptives, MAOIs → ↓ pseudocholinesterase activity → prolonged effect
  • Digoxin → arrhythmia risk (esp. with fasciculations releasing K+)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Successful endotracheal intubation
  • Adequate muscle relaxation for procedure (ECT, endoscopy, surgery)
  • Return of spontaneous respiration and movement within 5-10 minutes after dose
  • No malignant hyperthermia (no severe hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, dark urine, hypercarbia)
  • No prolonged paralysis (suspect pseudocholinesterase deficiency if > 20 min)
  • No serious hyperkalemia or cardiac arrhythmias
  • Full neurologic recovery

Medication Administration

  • Clients must receive continuous cardiac and respiratory monitoring during therapy.
  • Monitor clients following administration of a neuromuscular blocker for respiratory depression and have life support equipment available.
  • Continue to carefully monitor for return of respiratory function.
  • Succinylcholine is contraindicated for clients at risk for hyperkalemia (trauma, severe burns).

Nursing Interventions

  • Verify resuscitation equipment and qualified airway provider present BEFORE administering
  • Continuous cardiac AND respiratory monitoring during and after
  • Have dantrolene immediately available (malignant hyperthermia)
  • Have atropine available (bradycardia, especially with second dose)
  • Ensure adequate sedation AND analgesia given concurrently — succinylcholine does NOT provide either
  • Verify NO recent burn, crush injury, or denervation injury (hyperkalemia risk)
  • Verify NO personal/family history of malignant hyperthermia or muscular dystrophy
  • Use peripheral nerve stimulator (twitch monitor) to assess recovery
  • Do NOT extubate until full neuromuscular recovery (sustained head lift > 5 sec, hand grasp, train-of-four ratio > 0.9)
  • Monitor for prolonged apnea — may signal pseudocholinesterase deficiency
  • After: assess for post-procedure myalgia, report any unusual symptoms

Client Education

  • This medication will be given while you are under anesthesia for a brief surgical procedure or to help with breathing tube placement
  • You will be carefully monitored for breathing and heart rate the entire time
  • The effects wear off in 5-10 minutes
  • Some clients have muscle pain after (especially in chest, neck, abdomen) — usually resolves within a few days; over-the-counter pain relievers help
  • If you or family members have ever had malignant hyperthermia or muscle disease, tell ALL providers (anesthesia, surgery) BEFORE any future procedure
  • Carry a medical alert ID if you or a relative had this reaction
  • Tell providers if you have ever had unusual reaction to anesthesia
Worked Example Vecuronium (Nondepolarizing NMB) Ch 15 — Misc CNS Medications · NMB section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Vecuronium (Norcuron)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 15 — Misc CNS Medications
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker — competitively blocks acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors of the neuromuscular junction
  • Causes complete skeletal muscle paralysis — including respiratory muscles
  • NO sedative, analgesic, or amnestic properties — client is awake and feeling everything unless adequately sedated
  • Onset: 2–3 min IV; duration: 25–40 min
  • Reversal: neostigmine + glycopyrrolate, or sugammadex (selective binding)

Therapeutic Use

  • Facilitate endotracheal intubation
  • Maintain skeletal muscle paralysis during surgery (improves operating conditions)
  • Facilitate mechanical ventilation in ICU clients (ARDS, severe asthma)
  • Reduce metabolic demand in critically ill
  • Tetanus muscle spasms (refractory cases)

Complications

  • Respiratory paralysis — intentional but life-threatening if airway not secured; requires intubation and ventilation
  • Awareness during paralysis if inadequate sedation/analgesia — psychologically traumatic; ALWAYS sedate first
  • Prolonged paralysis (especially with renal/hepatic impairment, drug interactions)
  • Histamine release (less than other NMBs)
  • Cardiovascular effects: minimal compared to other NMBs
  • ICU-acquired weakness with prolonged use
  • Critical illness myopathy/neuropathy

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to vecuronium or other NMBs
  • Myasthenia gravis (increased sensitivity)
  • Inadequate airway management capabilities
  • Inadequate sedation/analgesia capabilities
  • Severe hepatic impairment (prolonged effect)
  • Burn clients (after 24 hr, resistance develops — need higher doses)
  • Pregnancy: assess risk vs benefit

Interactions

  • Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, vancomycin), magnesium, calcium channel blockers — potentiate NMB effect → prolonged paralysis
  • Volatile anesthetics — enhance NMB effect
  • Local anesthetics — can enhance
  • Beta blockers — potentiate
  • Corticosteroids (long-term) + NMB → severe myopathy
  • Anti-epileptics (chronic) — may shorten NMB duration

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Train-of-four (TOF) monitoring: aim for 1–2 twitches during paralysis (deeper for some procedures)
  • Adequate paralysis for intubation/procedure
  • Successful reversal: TOF ratio ≥ 0.9 with all 4 twitches, sustained head lift ≥ 5 sec, strong handgrip
  • No awareness during paralysis (adequate sedation maintained)
  • No prolonged paralysis after reversal

Medication Administration

  • Route: IV only
  • Intubation dose: 0.08–0.1 mg/kg IV bolus
  • Maintenance: 0.01 mg/kg IV bolus PRN, or 1–2 mcg/kg/min infusion (titrate to TOF)
  • Refrigerate; reconstitute with sterile water
  • NEVER give to non-intubated, non-sedated client (paralysis without ventilation = death)
  • Use TOF monitoring (peripheral nerve stimulator) to guide dosing

Nursing Interventions

  • Verify intubation AND adequate sedation/analgesia BEFORE giving NMB
  • Continuous ventilator monitoring; backup ambu bag at bedside
  • Apply bilateral lid tape or lubricant to protect corneas (no blinking)
  • Position changes every 2 hr to prevent pressure injuries
  • DVT prophylaxis (immobility)
  • Continuous sedation assessment (BIS monitor if available)
  • Train-of-four (TOF) monitoring to titrate dose
  • Drug interaction screening (especially aminoglycosides)
  • Communicate to all team members that client is paralyzed (cannot communicate distress)
  • Reversal: confirm adequate spontaneous respiratory effort before extubation

Client Education

  • (Family/proxy education): NMB causes paralysis to allow ventilator or surgery; sedation is also given to prevent awareness
  • Once reversed, weakness may persist briefly; physical therapy may be needed
  • If awareness occurred: psychological follow-up; PTSD screening; trauma-informed care
  • Future surgery: notify anesthesiology of any prior NMB issues, allergies, or family history of malignant hyperthermia
  • Critical illness recovery: ICU-acquired weakness can take weeks to months to fully resolve
  • Family communication during paralysis: speak to client even though unresponsive (they may be aware)
Worked Example Baclofen (Lioresal) Ch 15 — Misc CNS Medications · Relaxants section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Baclofen (Lioresal)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 15 — Misc CNS Medications
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant — GABA-B agonist; inhibits spinal cord reflexes
  • Reduces muscle spasticity without significantly affecting motor strength
  • Crosses BBB; CNS depressant properties

Therapeutic Use

  • Spasticity from multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, cerebral palsy
  • Intrathecal baclofen for severe refractory spasticity
  • Off-label: alcohol use disorder, hiccups, trigeminal neuralgia

Complications

  • ABRUPT WITHDRAWAL SYNDROME — rebound spasticity, hallucinations, seizures, fever, hyperthermia, multi-organ failure; can be fatal — especially with intrathecal pump failure
  • Drowsiness, dizziness, fatigue, weakness (very common, especially initial)
  • Nausea, constipation, urinary frequency or retention
  • Lowered seizure threshold
  • Mood changes: depression, anxiety, hallucinations (especially older adults)
  • Hypotonia
  • Intrathecal pump issues: catheter dislodgement, pump malfunction (emergency)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to baclofen
  • Seizure disorder (use with caution — lowers threshold)
  • Renal impairment — dose adjustment (renally cleared)
  • Psychiatric disorders — may worsen
  • Pregnancy: weigh risks; lactation: excreted in breast milk
  • Older adults — increased CNS effects, falls
  • Recent CVA or stroke history (may worsen function in some clients)

Interactions

  • CNS depressants (alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, sedatives) — additive sedation, respiratory depression
  • Antihypertensives — additive hypotension
  • TCAs — increased muscle weakness
  • MAOIs — potential interaction; use caution
  • Lithium — additive CNS effects

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Decreased spasticity (modified Ashworth Scale)
  • Improved function (mobility, ADLs, comfort)
  • Better sleep, less pain from spasms
  • Tolerable sedation
  • No withdrawal episodes
  • Stable mood and cognition

Medication Administration

  • Routes: oral (tablets) and intrathecal (continuous infusion via implanted pump)
  • Oral starting dose: 5 mg PO TID; titrate every 3 days; max 80 mg/day
  • Take with food to reduce GI upset
  • Last dose 4 hours before bedtime to minimize sleep disruption
  • Intrathecal: managed by specialist team; programmable pump refilled every 1–6 months
  • NEVER stop abruptly — taper over 1–2 weeks

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline: spasticity severity, ambulation status, renal function, mental status
  • Monitor for sedation, weakness, mood changes
  • Fall risk assessment; assistive devices
  • Educate family about gradual titration AND TAPERING required
  • For intrathecal pumps: monitor for catheter complications, refill schedule, withdrawal signs
  • If withdrawal symptoms develop: IV baclofen or oral baclofen (high dose); benzodiazepines for agitation; supportive care
  • Suicide risk assessment in mood changes
  • Coordinate with PT/OT

Client Education

  • NEVER stop suddenly — LIFE-THREATENING WITHDRAWAL can occur
  • Report missed doses; if > 2 doses missed, call provider before resuming
  • If intrathecal pump alarms, seek IMMEDIATE care
  • Take with food; may cause sedation (avoid driving until response known)
  • Avoid alcohol and CNS depressants
  • Carry medical alert ID listing baclofen
  • Report: hallucinations, fever, severe spasticity (signs of withdrawal); mood changes; new seizures
  • Rise slowly to prevent orthostatic hypotension
  • Continue PT/OT and home exercise program
Worked Example Malignant Hyperthermia (MH) Ch 15 — Misc CNS Medications · NMB section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure
Malignant Hyperthermia Management
Review Module Chapter
Ch 15 — Misc CNS Medications

Description of Procedure

Malignant Hyperthermia (MH) — a rare, life-threatening pharmacogenetic disorder of skeletal muscle calcium regulation triggered by exposure to certain anesthetic agents. Autosomal dominant inheritance (RYR1 gene mutation in most cases).

Trigger agents:

  • Volatile inhaled anesthetics: halothane, sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane, enflurane
  • Succinylcholine (depolarizing NMB)

Onset: from minutes to hours after exposure. Without rapid recognition and dantrolene treatment, mortality > 70%. With prompt treatment, mortality < 5%.

Indications

  • Suspected MH crisis during or after general anesthesia
  • Sudden unexplained rise in end-tidal CO2 despite increased ventilation (often the EARLIEST sign)
  • Generalized muscle rigidity (especially masseter rigidity after succinylcholine)
  • Tachycardia, hyperthermia, mixed acidosis
  • Hyperkalemia, rhabdomyolysis
  • Family history of MH — preventive measures

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre (prevention — for known/suspected susceptible clients):

  • Detailed pre-op history: personal/family history of MH or anesthesia complications
  • Susceptibility testing: caffeine-halothane contracture test (CHCT) or RYR1 genetic testing
  • Plan: AVOID trigger agents; use total IV anesthesia (TIVA) with propofol; non-depolarizing NMBs (vecuronium, rocuronium); flush anesthesia machine
  • Have dantrolene available and team familiar with MH protocol

Intra (active MH crisis — act IMMEDIATELY):

  1. STOP all triggering agents immediately
  2. Call for help / activate MH cart and MHAUS hotline (1-800-MH-HYPER for US)
  3. Hyperventilate with 100% oxygen at high flow rates (10–15 L/min)
  4. DANTROLENE 2.5 mg/kg IV bolus — reconstitute rapidly with sterile water; repeat every 5–10 min as needed (max 10 mg/kg)
  5. Active cooling: cool IV fluids, cooling blanket, ice packs to groin/axilla, gastric lavage with cold saline (target temp < 38°C)
  6. Treat hyperkalemia: insulin + glucose, calcium gluconate, bicarbonate, hyperventilation
  7. Treat arrhythmias per ACLS (avoid CCBs — cardiac arrest risk with dantrolene)
  8. Foley catheter; monitor urine output (rhabdo → AKI risk)
  9. Continuous ABG, electrolytes, CK monitoring
  10. ICU admission post-stabilization

Post:

  • Continue dantrolene 1 mg/kg q6h for at least 24–48 hr (recrudescence risk)
  • Document MH crisis in chart; medical alert bracelet for client
  • Refer client AND first-degree relatives for MH susceptibility testing
  • Counsel future surgery precautions (non-trigger anesthesia)
  • Report to North American MH Registry

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Temperature returns to baseline < 38°C
  • Resolution of muscle rigidity
  • Hemodynamic stability
  • Electrolytes (especially potassium) within normal range
  • Acid-base balance restored
  • No recrudescence in 48 hours
  • Client survives and avoids permanent organ damage
  • Family members tested and counseled appropriately

Potential Complications

  • Death — from arrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis, multi-organ failure (mortality < 5% with prompt treatment; > 70% without)
  • Hyperthermia-induced multi-organ damage — CNS, hepatic, renal injury
  • Rhabdomyolysis → acute kidney injury (massive CK elevation)
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
  • Cerebral edema, neurologic deficits
  • Recrudescence (recurrence) — 25% within 24–48 hr; requires ongoing dantrolene
  • Compartment syndrome from rigidity
  • Cardiac arrhythmias and arrest
  • If undiagnosed in family: future relatives at risk for crisis
Worked Example Diazepam Ch 16 — Sedative-Hypnotics · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Medication
Review Module Chapter
Ch 16 — Sedative-Hypnotics
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Diazepam is a long-acting benzodiazepine:

  • Enhances binding of GABA to GABA-A receptors → ↑ chloride influx → neuronal hyperpolarization → CNS depression
  • Produces: anxiolysis, sedation, hypnosis, muscle relaxation, anticonvulsant effects, anterograde amnesia
  • Long half-life (20-100 hr) with active metabolites — risk of accumulation, esp. in elderly
  • Onset: PO 15-60 min, IV 1-5 min
  • Reversal: flumazenil (use cautiously — can precipitate seizures in long-term users)

Therapeutic Use

  • Anxiety disorders
  • Seizure disorders
  • Insomnia
  • Muscle spasms
  • Alcohol withdrawal
  • Panic disorder
  • Induction of anesthesia

Complications

  • CNS depression: drowsiness, sedation, fatigue, ataxia, confusion (especially elderly)
  • Respiratory depression (esp. with opioids — fatal combination; FDA boxed warning)
  • Dependence and tolerance with long-term use; withdrawal syndrome (seizures, anxiety, insomnia, tremor) on abrupt discontinuation
  • Paradoxical reactions: agitation, hostility, hallucinations (especially elderly, children)
  • Anterograde amnesia
  • Falls and fractures (especially elderly)
  • Cognitive impairment with chronic use
  • Phlebitis with IV use; tissue necrosis with extravasation
  • Bradycardia, hypotension (IV use, especially rapid)
  • Teratogenic — cleft lip/palate, neonatal floppy infant syndrome / withdrawal
  • Suicide risk (especially in overdose with other CNS depressants)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Pregnancy: Benzodiazepines are Pregnancy Risk Category D (a high risk to the fetus)
  • Sleep apnea
  • Respiratory depression
  • Organic brain disease
  • Lactation
  • Cautious use in clients who have a history of substance use disorders, liver dysfunction, and kidney failure

Interactions

  • CNS depressants (alcohol, opioids, antihistamines, antipsychotics, anticonvulsants, sedatives) → additive respiratory depression — potentially fatal
  • Opioids — FDA black box warning for concurrent use
  • CYP3A4 inhibitors (cimetidine, erythromycin, fluoxetine, ketoconazole) → ↑ diazepam levels
  • CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin) → ↓ diazepam levels
  • Grapefruit juice → ↑ levels
  • Probenecid → ↑ levels

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Anxiety: ↓ anxiety symptoms, ↑ ability to function
  • Seizures: ↓ frequency, termination of status epilepticus
  • Alcohol withdrawal: ↓ tremors, anxiety, autonomic hyperactivity; prevention of seizures and DTs
  • Insomnia: improved sleep latency and duration
  • Muscle spasms: ↓ muscle tension and discomfort
  • No excessive sedation, respiratory depression, or paradoxical agitation
  • No development of dependence (with appropriate short-term use)

Medication Administration

  • Routes: oral, IV, IM, rectal gel (Diastat for seizures)
  • Adult dose:
    • PO anxiety: 2-10 mg PO BID-QID
    • IV/IM for status epilepticus: 5-10 mg slow IV push, may repeat
    • Alcohol withdrawal: 5-20 mg PO/IV q6h, titrate
  • IV: slow push (over ≥ 1 min), max 5 mg/min adults; do not mix with other meds (precipitates)
  • Have resuscitation equipment available (IV use)
  • Use lowest effective dose for shortest duration (typically < 4 weeks for anxiety to avoid dependence)
  • Taper gradually after long-term use — abrupt discontinuation causes withdrawal (seizures, anxiety, insomnia)

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess baseline mental status, anxiety level, seizure history, fall risk
  • Monitor respiratory status, especially with IV use or concurrent opioids
  • Monitor for excessive sedation, ataxia, dizziness
  • Watch for paradoxical reactions in elderly: increased agitation, aggression, hallucinations
  • Implement fall precautions (especially elderly)
  • Have flumazenil available for overdose (but use cautiously in long-term users)
  • Assess for signs of dependence (with prolonged use); plan tapered discontinuation
  • For status epilepticus: cardiac and respiratory monitoring, IV access, airway support available

Client Education

  • Report: severe drowsiness, confusion, paradoxical agitation, depression or suicidal thoughts, difficulty breathing, signs of dependence
  • Avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants — can be fatal
  • Avoid driving and hazardous activities until effects known
  • Do NOT abruptly stop after long-term use — taper under provider supervision (withdrawal can cause seizures)
  • Rise slowly to prevent falls (especially elderly)
  • Use for short-term only (typically < 4 weeks for anxiety)
  • Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding
  • Tell all providers about diazepam use
  • Avoid grapefruit juice
  • Store securely; controlled substance with abuse potential
Worked Example Zolpidem (Ambien) Ch 16 — Sedative-Hypnotics · Other section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Zolpidem (Ambien, Edluar, Intermezzo)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 16 — Sedative-Hypnotics
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Non-benzodiazepine GABA-A receptor agonist (Z-drug) — selectively binds the omega-1 (BZ1) subunit
  • Promotes sleep onset; minimal effect on sleep architecture compared to benzos
  • Schedule IV controlled substance — dependence and abuse potential (lower than benzos)
  • Short half-life (~2.5 hr) — reduces morning grogginess if taken correctly

Therapeutic Use

  • Short-term insomnia (sleep-onset difficulty primarily) — 7–10 days; max 4–5 weeks per ATI
  • Extended-release (Ambien CR) for sleep maintenance
  • Sublingual (Intermezzo) for middle-of-night awakening (low dose)
  • Not first-line; cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is preferred

Complications

  • Complex sleep behaviors (BLACK BOX WARNING) — sleep-walking, sleep-driving, sleep-eating, sleep-sex, with no memory of events; serious accidents reported
  • Next-morning impairment — particularly with extended-release or higher doses
  • Daytime drowsiness, dizziness, headache
  • Anterograde amnesia (loss of memory after dose)
  • Falls in older adults; Beers Criteria PIM
  • Paradoxical reactions (agitation, hallucinations) — especially older adults
  • Dependence and tolerance with prolonged use
  • Withdrawal: rebound insomnia, anxiety, tremor (severe with long-term high doses)
  • Respiratory depression (rare but possible, especially combined with opioids)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • History of complex sleep behaviors with zolpidem
  • Severe hepatic impairment
  • Sleep apnea (untreated) — can worsen apneas
  • Older adults — use lower doses; consider non-pharmacologic first
  • Pregnancy and lactation — avoid
  • History of substance abuse
  • Severe depression with suicidal ideation
  • Need for early morning driving (especially women — FDA recommends lower doses due to slower clearance)

Interactions

  • CNS depressants (alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, sedating antihistamines) — additive sedation, respiratory depression
  • CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, erythromycin, ritonavir, grapefruit juice) — increase zolpidem levels
  • CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine) — decrease levels
  • Other sleep aids (melatonin, doxylamine) — additive sedation
  • SSRIs — may potentiate hallucinations

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Reduced sleep latency (time to fall asleep)
  • Improved total sleep time
  • No complex sleep behaviors
  • No next-day impairment
  • Engagement in non-pharmacologic strategies (CBT-I, sleep hygiene)
  • Successful taper without rebound insomnia at end of therapy

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (tablet, ODT, sublingual, spray)
  • Standard IR dose: 5 mg (women) or 5–10 mg (men) PO at bedtime
  • Extended-release (CR): 6.25 mg (women) or 6.25–12.5 mg (men) PO at bedtime
  • Older adults: 5 mg max
  • Take ONLY when at least 7–8 hours of sleep opportunity available
  • Take immediately before bed, after lying down
  • Do NOT take with food (delays onset)
  • Schedule IV: lowest effective dose, shortest duration

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess sleep complaint thoroughly; rule out depression, anxiety, sleep apnea, substance issues
  • Recommend sleep hygiene and CBT-I first/concurrently
  • Lowest effective dose; shortest duration
  • For older adults or first-time users: consider observed initial dosing
  • Falls precautions: bed in low position, side rails up, call light within reach
  • Educate about complex sleep behaviors — discontinue immediately if they occur
  • Monitor for signs of dependence or escalating use
  • Coordinate gradual taper if used > 2–4 weeks

Client Education

  • Take ONLY when you have 7–8 hours to sleep — not for short naps
  • Take immediately before bed, after lying down
  • Do NOT take with alcohol or other sedatives — dangerous combination
  • Do NOT drive or operate heavy machinery until you know how you respond; next-day impairment can occur
  • Report any sleep-walking, sleep-driving, sleep-eating, or unusual nocturnal behaviors — STOP medication and call provider
  • Limit to short-term use (CBT-I is more effective long-term)
  • Do not stop abruptly after extended use — gradual taper
  • Avoid grapefruit juice
  • Practice good sleep hygiene: consistent schedule, dark/cool room, no screens before bed, no caffeine after noon
  • Pregnancy: discuss with provider
Worked Example Insomnia Ch 16 — Sedative-Hypnotics · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Insomnia
Review Module Chapter
Ch 16 — Sedative-Hypnotics

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Insomnia — difficulty initiating sleep, maintaining sleep, or non-restorative sleep that causes daytime impairment, despite adequate sleep opportunity.

  • DSM-5 requires: dissatisfaction with sleep quality/quantity + ≥ 1 of (difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, early morning awakening); ≥ 3 nights/week for ≥ 3 months; significant impairment
  • Acute: < 3 months (often triggered by stress)
  • Chronic: ≥ 3 months
  • Comorbid: with another medical or psychiatric condition (most common)
  • Prevalence: ~10–30% chronic; higher in women, older adults, shift workers

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Hyperarousal model: physiologic (elevated HR, cortisol), cognitive (rumination), and emotional (anxiety) hyperarousal
  • Dysregulation of sleep-wake cycle (suprachiasmatic nucleus)
  • Altered neurotransmitter balance: reduced GABA, elevated orexin/CRH
  • Conditioned arousal — bedroom becomes associated with wakefulness
  • Genetic predisposition — heritability 30–40%
  • Triggers: stress, life events, medical conditions, medications, environment

Expected Findings

Nighttime symptoms:

  • Prolonged sleep latency (> 30 min to fall asleep)
  • Frequent awakenings; difficulty returning to sleep
  • Early morning awakening (cannot return to sleep)
  • Reduced total sleep time
  • Non-restorative sleep

Daytime impairment:

  • Fatigue, sleepiness
  • Concentration and memory problems
  • Mood disturbance (irritability, depression, anxiety)
  • Reduced motivation, productivity
  • Increased errors, accidents
  • Social/occupational impairment

Assessment tools:

  • Sleep diary (gold standard for outpatient assessment, 2 weeks)
  • Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) — standardized scale
  • Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index
  • Polysomnography (only if suspect other sleep disorder — apnea, periodic limb movements)

Nursing Care

FIRST-LINE: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) — more effective long-term than medications. Components: sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring, relaxation, sleep hygiene.

Pharmacotherapy (short-term, when CBT-I inaccessible or inadequate):

  • Z-drugs (zolpidem, eszopiclone, zaleplon) — preferred over benzodiazepines
  • Benzodiazepines (temazepam, triazolam) — high addiction risk; avoid in older adults
  • Melatonin agonist (ramelteon) — non-controlled; preferred when worry about dependence
  • Orexin receptor antagonists (suvorexant, lemborexant) — newer; for chronic insomnia
  • Sedating antidepressants (trazodone, doxepin low-dose, mirtazapine) — off-label; useful if comorbid depression
  • Antihistamines (diphenhydramine) — OTC; AVOID in older adults (anticholinergic burden, Beers list)
  • Melatonin (OTC) — mild effect; safe for short-term

Sleep hygiene principles:

  • Consistent bedtime and wake time (including weekends)
  • Dark, cool, quiet bedroom
  • No electronic screens 30–60 min before bed
  • No caffeine after noon; limit alcohol (disrupts sleep)
  • Regular exercise (not late evening)
  • Bedroom for sleep only (not work, TV, eating)
  • If unable to sleep in 20 min: get up, do quiet activity, return when sleepy

Client Education

  • Sleep is a learned behavior; sleep hygiene matters
  • CBT-I is highly effective and durable — consider before medications
  • If medications used: short-term only (weeks, not months)
  • Avoid alcohol as sleep aid — worsens sleep architecture
  • Caffeine half-life is 6–8 hours — limit after noon
  • Address underlying causes: depression, anxiety, pain, GERD, sleep apnea
  • Older adults: most sleep aids are riskier; consider behavioral interventions, melatonin, ramelteon
  • Track sleep with a diary or app to identify patterns
  • Manage stress with relaxation techniques, mindfulness, exercise
  • Naps should be < 30 min and before 3 PM
  • Light exposure in morning helps regulate circadian rhythm
  • Seek evaluation for snoring/gasping (sleep apnea) or leg movements (PLMD)
Worked Example Flumazenil (Benzodiazepine Reversal) Ch 16 — Sedative-Hypnotics · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Flumazenil (Romazicon)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 16 — Sedative-Hypnotics
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Benzodiazepine receptor antagonist — competitively binds GABA-A benzodiazepine site, displacing benzos
  • Reverses benzodiazepine sedation, respiratory depression, and amnesia
  • Onset 1–2 min IV; duration 30–60 min (often SHORTER than the benzo) — re-sedation likely
  • Does NOT reverse opioids or other CNS depressants

Therapeutic Use

  • Benzodiazepine overdose — reversal of respiratory depression and severe sedation
  • Reversal of conscious sedation (post-procedure)
  • Diagnostic in suspected mixed drug overdose
  • NOT routinely first-line in overdose — many providers prefer supportive care due to seizure risk

Complications

  • Seizures — especially in benzo-dependent clients (precipitated withdrawal seizures); also in mixed overdose with TCAs or other seizure-inducing drugs
  • Re-sedation — when flumazenil wears off before the benzo (longer-acting benzos like diazepam, lorazepam)
  • Acute withdrawal syndrome in chronic benzo users: agitation, sweating, tachycardia, hypertension
  • Cardiac arrhythmias (rare)
  • Nausea, vomiting, anxiety, dizziness on reversal
  • Increased intracranial pressure (avoid in TBI)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Known seizure disorder treated with benzodiazepines (will precipitate seizures)
  • Suspected mixed overdose with TCAs or other proconvulsants
  • Long-term benzodiazepine use (chronic dependence → severe withdrawal)
  • Hypersensitivity to flumazenil
  • Increased intracranial pressure
  • Pregnancy — use only if benefits outweigh risks
  • Severe TCA overdose

Interactions

  • All benzodiazepines — reverses effects
  • Zolpidem and Z-drugs — partial reversal (also GABA-A site)
  • TCAs, cocaine, isoniazid, theophylline — seizure risk amplified
  • Does NOT reverse: opioids, alcohol, barbiturates, GHB

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Improved level of consciousness
  • Return of spontaneous adequate respiration
  • Reversal of respiratory depression and severe sedation
  • Stable vital signs without re-sedation
  • No seizure activity
  • Continued monitoring for at least 2–4 hours (longer if long-acting benzo involved)

Medication Administration

  • Route: IV only
  • Adult dose: 0.2 mg IV over 15 sec; if no response after 45 sec, repeat 0.2 mg every minute (max 1 mg per attempt; max 3 mg/hr total)
  • Most clients respond to total dose < 1 mg
  • Infusion may be needed for long-acting benzo overdose (0.1–0.5 mg/hr)
  • Continuous monitoring during and after administration
  • Have benzodiazepines available to treat seizures if precipitated

Nursing Interventions

  • Verify history: rule out chronic benzo use, seizure disorder, mixed overdose (TCA toxicity = anticholinergic signs, ECG widening)
  • Obtain EKG before reversal (check for TCA toxicity)
  • Establish IV; prepare for seizure precautions (suction, padded rails, oxygen)
  • Have IV benzodiazepines (lorazepam) available to treat precipitated seizures — seems paradoxical but seizures may need benzo treatment
  • Continuous cardiopulmonary monitoring
  • Reassess every 5–15 min for re-sedation; redose flumazenil as needed
  • Provide reorientation and reassurance (acute withdrawal can be distressing)
  • Document time, dose, response
  • Mental health and substance use evaluation after stabilization

Client Education

  • (Post-event) Flumazenil rapidly reversed the benzodiazepine effects
  • Re-sedation can occur as flumazenil wears off — continued monitoring is required
  • Do NOT drive or operate machinery for 24 hours
  • Avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants for at least 24 hr
  • If reversal was for overdose: mental health and substance use evaluation recommended
  • If chronic benzo user: do not abruptly stop benzodiazepines (severe withdrawal); coordinate gradual taper
  • If accidental: review medication list and pillbox use; consider drug interactions
  • Family: learn signs of overdose and when to call 911
Worked Example Albuterol Ch 17 — Airflow Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Albuterol
Review Module Chapter
Ch 17 — Airflow Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Albuterol is a short-acting beta-2 adrenergic agonist (SABA) that:

  • Selectively stimulates β2 receptors in bronchial smooth muscle → bronchodilation
  • Onset: 5-15 min (inhaled), peak 30-60 min, duration 4-6 hr
  • Rescue/quick-relief medication for acute bronchospasm
  • Selectivity decreases at higher doses → β1 effects emerge (tachycardia)
  • Does NOT treat underlying airway inflammation (use ICS for that)

Therapeutic Use

Beta2-adrenergic agonists act by selectively activating the beta2-receptors in the bronchial smooth muscle, resulting in bronchodilation. They also suppress histamine release and promote ciliary motility.

Complications

  • Oral agents can cause tachycardia and angina due to activation of alpha1 receptors in the heart.
  • Activation of beta2 receptors in skeletal muscle causes tremors.

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to albuterol or other sympathomimetics
  • Caution: cardiovascular disease (CAD, arrhythmias, HTN)
  • Caution: hyperthyroidism, diabetes mellitus (may ↑ glucose)
  • Caution: seizure disorder
  • Caution: hypokalemia (albuterol can lower K+ further)
  • Pregnancy Cat C (benefit usually outweighs risk in acute asthma)

Interactions

  • Beta-blockers (esp. non-selective like propranolol) → antagonize albuterol effect; can trigger bronchospasm
  • MAO inhibitors, tricyclic antidepressants → ↑ cardiovascular effects
  • Other sympathomimetics → additive effects, ↑ adverse effects
  • Loop and thiazide diuretics → additive hypokalemia
  • Digoxin → ↓ digoxin levels (theoretical)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ wheezing, coughing, dyspnea
  • ↑ peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR)
  • ↑ oxygen saturation (SpO₂)
  • ↑ ability to speak in full sentences
  • ↓ accessory muscle use
  • Improved tolerance to activity/exercise
  • Use frequency < 2 days/week (well-controlled asthma)

Medication Administration

  • Routes: MDI (metered-dose inhaler), nebulizer, oral, IV (rare)
  • MDI: 1-2 puffs q4-6h PRN; use spacer for proper deposition
  • Nebulizer: 2.5 mg in 3 mL NS over 5-15 min
  • If using daily controller (ICS), use albuterol FIRST, wait 5 min, then ICS
  • Rinse mouth after use to ↓ throat irritation
  • Frequent use (> 2x/week) indicates poor asthma control → reassess plan
  • Use 15-30 min before exercise for exercise-induced bronchospasm

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess respiratory status before and after administration (RR, breath sounds, SpO₂, accessory muscle use)
  • Monitor for adverse effects: tachycardia, tremor, nervousness, palpitations, headache
  • Monitor serum potassium (especially with frequent or high-dose use)
  • Teach proper inhaler technique; verify with return demonstration
  • Encourage spacer use (improves drug delivery, decreases oropharyngeal deposition)
  • Have client rinse mouth after each use
  • If using daily, document frequency — > 2 days/week signals need for controller medication

Client Education

  • Report: palpitations, chest pain, severe tremors, paradoxical worsening of breathing, frequent need to use (> 2 days/week)
  • Use SABA before any inhaled corticosteroid (5 min apart) so airways open for ICS
  • Proper MDI technique: shake → exhale → seal lips → press canister + slow deep breath → hold 10 sec → exhale → wait 1 min between puffs
  • Use a spacer for best results
  • Rinse mouth and gargle after each use
  • Carry rescue inhaler at ALL times
  • Use 15-30 min before exercise if exercise-induced asthma
  • Keep written asthma action plan; know when to seek emergency care
Worked Example Guaifenesin Ch 18 — Upper Respiratory Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Guaifenesin
Review Module Chapter
Ch 18 — Upper Respiratory Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Guaifenesin is an expectorant that:

  • Reduces the viscosity and surface tension of bronchial secretions
  • Increases airway hydration → loosens mucus → easier to cough up
  • Does NOT suppress cough — works WITH productive cough to clear airways
  • Onset 30 min, peak 1-2 hr, duration 4-6 hr (extended release: up to 12 hr)

Therapeutic Use

  • Symptomatic relief of productive cough with thick mucus
  • Common cold, bronchitis, sinusitis (when mucus is thick)
  • Adjunct in chronic conditions with mucus retention (COPD, cystic fibrosis)

Complications

  • GI upset
  • Drowsiness
  • Dizziness
  • Rash

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to guaifenesin
  • Persistent cough > 1 week — needs evaluation, NOT continued OTC use
  • Productive cough caused by chronic conditions (asthma, smoking, emphysema) — only use under provider guidance
  • Children < 4 years (avoid all OTC cough/cold products)
  • Caution in pregnancy and breastfeeding

Interactions

  • Few clinically significant interactions (low protein binding, minimal metabolism)
  • May interfere with urine 5-HIAA test (false positive)
  • Often combined with other ingredients in OTC products (decongestants, antihistamines, dextromethorphan) — read labels to avoid duplication

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Cough is more productive, mucous is easier to expectorate.
  • Chest congestion is decreased.

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (tablet, capsule, liquid, ER tablet)
  • Adult dose: 200-400 mg PO q4h PRN (immediate-release) or 600-1200 mg PO q12h (ER)
  • Max: 2,400 mg/day
  • Pediatric (4-11 yr): 100-200 mg PO q4h (max 1,200 mg/day)
  • Take with a full glass of water (8 oz)
  • Do NOT crush or chew extended-release tablets
  • Encourage ↑ fluid intake (≥ 2-3 L/day) — water is the best expectorant

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess respiratory status, character of cough, sputum production/consistency
  • Encourage adequate hydration (water is more important than the drug)
  • Teach effective cough technique (incentive spirometry if appropriate)
  • Reposition q2h; encourage ambulation to mobilize secretions
  • Humidify air if dry environment
  • Monitor for nausea, vomiting, dizziness, drowsiness (uncommon)

Client Education

  • Report: cough persisting > 1 week, high fever, chest pain, blood-tinged sputum, severe headache, rash
  • Drink plenty of fluids (≥ 2 L/day) — most important for thinning mucus
  • Take with a full glass of water
  • Do NOT use to suppress cough — purpose is to make coughing more productive
  • Avoid combining with cough suppressants (defeats the purpose)
  • Read OTC labels carefully — many combination products contain guaifenesin
  • If pregnant, breastfeeding, or treating a child < 4 yr, consult provider
Worked Example Furosemide Ch 19 — Medications Affecting Urinary Output · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Medication
Review Module Chapter
Ch 19 — Medications Affecting Urinary Output
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Furosemide is a loop diuretic:

  • Inhibits the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending loop of Henle
  • Blocks sodium, potassium, and chloride reabsorption → ↑ water excretion
  • Most potent diuretic class — useful when rapid or large diuresis needed
  • Onset: PO 30-60 min, IV 5 min
  • Duration: PO 6-8 hr, IV 2 hr
  • Also causes venodilation (↓ preload) — useful in acute pulmonary edema

Therapeutic Use

  • Used when there is an emergent need for rapid mobilization of fluid
  • Pulmonary edema caused by heart failure
  • Liver, cardiac, or kidney disease
  • Hypertension
  • Unlabeled use: hypercalcemia

Complications

  • Dehydration
  • Hypotension
  • Ototoxicity
  • Hypokalemia

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Anuria
  • Hypersensitivity to furosemide or sulfonamides (cross-reactivity possible)
  • Severe hypovolemia, dehydration
  • Severe electrolyte imbalances (esp. hypokalemia)
  • Hepatic coma (precipitate by hypokalemia)
  • Caution: gout, diabetes (↑ glucose), SLE, renal impairment
  • Caution: ototoxicity risk with rapid IV push or high doses
  • Pregnancy Cat C; breastfeeding (suppresses lactation)

Interactions

  • Aminoglycosides, vancomycin → additive ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity
  • Digoxin → hypokalemia ↑ digoxin toxicity
  • Lithium → ↓ lithium clearance → ↑ toxicity
  • NSAIDs → ↓ diuretic effect, ↑ nephrotoxicity
  • Antihypertensives → additive hypotension
  • Corticosteroids → ↑ hypokalemia
  • Antidiabetics → ↓ effect (furosemide ↑ glucose)
  • Probenecid → ↓ diuretic effect

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↑ urine output (target depends on indication)
  • Weight loss appropriate to goal (e.g., 1-2 lb/day for HF)
  • ↓ peripheral edema, ↓ ascites, ↓ JVD
  • ↑ ease of breathing, ↓ crackles, ↓ orthopnea (HF, pulmonary edema)
  • BP at goal (HTN indication)
  • Electrolytes stable: K+ 3.5-5.0, Mg++ 1.5-2.5, Na+ 135-145
  • No signs of dehydration (BP, HR, mucous membranes, skin turgor)
  • No ototoxicity (hearing intact, no tinnitus)

Medication Administration

  • Routes: oral, IV, IM
  • Adult: 20-80 mg PO daily-BID; titrate based on response
  • IV: 20-40 mg slow IV push over 1-2 min; max 4 mg/min (faster ↑ ototoxicity)
  • Take in the morning (BID dosing: 2nd dose by mid-afternoon) to avoid nocturia
  • Take with food if GI upset
  • Monitor daily weights (same time, same scale, similar clothing) — most accurate fluid status indicator
  • Strict I&O, daily electrolyte monitoring (esp. K+) initially
  • Encourage potassium-rich foods (bananas, oranges, potatoes, leafy greens) or supplement as prescribed

Nursing Interventions

  • Dehydration: Assess for dry mouth, increased thirst, low urine output, weight loss.
  • Hypotension: monitor orthostatic blood pressure and pulse; monitor for manifestations of postural hypotension.
  • Ototoxicity: Assess for tinnitus; avoid administering ototoxic medications.
  • Hypokalemia: monitor laboratory values; offer potassium-rich foods; assess for general weakness, nausea, and vomiting.

Client Education

  • Report: dizziness on standing, severe muscle weakness or cramps (hypokalemia), hearing changes or ringing in ears, dramatic weight loss, ↓ urine output despite medication, signs of dehydration
  • Take in the morning (and afternoon if BID) — avoid late doses
  • Weigh yourself daily at the same time; report weight gain > 2 lb/day or 5 lb/week (HF)
  • Eat potassium-rich foods (bananas, oranges, potatoes, spinach, cantaloupe) unless contraindicated
  • Rise slowly to prevent dizziness (orthostatic hypotension)
  • Use sunscreen — photosensitivity
  • Avoid NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) unless approved by provider
  • Limit alcohol (↑ hypotension)
  • Diabetic clients: monitor glucose more closely
  • Take potassium supplement if prescribed
  • If sulfa-allergic, ensure provider knows (cross-reactivity possible)
Worked Example Aliskiren Ch 20 — Medications Affecting Blood Pressure · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Aliskiren
Review Module Chapter
Ch 20 — Medications Affecting Blood Pressure
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Aliskiren is a direct renin inhibitor (DRI) — antihypertensive:

  • Inhibits renin (the enzyme that initiates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system)
  • ↓ angiotensin I production → ↓ angiotensin II → ↓ vasoconstriction and ↓ aldosterone → ↓ BP
  • Unique mechanism — different point of intervention in RAAS compared to ACE inhibitors and ARBs
  • Onset: 1-2 weeks for full effect; half-life ~24 hours → once-daily dosing

Therapeutic Use

Aliskiren binds with renin to inhibit production of angiotensin I, thus decreasing production of both angiotensin II and aldosterone. Aliskiren is used solely for treating hypertension alone or in combination with other antihypertensives.

Complications

  • Diarrhea: dose-related, occurs most frequently in females and older adult clients
  • Risk for angioedema and rash caused by allergy to the medication
  • Hyperkalemia
  • Hypotension

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Pregnancy — fetal injury/death possible (Cat D in 2nd/3rd trimesters)
  • Concurrent use with ACE inhibitors or ARBs in clients with diabetes or moderate-severe renal impairment (contraindicated — ↑ hyperkalemia, hypotension, renal impairment)
  • Hypersensitivity to aliskiren or history of angioedema
  • Caution: renal artery stenosis (bilateral or in solitary kidney)
  • Caution: hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, volume depletion
  • Caution: severe hepatic impairment

Interactions

  • ACE inhibitors, ARBs in diabetics or those with renal impairment → contraindicated
  • Potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone), K supplements, salt substitutes → hyperkalemia
  • NSAIDs → ↓ antihypertensive effect, ↑ renal impairment
  • Cyclosporine, itraconazole → ↑ aliskiren levels — avoid combination
  • High-fat meals → ↓ absorption by 70% — take consistently with or without food
  • Other antihypertensives → additive hypotension

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • BP at target range (typically < 130/80 for most adults)
  • ↓ symptoms of hypertension (headache, dizziness, blurred vision)
  • No hyperkalemia (K+ < 5.5 mEq/L)
  • Stable renal function (BUN, creatinine)
  • No angioedema or severe hypotension

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral
  • Dose: 150 mg PO daily, may titrate to 300 mg PO daily
  • Take consistently with or without food (high-fat meals ↓ absorption significantly)
  • Take at same time each day
  • Monitor BP, potassium, renal function (BUN, creatinine) at baseline and periodically
  • If a dose is missed, take when remembered unless close to next dose; do not double up
  • Allow 2-4 weeks for full antihypertensive effect

Nursing Interventions

Monitor blood electrolytes, paying close attention to potassium levels, because the client is at risk for hyperkalemia. This is especially important when the client takes ACE inhibitors concurrently, because these medications also raise potassium levels.

Client Education

  • Do not take aliskiren with foods high in fat, which decreases absorption of the medication.
  • Do not take potassium supplements or salt substitutes containing potassium.
  • Clients should not take aliskiren during pregnancy.
  • If a rash or angioedema occurs, discontinue aliskiren and notify the provider.
  • Call 911 if severe manifestations of allergy are present.
Worked Example Digoxin Ch 21 — Cardiac Glycosides and Heart Failure · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Digoxin
Review Module Chapter
Ch 21 — Cardiac Glycosides and Heart Failure
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Digoxin is a cardiac glycoside that:

  • Positive inotrope — increases force of myocardial contraction (inhibits Na+/K+-ATPase → ↑ intracellular calcium)
  • Negative chronotrope — slows heart rate (↑ vagal tone)
  • Negative dromotrope — slows AV node conduction
  • Net effect: ↑ cardiac output, ↑ stroke volume, ↓ heart rate, ↓ AV conduction
  • Narrow therapeutic window: 0.5-2.0 ng/mL (some sources 0.8-2.0)

Therapeutic Use

Digoxin improves the heart's pumping effectiveness and increases cardiac output and stroke volume. It decreases heart rate by slowing depolarization through the SA node, thus allowing more time for the ventricles to fill with blood. Due to these effects, digoxin is used to treat heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and some other tachydysrhythmias.

Complications

The client should monitor for manifestations of digoxin toxicity, which include GI effects (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea), CNS effects (fatigue, weakness), visual effects (yellow-tinged vision, halos around lights, diplopia), heart rate less than 60/ min in adults, or skipped beats when checking the pulse.

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Digoxin toxicity (active or recent)
  • Ventricular fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia
  • Second/third-degree heart block (without pacemaker)
  • Hypokalemia ↑ toxicity risk substantially
  • Hypercalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hypothyroidism
  • Acute MI (caution)
  • Renal impairment — dose-adjust (digoxin renally cleared)
  • Caution: elderly (↓ renal function), pregnancy Cat C

Interactions

  • Thiazide and loop diuretics → cause hypokalemia → ↑ digoxin toxicity
  • Quinidine, verapamil, amiodarone, dronedarone → ↑ digoxin levels
  • Antacids, cholestyramine, kaolin-pectin → ↓ digoxin absorption
  • ACE inhibitors, ARBs → ↑ digoxin levels (renal effect)
  • NSAIDs → ↑ digoxin levels
  • St. John's wort → ↓ digoxin levels
  • Hawthorn, licorice, ginseng → potentiated effects

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Improved cardiac output: ↑ urine output, ↓ peripheral edema, ↓ dyspnea, ↓ fatigue
  • HR within target range (typically 60-100; provider sets parameters)
  • ↓ symptoms of heart failure (clear lungs, ↓ JVD, ↓ S3)
  • For atrial fibrillation: rate control achieved
  • Digoxin level 0.5-2.0 ng/mL
  • No signs of toxicity (nausea, vomiting, visual changes, dysrhythmias)

Medication Administration

  • Routes: oral (most common), IV (rapid digitalization)
  • Adult maintenance dose: 0.125-0.25 mg/day PO
  • Pediatric: weight-based microgram dosing
  • Check apical pulse for full 1 minute BEFORE each dose
  • Hold and notify provider if:
    • Adult HR < 60
    • Children < 70
    • Infants < 90-110
  • IV: infuse slowly over ≥ 5 minutes
  • Monitor: digoxin level (0.5-2.0 ng/mL), K+, Mg++, renal function
  • Antidote: digoxin immune Fab (Digibind)

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor digoxin blood levels periodically during treatment. The expected reference range is 0.5 to 0.8 ng/mL.
  • Monitor blood potassium levels because hypokalemia can cause cardiac dysrhythmias, especially in older adult clients. monitoring ECG is also important to check for dysrhythmias.

Client Education

  • Take oral digoxin at the same time each day. Do not skip a dose or take more than the prescribed dose each day.
  • Monitor for manifestations of toxicity.
  • Report any new prescriptions and to contact provider before taking OTC medications, because digoxin interacts with many other substances.
Worked Example Dopamine (Dose-Dependent Inotrope) Ch 21 — Cardiac Glycosides and Heart Failure · Inotropes section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Dopamine
Review Module Chapter
Ch 21 — Cardiac Glycosides and Heart Failure
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Endogenous catecholamine with DOSE-DEPENDENT receptor effects:

  • Low dose (1–5 mcg/kg/min): dopaminergic receptors → renal/mesenteric vasodilation → increased renal perfusion (“renal dose”; clinical benefit debated)
  • Moderate dose (5–10 mcg/kg/min): beta-1 stimulation → increased contractility, heart rate, cardiac output
  • High dose (> 10 mcg/kg/min): alpha-1 stimulation → vasoconstriction → increased BP and SVR

Therapeutic Use

  • Shock (cardiogenic, septic, hypovolemic after volume repletion)
  • Hypotension unresponsive to fluids
  • Acute heart failure with hypotension
  • Symptomatic bradycardia (alternative to other agents)
  • To improve cardiac output and BP in critically ill

Complications

  • Tachycardia, arrhythmias (ventricular ectopy, tachyarrhythmias)
  • Tissue necrosis from extravasation — vesicant; can cause severe tissue damage (antidote: phentolamine SC around site)
  • Excessive vasoconstriction → reduced peripheral/organ perfusion at high doses
  • Increased myocardial oxygen demand → ischemia
  • Hypertension (high dose)
  • Nausea, vomiting, headache
  • Gangrene of extremities (prolonged high dose)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Pheochromocytoma
  • Uncorrected tachyarrhythmias or ventricular fibrillation
  • Hypovolemia (correct volume FIRST before vasopressors)
  • Caution: occlusive vascular disease, recent MI
  • Requires central line for higher doses (extravasation risk)
  • Sulfite sensitivity (some formulations)

Interactions

  • MAOIs — potentiate effects dramatically (reduce dopamine dose to 1/10)
  • Beta blockers — antagonize beta effects
  • Alpha blockers — antagonize alpha (vasoconstrictor) effects
  • Phenytoin — hypotension and bradycardia
  • TCAs — potentiate cardiovascular effects
  • General anesthetics (halothane) — increased arrhythmia risk

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Improved BP and MAP (target MAP ≥ 65 mmHg typically)
  • Improved cardiac output and tissue perfusion
  • Improved urine output (≥ 0.5 mL/kg/hr)
  • Improved mentation, capillary refill, skin warmth
  • Resolution of shock state
  • Stable or controlled heart rate/rhythm

Medication Administration

  • Route: IV continuous infusion ONLY (via infusion pump)
  • CENTRAL LINE preferred (extravasation = tissue necrosis)
  • Dose titrated to effect: start 2–5 mcg/kg/min, titrate to clinical response
  • Weight-based dosing — verify weight in kg
  • Use a dedicated line; do not mix with alkaline solutions (sodium bicarbonate inactivates dopamine)
  • Protect from light; discard if discolored (pink/yellow/brown)
  • Wean gradually — do not stop abruptly (rebound hypotension)

Nursing Interventions

  • Continuous cardiac and BP monitoring (arterial line ideal); titrate to MAP/BP goal
  • Hourly (or more frequent) urine output via indwelling catheter
  • Verify central line placement; assess IV site frequently for extravasation
  • Have phentolamine available for extravasation (inject SC around site to reverse vasoconstriction)
  • Monitor for arrhythmias, chest pain (increased O2 demand)
  • Assess perfusion: extremities (color, temp, pulses), capillary refill, mentation
  • Correct hypovolemia before/during vasopressor use
  • Use infusion pump; double-check calculations (high-alert medication; independent double-check)
  • Wean slowly under monitoring

Client Education

  • (Critical care setting; family education) Dopamine supports blood pressure and heart function during a serious illness
  • Continuous monitoring of heart rhythm, blood pressure, and urine output is needed
  • The IV site is checked frequently because the medication can damage tissue if it leaks
  • Report any pain, burning, or swelling at the IV site immediately
  • The medication will be slowly decreased as the condition improves
  • Frequent vital signs and blood draws are expected in this setting
Worked Example Dobutamine Ch 21 — Cardiac Glycosides and Heart Failure · Inotropes section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Dobutamine
Review Module Chapter
Ch 21 — Cardiac Glycosides and Heart Failure
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Selective beta-1 adrenergic agonist (synthetic catecholamine)
  • Increases myocardial contractility (positive inotropy) and cardiac output
  • Minimal effect on heart rate at therapeutic doses (less tachycardia than dopamine)
  • Mild vasodilation (beta-2) → reduced afterload, which can aid failing heart
  • Does NOT significantly raise BP (not a vasopressor)

Therapeutic Use

  • Acute decompensated heart failure — short-term improvement of cardiac output
  • Cardiogenic shock (often with a vasopressor)
  • Low cardiac output states
  • Cardiac stress testing (pharmacologic stress echo)
  • Bridge to definitive therapy (transplant, device)

Complications

  • Tachycardia, arrhythmias (atrial and ventricular)
  • Increased myocardial oxygen demand → ischemia/angina
  • Hypotension (from vasodilation, especially if hypovolemic)
  • Hypertension (less common)
  • Headache, nausea, tremor
  • Hypokalemia (intracellular potassium shift)
  • Tolerance with prolonged infusion (receptor downregulation)
  • Increased mortality with long-term continuous use

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to dobutamine or sulfites
  • Idiopathic hypertrophic subaortic stenosis (IHSS/HOCM) — worsens obstruction
  • Uncorrected hypovolemia (correct first)
  • Severe aortic stenosis (caution)
  • Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response (may accelerate rate)
  • Caution: recent MI, active ischemia

Interactions

  • Beta blockers — antagonize dobutamine’s effects
  • MAOIs — potentiate effects
  • TCAs — enhanced cardiovascular effects
  • General anesthetics (halothane) — arrhythmia risk
  • Nitroprusside — synergistic increase in cardiac output (sometimes used together)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Improved cardiac output and cardiac index
  • Improved tissue perfusion (urine output, mentation, skin warmth, capillary refill)
  • Reduced symptoms of heart failure (dyspnea)
  • Stable or improved hemodynamics without excessive tachycardia
  • No significant arrhythmias or ischemia

Medication Administration

  • Route: IV continuous infusion via pump
  • Dose: 2–20 mcg/kg/min, titrated to hemodynamic response
  • Weight-based — verify kg
  • Central line preferred (peripheral acceptable; less vesicant than dopamine but still caution)
  • Do not mix with sodium bicarbonate or alkaline solutions
  • May discolor slightly (pink) from oxidation — does not indicate loss of potency, but follow facility policy
  • Wean gradually

Nursing Interventions

  • Continuous cardiac monitoring (rhythm), BP (arterial line ideal), hemodynamics
  • Monitor heart rate — report increase > 10% (increased O2 demand)
  • Hourly urine output; assess perfusion
  • Monitor potassium (hypokalemia risk) and for arrhythmias
  • Assess for chest pain/ischemia
  • Ensure adequate volume status before starting
  • Use infusion pump; high-alert medication (independent double-check)
  • Assess IV site; wean slowly under monitoring

Client Education

  • (Critical care; family education) Dobutamine helps the heart pump more effectively during acute heart failure
  • Continuous heart and blood pressure monitoring is necessary
  • Report chest pain, palpitations, or feeling your heart race
  • The medication is given temporarily and weaned as the heart improves
  • Frequent vital signs and lab draws are part of close monitoring
  • For stress test use: the medication briefly stresses the heart to evaluate function
Worked Example Digoxin Toxicity Ch 21 — Cardiac Glycosides and Heart Failure · HF section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Digoxin Toxicity

Defining Characteristics

Digoxin toxicity is a potentially life-threatening condition resulting from excessive digoxin effect, due to digoxin’s narrow therapeutic index.

  • Therapeutic serum level: 0.5–2.0 ng/mL (some target 0.5–0.8 for HF)
  • Toxicity often > 2.0 ng/mL, but can occur within “therapeutic” range if hypokalemic

Early signs: anorexia, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, weakness.
Visual: blurred vision, yellow-green halos around lights (classic), photophobia.
Cardiac: bradycardia, any new dysrhythmia (PVCs, AV block, atrial tachycardia with block, ventricular dysrhythmias).
Neuro: confusion, especially in older adults.

Antecedents

  • Hypokalemia (the most important precipitant) — often from concurrent diuretics; low K+ increases digoxin binding to cardiac cells
  • Hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia
  • Renal impairment (digoxin is renally cleared) — accumulation
  • Older age (reduced clearance, lower lean mass)
  • Dehydration
  • Drug interactions: amiodarone, verapamil, quinidine, spironolactone (raise digoxin levels)
  • Dosing errors (narrow margin)
  • Hypothyroidism

Negative Consequences

  • Life-threatening dysrhythmias — ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, complete heart block, asystole
  • Cardiac arrest and death
  • Falls (from confusion, weakness, bradycardia)
  • Hospitalization, ICU admission
  • In severe overdose: severe hyperkalemia (efflux of potassium from cells) paradoxically signals poor prognosis

Related Concepts

Narrow therapeutic index, therapeutic drug monitoring, hypokalemia, loop/thiazide diuretics, renal clearance, digoxin immune Fab (DigiFab/Digibind), apical pulse assessment, drug interactions (amiodarone, verapamil, quinidine), heart failure, atrial fibrillation.

Exemplars

  • Classic case: Older adult on digoxin + furosemide reports nausea, sees “yellow halos,” HR 48. Check digoxin level AND potassium — likely hypokalemia-potentiated toxicity.
  • Prevention: Check apical pulse for full 60 seconds before EVERY dose; HOLD if < 60 bpm (adults) and notify provider. Monitor potassium, magnesium, renal function, and digoxin levels.
  • Hold parameters: apical HR < 60 (adults), < 70 (children), < 90–110 (infants).
  • Treatment of toxicity:
    • Stop digoxin
    • Correct electrolytes (potassium if low — cautiously; magnesium)
    • Continuous cardiac monitoring
    • Treat dysrhythmias (atropine for bradycardia; antiarrhythmics for ventricular)
    • Digoxin immune Fab (DigiFab) for severe toxicity, life-threatening dysrhythmias, or severe hyperkalemia
  • Drug interaction example: starting amiodarone in a digoxin patient can raise digoxin levels by 50–100% — reduce digoxin dose and monitor.
  • Patient teaching: take pulse before dose; report nausea, visual changes, palpitations; maintain consistent potassium intake; keep lab appointments; report all new medications.
Worked Example Nitroglycerin Ch 22 — Angina · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Oral
Review Module Chapter
Ch 22 — Angina
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Nitroglycerin is an organic nitrate vasodilator:

  • Converted to nitric oxide (NO) in vascular smooth muscle
  • NO activates guanylate cyclase → ↑ cGMP → smooth muscle relaxation → vasodilation
  • Effects:
    • Primarily venous dilation at low doses → ↓ preload → ↓ myocardial O₂ demand
    • Arterial dilation at higher doses → ↓ afterload
    • Coronary artery dilation → ↑ O₂ supply to ischemic myocardium
  • Onset: sublingual 1-3 min, IV immediate, transdermal 30 min
  • Tolerance develops with continuous exposure — need nitrate-free interval (10-12 hr daily)

Therapeutic Use

Sublingual tablets or spray are used to treat an angina attack after it begins, while the oral tablets, transdermal patch, and transdermal ointment are used for prevention of angina. The capsules and transdermal forms have a slower onset and longer duration of action than the sublingual forms. Sublingual nitroglycerin begins working within 2 min, but the duration of action is only 30 min. Oral forms are taken several times daily, but duration of action is several hours.

Complications

Major adverse effects include headache, dizziness caused by hypotension, and rebound tachycardia.
