Contraindications/Precautions

  • Concurrent PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil) — severe hypotension, MI, death
  • Concurrent riociguat
  • Severe hypotension or hypovolemia
  • Increased intracranial pressure
  • Severe anemia
  • Constrictive pericarditis, cardiac tamponade
  • Right ventricular MI (preload-dependent)
  • Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (worsens obstruction)
  • Hypersensitivity to nitrates

Interactions

  • Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (sildenafil/Viagra, tadalafil/Cialis, vardenafil/Levitra) — life-threatening hypotension; wait 24 hours after sildenafil/vardenafil and 48 hours after tadalafil before nitroglycerin
  • Antihypertensives, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers → additive hypotension
  • Alcohol → additive hypotension
  • TCAs, phenothiazines → additive hypotension
  • Heparin → ↓ heparin effect with concurrent IV NTG

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Acute angina: chest pain relieved within 5 minutes of sublingual dose
  • Chronic angina prevention: ↓ frequency and severity of attacks
  • ↑ exercise tolerance
  • No serious hypotension (SBP > 90, no orthostatic symptoms)
  • No medication overuse (using > 3x in 15 min indicates emergency)
  • No serious headaches (usually improves with continued use)

Medication Administration

  • Routes: sublingual (tablet, spray), transdermal (patch, ointment), oral SR, IV, buccal, translingual
  • Acute angina (sublingual):
    • Sit or lie down (hypotension risk)
    • 1 tablet under tongue OR 1 spray; do NOT swallow tablet
    • If chest pain not relieved in 5 min, call 911, then may repeat dose; max 3 doses in 15 min
    • Tingling/burning under tongue indicates potency
  • Transdermal patch:
    • Apply to clean, dry, non-hairy chest or upper arm
    • Rotate sites daily
    • Remove for 10-12 hours daily (typically overnight) to prevent tolerance
  • Sublingual tablet storage: keep in original dark glass container; replace every 6 months; do NOT carry in pocket near body heat (degrades)

Nursing Interventions

  • Teach the client that the oral sustained-release form of nitroglycerin should not be used to abort an angina attack. In addition, it should be taken on an empty stomach with at least 8 oz of water and must be swallowed whole.
  • Teach the client not to perform activities that require alertness if dizziness is experienced while taking oral nitroglycerin.
  • The client should inform the provider if headaches are persistent because the dose of nitroglycerin might need to be decreased.
  • The client should inform the provider if tachycardia occurs, because a beta-adrenergic blocker or other medication can be prescribed to slow the pulse rate.

Client Education

  • Report: chest pain not relieved by 1 SL dose after 5 minutes (CALL 911), severe headache, fainting, blurred vision
  • For acute chest pain (SL tablet/spray):
    1. Sit or lie down (prevent dizziness/falling)
    2. Place 1 tablet under tongue (or 1 spray) — let it dissolve, do not swallow
    3. If chest pain not relieved in 5 minutes, CALL 911
    4. While waiting, may take up to 2 more doses 5 minutes apart (3 total in 15 minutes)
    5. Tingling/burning under tongue indicates the drug is still potent
  • Carry sublingual tablets/spray AT ALL TIMES
  • Store SL tablets in original dark glass bottle; replace every 6 months; do NOT carry in pocket near body (heat degrades)
  • For transdermal patch: apply to clean, dry, hairless skin (chest, upper arm); rotate sites daily; remove for 10-12 hours daily (typically overnight) to prevent tolerance
  • Take oral sustained-release tablets on empty stomach with full glass of water; swallow whole
  • DO NOT take with sildenafil (Viagra), tadalafil (Cialis), or vardenafil (Levitra) — fatal hypotension. Wait 24 hr after sildenafil/vardenafil; 48 hr after tadalafil
  • Avoid alcohol (additive hypotension)
  • Rise slowly to prevent dizziness
  • Headache is common; usually improves; treat with acetaminophen
  • Remove patches before defibrillation, MRI, or cardioversion — fire/burn hazard
Worked Example Angina Pectoris Ch 22 — Angina · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Angina Pectoris
Review Module Chapter
Ch 22 — Angina

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Angina Pectoris — chest pain or discomfort resulting from myocardial ischemia (oxygen demand exceeds supply), usually due to coronary artery disease.

Types:

  • Stable (exertional) angina: predictable; triggered by exertion/stress; relieved by rest or nitroglycerin; < 15 min
  • Unstable angina: new, worsening, or at rest; medical emergency; part of acute coronary syndrome (ACS); NOT relieved predictably
  • Variant (Prinzmetal) angina: coronary vasospasm; often at rest, cyclical; responds to calcium channel blockers

Unstable angina vs MI: angina has no/minimal troponin elevation; MI has myocardial necrosis (elevated troponin).

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Atherosclerosis narrows coronary arteries → reduced blood flow
  • When myocardial oxygen demand (exertion, stress, tachycardia) exceeds supply → ischemia → anaerobic metabolism → lactic acid → pain
  • Stable: fixed plaque; ischemia only with increased demand
  • Unstable: plaque rupture → partial thrombus → ischemia at rest (impending MI)
  • Variant: coronary artery spasm (may have minimal atherosclerosis)
  • Risk factors: smoking, HTN, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, obesity, family history, sedentary lifestyle

Expected Findings

Symptoms:

  • Substernal chest pain/pressure (“squeezing,” “tightness,” “elephant on chest”)
  • Radiation to left arm, jaw, neck, back, shoulder
  • Dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea
  • Anxiety, sense of doom
  • Atypical presentations (women, older adults, diabetics): fatigue, indigestion, jaw/back pain, dyspnea without chest pain

Diagnostic:

  • 12-lead EKG: ST depression or T-wave inversion (ischemia); transient ST elevation (variant)
  • Cardiac biomarkers (troponin) — to differentiate from MI
  • Stress testing (exercise or pharmacologic)
  • Coronary angiography (definitive for CAD extent)
  • Lipid panel, fasting glucose, CBC

Nursing Care

Acute angina episode:

  • Stop activity, rest, sit or lie down
  • Administer sublingual nitroglycerin (up to 3 doses, 5 min apart)
  • Oxygen if hypoxic (SpO2 < 90%)
  • 12-lead EKG; assess pain (PQRST); vital signs
  • If pain unrelieved after first NTG or new/worsening: call 911 / activate emergency response (possible ACS)
  • Aspirin (chewed) for suspected ACS

Chronic pharmacotherapy:

  • Nitrates (nitroglycerin) — acute relief and prophylaxis (long-acting)
  • Beta blockers — reduce HR and contractility → reduced O2 demand (first-line chronic)
  • Calcium channel blockers — vasodilation; first-line for variant angina
  • Ranolazine — chronic stable angina (adjunct)
  • Antiplatelet (aspirin, clopidogrel) — prevent thrombosis
  • Statins — plaque stabilization, lipid lowering
  • ACE inhibitors if HTN/diabetes/HF

Revascularization: PCI (stent) or CABG for significant CAD.

Client Education

  • Recognize angina vs emergency: stable pattern relieved by rest/NTG is expected; new, worsening, prolonged, or rest pain = call 911
  • Sublingual NTG protocol: 1 tablet under tongue; if no relief in 5 min, call 911, may take up to 3 doses 5 min apart
  • Carry NTG at all times; store in original dark glass container; replace every 6 months
  • Take NTG prophylactically before known triggers (exertion, sex, cold exposure)
  • Lifestyle: smoking cessation, heart-healthy diet, regular exercise (as tolerated), weight management, stress reduction
  • Control comorbidities: HTN, diabetes, hyperlipidemia
  • Take aspirin and statins as prescribed
  • Recognize MI symptoms; act FAST
  • Cardiac rehabilitation participation
  • Avoid PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil) with nitrates (fatal hypotension)
Worked Example Ranolazine (Ranexa) Ch 22 — Angina · Other section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Ranolazine (Ranexa)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 22 — Angina
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Anti-anginal — inhibits the late sodium current in cardiac cells, reducing intracellular calcium overload
  • Improves myocardial oxygen efficiency WITHOUT significantly affecting heart rate or blood pressure
  • Mechanism distinct from nitrates, beta blockers, CCBs (no hemodynamic effect)

Therapeutic Use

  • Chronic stable angina — usually as add-on when other anti-anginals are inadequate
  • Not for acute angina attacks (no rapid effect)
  • Useful when beta blockers/CCBs are limited by low HR or BP

Complications

  • QT prolongation — dose-dependent; risk of torsades de pointes (especially with other QT-prolonging drugs)
  • Dizziness, headache
  • Constipation, nausea
  • Peripheral edema
  • Renal failure can increase levels (caution in severe renal impairment)
  • Confusion, hallucinations (rare, especially older adults)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hepatic impairment (cirrhosis) — contraindicated
  • Concurrent strong CYP3A4 inhibitors or inducers
  • Pre-existing QT prolongation or concurrent QT-prolonging drugs
  • Severe renal impairment (caution)
  • Pregnancy/lactation — limited data

Interactions

  • Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir, grapefruit juice) — raise ranolazine levels (avoid)
  • CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin) — reduce effectiveness
  • QT-prolonging drugs (amiodarone, sotalol, certain antipsychotics, fluoroquinolones) — additive torsades risk
  • Increases levels of: digoxin, simvastatin (limit simvastatin dose), metformin
  • Diltiazem, verapamil (CYP3A4 inhibition) — increase ranolazine

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Reduced frequency of angina episodes
  • Increased exercise tolerance
  • Reduced use of short-acting nitroglycerin
  • No prolonged QT or torsades
  • Tolerable side effects

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral, extended-release tablets
  • Dose: 500 mg PO BID, may increase to 1,000 mg BID
  • Swallow whole — do not crush, chew, or break
  • Take with or without food (consistent)
  • Avoid grapefruit juice
  • Not for acute attacks — this is a maintenance medication

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline and periodic EKG (QT interval), renal function, hepatic function
  • Comprehensive medication reconciliation for CYP3A4 and QT-prolonging interactions
  • Monitor for dizziness, palpitations, syncope
  • Assess angina frequency and exercise tolerance
  • Educate that this does NOT replace rescue nitroglycerin
  • Monitor digoxin level if co-prescribed (ranolazine raises it)
  • Limit simvastatin dose if co-prescribed

Client Education

  • This medication PREVENTS angina; it does NOT relieve an acute attack — continue to carry rescue nitroglycerin
  • Swallow tablets whole; do not crush or chew
  • Take regularly twice daily
  • Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice
  • Report palpitations, fainting, or irregular heartbeat (QT effects)
  • Tell all providers about this medication (many interactions)
  • Increase fluids and fiber for constipation
  • Rise slowly if dizzy
  • Do not stop abruptly without provider guidance
  • Keep follow-up appointments for EKG monitoring
Worked Example Sublingual Nitroglycerin Administration Ch 22 — Angina · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill
Sublingual Nitroglycerin Administration
Review Module Chapter
Ch 22 — Angina

Description of Skill

Administration of sublingual nitroglycerin (SL NTG) for acute angina — a fast-acting vasodilator that relieves anginal chest pain by reducing preload (venodilation) and improving coronary perfusion.

The 3-dose protocol and recognizing when to activate emergency response are critical patient-safety skills. Onset is 1–3 minutes; tablet should produce a tingling/fizzing sensation under the tongue (indicates potency).

Indications

  • Acute anginal chest pain (stable angina)
  • Prophylaxis before known triggers (exertion, emotional stress, cold, sexual activity)
  • Acute coronary syndrome management (in monitored settings)
  • Acute hypertensive episodes with chest pain (clinical settings)

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre:

  • Assess chest pain (PQRST: provocation, quality, radiation, severity, timing)
  • Obtain baseline vital signs — check BP (hold if SBP < 90 mmHg); heart rate
  • 12-lead EKG if in clinical setting
  • Verify NO PDE5 inhibitor use (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil within 24–48 hr) — fatal hypotension risk
  • Confirm tablet potency: should be stored in original dark glass bottle, replaced every 6 months

Intra (3-dose protocol):

  1. Have client sit or lie down (prevents falls from hypotension)
  2. Place ONE tablet under the tongue; do not swallow; let dissolve
  3. Client should feel tingling/fizzing (indicates potency)
  4. Wait 5 minutes; reassess pain and BP
  5. If pain unrelieved after FIRST dose — call 911 / activate EMS (current AHA guidance), then may give up to 2 more doses 5 min apart (max 3 doses total)
  6. Recheck BP before each subsequent dose (hold if SBP < 90)
  7. Monitor continuously for hypotension

Post:

  • Document pain relief, number of doses, vital signs response, EKG changes
  • Reassess and continue monitoring
  • If relieved: identify trigger; reinforce teaching
  • If unrelieved: prepare for ACS workup (troponin, continued monitoring, possible PCI)
  • Wear gloves if applying topical/paste forms (absorption through skin)

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Chest pain relieved (ideally within 5 min of first dose for stable angina)
  • Stable hemodynamics; no symptomatic hypotension
  • Client/family demonstrate correct self-administration technique and 3-dose protocol
  • Client knows when to call 911
  • Appropriate escalation to emergency care if unrelieved

Potential Complications

  • Hypotension — can cause dizziness, syncope, falls; worse if volume-depleted or with other vasodilators
  • Severe/fatal hypotension with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil) — absolute contraindication
  • Reflex tachycardia
  • Headache (very common — from vasodilation; treat with acetaminophen)
  • Tolerance with continuous use (need nitrate-free interval for long-acting forms)
  • Flushing, dizziness
  • Masking an MI — delaying emergency care if relying solely on NTG for unrelieved pain
  • Loss of potency if improperly stored (no tingling = possibly expired/inactive)
Worked Example Verapamil Ch 23 — Medications Affecting Cardiac Rhythm · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Verapamil
Review Module Chapter
Ch 23 — Medications Affecting Cardiac Rhythm
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Verapamil is a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that blocks L-type calcium channels in:

  • Myocardium — negative inotrope (↓ contractility)
  • SA and AV nodes — negative chronotrope (↓ HR) and negative dromotrope (↓ AV conduction)
  • Vascular smooth muscle — vasodilation (mainly arterial)

Net effects: ↓ HR, ↓ contractility, ↓ AV conduction, ↓ BP, ↓ myocardial O₂ demand → useful for angina, dysrhythmias, HTN.

Therapeutic Use

Verapamil is a calcium channel blocker and a class IV antidysrhythmic medication that decreases heart rate, slows conduction through both the SA and AV nodes, and decreases force of contraction of the heart. It is used to treat supraventricular tachycardia (SVT).

Complications

  • Bradycardia
  • Hypotension
  • Heart failure
  • Constipation

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Severe hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg)
  • Cardiogenic shock
  • Second/third-degree AV block (without pacemaker)
  • Sick sinus syndrome
  • Severe heart failure with ↓ EF (negative inotrope worsens HF)
  • Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome with atrial fib (paradoxical ventricular response)
  • Concurrent IV beta-blocker (additive cardiac depression)
  • Hepatic impairment — dose adjust
  • Pregnancy Cat C

Interactions

  • Beta-blockers → additive bradycardia, AV block, HF → AVOID combination (esp. IV)
  • Digoxin → ↑ digoxin levels → toxicity risk
  • Statins (esp. simvastatin) → ↑ statin levels → rhabdomyolysis risk
  • Grapefruit juice → ↑ verapamil levels (CYP3A4 inhibition)
  • Amiodarone → ↑ bradycardia, AV block
  • Antihypertensives → additive hypotension
  • Carbamazepine → ↑ carbamazepine levels (toxicity)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Angina: ↓ frequency and severity of chest pain, ↑ exercise tolerance
  • HTN: BP within target range
  • SVT: conversion to sinus rhythm; ↓ ventricular rate in afib/aflutter
  • HR within target (typically 60-100)
  • No signs of HF worsening (no new dyspnea, edema, weight gain)

Medication Administration

  • Routes: oral (immediate or sustained release), IV (for acute dysrhythmias)
  • Adult oral dose: 80-120 mg PO TID (immediate); 120-240 mg PO daily (SR)
  • IV: 5-10 mg slow IV push over 2 min for SVT (cardiac monitoring required)
  • Take with food to ↓ GI upset
  • Do NOT crush or split SR formulations
  • Avoid grapefruit juice
  • Monitor BP and HR before each dose; hold for HR < 60 or SBP < 90

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor both kidney and liver function because the medication dosage might need to be lowered if either kidney or liver impairment are present.
  • Monitor blood pressure and pulse.
  • Monitor periodic ECG testing for dysrhythmias and for improvement of SVT.
  • Assess for manifestations of heart failure, such as dyspnea and crackles in the lungs.
  • Question the client about dizziness, which can occur due to hypotension.
  • Teach the client to move slowly from lying to sitting or standing and to avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until effects of verapamil are known.

Client Education

  • Report immediately: dizziness, fainting, slow pulse (< 60), worsening shortness of breath, swelling, palpitations
  • Take pulse before each dose; hold and call provider if HR < 60
  • Rise slowly to prevent orthostatic hypotension
  • Constipation is common — increase fiber and fluids, stay active
  • Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice
  • Do not crush or split sustained-release tablets
  • Take with food
  • Tell all providers (esp. before any new beta-blocker)
Worked Example Atorvastatin Ch 24 — Antilipemic Agents · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Atorvastatin
Review Module Chapter
Ch 24 — Antilipemic Agents
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Atorvastatin is an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (statin) that:

  • Inhibits the rate-limiting enzyme in hepatic cholesterol synthesis
  • ↓ LDL ("bad" cholesterol) — primary effect, 30-60% reduction
  • ↓ triglycerides modestly
  • ↑ HDL ("good" cholesterol) slightly
  • Has pleiotropic effects: plaque stabilization, anti-inflammatory, improved endothelial function
  • Reduces cardiovascular events and mortality in at-risk clients

Therapeutic Use

Atorvastatin decreases LDL and triglycerides, and elevates hDL. It reduces the risk for cardiovascular events (myocardial infarction) and also provides secondary prevention in clients who have had a cardiovascular event. In clients who have diabetes mellitus and hypertension, atorvastatin can reduce mortality by controlling cholesterol levels.

Complications

  • Muscle pain/tenderness (myopathy)
  • Liver toxicity with findings (jaundice, upper abdominal pain, anorexia, and nausea)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Active liver disease or unexplained persistent ↑ liver enzymes
  • Pregnancy Category X — fetal harm (cholesterol needed for fetal development)
  • Breastfeeding
  • Caution: history of liver disease, heavy alcohol use, renal impairment, hypothyroidism (treat first), elderly
  • Caution with concurrent fibrates, niacin, cyclosporine, certain antifungals/antibiotics (↑ rhabdomyolysis risk)

Interactions

  • Grapefruit juice → ↑ statin levels → ↑ rhabdomyolysis risk (esp. simvastatin, atorvastatin)
  • Fibrates (gemfibrozil) → ↑ myopathy/rhabdomyolysis
  • Niacin (high-dose) → ↑ myopathy
  • Cyclosporine, erythromycin, clarithromycin, itraconazole, ketoconazole → ↑ statin levels
  • Warfarin → ↑ INR (monitor closely)
  • Digoxin → ↑ digoxin levels (atorvastatin specifically)
  • St. John's wort → ↓ statin effect

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • LDL reduction to target (varies by ASCVD risk; commonly < 100, or < 70 if high risk)
  • ↓ total cholesterol and triglycerides
  • ↑ or stable HDL
  • No new cardiovascular events (MI, stroke, revascularization)
  • No hepatotoxicity (stable LFTs)
  • No myopathy (no muscle pain or weakness, CK within normal)

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral, once daily
  • Dose: 10-80 mg PO daily
  • Can be taken any time of day (atorvastatin has long half-life; unlike simvastatin which is bedtime)
  • Take with or without food
  • Avoid grapefruit juice
  • Baseline and periodic monitoring:
    • LFTs (ALT/AST) at baseline, 12 weeks, then annually
    • CK if muscle symptoms develop
    • Lipid panel q4-12 weeks initially, then annually

Nursing Interventions

Monitor baseline and periodic cholesterol levels (including LDL, hDL, and triglycerides), creatine kinase levels for myopathy, and liver function tests for liver toxicity.

Client Education

  • Perform additional ways to help decrease cholesterol and improve health (exercise, low-fat diet, weight control, and smoking cessation).
  • Take atorvastatin in the evening without regard to meals. (Antilipemic agents are given in the evening because cholesterol is mostly synthesized during the night.)
Worked Example Cholestyramine (Bile-Acid Sequestrant) Ch 24 — Antilipemic Agents · Other section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Cholestyramine (Questran)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 24 — Antilipemic Agents
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Bile-acid sequestrant — binds bile acids in the intestine, forming an insoluble complex excreted in feces
  • The liver then uses cholesterol to make more bile acids → lowers LDL cholesterol
  • Not absorbed systemically (acts within the GI tract)
  • Lowers LDL ~15–30%; may slightly raise triglycerides

Therapeutic Use

  • Hypercholesterolemia (elevated LDL) — adjunct to statins or when statins not tolerated
  • Pruritus from bile acid accumulation (partial biliary obstruction, cholestasis)
  • Off-label: bile acid diarrhea, digoxin toxicity (binds digoxin), C. difficile (binds toxin)

Complications

  • Constipation (most common) — can be severe; fecal impaction
  • Bloating, flatulence, abdominal discomfort, nausea
  • Malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) with long-term use
  • Decreased absorption of many other medications
  • Hyperchloremic acidosis (high doses, prolonged)
  • May increase triglycerides
  • GI obstruction (rare, with pre-existing motility issues)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Complete biliary obstruction (no bile to bind)
  • Hypersensitivity
  • Severe constipation; bowel obstruction history
  • Hypertriglyceridemia > 400 mg/dL (can worsen)
  • Phenylketonuria (some formulations contain aspartame)
  • Caution: pre-existing GI disorders, vitamin deficiencies

Interactions

  • Binds and reduces absorption of MANY drugs: warfarin, digoxin, thyroid hormones (levothyroxine), thiazides, statins, some antibiotics, fat-soluble vitamins
  • KEY RULE: take other medications 1 hour BEFORE or 4–6 hours AFTER cholestyramine
  • Reduces absorption of fat-soluble vitamins — may need supplementation
  • Can affect oral contraceptive absorption

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Reduced LDL cholesterol on lipid panel
  • Reduced pruritus (cholestasis indication)
  • No severe constipation or GI obstruction
  • Adequate fat-soluble vitamin levels
  • No interference with other medication effectiveness (proper timing)

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral powder (mixed with fluid) or tablets
  • NEVER take dry — mix powder thoroughly with 4–8 oz water, juice, or other fluid; let stand 1–2 min
  • Take with meals
  • Usual dose: 4 g 1–2 times daily, titrate
  • Separate other medications: 1 hr before OR 4–6 hr after
  • Increase fluids and fiber to prevent constipation

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline and periodic lipid panel
  • Assess bowel function; implement constipation prevention (fluids, fiber, activity)
  • Carefully time other medications (1 hr before/4–6 hr after); review full medication list
  • Monitor for fat-soluble vitamin deficiency with long-term use
  • Monitor INR if on warfarin (absorption affected)
  • Monitor digoxin and thyroid levels if co-prescribed
  • Educate on proper mixing (never take dry — esophageal obstruction/aspiration risk)

Client Education

  • Always mix powder with liquid — never take dry (choking/obstruction risk)
  • Mix with 4–8 oz water/juice; stir well; can mix with applesauce or soup
  • Take other medications 1 hour before or 4–6 hours after cholestyramine
  • Increase fluids and dietary fiber to prevent constipation
  • Take with meals
  • Continue low-fat, low-cholesterol diet
  • May need fat-soluble vitamin supplements (A, D, E, K) — discuss with provider
  • Report severe constipation, abdominal pain, unusual bleeding (vitamin K), or no bowel movement
  • Keep lab appointments for lipid monitoring
Worked Example Ezetimibe (Zetia) Ch 24 — Antilipemic Agents · Other section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Ezetimibe (Zetia)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 24 — Antilipemic Agents
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Cholesterol absorption inhibitor — blocks the NPC1L1 transporter in the small intestine brush border
  • Reduces absorption of dietary and biliary cholesterol → lowers LDL
  • Complementary to statins (different mechanism) — additive LDL lowering
  • Lowers LDL ~18% as monotherapy; more when combined with a statin

Therapeutic Use

  • Hypercholesterolemia — adjunct to statin or when statin alone is insufficient/not tolerated
  • Homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (with statin)
  • Homozygous sitosterolemia
  • Combination product with simvastatin (Vytorin)

Complications

  • Generally well-tolerated
  • Diarrhea, abdominal pain
  • Fatigue
  • Myopathy/rhabdomyolysis (rare; increased when combined with statins)
  • Hepatotoxicity (rare; transaminase elevations, especially with statins)
  • Arthralgia, back pain
  • Hypersensitivity (angioedema, rash — rare)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to ezetimibe
  • Active liver disease or unexplained persistent transaminase elevation (when combined with a statin)
  • Moderate-severe hepatic impairment (not recommended)
  • Pregnancy/lactation — avoid (especially with statin)
  • Caution combining with fibrates (gallstone risk)

Interactions

  • Statins — additive LDL lowering (intended); slightly increased myopathy/hepatotoxicity risk
  • Bile-acid sequestrants (cholestyramine) — reduce ezetimibe absorption; take ezetimibe ≥ 2 hr before or ≥ 4 hr after
  • Fibrates (gemfibrozil) — increase ezetimibe levels and gallstone risk
  • Cyclosporine — increases ezetimibe levels (monitor)
  • Warfarin — monitor INR

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Reduced LDL cholesterol on lipid panel
  • Achievement of LDL goal (especially combined with statin)
  • No myopathy or hepatotoxicity
  • Tolerable side effects
  • Adherence to therapy and lifestyle modifications

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral tablet
  • Dose: 10 mg PO once daily
  • Take with or without food, same time daily
  • Can be taken with a statin (often combined)
  • If on a bile-acid sequestrant: take ezetimibe ≥ 2 hr before or ≥ 4 hr after

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline and periodic lipid panel, LFTs (especially if combined with statin)
  • Assess for muscle pain, weakness, tenderness (myopathy, especially with statin)
  • Educate on timing with bile-acid sequestrants
  • Reinforce lifestyle measures (diet, exercise)
  • Monitor INR if on warfarin
  • Assess adherence at follow-up

Client Education

  • Take once daily at the same time
  • Continue heart-healthy, low-cholesterol diet and exercise
  • Report unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness (especially with a statin)
  • Report yellowing of skin/eyes, dark urine, persistent fatigue (liver)
  • If taking cholestyramine: separate doses (ezetimibe 2 hr before or 4 hr after)
  • Do not stop without consulting provider
  • Keep lab appointments for cholesterol and liver monitoring
  • Inform provider if pregnant or planning pregnancy (especially with statin)
Worked Example Hyperlipidemia / Dyslipidemia Ch 24 — Antilipemic Agents · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Hyperlipidemia / Dyslipidemia
Review Module Chapter
Ch 24 — Antilipemic Agents

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Hyperlipidemia / Dyslipidemia — abnormal levels of lipids (cholesterol, triglycerides) in the blood, a major modifiable risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD).

Lipid components:

  • LDL (“bad”): primary target; optimal < 100 mg/dL (< 70 for high risk)
  • HDL (“good”): protective; desirable ≥ 60 mg/dL; low < 40 (men) / < 50 (women)
  • Triglycerides: normal < 150 mg/dL; very high > 500 (pancreatitis risk)
  • Total cholesterol: desirable < 200 mg/dL

Often asymptomatic; detected on screening lipid panel. May be primary (genetic, e.g., familial hypercholesterolemia) or secondary (diet, diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, medications).

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Elevated LDL deposits cholesterol in arterial walls → atherosclerotic plaque formation
  • Plaque narrows arteries → reduced perfusion (CAD, PAD, cerebrovascular disease)
  • Plaque rupture → thrombosis → MI, stroke
  • Low HDL reduces reverse cholesterol transport (removal from tissues)
  • High triglycerides contribute to atherogenesis; very high levels → pancreatitis
  • Genetic factors (LDL receptor defects), diet (saturated/trans fats), obesity, sedentary lifestyle, diabetes, metabolic syndrome

Expected Findings

Usually asymptomatic. With severe or familial forms:

  • Xanthomas — lipid deposits in skin/tendons
  • Xanthelasma — yellow plaques on eyelids
  • Corneal arcus — gray ring around cornea (premature in young = familial)

Signs of complications:

  • Angina, MI (CAD)
  • Claudication (PAD)
  • TIA/stroke symptoms
  • Acute pancreatitis (very high triglycerides)

Diagnostic:

  • Fasting lipid panel (9–12 hr fast): total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides
  • ASCVD risk calculator (10-year risk)
  • Secondary cause workup: glucose/A1c, TSH, liver/renal function
  • Consider coronary artery calcium score for risk refinement

Nursing Care

Statin therapy (first-line) based on ASCVD risk:

  • High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 40–80 mg, rosuvastatin 20–40 mg): clinical ASCVD, LDL ≥ 190, diabetes 40–75 yr with high risk, 10-yr risk ≥ 20%
  • Moderate-intensity statin: diabetes, intermediate risk

Add-on / alternative agents:

  • Ezetimibe — add if LDL goal not met on max statin
  • PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab) — injectable; for familial or refractory
  • Bile-acid sequestrants (cholestyramine)
  • Fibrates (gemfibrozil, fenofibrate) — primarily for high triglycerides
  • Omega-3 fatty acids / icosapent ethyl — high triglycerides
  • Niacin — less used now (flushing, limited benefit)

Nursing care:

  • Lipid panel monitoring (baseline, 4–12 weeks after starting/changing, then periodically)
  • LFT monitoring with statins
  • Assess for muscle symptoms (statin myopathy)
  • Reinforce lifestyle interventions
  • Medication adherence support (asymptomatic condition)

Client Education

  • Therapeutic lifestyle changes are foundational: heart-healthy diet (reduce saturated/trans fats, increase fiber, fruits, vegetables, whole grains, fish)
  • Regular aerobic exercise (150 min/week)
  • Weight management; smoking cessation; limit alcohol
  • Take statins as prescribed (usually evening — cholesterol synthesis peaks at night; though atorvastatin/rosuvastatin can be any time)
  • Report muscle pain, tenderness, weakness, or dark urine (statin myopathy/rhabdomyolysis)
  • Report yellowing skin/eyes, persistent fatigue (liver)
  • Avoid grapefruit juice with some statins (simvastatin, atorvastatin)
  • This is a long-term condition; medication usually continued indefinitely
  • Keep lab appointments (lipids, liver function)
  • Manage related conditions: diabetes, hypertension, obesity
  • Family screening for familial hypercholesterolemia if early/severe
Worked Example Clopidogrel Ch 25 — Medications Affecting Coagulation · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Clopidogrel
Review Module Chapter
Ch 25 — Medications Affecting Coagulation
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Clopidogrel is an antiplatelet (ADP P2Y12 receptor inhibitor):

  • Irreversibly inhibits ADP binding to platelet P2Y12 receptors
  • Prevents platelet activation, aggregation, and clot formation
  • Effect lasts for the lifespan of the platelet (~7-10 days) — irreversible
  • Prodrug — requires hepatic activation by CYP2C19
  • Used to prevent arterial thrombosis (different from anticoagulants like warfarin, which prevent venous/atrial clots)

Therapeutic Use

Clopidogrel inhibits platelet aggregation and prolongs bleeding time. It is used to prevent myocardial infarction (mI) or stroke in clients who have already had an mI or stroke.

Complications

Like other platelet inhibitors, clopidogrel can cause bleeding due to thrombocytopenia. It can also cause GI effects (abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea).

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Active pathologic bleeding (peptic ulcer, intracranial hemorrhage)
  • Severe hepatic impairment
  • Hypersensitivity to clopidogrel
  • CYP2C19 poor metabolizers — reduced efficacy (genetic testing available)
  • Caution: recent surgery, history of GI bleed, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) — rare but serious
  • Discontinue 5-7 days before elective surgery

Interactions

  • NSAIDs, aspirin, warfarin, heparin → ↑ bleeding risk (sometimes combined intentionally for ACS; otherwise caution)
  • Proton pump inhibitors (especially omeprazole and esomeprazole) → ↓ clopidogrel activation via CYP2C19 inhibition → ↓ antiplatelet effect; pantoprazole or H2 blockers are preferred for GI protection
  • SSRIs/SNRIs → ↑ bleeding risk
  • Ginkgo, garlic, ginger → ↑ bleeding risk
  • St. John's wort, rifampin → ↑ clopidogrel activation (theoretical ↑ effect/bleeding)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Prevention of thrombotic events: no new MI, stroke, or stent thrombosis
  • Patency of coronary stents (per imaging/clinical)
  • ↓ recurrent ischemic events in ACS, PAD
  • No bleeding complications: stable Hgb/Hct, no bruising, no GI bleeding

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral
  • Loading dose (ACS/PCI): 300-600 mg PO once
  • Maintenance: 75 mg PO daily
  • Take with or without food
  • Often combined with aspirin (dual antiplatelet therapy) after stent placement
  • Avoid omeprazole/esomeprazole; if PPI needed, use pantoprazole
  • Hold 5-7 days before elective surgery (irreversible — platelet recovery takes time)

Nursing Interventions

  • The nurse should plan to monitor the platelet count periodically while the client takes clopidogrel.
  • Teach the client to monitor for bleeding. The client should watch for black stools, coffee-ground emesis, blood in the urine, nose bleeds, unusual bruising, or petechiae. The client should inform the provider if these occur and about GI effects.
  • The nurse should be aware of all medications the client is taking, because risk for bleeding increases if the medication is taken with anticoagulants or antiplatelet medications. Clopidogrel is sometimes administered concurrently with aspirin, and that increases the risk for bleeding. The medication should be discontinued 7 days before any elective surgery.

Client Education

  • Report immediately: unusual bruising, prolonged bleeding from minor cuts, blood in urine/stool, black tarry stools, severe headache, vision changes, weakness
  • Take as prescribed daily — missing doses ↑ thrombosis risk (esp. after stent)
  • Use soft toothbrush, electric razor; avoid contact sports
  • Tell ALL providers (esp. dentists, surgeons) before any procedure
  • Do NOT stop without consulting prescriber (esp. after recent stent)
  • Avoid aspirin or NSAIDs unless prescribed
  • Use pantoprazole, NOT omeprazole, if antacid/PPI needed
  • Wear medical alert ID
Worked Example Epoetin Alfa Ch 26 — Growth Factors · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Subcutaneous
Review Module Chapter
Ch 26 — Growth Factors
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Epoetin alfa is a recombinant human erythropoietin (erythropoiesis-stimulating agent, ESA):

  • Stimulates erythroid progenitor cells in bone marrow → ↑ red blood cell production
  • Same mechanism as endogenous erythropoietin (produced by kidneys)
  • Onset of reticulocyte response: 7-10 days; clinical Hgb response: 2-6 weeks
  • Used to treat or prevent anemia when endogenous EPO is inadequate
  • Boxed warning: ↑ risk of cardiovascular events, thrombosis, tumor progression

Therapeutic Use

Erythropoietin, a substance that stimulates bone marrow to produce red blood cells, is produced by the kidney. In clients who have chronic kidney disease, erythropoietin is no longer present and anemia results. Epoetin alfa stimulates production of red blood cells in these clients.

Complications

  • Headaches and myalgia (body aches)
  • Thrombotic events, such as myocardial infarction and stroke
  • Hypertension (common, sometimes serious)
  • A too-rapid increase (hgb greater than 1 g/dL over 2 weeks, or hgb greater than 10 g/dL) can worsen hypertension, increase risk of thrombosis, and cause seizures.

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Uncontrolled hypertension
  • Pure red cell aplasia following ESA therapy
  • Hypersensitivity to epoetin or albumin (human or other components)
  • Boxed warning: ↑ mortality, MI, stroke, VTE, tumor progression — use lowest dose to avoid transfusion
  • Caution: cardiovascular disease, stroke history, thrombosis history, seizure disorder
  • Caution: cancer (avoid in clients with anticipated cure if non-myeloid)
  • Pregnancy Cat C

Interactions

  • Iron, folate, B12 deficiency → must be corrected for response; check and supplement
  • ACE inhibitors, ARBs → may potentiate hypertensive effects in dialysis
  • Antihypertensives — may need adjustment as Hgb rises (↑ BP common)
  • Heparin requirements may ↑ during hemodialysis (↑ blood viscosity)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Hgb rising at appropriate rate: 1-2 g/dL per 2-4 weeks (target 10-11 g/dL)
  • ↑ reticulocyte count within 7-10 days
  • ↓ fatigue, ↑ exercise tolerance, improved quality of life
  • ↓ need for blood transfusions
  • BP controlled (no hypertensive crisis)
  • No thrombotic events (DVT, MI, stroke)
  • Adequate iron stores maintained

Medication Administration

  • Routes: subcutaneous or intravenous
  • CKD on dialysis: 50-100 units/kg IV 3x/week initially
  • CKD not on dialysis: 50-100 units/kg SC weekly
  • Chemotherapy-induced anemia: 40,000 units SC weekly or 150 units/kg SC 3x/week
  • Target Hgb: 10-11 g/dL (NOT > 11-12 g/dL — ↑ adverse events)
  • If Hgb rises > 1 g/dL in 2 weeks, reduce dose by 25%
  • Adjust based on Hgb response every 2-4 weeks
  • Hold if Hgb > 11-12 g/dL until Hgb declines
  • Ensure adequate iron stores: ferritin > 100 ng/mL, TSAT > 20%
  • Refrigerate vials; do not shake

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor baseline iron levels, CBC with differential, and platelet count.
  • Monitor hgb and hct twice weekly until blood counts stabilize.
  • Calculate dosages carefully. Both subcutaneous and IV epoetin alfa have dosages based on the client's weight. Do not shake the epoetin alfa vial, and discard vial after one dose is removed.
  • Monitor blood pressure carefully, and report increases to the provider. Question the client about frequency and severity of headaches, which could be an indication of increasing blood pressure or a simple adverse effect.

Client Education

  • Report immediately: chest pain, shortness of breath, sudden numbness/weakness, severe headache, vision changes (signs of MI/stroke/HTN crisis); leg pain or swelling (DVT); seizures; severe HTN
  • Take iron supplement as prescribed (essential for response)
  • Eat iron-rich foods: lean red meat, beans, fortified cereals
  • Monitor BP at home — keep a log
  • If self-administering: teach SC injection technique, site rotation
  • Refrigerate; do not freeze; do not shake vial
  • Keep all lab appointments (Hgb every 2-4 weeks; iron studies periodically)
  • Do NOT discontinue without provider direction
  • Discuss any planned pregnancy or surgery with provider
Worked Example Filgrastim (Neupogen) Ch 26 — Growth Factors · Leukopoietic section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Filgrastim (Neupogen)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 26 — Growth Factors
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) — recombinant; stimulates bone marrow to produce and release neutrophils
  • Increases neutrophil count, function, and migration
  • Reduces duration and severity of neutropenia

Therapeutic Use

  • Chemotherapy-induced neutropenia — reduces infection risk
  • Febrile neutropenia prevention/treatment
  • Bone marrow transplant support
  • Severe chronic neutropenia
  • Mobilization of peripheral blood stem cells for collection

Complications

  • Bone pain (most common) — from marrow expansion; often in lower back, pelvis, long bones
  • Splenic rupture (rare but serious) — left upper quadrant or shoulder tip pain
  • Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) (rare)
  • Capillary leak syndrome
  • Leukocytosis (excessive WBC)
  • Injection site reactions
  • Sickle cell crisis in clients with sickle cell disease
  • Allergic reactions

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to filgrastim or E. coli-derived proteins
  • Sickle cell disease (caution — can precipitate crisis)
  • Do NOT give within 24 hr before or after cytotoxic chemotherapy (rapidly dividing cells more sensitive)
  • Pre-existing splenomegaly (rupture risk)
  • Pregnancy/lactation — weigh risk/benefit

Interactions

  • Cytotoxic chemotherapy — do not give within 24 hr before/after (timing critical)
  • Lithium — may potentiate neutrophil release
  • Drugs causing neutropenia — may counteract
  • Few other clinically significant interactions

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Increased absolute neutrophil count (ANC)
  • Reduced incidence/duration of febrile neutropenia
  • Fewer infections during chemotherapy
  • Successful stem cell mobilization (if that indication)
  • Maintenance of chemotherapy schedule (fewer dose delays)

Medication Administration

  • Route: subcutaneous or IV
  • Dose: 5 mcg/kg/day (chemo-induced neutropenia); individualized
  • Start 24 hr AFTER chemotherapy; continue until ANC recovers
  • Refrigerate; allow to reach room temperature before injection; do not shake
  • Rotate SC injection sites
  • Pegfilgrastim (Neulasta) is a long-acting form — once per chemo cycle

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline and frequent CBC with differential (monitor ANC)
  • Time administration correctly relative to chemotherapy (≥ 24 hr gap)
  • Assess for bone pain — treat with acetaminophen or NSAIDs (often non-opioid responsive); reassure it indicates marrow response
  • Monitor for splenic rupture — left upper quadrant/shoulder pain (emergency)
  • Monitor for respiratory distress
  • Teach SC self-injection technique
  • Neutropenic precautions until ANC recovers
  • Proper storage education (refrigerate, don’t shake)

Client Education

  • Bone pain is common and expected — means the medication is working; treat with acetaminophen (consult provider)
  • Report left upper abdominal or shoulder pain immediately (possible splenic rupture)
  • Report difficulty breathing, fever, signs of infection
  • Store in refrigerator; let warm to room temp before injecting; do not shake
  • Rotate injection sites; proper SC technique
  • Maintain neutropenic precautions: hand hygiene, avoid crowds and sick people, avoid raw foods, monitor temperature
  • Keep all lab appointments (ANC monitoring)
  • Do not receive live vaccines during therapy
  • Report fever ≥ 100.4°F (38°C) immediately — medical emergency in neutropenia
Worked Example Anemia Ch 26 — Growth Factors · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Anemia
Review Module Chapter
Ch 26 — Growth Factors

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Anemia — a reduction in red blood cell mass, hemoglobin, or hematocrit below normal, resulting in decreased oxygen-carrying capacity.

Common types:

  • Iron-deficiency anemia (most common): microcytic, hypochromic; from blood loss, poor intake, malabsorption
  • Vitamin B12 deficiency / pernicious anemia: macrocytic; impaired absorption (lack of intrinsic factor) → neurologic symptoms
  • Folate deficiency: macrocytic; poor intake, alcoholism, pregnancy
  • Anemia of chronic disease: inflammation, CKD (reduced erythropoietin)
  • Hemolytic anemia: increased RBC destruction
  • Aplastic anemia: bone marrow failure

Normal Hgb: ~12–16 g/dL (women), ~14–18 (men).

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Three mechanisms: decreased production, increased destruction, or blood loss
  • Iron deficiency: insufficient iron for hemoglobin synthesis → small, pale RBCs
  • B12/folate deficiency: impaired DNA synthesis → large, immature RBCs (megaloblasts)
  • Pernicious anemia: autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor → B12 not absorbed in terminal ileum
  • CKD: reduced erythropoietin production by kidneys → reduced RBC production
  • Reduced oxygen-carrying capacity → tissue hypoxia → compensatory tachycardia, increased respiratory rate

Expected Findings

General anemia symptoms (from tissue hypoxia):

  • Fatigue, weakness, lethargy
  • Pallor (skin, conjunctiva, nail beds)
  • Dyspnea on exertion, tachycardia, palpitations
  • Dizziness, headache, cold intolerance
  • Tachypnea

Type-specific:

  • Iron deficiency: spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia), pica, glossitis, cheilosis
  • B12 deficiency: neurologic symptoms — paresthesias, ataxia, impaired proprioception, cognitive changes; beefy red tongue
  • Hemolytic: jaundice, splenomegaly

Diagnostic:

  • CBC: Hgb, Hct, RBC indices (MCV distinguishes micro/normo/macrocytic)
  • Iron studies: ferritin, serum iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation
  • B12 and folate levels; reticulocyte count
  • Peripheral smear; Schilling test (historical) for pernicious anemia
  • Stool occult blood (GI loss)

Nursing Care

Treatment by type:

  • Iron deficiency: oral iron (ferrous sulfate) — take on empty stomach with vitamin C; IV iron if intolerant/malabsorption; treat underlying cause (find blood loss source)
  • B12 deficiency / pernicious: B12 injections (IM) or high-dose oral; lifelong for pernicious anemia
  • Folate deficiency: folic acid supplementation; dietary improvement
  • CKD anemia: erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (epoetin alfa, darbepoetin) + iron
  • Severe: packed RBC transfusion

Nursing care:

  • Monitor CBC, iron studies, reticulocyte response
  • Energy conservation; activity pacing; rest periods
  • Fall precautions (dizziness)
  • Oxygen if symptomatic hypoxia
  • Dietary counseling (iron-rich foods, B12 sources, folate)
  • Assess for bleeding source (GI, GU, menstrual)
  • Safe transfusion administration if ordered

Client Education

  • Oral iron: take on empty stomach (1 hr before/2 hr after meals) with vitamin C (orange juice) for absorption; take with food if GI upset (reduces absorption but improves tolerance)
  • Iron causes dark/black stools (harmless) and constipation (increase fiber/fluids)
  • Use a straw for liquid iron (stains teeth); rinse mouth
  • Separate iron from antacids, dairy, tea, coffee (reduce absorption)
  • Pernicious anemia: B12 injections are LIFELONG — cannot be cured by diet alone
  • Iron-rich foods: red meat, beans, fortified cereals, leafy greens
  • B12 sources: meat, fish, dairy, eggs, fortified foods
  • Folate: leafy greens, citrus, legumes, fortified grains
  • Energy conservation; pace activities; rest as needed
  • Report worsening fatigue, shortness of breath, chest pain, or bleeding
  • Keep lab appointments to monitor response
  • Take iron away from children (overdose dangerous)
Worked Example Neutropenia & Infection Precautions Ch 26 — Growth Factors · Leukopoietic section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Neutropenia & Infection Precautions

Defining Characteristics

Neutropenia — abnormally low absolute neutrophil count (ANC), increasing susceptibility to infection. Neutrophils are the primary defense against bacterial and fungal infections.

ANC severity (cells/mm³):

  • Mild: 1,000–1,500
  • Moderate: 500–1,000
  • Severe: < 500 (highest infection risk)

ANC calculation: ANC = WBC × (% segs + % bands) / 100

Febrile neutropenia (ANC < 500 + temp ≥ 38.3°C / 101°F once, or ≥ 38°C / 100.4°F sustained) is a MEDICAL EMERGENCY requiring immediate antibiotics.

Antecedents

  • Chemotherapy (most common cause — nadir typically 7–14 days post-treatment)
  • Radiation therapy
  • Bone marrow disorders (leukemia, aplastic anemia, MDS)
  • Medications (clozapine, methimazole, some antibiotics)
  • Autoimmune conditions
  • Severe infections (sepsis)
  • Bone marrow transplant
  • Congenital neutropenia

Negative Consequences

  • Life-threatening infections — bacterial, fungal; can progress rapidly to sepsis
  • Septic shock and death — especially with severe neutropenia
  • Classic signs of infection may be ABSENT or muted (no pus, minimal inflammation) due to lack of neutrophils — fever may be the ONLY sign
  • Treatment delays for chemotherapy
  • Prolonged hospitalization
  • Need for protective isolation

Related Concepts

Absolute neutrophil count (ANC), febrile neutropenia, G-CSF (filgrastim), chemotherapy nadir, protective/reverse isolation, neutropenic diet, sepsis, immunocompromise, prophylactic antibiotics, hand hygiene.

Exemplars

  • Neutropenic precautions:
    • Strict hand hygiene (staff, visitors, client)
    • Private room; consider protective/reverse isolation; positive-pressure room for severe cases
    • No fresh flowers or plants (fungal/bacterial reservoir)
    • Limit visitors; no sick visitors
    • Avoid invasive procedures when possible (no rectal temps, suppositories, enemas)
    • Meticulous skin and oral care
    • Monitor temperature frequently
  • Neutropenic diet: avoid raw/undercooked meats, eggs, unwashed fruits/vegetables, unpasteurized products, soft cheeses; well-cooked foods only
  • Febrile neutropenia response: blood cultures × 2, then broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour (do not wait for culture results); this is an oncologic emergency.
  • Filgrastim (G-CSF): stimulates neutrophil production to shorten neutropenic period.
  • Patient teaching: report fever ≥ 100.4°F (38°C) IMMEDIATELY; avoid crowds, sick contacts, raw foods; meticulous hygiene; no live vaccines; recognize that fever may be the only infection sign.
  • ANC calculation example: WBC 2,000, segs 30%, bands 5% → ANC = 2,000 × 0.35 = 700 (moderate neutropenia).
Worked Example Calcium Carbonate Ch 28 — Peptic Ulcer Disease · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Calcium
Review Module Chapter
Ch 28 — Peptic Ulcer Disease
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Calcium carbonate is a non-systemic antacid:

  • Reacts with hydrochloric acid in stomach → forms calcium chloride, CO₂, and water → ↑ gastric pH
  • Provides rapid (5-15 min) but short-duration (30-60 min) relief of heartburn and reflux
  • Reduces irritation of inflamed gastric and esophageal mucosa
  • Also serves as a calcium supplement (40% elemental calcium by weight)
  • Promotes wound healing in peptic ulcer disease (in combination with other therapies)

Therapeutic Use

Calcium carbonate is an antacid that raises the ph of gastric contents, which reduces irritation of stomach mucosa, resulting in relief of pain.

Complications

  • Constipation (most common) — encourage fiber and fluids
  • Hypercalcemia with chronic high-dose use — nausea, vomiting, lethargy, confusion, polyuria, polydipsia
  • Acid rebound — paradoxical hyperacidity after calcium effect ends
  • Gas, belching, flatulence (CO₂ released during gastric acid neutralization)
  • Kidney stones (calcium-containing) in predisposed clients
  • Milk-alkali syndrome — hypercalcemia + metabolic alkalosis + renal impairment
  • ↓ absorption of certain medications (tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, iron, levothyroxine, bisphosphonates)
  • Allergic reactions (rare)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypercalcemia (cancer, hyperparathyroidism, milk-alkali syndrome)
  • Renal calculi (calcium-containing stones)
  • Severe renal impairment (↑ calcium retention)
  • Caution: heart failure (sodium load in chewables), hypertension
  • Caution: digoxin therapy (hypercalcemia ↑ digoxin toxicity)
  • Caution: pregnancy (limit total calcium intake; Cat C)

Interactions

  • ↓ absorption of many drugs when given concurrently — separate by at least 1-2 hours:
    • Tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones (chelation)
    • Iron, levothyroxine, bisphosphonates
    • Digoxin, phenytoin
  • Thiazide diuretics → ↑ calcium retention → hypercalcemia
  • Other antacids — usually given alone
  • Excessive milk + calcium = milk-alkali syndrome (hypercalcemia, alkalosis, renal impairment)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Relief of heartburn, indigestion within 5-15 min
  • ↓ epigastric pain in peptic ulcer disease
  • No constipation (common side effect)
  • No signs of hypercalcemia (nausea, vomiting, lethargy, confusion, polyuria)
  • No acid rebound (paradoxical hyperacidity with excessive use)

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (chewable, tablet, liquid)
  • Adult dose: 500-1500 mg PO PRN for symptoms; max 7,000 mg elemental calcium/24 hr
  • Chew chewable tablets thoroughly; do NOT swallow whole
  • Shake liquid suspensions before each dose
  • Separate from other medications by 1-2 hours
  • Take with or after meals for best buffering effect
  • Use with adequate water
  • Limit duration to 2 weeks without provider evaluation

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess GI symptoms (heartburn, indigestion, abdominal pain) before and after dose
  • Assess for constipation — common side effect; ↑ fluid and fiber intake
  • Monitor for hypercalcemia in long-term or high-dose users
  • Verify timing relative to other medications (separation needed)
  • If used for ulcer disease, ensure not masking serious GI condition; refer if symptoms > 2 weeks
  • Educate on lifestyle modifications (avoid trigger foods, weight management, head of bed elevation)

Client Education

  • Shake liquid suspensions prior to taking each dose in order to disperse the medication.
  • Take other medications at least 1 hr before or after taking aluminum hydroxide.
  • Calcium carbonate can cause constipation. Notify the provider if it persists. You might need to alternate this antacid with one that is a magnesium compound and has diarrhea as an adverse effect.
  • Report manifestations of hypercalcemia (constipation, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, confusion) to the provider.
Worked Example Sulfasalazine Ch 29 — Gastrointestinal Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Sulfasalazine
Review Module Chapter
Ch 29 — Gastrointestinal Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Sulfasalazine is a 5-aminosalicylate (5-ASA) anti-inflammatory:

  • Pro-drug — cleaved by colonic bacteria into:
    • 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) — local anti-inflammatory effect on intestinal mucosa
    • Sulfapyridine — absorbed systemically (causes most side effects)
  • Inhibits prostaglandin synthesis, ↓ inflammatory mediators in the gut
  • Anti-inflammatory and disease-modifying effects

Therapeutic Use

Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis

Complications

Complications that occur with the use of sulfasalazine include agranulocytosis, and hemolytic and macrocytic anemia.

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to sulfa drugs, salicylates, or aspirin
  • G6PD deficiency (hemolytic anemia risk)
  • Intestinal or urinary obstruction
  • Severe hepatic or renal impairment
  • Porphyria
  • Pregnancy Cat B; caution in third trimester (kernicterus risk)
  • Breastfeeding (transferred in breast milk)
  • Infants < 2 yr

Interactions

  • Folate antagonist — supplement with folic acid 1 mg/day
  • Digoxin → ↓ digoxin absorption
  • Methotrexate → ↑ adverse effects (additive folate antagonism, hepatotoxicity)
  • Warfarin → ↑ INR / bleeding risk
  • Sulfonylureas → ↑ hypoglycemia
  • Other hepatotoxic or bone marrow-suppressing drugs → additive toxicity

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • UC: ↓ stool frequency, ↓ blood/mucus in stool, ↓ abdominal pain; mucosal healing on endoscopy
  • RA: ↓ joint pain, swelling, stiffness; ↑ function; ↓ ESR/CRP
  • No hematologic toxicity (CBC stable)
  • No hepatic toxicity (LFTs stable)
  • No serious hypersensitivity reactions

Medication Administration

The client should take sulfasalazine four times per day in divided doses.

Nursing Interventions

  • Verify sulfa allergy history before first dose
  • Baseline labs: CBC, LFTs, BUN, creatinine, G6PD screen if at risk
  • Monitor CBC every 2 weeks for first 3 months, then periodically (blood dyscrasias)
  • Monitor LFTs and renal function monthly initially
  • Encourage ↑ fluid intake (2-3 L/day)
  • Assess for hypersensitivity: rash, fever, sore throat (sign of agranulocytosis), photosensitivity
  • Watch for Stevens-Johnson syndrome — rare but serious; discontinue if rash
  • Administer folic acid as prescribed
  • Counsel that urine and skin may turn yellow-orange (harmless)

Client Education

  • Report immediately: rash, fever, sore throat, severe diarrhea, unusual bruising/bleeding, yellow skin/eyes, joint pain worsening, difficulty breathing
  • Take with food and 8 oz of water
  • Drink at least 2 L of water daily
  • Continue folic acid supplement
  • Urine and skin may turn yellow-orange — this is harmless
  • Use sunscreen — photosensitivity
  • Do not take if allergic to sulfa drugs, aspirin, or salicylates
  • Effect takes weeks — do not stop early if no immediate benefit
  • Keep all lab appointments
  • Discuss pregnancy plans with provider (may impact fertility in men)
Worked Example Cyanocobalamin Ch 30 — Vitamins and Minerals · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Cyanocobalamin
Review Module Chapter
Ch 30 — Vitamins and Minerals
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Cyanocobalamin converts folic acid from an inactive form to an active form. It corrects megaloblastic anemia related to a deficiency of vitamin B12.

Therapeutic Use

  • Vitamin B12 deficiency from any cause:
    • Pernicious anemia (lack of intrinsic factor)
    • Malabsorption (Crohn's, celiac, ileal resection)
    • Post-gastrectomy / post-bariatric surgery
    • Strict vegan diet (no animal sources)
    • Long-term PPI or metformin use
  • Schilling test (historical, less used now)
  • Cyanide poisoning (high-dose hydroxocobalamin — different form)

Complications

  • Hypokalemia during initial treatment of severe deficiency (rapid RBC production drives K+ into cells)
  • Anaphylaxis (rare; more often with parenteral)
  • Injection site pain, itching, swelling (parenteral)
  • Mild diarrhea, itching, rash
  • Peripheral edema
  • Headache
  • Hyperuricemia (rare)
  • Fluid overload from rapid erythropoiesis (in cardiac clients)
  • Mild hyperglycemia
  • Polycythemia rebound if overdosed

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to cobalt or vitamin B12
  • Optic nerve damage (Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy) — rare
  • Hypokalemia (correction of megaloblastic anemia → rapid cellular K uptake → hypokalemia)
  • Caution: cardiac disease (volume changes with rapid erythropoiesis)
  • Caution: iron, folate deficiency (often coexists)
  • Pregnancy Cat A (oral); Cat C (parenteral)

Interactions

  • Drugs that ↓ absorption: PPIs, H2 blockers, metformin, colchicine, neomycin, cholestyramine
  • Alcohol (chronic) → impaired absorption
  • Chloramphenicol → ↓ response to B12 therapy
  • Iron, folate deficiency may coexist — treat all
  • Nitrous oxide (chronic exposure) → inactivates B12

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Review laboratory values for increased reticulocyte count and macrocytes and hgb and hct levels within the expected reference range.
  • Assess for improvement of neurologic manifestations (numbness, tingling of hands and feet).

Medication Administration

  • Routes: oral, IM, SC, intranasal
  • Parenteral (IM/SC) for pernicious anemia, severe deficiency:
    • 1,000 mcg IM daily × 7 days, then weekly × 4 weeks, then monthly for life
  • Oral: 1,000-2,000 mcg PO daily (even with malabsorption — high doses absorbed by passive diffusion)
  • Intranasal (Nascobal): 500 mcg one nostril once weekly
  • Inspect IM injection sites; rotate
  • Check serum B12, methylmalonic acid, homocysteine at baseline and to monitor response
  • Replace concurrent iron and folate deficiencies as indicated

Nursing Interventions

  • Obtain baseline CBC, B12, folate, iron, methylmalonic acid, homocysteine
  • Assess for neurologic symptoms (numbness, tingling, balance, gait, cognition) at baseline and follow-up
  • Administer parenteral therapy promptly for symptomatic deficiency — neurologic damage may be permanent if untreated
  • Monitor potassium during initial treatment (rapid RBC production can cause hypokalemia)
  • Monitor for fluid overload in cardiac clients (rapid erythropoiesis)
  • Teach proper self-injection technique if home parenteral therapy
  • Coordinate ongoing monthly injections; review at each visit
  • Identify and treat underlying cause when possible

Client Education

  • Review manifestations of hypokalemia.
  • Discuss the use of potassium supplements, if prescribed.
  • Discuss dietary sources of potassium.
  • Consume foods high in vitamin B12.
  • Administer intranasal cyanocobalamin 1 hr before or after eating hot foods when nasal secretions are decreased.
  • Periodic laboratory testing of hgb, hct, RBC, reticulocyte count, and folate levels is advised.
Worked Example Finasteride Ch 31 — Medications Affecting the Reproductive Tract · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Finasteride
Review Module Chapter
Ch 31 — Medications Affecting the Reproductive Tract
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Finasteride slows the production of testosterone, which reduces the size of the prostate and subsequently promotes urinary elimination.

Therapeutic Use

  • Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) (Proscar 5 mg) — ↓ urinary symptoms, ↓ risk of urinary retention and surgery
  • Male pattern baldness (androgenic alopecia) (Propecia 1 mg)
  • Off-label: hirsutism in women (rare; significant pregnancy risk)

Complications

  • Decreased libido
  • Decreased ejaculate volume
  • Gynecomastia
  • Orthostatic hypotension

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Pregnancy and women of childbearing age — causes feminization of male fetuses (genital abnormalities)
  • Crushed/broken tablets must NOT be handled by pregnant women
  • Hypersensitivity to finasteride
  • Caution: hepatic impairment (extensively metabolized)
  • Caution: clients with risk of prostate cancer (drug ↓ PSA — interpret PSA cautiously; may mask cancer)

Interactions

  • Few clinically significant drug-drug interactions
  • Alpha-blockers (tamsulosin, doxazosin) → often combined for BPH (additive symptom relief)
  • St. John's wort → may ↓ levels (CYP3A4 induction)
  • Effect on PSA — informs lab teams; multiply measured PSA by 2 for cancer screening

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • BPH: ↓ urinary frequency, urgency, nocturia, hesitancy, weak stream; ↓ post-void residual; ↑ urinary flow rate
  • ↓ prostate volume on exam/imaging (over months)
  • Hair loss: stabilization, then gradual regrowth (most visible 3-12 months)
  • ↓ PSA (approximately 50% reduction)
  • No serious adverse events (depression, suicidal thoughts, breast changes, severe sexual dysfunction)

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral once daily
  • BPH: 5 mg PO daily
  • Male pattern baldness: 1 mg PO daily
  • Take with or without food, at the same time each day
  • Swallow whole — do NOT crush, break, or chew
  • Therapeutic benefit may take 6-12 months for BPH; 3-6 months for hair
  • Effects on hair reverse within 12 months of discontinuation
  • Effects on BPH reverse within months of discontinuation

Nursing Interventions

  • Educate male client about possible sexual side effects (decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, ejaculatory disorders) and risk for persistent dysfunction even after stopping
  • Assess baseline PSA, DRE; recheck periodically (interpret with finasteride adjustment factor of 2x)
  • Monitor for breast changes (tenderness, enlargement, lumps) — rare; report immediately (breast cancer reported)
  • Counsel about mood changes/depression (post-marketing reports)
  • Verify NO pregnancy in household or female partner of childbearing age handling tablets
  • Use condoms during sexual activity if partner is pregnant (semen contains small amounts)

Client Education

  • Report: breast lumps, tenderness, or discharge; depression or suicidal thoughts; difficulty with sexual function that persists; rash or allergic reaction
  • Take at the same time each day — patience needed (months for full effect)
  • Do NOT crush or break tablets
  • Pregnant women must not handle broken or crushed tablets (skin absorption — fetal harm)
  • Use a condom during sex if female partner is pregnant (small amounts in semen)
  • Sexual side effects (↓ libido, erectile dysfunction, ↓ ejaculate volume) may occur and may persist after discontinuation
  • Do NOT donate blood for at least 1 month after stopping (protect pregnant transfusion recipients)
  • Tell providers about finasteride — affects PSA interpretation
  • Hair loss may resume within a year of stopping
Worked Example Sildenafil (PDE5 Inhibitor) Ch 31 — Medications Affecting the Reproductive Tract · Men’s health section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Sildenafil (Viagra, Revatio)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 31 — Medications Affecting the Reproductive Tract
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitor — inhibits PDE5, increasing cyclic GMP → smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilation
  • In the penis: enhances nitric-oxide-mediated vasodilation → increased blood flow → erection (with sexual stimulation)
  • In pulmonary vasculature: vasodilation (for pulmonary hypertension)

Therapeutic Use

  • Erectile dysfunction (ED)
  • Pulmonary arterial hypertension (Revatio brand)
  • Requires sexual stimulation to produce erection (does not work alone)

Complications

  • Severe/fatal hypotension with nitrates (absolute contraindication)
  • Priapism — erection > 4 hr; medical emergency (tissue damage)
  • Headache, flushing, dyspepsia, nasal congestion
  • Visual disturbances — blue-tinged vision, light sensitivity; rare: NAION (sudden vision loss)
  • Sudden hearing loss (rare)
  • Hypotension, dizziness, syncope
  • MI/arrhythmia in cardiac-compromised clients during sexual activity

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Concurrent nitrates (any form) or riociguat — ABSOLUTE contraindication (fatal hypotension)
  • Severe cardiovascular disease; unstable angina; recent MI/stroke
  • Severe hepatic/renal impairment (dose adjust)
  • Hypotension (< 90/50)
  • Retinitis pigmentosa
  • Caution with alpha blockers (additive hypotension)
  • History of NAION

Interactions

  • Nitrates (nitroglycerin, isosorbide) — CONTRAINDICATED (fatal hypotension)
  • Alpha blockers (tamsulosin, doxazosin) — additive hypotension; separate dosing/start low
  • CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, ritonavir, erythromycin, grapefruit) — increase sildenafil levels (reduce dose)
  • Other antihypertensives — additive hypotension
  • Riociguat — contraindicated

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Improved erectile function (ED indication)
  • Improved exercise capacity and reduced symptoms (pulmonary hypertension)
  • No hypotensive events or priapism
  • No visual/hearing complications
  • Tolerable side effects

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral
  • ED: 50 mg (range 25–100 mg) about 30–60 min before sexual activity; max once daily
  • Pulmonary HTN: 20 mg three times daily (different dosing)
  • High-fat meals delay absorption
  • Reduce dose with CYP3A4 inhibitors, hepatic/renal impairment, older adults

Nursing Interventions

  • Verify NO nitrate use (scheduled or PRN, including recreational “poppers”) — absolute contraindication
  • Assess cardiovascular status (sexual activity is cardiac stress)
  • Review medications for alpha blockers, CYP3A4 inhibitors
  • Baseline BP; monitor for hypotension
  • Educate on priapism emergency
  • Counsel on visual/hearing changes
  • For pulmonary HTN use: different dosing and monitoring

Client Education

  • NEVER take with nitrates (nitroglycerin, isosorbide) or chest-pain medications containing nitrates — can cause fatal blood pressure drop
  • Requires sexual stimulation to work; takes ~30–60 min
  • Take no more than once daily
  • Seek emergency care for an erection lasting more than 4 hours (priapism)
  • Stop and seek care for sudden vision or hearing loss, chest pain during activity
  • Avoid grapefruit juice
  • Limit alcohol (worsens hypotension and ED)
  • Tell all providers you take this (interaction with nitrates in emergencies)
  • Sexual activity is exertion — discuss cardiac safety with provider if heart disease
  • Rise slowly (dizziness)
Worked Example Tamsulosin (Flomax) Ch 31 — Medications Affecting the Reproductive Tract · Men’s health section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Tamsulosin (Flomax)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 31 — Medications Affecting the Reproductive Tract
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Selective alpha-1A adrenergic antagonist — targets receptors in the prostate and bladder neck
  • Relaxes smooth muscle in prostate and bladder neck → improved urine flow
  • More uroselective than older alpha blockers → less effect on blood pressure (but still some)
  • Does NOT shrink the prostate (symptomatic relief only)

Therapeutic Use

  • Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) — relieve urinary symptoms
  • Off-label: facilitate passage of ureteral/kidney stones (medical expulsive therapy)

Complications

  • Orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, syncope (especially first dose)
  • Intraoperative Floppy Iris Syndrome (IFIS) — complicates cataract surgery; must inform ophthalmologist
  • Retrograde/abnormal ejaculation
  • Nasal congestion, headache
  • Priapism (rare)
  • Reflex tachycardia

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to tamsulosin or sulfa (some caution)
  • History of orthostatic hypotension/syncope
  • Planned cataract surgery (IFIS — inform surgeon)
  • Concurrent PDE5 inhibitors (additive hypotension)
  • Concurrent strong CYP3A4/2D6 inhibitors
  • Older adults — fall risk

Interactions

  • PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) — additive hypotension
  • Other antihypertensives, alpha blockers — additive hypotension
  • Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole) and CYP2D6 inhibitors (paroxetine) — increase tamsulosin levels
  • Cimetidine — increases levels

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Improved urinary flow rate
  • Reduced BPH symptoms: hesitancy, frequency, urgency, nocturia, weak stream
  • Reduced post-void residual
  • No symptomatic hypotension or falls
  • Improved quality of life (AUA symptom score)

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral capsule
  • Dose: 0.4 mg PO once daily; may increase to 0.8 mg
  • Take 30 minutes after the same meal each day (consistent)
  • Swallow whole — do not crush, chew, or open capsule
  • Take first dose at bedtime to reduce first-dose hypotension risk (per some protocols)

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline and orthostatic BP (sitting/standing)
  • Fall precautions, especially first dose and dose increases
  • Ask about planned cataract surgery (IFIS); notify ophthalmologist if so
  • Review for PDE5 inhibitors and antihypertensives
  • Assess urinary symptoms and response
  • Educate on consistent timing (after same meal)
  • Rule out prostate cancer (BPH symptoms overlap; check PSA/DRE per provider)

Client Education

  • Take 30 minutes after the same meal daily
  • Swallow capsule whole; do not crush or chew
  • Rise slowly from sitting/lying (dizziness, especially first doses)
  • If dizzy, sit or lie down; avoid driving after first dose until response known
  • Tell your eye surgeon you take this if you have cataract surgery (floppy iris syndrome)
  • May cause abnormal/retrograde ejaculation (harmless but report concerns)
  • Do not combine with ED medications without provider approval (low BP)
  • Continue medication — it manages symptoms but does not cure BPH
  • Report fainting, prolonged erection, or worsening urinary symptoms
  • Keep follow-up for prostate evaluation
Worked Example Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) Ch 31 — Medications Affecting the Reproductive Tract · Men’s health section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 31 — Medications Affecting the Reproductive Tract

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) — non-cancerous enlargement of the prostate gland, common in aging men, causing lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) from urethral compression.

  • Very common: ~50% of men by age 60, ~90% by age 85
  • Not cancer and does not increase prostate cancer risk (but symptoms overlap — must evaluate)
  • Symptoms range from mild to severe urinary obstruction
  • Can lead to complications: urinary retention, UTIs, bladder stones, renal damage

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Age-related hormonal changes (dihydrotestosterone, DHT) stimulate prostate cell proliferation
  • Prostate gland enlarges, compressing the urethra
  • Static component: physical enlargement of glandular tissue
  • Dynamic component: increased smooth muscle tone (alpha-1 receptors) in prostate and bladder neck
  • Urethral compression → obstruction → bladder must work harder → bladder muscle hypertrophy, then decompensation
  • Incomplete emptying → residual urine → UTIs, stones, eventually retention

Expected Findings

Obstructive symptoms (voiding):

  • Weak/intermittent urine stream
  • Hesitancy (difficulty starting)
  • Straining to void
  • Incomplete emptying; post-void dribbling

Irritative symptoms (storage):

  • Frequency, urgency
  • Nocturia
  • Urge incontinence

Diagnostic:

  • Digital rectal exam (DRE): smooth, enlarged, firm prostate
  • AUA/IPSS symptom score
  • PSA (rule out cancer; BPH can mildly elevate)
  • Urinalysis (rule out infection/hematuria)
  • Post-void residual; uroflowmetry
  • Renal function if obstruction suspected

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Alpha-1 blockers (tamsulosin, alfuzosin, doxazosin, terazosin) — relax smooth muscle; rapid symptom relief; orthostatic hypotension
  • 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) — shrink prostate over months; lower PSA; sexual side effects; teratogenic (pregnant women avoid handling)
  • Combination therapy (alpha blocker + 5-ARI) for larger prostates
  • PDE5 inhibitors (tadalafil) — for BPH + ED
  • Anticholinergics — cautiously for storage symptoms (retention risk)

Procedural/surgical: TURP (transurethral resection), laser therapy, prostatic urethral lift, for refractory cases.

Nursing care:

  • Assess urinary symptoms, post-void residual, signs of retention
  • Monitor for acute urinary retention (emergency — catheterization)
  • Monitor BP (alpha blockers); fall precautions
  • Post-TURP care: continuous bladder irrigation, monitor for hemorrhage, TURP syndrome
  • Distinguish from prostate cancer (PSA, DRE)

Client Education

  • BPH is benign (not cancer) but needs management to prevent complications
  • Alpha blockers: rise slowly (orthostatic hypotension); inform eye surgeon (cataract/floppy iris); symptom relief is quick
  • 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors: take months to work; sexual side effects; lower PSA (tell providers); pregnant women should not handle crushed/broken tablets (teratogenic)
  • Avoid medications that worsen retention: antihistamines, decongestants, anticholinergics (read OTC labels)
  • Lifestyle: limit fluids in evening, limit caffeine/alcohol, double voiding, timed voiding
  • Seek emergency care if unable to urinate (acute retention)
  • Report fever, dysuria (UTI), blood in urine
  • Keep prostate cancer screening per provider
  • Do not stop medications without provider guidance
Worked Example Methylergonovine Ch 32 — Medications Affecting Labor and Delivery · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Methylergonovine
Review Module Chapter
Ch 32 — Medications Affecting Labor and Delivery
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Methylergonovine is an ergot alkaloid uterine stimulant:

  • Stimulates contraction of uterine smooth muscle directly
  • Produces sustained tetanic contractions (NOT rhythmic like oxytocin) → compress uterine vessels → control bleeding
  • Also causes peripheral vasoconstriction (cause of HTN side effect)
  • Onset: PO 5-15 min, IM 2-5 min, IV immediate
  • Duration: 3 hr (PO/IM), 45 min (IV)

Therapeutic Use

Prevent postpartum hemorrhage

Complications

Hypertensive crisis

Contraindications/Precautions

Hypertension, preeclampsia, cardiac disease: Use with caution with maternal history of severe renal or hepatic disease, and sepsis.

Interactions

  • Vasoconstrictors, other sympathomimetics → severe HTN
  • CYP3A4 inhibitors (erythromycin, clarithromycin, azole antifungals, HIV protease inhibitors) → ↑ ergot toxicity (vasospasm, ischemia)
  • Beta-blockers (esp. propranolol) → ↑ vasoconstriction → peripheral ischemia
  • Triptans, other ergots → additive vasoconstriction (avoid)
  • Tobacco → ↑ vasoconstriction

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Firm, contracted uterus on palpation (no boggy uterus)
  • ↓ uterine bleeding, normal lochia rubra → serosa progression
  • Stable vital signs (BP, HR, no signs of shock)
  • Adequate uterine involution (descending fundal height postpartum)
  • No signs of ergot toxicity: chest pain, severe HA, vision changes, peripheral coldness/numbness

Medication Administration

  • Routes: IM (most common in postpartum), oral, IV (only in emergency, with caution)
  • Postpartum: 0.2 mg IM after delivery of placenta; may repeat q2-4h up to 5 doses
  • Oral maintenance: 0.2 mg PO q6-8h × up to 7 days
  • IV use ONLY in life-threatening emergencies due to severe HTN risk
  • Assess BP and HR BEFORE each dose; hold if BP > 140/90 or per protocol
  • Monitor uterine fundus (firmness, position, lochia)
  • Have calcium gluconate available (used for ergot poisoning vasospasm)

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor vital signs for increase in blood pressure.
  • Monitor for manifestations of hypertensive crisis (headache, nausea, vomiting, and increased blood pressure).
  • Monitor for uterine tone and vaginal bleeding.
  • Provide emergency interventions.

Client Education

  • Report: chest pain, severe headache, blurred vision, numbness or tingling in fingers/toes, calf pain, palpitations, sudden cold extremities
