  • DASH diet: rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, low-fat dairy; reduce saturated fat
  • Sodium restriction (< 2,300 mg/day, ideally < 1,500 mg)
  • Limit alcohol; quit smoking
  • Regular aerobic exercise (150 min/week)
  • Weight loss if overweight (~1 mmHg per kg lost)
  • Home BP monitoring; keep a log; bring to appointments
  • Rise slowly to prevent orthostatic dizziness
  • Report: severe headache, chest pain, vision changes, shortness of breath (possible crisis)
  • ACE inhibitors: report dry cough, facial/lip swelling (angioedema), avoid salt substitutes (K+)
  • Manage stress; adequate sleep (screen for sleep apnea)
  • Keep all follow-up appointments and labs
Worked Example Prazosin (Alpha-Adrenergic Blocker) Ch 20 — Medications Affecting Blood Pressure · Sympatholytics section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Prazosin (Minipress)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 20 — Medications Affecting Blood Pressure
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Selective alpha-1 adrenergic antagonist — blocks alpha-1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle → vasodilation (arterial and venous) → reduced BP
  • Also relaxes smooth muscle in bladder neck and prostate
  • Reduces peripheral vascular resistance

Therapeutic Use

  • Hypertension (not first-line; usually add-on)
  • Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) — improves urinary flow
  • PTSD-associated nightmares (off-label; well-supported)
  • Raynaud’s phenomenon, pheochromocytoma (perioperative)

Complications

  • First-dose orthostatic hypotension / syncope — pronounced drop in BP with first dose or dose increases; can cause fainting
  • Dizziness, lightheadedness, headache
  • Reflex tachycardia, palpitations
  • Nasal congestion (alpha blockade)
  • Fluid retention/edema (may need diuretic)
  • Priapism (rare)
  • Fatigue, drowsiness
  • Intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (cataract surgery)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to prazosin or other quinazolines
  • History of orthostatic hypotension / syncope
  • Older adults — fall risk (Beers Criteria caution)
  • Concurrent PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil) — severe hypotension
  • Planned cataract surgery (floppy iris syndrome — inform ophthalmologist)
  • Pregnancy and lactation — limited data

Interactions

  • PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) — additive hypotension (severe)
  • Other antihypertensives, diuretics — additive hypotension
  • Beta blockers — enhanced first-dose hypotension
  • NSAIDs — reduce antihypertensive effect
  • Alcohol — additive hypotension

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • BP reduction to target
  • Improved urinary symptoms (BPH): stream, frequency, urgency
  • Reduced nightmares (PTSD use)
  • No syncope or significant orthostatic symptoms
  • Tolerable side effects

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral
  • Start LOW: 1 mg PO at BEDTIME (first-dose effect) — titrate slowly; usual 6–15 mg/day in divided doses
  • PTSD nightmares: start 1 mg at bedtime; titrate up
  • Take first dose at bedtime to minimize syncope risk
  • Take with or without food (consistent)

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline and ongoing BP (sitting and standing) — assess orthostatic changes
  • Administer first dose at bedtime; have client stay in bed and rise slowly
  • Fall precautions, especially first 24 hours and after dose changes
  • Educate about first-dose phenomenon
  • Monitor for edema (may need diuretic)
  • Assess urinary symptoms if BPH indication
  • Inform of cataract surgery interaction (notify ophthalmologist)
  • Screen for PDE5 inhibitor use

Client Education

  • Take the FIRST dose at bedtime — may cause dizziness or fainting
  • Rise slowly from sitting/lying, especially when starting or increasing dose
  • If you feel dizzy, sit or lie down immediately
  • Do not drive after first dose until you know how it affects you
  • Avoid alcohol (worsens hypotension)
  • Do not combine with erectile dysfunction drugs (sildenafil) without provider approval — dangerous BP drop
  • Continue medication even if feeling well; do not stop abruptly
  • Report fainting, persistent dizziness, prolonged erection (emergency), or swelling
  • If having cataract surgery, tell your eye surgeon you take this medication
  • For BPH: may take a few weeks for urinary improvement
Worked Example Enoxaparin Ch 25 — Medications Affecting Coagulation · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Enoxaparin
Review Module Chapter
Ch 25 — Medications Affecting Coagulation
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) — preferentially inhibits factor Xa (via antithrombin) to prevent clot formation; more predictable effect than unfractionated heparin

Therapeutic Use

  • VTE prophylaxis (post-surgery, immobility) and treatment of DVT/PE
  • Acute coronary syndrome

Complications

  • Bleeding, injection-site bruising/hematoma
  • Thrombocytopenia (HIT — less common than with UFH)
  • Rarely osteoporosis with long-term use

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Active bleeding, history of HIT
  • Hypersensitivity to heparin/pork products
  • Caution: renal impairment (accumulation), recent surgery, spinal/epidural procedures

Interactions

  • Anticoagulants, antiplatelets, NSAIDs, thrombolytics → ↑ bleeding
  • Bleeding-promoting herbals (ginkgo, garlic)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • No new clot formation; resolution of VTE
  • No bleeding; routine aPTT not required (anti-Xa level if monitored)

Medication Administration

  • Route: SubQ only (alternate sides of the abdomen)
  • Do not expel the air bubble in the prefilled syringe; do not aspirate or rub the site
  • No routine coagulation monitoring needed
  • Antidote: protamine sulfate (partial reversal)

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor for bleeding, CBC/platelets, and renal function
  • Use correct SubQ technique; rotate sites
  • Have protamine sulfate available
  • Hold before spinal/epidural procedures per protocol

Client Education

  • Report bleeding/bruising, blood in urine or stool, severe headache
  • Use a soft toothbrush and electric razor
  • Learn proper self-injection technique; rotate sites
  • Avoid NSAIDs/aspirin and new supplements without approval
Worked Example Ondansetron Ch 29 — Gastrointestinal Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Ondansetron
Review Module Chapter
Ch 29 — Gastrointestinal Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Selective serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonist — blocks serotonin centrally (chemoreceptor trigger zone) and peripherally (vagal/GI) to prevent nausea and vomiting

Therapeutic Use

  • Prevention/treatment of chemotherapy- and radiation-induced and postoperative nausea and vomiting

Complications

  • Headache, constipation, dizziness
  • QT prolongation (dysrhythmia risk)
  • Rarely serotonin syndrome (with serotonergic drugs)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Congenital long QT syndrome
  • Concurrent apomorphine
  • Caution: other QT-prolonging drugs, electrolyte imbalances (low K/Mg)

Interactions

  • Other QT-prolonging drugs → ↑ dysrhythmia risk
  • Serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs) → serotonin syndrome
  • Apomorphine → severe hypotension

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Absence or reduction of nausea/vomiting
  • Maintained hydration and nutrition

Medication Administration

  • Routes: PO (tablet, orally disintegrating tablet), IV (give slowly/diluted), IM
  • Give before emetogenic chemotherapy or at the end of surgery
  • Monitor ECG/electrolytes in at-risk clients

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess nausea/vomiting and hydration status
  • Monitor ECG and electrolytes (potassium, magnesium) in at-risk clients
  • Administer prophylactically before chemotherapy
  • Manage constipation

Client Education

  • Report palpitations, chest pain, or fainting
  • Prevent constipation with fluids and fiber
  • ODT: let it dissolve on the tongue
  • Take before situations likely to cause nausea
Worked Example Naloxone Ch 36 — Opioid Agonists and Antagonists · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Naloxone
Review Module Chapter
Ch 36 — Opioid Agonists and Antagonists
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Pure opioid antagonist — competitively blocks opioid receptors, rapidly reversing opioid effects including respiratory depression, sedation, and analgesia

Therapeutic Use

  • Opioid overdose / reversal of opioid-induced respiratory depression
  • Reversal of excessive opioid sedation

Complications

  • Acute opioid withdrawal in dependent clients (pain, agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, nausea/vomiting)
  • Resedation when it wears off (short duration)
  • Rarely pulmonary edema, dysrhythmias

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity
  • Caution in opioid-dependent clients (precipitates withdrawal) and cardiovascular disease

Interactions

  • Reverses all opioid effects (including analgesia)
  • Reversal of buprenorphine may be incomplete (high receptor affinity)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Restored adequate respiratory rate and depth
  • Improved level of consciousness and oxygenation
  • Reversal of overdose without precipitating severe complications

Medication Administration

  • Routes: IV (fastest), IM, SubQ, intranasal
  • Titrate to restore effective respirations
  • Short half-life → repeat dosing and continuous monitoring often required (may outlast naloxone)

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor respiratory rate/depth, LOC, and oxygen saturation continuously
  • Be prepared to give repeat doses (drug duration shorter than many opioids)
  • Monitor for opioid withdrawal and resedation
  • Ensure airway support available

Client Education

  • Caregivers: recognize overdose (slow/absent breathing, unresponsive, pinpoint pupils) and give intranasal naloxone
  • Call emergency services and stay with the person
  • Expect possible withdrawal/agitation after reversal
  • Watch for return of symptoms (resedation) — repeat dose may be needed
Worked Example Buspirone Ch 7 — Anxiety and Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Buspirone
Review Module Chapter
Ch 7 — Anxiety and Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Atypical anxiolytic — partial serotonin (5-HT1A) agonist that relieves anxiety without sedation, muscle relaxation, or dependence

Therapeutic Use

  • Generalized anxiety disorder (long-term management)
  • Adjunct for depression

Complications

  • Dizziness, lightheadedness, headache, nausea
  • Restlessness (uncommon)
  • No significant sedation or abuse potential

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Concurrent MAOIs (hypertensive crisis)
  • Caution: hepatic/renal impairment

Interactions

  • MAOIs → hypertensive crisis
  • Grapefruit juice → ↑ buspirone level
  • Other serotonergic drugs → serotonin syndrome

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ anxiety symptoms over 3–4 weeks of consistent use

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, taken consistently (with or without food, but be consistent)
  • Not for PRN use — full effect takes weeks
  • Avoid grapefruit juice

Nursing Interventions

  • Reinforce that relief is delayed (weeks), not immediate
  • Assess anxiety symptoms; encourage adherence
  • Review for MAOI/serotonergic interactions

Client Education

  • Take regularly as scheduled, not as needed
  • Full effect takes 3–4 weeks — continue even without immediate relief
  • No dependence or sedation, but avoid grapefruit juice
  • Report persistent dizziness
Worked Example Alprazolam Ch 7 — Anxiety and Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Alprazolam
Review Module Chapter
Ch 7 — Anxiety and Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Benzodiazepine — enhances GABA inhibition in the CNS, producing rapid anxiolytic and sedative effects

Therapeutic Use

  • Anxiety and panic disorder (short-term)

Complications

  • Sedation, drowsiness, dizziness, ataxia
  • Tolerance and physical dependence
  • Respiratory depression (with other CNS depressants)
  • Paradoxical excitation (older adults); anterograde amnesia

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Sleep apnea, severe respiratory disease, acute narrow-angle glaucoma
  • Pregnancy; substance use disorder history
  • Caution: older adults (Beers — falls)

Interactions

  • Alcohol, opioids, other CNS depressants → additive respiratory depression
  • CYP3A4 inhibitors (grapefruit, azoles) → ↑ levels

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ anxiety/panic symptoms; client able to function
  • No oversedation or respiratory depression

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO; Schedule IV controlled substance
  • Short-term use; taper to discontinue (never stop abruptly)
  • Antidote for overdose: flumazenil (use cautiously)

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor for sedation, respiratory status, and fall risk
  • Assess for dependence; reinforce taper
  • Screen for concurrent CNS depressants/alcohol

Client Education

  • Avoid alcohol and other sedatives
  • Do not stop abruptly (withdrawal/seizures) — taper with provider
  • Risk of dependence; use lowest dose for shortest time
  • Avoid driving until response known; rise slowly
Worked Example Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) Ch 7 — Anxiety and Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 7 — Anxiety and Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) — persistent, excessive worry about multiple life areas (work, health, family, finances) for ≥ 6 months that is difficult to control and interferes with daily functioning.

  • DSM-5 criteria: excessive anxiety + 3+ physical symptoms (restlessness, fatigue, concentration difficulty, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance)
  • Distinct from panic disorder (acute episodes) and OCD (specific intrusive thoughts)
  • Lifetime prevalence ~6%; twice as common in women
  • Often comorbid with depression (~50%) and substance use disorders

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Neurotransmitter dysregulation: reduced GABA (inhibitory) activity, altered serotonin/norepinephrine signaling
  • HPA axis dysfunction: chronic activation → elevated cortisol → physical and cognitive effects
  • Amygdala hyperactivity: fear-processing center over-responds to perceived threats
  • Prefrontal cortex underactivity: diminished top-down regulation of fear responses
  • Genetic predisposition — heritability ~30–40%
  • Environmental: childhood adversity, chronic stress, substance use (caffeine, stimulants exacerbate)

Expected Findings

Psychological:

  • Excessive, uncontrollable worry across multiple domains
  • Difficulty concentrating, mind “going blank”
  • Irritability, feeling on edge
  • Catastrophizing, hypervigilance for threat

Physical:

  • Muscle tension (headaches, back/neck pain)
  • Restlessness, fatigue
  • Sleep disturbance (initial insomnia, restless sleep)
  • GI symptoms (IBS-like)
  • Sympathetic activation: palpitations, sweating, tremor

Assessment tools: GAD-7 questionnaire (score ≥ 10 suggests moderate-severe GAD).

Nursing Care

First-line treatment: combination of psychotherapy + pharmacology

Pharmacotherapy:

  • SSRIs (escitalopram, sertraline, paroxetine) — first-line; 2–6 weeks for full effect; start low, go slow
  • SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine) — alternative first-line
  • Buspirone — non-addictive; 2–4 weeks to effect
  • Benzodiazepines (lorazepam, alprazolam) — SHORT-TERM ONLY for acute distress while SSRI takes effect; high addiction risk
  • Hydroxyzine — non-addictive option for acute anxiety
  • Gabapentin/pregabalin — adjunct options
  • Beta blockers — for performance/situational anxiety (physical symptoms)

Non-pharm: CBT (gold standard), exposure therapy, mindfulness, sleep hygiene, exercise, limit caffeine/alcohol.

Suicide risk assessment — comorbidity with depression elevates risk; assess at every visit.

Client Education

  • SSRIs/SNRIs take 2–6 weeks for full effect — do NOT stop because they “aren’t working”
  • Side effects (GI, sexual, insomnia) often improve after 1–2 weeks
  • Do NOT stop abruptly — discontinuation syndrome (flu-like, dizziness, electric-shock sensations) — taper
  • Avoid alcohol (worsens anxiety, dangerous with benzos)
  • Limit caffeine; avoid stimulants
  • Practice relaxation techniques daily; engage in regular exercise
  • Crisis plan: contact provider/hotline if suicidal thoughts emerge
  • If on benzodiazepines: NO alcohol, NO driving until known response, NEVER stop abruptly
Worked Example Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) Ch 7 — Anxiety and Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 7 — Anxiety and Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) — develops after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence (direct, witnessing, or learning of an event affecting a loved one).

  • DSM-5 requires 4 symptom clusters for > 1 month: intrusion (flashbacks, nightmares), avoidance, negative cognitions/mood, alterations in arousal/reactivity
  • Onset may be delayed (years after trauma)
  • Lifetime prevalence ~7–8% (higher in military veterans, abuse survivors)
  • Frequently comorbid with depression, substance use, anxiety, suicide risk
  • Children may exhibit through play, regression, or behavioral changes

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • HPA axis dysregulation: chronic stress hormone exposure alters cortisol response
  • Amygdala hyperreactivity: heightened threat detection persists after danger has passed
  • Hippocampal volume reduction: impairs memory consolidation; trauma memories remain “raw”
  • Prefrontal cortex hypoactivity: reduced capacity to inhibit fear response
  • Conditioned fear response: environmental cues become associated with trauma → triggered re-experiencing
  • Risk factors: prior trauma, lack of social support, severity/duration of trauma, female sex, genetic predisposition

Expected Findings

Intrusion symptoms:

  • Recurrent intrusive memories, distressing dreams/nightmares
  • Flashbacks (dissociative reactions) — feel/act as if reliving trauma
  • Intense psychological/physiological distress at trauma reminders

Avoidance:

  • Avoidance of trauma-related memories, thoughts, feelings
  • Avoidance of external reminders (people, places, situations)

Negative cognitions/mood:

  • Inability to remember key aspects of trauma
  • Persistent negative beliefs (“I am bad,” “the world is dangerous”)
  • Distorted blame of self/others
  • Detachment, anhedonia, restricted positive affect

Arousal/reactivity:

  • Irritability, anger outbursts, reckless behavior
  • Hypervigilance, exaggerated startle response
  • Sleep disturbance, concentration problems

Nursing Care

Trauma-informed care principles: safety, trustworthiness, peer support, collaboration, empowerment, cultural humility. Survivor never to blame.

Pharmacotherapy:

  • SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) — FDA-approved for PTSD; first-line
  • SNRIs (venlafaxine) — alternative
  • Prazosin — specifically for trauma-related nightmares (alpha-1 blocker)
  • Mirtazapine — for insomnia/appetite
  • AVOID benzodiazepines — may worsen PTSD; high addiction risk in this population
  • Atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, quetiapine) — adjunct for refractory cases

Non-pharm (gold standards):

  • Trauma-focused CBT, Prolonged Exposure (PE), Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT)
  • EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing)
  • Group therapy with trauma survivors
  • Suicide risk assessment at every visit

Client Education

  • Recovery is possible — evidence-based treatments work; many recover or significantly improve
  • SSRIs/SNRIs take 4–12 weeks for PTSD response (longer than depression)
  • Prazosin: take at bedtime; start low to avoid first-dose hypotension; report dizziness
  • Sleep hygiene, regular exercise, limit alcohol/substances (worsen PTSD)
  • Identify and use coping strategies; build social support
  • Recognize triggers; develop a safety plan for distress episodes
  • Therapy is essential adjunct to medication
  • Crisis lines: 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline; Veterans Crisis Line
Worked Example Serotonin Syndrome Ch 7 — Anxiety and Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders · Antidepressants section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Serotonin Syndrome

Defining Characteristics

Serotonin Syndrome is a potentially life-threatening condition caused by excessive serotonergic activity in the central and peripheral nervous systems, usually from drug interactions or overdose of serotonergic medications.

Classic triad:

  • Mental status changes — agitation, anxiety, delirium, confusion
  • Autonomic instability — hyperthermia, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis
  • Neuromuscular abnormalities — clonus (especially lower extremity), tremor, hyperreflexia, rigidity

Onset is typically rapid (within hours of dose change or new drug interaction). Severity ranges from mild to fatal.

Antecedents

  • Combining two or more serotonergic drugs
  • Dose increase of serotonergic drug
  • Switching from MAOI to SSRI without adequate washout (need 2-week washout)
  • Concurrent use of serotonergic medications with triptans, tramadol, linezolid, methylene blue
  • Recreational drug use (MDMA, cocaine) with serotonergic medications
  • St. John’s wort taken with SSRIs/SNRIs
  • Inadequate prescriber awareness of serotonergic drug interactions

Negative Consequences

  • Hyperthermia (> 41°C / 105°F) — can cause irreversible CNS damage, multi-organ failure
  • Rhabdomyolysis — from rigidity and hyperthermia → AKI
  • Seizures, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
  • Death if untreated
  • Confusion with neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) — delayed diagnosis
  • Need for ICU admission and intensive supportive care

Related Concepts

SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, tramadol, triptans (sumatriptan), linezolid, methylene blue, St. John’s wort, MDMA/ecstasy, neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS — differential), CYP450 interactions, washout periods, cyproheptadine (5-HT2A antagonist used as antidote).

Exemplars

  • Drug combinations to AVOID: SSRI + MAOI; SSRI + tramadol; SSRI + St. John’s wort; SSRI + linezolid; triptans + SSRI/SNRI (use caution); MAOI + meperidine
  • Required washout: 2 weeks off SSRI/SNRI before MAOI (5 weeks for fluoxetine due to long half-life); 2 weeks off MAOI before SSRI
  • Classic case: Client on sertraline starts tramadol for pain → develops agitation, hyperthermia, clonus within 24 hr
  • Recognition: ask “What new medication or dose change in the last week?” Check for clonus (Babinski-like ankle clonus is highly specific)
  • Treatment: (1) STOP all serotonergic agents IMMEDIATELY; (2) supportive care: cooling (ice packs, evaporative cooling), IV fluids, sedation with benzodiazepines; (3) cyproheptadine (5-HT2A antagonist) PO for moderate-severe cases; (4) ICU admission for severe cases (intubation, paralysis with non-depolarizing NMB, NOT succinylcholine due to hyperkalemia risk)
  • Resolution: mild cases resolve within 24–72 hr after discontinuation; severe cases may need ICU days

Fluoxetine
Review Module Chapter
Ch 8 — Depressive Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) — blocks serotonin reuptake, increasing serotonin availability in the CNS

Therapeutic Use

  • Major depressive disorder, OCD, panic disorder, bulimia, PMDD
  • Often first-line; long half-life

Complications

  • GI upset, headache, insomnia or somnolence
  • Sexual dysfunction, weight changes
  • Serotonin syndrome (with other serotonergics)
  • Hyponatremia; ↑ bleeding risk; early ↑ anxiety

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Concurrent MAOIs (or within 14 days; 5 weeks after fluoxetine)
  • Black box: increased suicidality in clients < 25 years
  • Caution: bipolar disorder (mania), bleeding risk

Interactions

  • MAOIs, triptans, tramadol, St. John’s wort → serotonin syndrome
  • NSAIDs/anticoagulants → ↑ bleeding
  • Inhibits CYP enzymes → ↑ levels of some drugs

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ depressive/target symptoms over 4–6 weeks
  • No serotonin syndrome or worsening suicidality

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, usually in the morning (may cause insomnia)
  • Effect takes 4–6 weeks; taper to discontinue (long half-life reduces discontinuation effects)
  • Observe 14-day washout to/from MAOIs (5 weeks after fluoxetine)

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess suicide risk, especially early and in young clients
  • Monitor mood, for serotonin syndrome, and bleeding
  • Reinforce delayed onset and adherence

Client Education

  • Full effect takes 4–6 weeks — continue even if not improved yet
  • Report worsening mood or suicidal thoughts immediately
  • Report agitation, fever, tremor, sweating (serotonin syndrome)
  • Do not stop abruptly; avoid alcohol; report unusual bleeding
Worked Example Amitriptyline Ch 8 — Depressive Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Amitriptyline
Review Module Chapter
Ch 8 — Depressive Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) — blocks reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin, increasing their availability in the CNS

Therapeutic Use

  • Depression (second-line)
  • Neuropathic pain and migraine prophylaxis (low dose)

Complications

  • Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision)
  • Orthostatic hypotension, sedation, weight gain
  • Cardiotoxic in overdose (wide QRS, dysrhythmias) — narrow margin
  • Lowered seizure threshold

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Recent MI, dysrhythmias
  • Concurrent MAOIs
  • Beers — avoid in older adults
  • Black box: suicidality in clients < 25; caution glaucoma, BPH

Interactions

  • MAOIs → hypertensive crisis/serotonin syndrome
  • Other anticholinergics → additive effects
  • CNS depressants → sedation; antihypertensives → ↑ hypotension

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ depressive symptoms or neuropathic pain over weeks
  • No cardiac toxicity or excessive anticholinergic effects

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, often at bedtime (sedation)
  • Effect takes several weeks; lower doses for pain than depression
  • Taper to discontinue; overdose is a medical emergency (cardiac monitoring)

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess suicide risk and cardiac status (ECG baseline in at-risk)
  • Monitor for anticholinergic effects and orthostatic hypotension
  • Manage constipation/dry mouth

Client Education

  • Full effect takes weeks
  • Rise slowly (orthostatic hypotension); relieve dry mouth with sugar-free gum
  • Report difficulty urinating, irregular heartbeat, or worsening mood
  • Do not stop abruptly; keep out of reach (overdose danger)
Worked Example Clozapine Ch 10 — Psychotic Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Clozapine
Review Module Chapter
Ch 10 — Psychotic Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic — blocks dopamine and serotonin receptors; effective for treatment-resistant schizophrenia

Therapeutic Use

  • Treatment-resistant schizophrenia
  • Reduction of recurrent suicidal behavior in schizophrenia

Complications

  • Agranulocytosis (life-threatening — requires ANC monitoring)
  • Seizures (dose-related)
  • Metabolic syndrome (weight gain, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia)
  • Myocarditis, severe constipation/ileus, orthostatic hypotension, sedation, hypersalivation

Contraindications/Precautions

  • History of clozapine-induced agranulocytosis
  • Severe neutropenia (low ANC)
  • Caution: cardiac disease, seizure disorder, diabetes

Interactions

  • Other myelosuppressive drugs → ↑ agranulocytosis risk
  • CNS depressants → sedation
  • Smoking → ↓ clozapine level (changes in smoking alter levels)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ psychotic symptoms when other agents failed
  • ANC within safe range; no metabolic or cardiac complications

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO; requires enrollment in a REMS program with scheduled ANC monitoring
  • Dispensed only when ANC is acceptable; titrate slowly
  • Monitor weight, glucose, lipids, and for myocarditis early in therapy

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor ANC/WBC on the required schedule; hold for low ANC
  • Assess for fever/sore throat (infection), seizures, constipation, cardiac symptoms
  • Monitor metabolic parameters

Client Education

  • Report fever, sore throat, or signs of infection immediately
  • Keep all blood-draw appointments (mandatory)
  • Report chest pain, palpitations, severe constipation, or seizures
  • Rise slowly; tell provider about smoking changes
Worked Example Levodopa/Carbidopa Ch 13 — Chronic Neurologic Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Levodopa/Carbidopa
Review Module Chapter
Ch 13 — Chronic Neurologic Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Antiparkinson agent — levodopa converts to dopamine in the brain (replacing deficient dopamine); carbidopa prevents peripheral breakdown so more levodopa reaches the CNS and reduces peripheral side effects

Therapeutic Use

  • Parkinson disease — reduces tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia

Complications

  • Nausea, orthostatic hypotension, dizziness
  • Dyskinesias and ‘wearing-off’/‘on-off’ fluctuations
  • Hallucinations, confusion; darkened sweat/urine (harmless)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Concurrent nonselective MAOIs (hypertensive crisis)
  • Narrow-angle glaucoma; caution: psychiatric illness, cardiac disease, melanoma history

Interactions

  • High-protein meals and vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) → ↓ levodopa effect
  • Nonselective MAOIs → hypertensive crisis
  • Antipsychotics (dopamine blockers) → ↓ effect

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Improved mobility — ↓ tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia
  • Manageable motor fluctuations

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO; take consistently; separate from high-protein meals
  • Effect may take weeks; do not stop abruptly (risk of NMS-like crisis)
  • Monitor for orthostatic hypotension and dyskinesias

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess motor function and for ‘wearing-off’
  • Monitor BP (orthostasis) and for hallucinations/confusion
  • Educate on protein/B6 timing

Client Education

  • Take consistently; space from high-protein meals; avoid B6 supplements unless approved
  • Sweat/urine may darken (harmless)
  • Rise slowly; report uncontrolled movements, hallucinations, or marked symptom fluctuations
  • Do not stop abruptly
Worked Example Donepezil Ch 13 — Chronic Neurologic Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Donepezil
Review Module Chapter
Ch 13 — Chronic Neurologic Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Cholinesterase inhibitor — inhibits acetylcholinesterase, increasing acetylcholine in the CNS to support memory/cognition

Therapeutic Use

  • Alzheimer disease (all stages) — slows symptom progression (does not cure)

Complications

  • GI: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia/weight loss
  • Bradycardia, dizziness, insomnia (vivid dreams)
  • Cholinergic effects; excess → cholinergic crisis

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity
  • Caution: bradycardia/heart block, peptic ulcer disease, asthma/COPD, seizures

Interactions

  • Anticholinergic drugs → ↓ effect
  • NSAIDs → ↑ GI bleeding risk
  • Beta blockers → additive bradycardia

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Slowed cognitive/functional decline; modest improvement or stabilization of memory

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, usually at bedtime
  • Titrate gradually; take consistently
  • Monitor heart rate, weight, and GI tolerance

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor heart rate (bradycardia), weight, and GI effects
  • Assess cognition/function over time
  • Educate family on realistic expectations (slows, not cures)

Client Education

  • Give at bedtime; report persistent GI upset, fainting, or slow heart rate
  • Effect is to slow decline, not reverse the disease
  • Report changes in alertness; ensure safety/supervision
  • Do not combine with anticholinergic OTC drugs without approval
Worked Example Parkinson’s Disease Ch 13 — Chronic Neurologic Disorders · Parkinson’s section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Parkinson’s Disease
Review Module Chapter
Ch 13 — Chronic Neurologic Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Parkinson’s Disease (PD) — progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra of the midbrain.

  • Classic motor tetrad: TRAP — Tremor (resting, “pill-rolling”), Rigidity (cogwheel), Akinesia/bradykinesia, Postural instability
  • Onset typically > 60 yr; affects ~1% over 60
  • Diagnosis is clinical; no specific test confirms
  • Non-motor symptoms often precede motor: anosmia, REM sleep behavior disorder, constipation, depression
  • Progressive course; medications manage symptoms but do not halt disease

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta → reduced dopamine in basal ganglia (nigrostriatal pathway)
  • Imbalance of dopamine (deficient) and acetylcholine (relatively excess) → motor symptoms
  • Lewy bodies (alpha-synuclein protein aggregates) in remaining neurons
  • Symptoms appear when ~70–80% of dopaminergic neurons are lost
  • Multi-system involvement — autonomic, cognitive, mood regulation pathways affected
  • Etiology: combination of genetic predisposition + environmental factors (pesticides, head trauma)

Expected Findings

Motor symptoms (TRAP):

  • Resting tremor (pill-rolling); diminishes with movement
  • Cogwheel rigidity (ratcheting resistance to passive motion)
  • Bradykinesia (slowness initiating/completing movements); shuffling gait, micrographia (small handwriting), masked facies (hypomimia)
  • Postural instability (later stage); falls; festinating gait

Non-motor symptoms:

  • Autonomic: constipation, orthostatic hypotension, urinary urgency, drooling
  • Cognitive: dementia (50%+ at late stages); executive dysfunction
  • Mood: depression (~50%), anxiety, apathy
  • Sleep: REM behavior disorder, insomnia, daytime sleepiness
  • Sensory: anosmia (loss of smell — often early)

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Levodopa/carbidopa (Sinemet) — GOLD STANDARD; carbidopa prevents peripheral levodopa breakdown, reducing peripheral side effects
  • Dopamine agonists: pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine (early disease; may delay levodopa start)
  • MAO-B inhibitors: selegiline, rasagiline
  • COMT inhibitors: entacapone, tolcapone (extend levodopa effect)
  • Anticholinergics: benztropine, trihexyphenidyl (for tremor in younger clients; avoid in older adults — cognitive impairment)
  • Amantadine (for dyskinesias)
  • Deep brain stimulation (DBS) for advanced disease

Nursing care:

  • Fall prevention: assistive devices, environmental modification, PT/OT
  • Swallowing assessment (aspiration risk); speech therapy
  • Constipation management: fluids, fiber, mobility
  • Nutrition: protein can compete with levodopa absorption — separate protein meals
  • Mental health screening: depression, anxiety, hallucinations
  • Caregiver support and education

Client Education

  • Take levodopa exactly on schedule — missed doses cause “off” periods (sudden return of symptoms)
  • Take on empty stomach if possible (high-protein meals reduce absorption) — separate from protein by ≥ 30 min
  • Expect “wearing off” and on/off fluctuations as disease progresses; report to provider for dose adjustment
  • Report dyskinesias (involuntary movements), hallucinations, severe nausea
  • Rise slowly to prevent orthostatic hypotension
  • Increase fiber and fluids for constipation
  • Maintain physical activity (walking, tai chi, dancing — shown to slow motor decline)
  • Speech and swallowing therapy as needed
  • Do NOT abruptly stop dopaminergic medications (can precipitate parkinsonian crisis)
  • Avoid first-generation antipsychotics (worsen PD); if antipsychotic needed for hallucinations, use pimavanserin or quetiapine/clozapine
  • Carry medical ID; inform all providers
Worked Example Alzheimer’s Disease Ch 13 — Chronic Neurologic Disorders · Alzheimer’s section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Alzheimer’s Disease
Review Module Chapter
Ch 13 — Chronic Neurologic Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) — the most common cause of dementia in older adults; a progressive, irreversible neurodegenerative disorder characterized by gradual loss of memory, cognition, language, and ultimately motor function.

  • Onset typically > 65 yr; prevalence doubles every 5 years after 65
  • Three stages: mild (early), moderate (middle), severe (late)
  • Mean duration ~8–10 years from diagnosis to death
  • Diagnosis: clinical assessment + cognitive testing (MMSE, MoCA) + imaging to rule out other causes; definitive only on autopsy
  • Risk factors: age, family history, ApoE4 allele, cardiovascular risk factors, head trauma, low education

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Amyloid-beta plaques — extracellular protein aggregates disrupt neuronal communication
  • Neurofibrillary tangles — intracellular hyperphosphorylated tau protein
  • Cholinergic deficit — loss of cholinergic neurons in basal nucleus of Meynert → reduced acetylcholine
  • Glutamate excitotoxicity — excess glutamate damages neurons
  • Brain atrophy progresses from medial temporal lobe (memory) outward
  • Synaptic dysfunction → neurotransmitter loss → cell death

Expected Findings

Early/mild:

  • Short-term memory loss; difficulty learning new info
  • Word-finding difficulty
  • Mild executive dysfunction; difficulty with complex tasks (finances, planning)
  • Mood changes: depression, anxiety, social withdrawal

Moderate:

  • Confusion, disorientation to time and place
  • Apraxia (difficulty with familiar tasks), agnosia
  • Behavioral disturbances: agitation, wandering, sundowning, paranoia, hallucinations
  • Sleep disturbance
  • Inability to manage ADLs independently

Severe/late:

  • Severe memory loss; inability to recognize family
  • Loss of communication (aphasia, mutism)
  • Loss of motor function: incontinence, immobility
  • Dysphagia; aspiration risk
  • Total dependence; eventually bed-bound

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) — mild-moderate AD; slow decline by ~6–12 months
  • NMDA antagonist (memantine) — moderate-severe AD; can combine with cholinesterase inhibitor
  • Newer disease-modifying agents (aducanumab, lecanemab) — controversial; high cost, modest benefit, brain edema risk
  • Symptomatic: SSRIs for depression; antipsychotics (cautious) for severe agitation/psychosis — BBW for increased mortality in dementia

Non-pharm (more important than meds):

  • Structured environment, consistent routine, orientation cues
  • Safety: door alarms (wandering), remove hazards, supervision
  • Communication: short sentences, eye contact, validation rather than correction
  • Caregiver education and support
  • Adult day programs, respite care
  • Advance care planning EARLY (while client can participate)
  • Avoid restraints; minimize anticholinergic burden (worsens cognition)

Client Education

  • Diagnosis and prognosis discussed honestly; engage in advance directives and POA decisions while still able
  • Medication takes weeks to show effect; expect slowed decline, not improvement
  • Cholinesterase inhibitor side effects: GI (most common — titrate slowly), bradycardia, syncope
  • Use memory aids: calendars, labels, simple lists
  • Maintain physical activity, social engagement, cognitive stimulation
  • Mediterranean-style diet may slow progression
  • Sleep regularly; avoid alcohol
  • Caregivers: join support groups (Alzheimer’s Association); learn de-escalation techniques; address own self-care
  • Driving cessation conversations — safety priority
  • Plan for eventual long-term care needs
Worked Example Status Epilepticus Management Ch 13 — Chronic Neurologic Disorders · Status epilepticus section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure
Status Epilepticus Management
Review Module Chapter
Ch 13 — Chronic Neurologic Disorders

Description of Procedure

Status epilepticus (SE) — a neurologic emergency defined as a single seizure lasting ≥ 5 minutes OR two or more seizures without return to baseline consciousness between them.

Time is brain — prolonged seizures cause neuronal injury via excitotoxicity. Treatment becomes progressively harder the longer SE continues (refractory SE after 2 lines of treatment; super-refractory after > 24 hr).

The treatment ladder uses progressively stronger anticonvulsants while supporting airway, breathing, and circulation.

Indications

  • Convulsive seizure activity lasting ≥ 5 minutes
  • Recurrent seizures without recovery of consciousness in between
  • Subtle or non-convulsive SE (continuous EEG seizures with altered mental status)
  • Witnessed seizure plus continued altered mental status of unclear etiology

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre / immediate during seizure:

  • Call for help / activate rapid response
  • Note time of onset and duration
  • Protect airway: position lateral (recovery position), suction secretions, suppl. O2; do NOT insert anything into mouth
  • Protect from injury: pad rails, move objects; do NOT restrain
  • Continuous monitoring: pulse ox, cardiac, BP

Intra (treatment ladder):

  1. Stage 1 (0–5 min): ABCs; check glucose (give D50W if hypoglycemic, thiamine first if alcoholic); establish IV access
  2. Stage 2 (5–20 min): First-line: IV benzodiazepine
    • Lorazepam 4 mg IV (preferred — longer duration than diazepam)
    • Or diazepam 10 mg IV
    • Or midazolam 10 mg IM if no IV access
    • May repeat once after 5 min if seizure continues
  3. Stage 3 (20–40 min): Second-line: IV antiepileptic
    • Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (preferred — no cardiac effects, no interactions)
    • Or fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg IV (cardiac monitoring; slower infusion)
    • Or valproate 40 mg/kg IV
  4. Stage 4 (> 40 min — refractory SE): ICU admission, continuous EEG; continuous IV infusion:
    • Midazolam infusion, propofol infusion, or pentobarbital
    • Intubation often required

Post:

  • Identify underlying cause: head CT, EEG, labs (glucose, electrolytes, drug levels, toxicology, infection workup)
  • If known epilepsy: check antiepileptic levels, adherence; restart home regimen
  • If new-onset: full workup for cause (stroke, tumor, infection, metabolic)
  • Document seizure characteristics for future reference
  • Continuous EEG monitoring if persistent altered mental status
  • Education for client and family on seizure precautions and medication adherence

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Seizure terminates within 5–30 min of treatment initiation
  • Return to baseline mental status
  • Stable airway, breathing, circulation throughout
  • No injury during seizure
  • Underlying cause identified and addressed
  • Discharge with appropriate antiepileptic regimen and follow-up

Potential Complications

  • Permanent neurologic injury — from prolonged excitotoxicity (mortality 10–30% for refractory SE)
  • Respiratory depression / failure — from seizure activity AND from treatment medications; need intubation
  • Aspiration pneumonia — from impaired airway protection
  • Rhabdomyolysis from sustained motor activity → AKI
  • Cardiac arrhythmias (especially with fosphenytoin/phenytoin or hypotension)
  • Hypoglycemia (especially in children)
  • Hyperthermia from prolonged activity
  • Hypotension from benzodiazepines, propofol, or barbiturates — vasopressor support may be needed
Worked Example Fluticasone (Inhaled) Ch 17 — Airflow Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Fluticasone (Inhaled)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 17 — Airflow Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Inhaled glucocorticoid (corticosteroid) — reduces airway inflammation, edema, and mucus production for long-term asthma control

Therapeutic Use

  • Long-term control/prevention of asthma (not for acute attacks)
  • Maintenance therapy in COPD (combination products)

Complications

  • Oral candidiasis (thrush) and hoarseness
  • Throat irritation, cough
  • Systemic effects rare at inhaled doses (high-dose/long-term: bone loss, slowed growth in children)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Acute asthma attack/status asthmaticus (not a rescue drug)
  • Hypersensitivity
  • Caution: active oral/respiratory infection

Interactions

  • Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ritonavir, ketoconazole) → ↑ systemic corticosteroid effect
  • Minimal interactions at inhaled doses

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ frequency/severity of asthma symptoms and exacerbations
  • Improved peak flow; reduced rescue-inhaler use

Medication Administration

  • Route: inhaled (MDI or DPI); use a spacer with MDI
  • Take on a scheduled basis (not PRN); effect builds over time
  • Rinse mouth after each use; if used with a bronchodilator, give the bronchodilator first

Nursing Interventions

  • Reinforce daily/scheduled use and correct inhaler technique
  • Teach mouth rinsing and spacer use to prevent thrush
  • Assess for oral candidiasis; monitor growth in children

Client Education

  • This is a controller, not a rescue inhaler — use a SABA for acute attacks
  • Use every day even when feeling well
  • Rinse mouth after use; report white patches in the mouth
  • Use a spacer; carry a rescue inhaler separately
Worked Example Montelukast Ch 17 — Airflow Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Montelukast
Review Module Chapter
Ch 17 — Airflow Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Leukotriene receptor antagonist — blocks leukotrienes to reduce airway inflammation, bronchoconstriction, edema, and mucus

Therapeutic Use

  • Long-term asthma control/prophylaxis (including exercise-induced)
  • Allergic rhinitis

Complications

  • Headache, GI upset
  • Neuropsychiatric effects (mood/behavior changes, depression, sleep disturbances) — black box
  • Not effective for acute bronchospasm

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Acute asthma attack
  • Caution: history of psychiatric illness

Interactions

  • Phenobarbital, rifampin → ↓ montelukast level
  • Generally few significant interactions

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ asthma symptoms and exacerbations
  • Reduced rescue-inhaler use; controlled allergic rhinitis

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, usually once daily in the evening
  • For exercise-induced asthma, take at least 2 hr before exercise (per regimen)
  • Not for acute attacks; chewable/granule forms for children

Nursing Interventions

  • Reinforce scheduled use (not for acute attacks)
  • Monitor for mood/behavior changes and educate family to report them
  • Assess asthma control

Client Education

  • Take daily as prescribed, even when well
  • Report mood changes, agitation, depression, or unusual behavior
  • Keep a rescue inhaler for acute symptoms
  • Do not use to treat an asthma attack
Worked Example Asthma Ch 17 — Airflow Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Asthma
Review Module Chapter
Ch 17 — Airflow Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Asthma — chronic inflammatory disease of the airways characterized by reversible airflow obstruction, bronchial hyperresponsiveness, and episodes of wheezing, dyspnea, chest tightness, and cough.

  • Affects ~8% of US population; common in children
  • Triggers vary: allergens, exercise, cold air, viral infections, irritants (smoke), aspirin/NSAIDs, stress
  • Severity classified by symptom frequency and pulmonary function (NAEPP/GINA guidelines): intermittent, mild persistent, moderate persistent, severe persistent
  • Goal of management: control inflammation, prevent attacks, maintain normal activity, minimize medication side effects

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Airway inflammation — mast cells, eosinophils, T-lymphocytes release inflammatory mediators
  • Bronchospasm — smooth muscle contraction narrows airways
  • Airway edema from inflammation
  • Mucus hypersecretion — thick mucus plugs further narrow airways
  • Airway remodeling (chronic) — permanent thickening of airway walls
  • Result: increased airway resistance, decreased airflow, particularly on expiration (air trapping)
  • Triggers: allergens (dust mites, pollen, pet dander), irritants (smoke, pollution), exercise, infection, cold air, emotional stress, GERD, certain meds (aspirin, beta blockers)

Expected Findings

Asthma attack symptoms:

  • Wheezing (expiratory; may be inspiratory in severe)
  • Dyspnea, shortness of breath
  • Chest tightness
  • Persistent cough (especially at night/early morning)
  • Use of accessory muscles, retractions (severe)
  • Tachypnea, tachycardia
  • Pulsus paradoxus (severe)
  • Cyanosis, decreased oxygen saturation
  • Silent chest (extremely severe — ominous; cannot move air)

Diagnostic findings:

  • Spirometry: reduced FEV1, reduced FEV1/FVC ratio, reversibility (≥ 12% improvement after bronchodilator)
  • Peak flow monitoring at home (personal best, zones)
  • Eosinophilia on CBC
  • Elevated IgE in atopic asthma
  • Methacholine challenge if diagnosis unclear

Nursing Care

Stepwise pharmacologic management (NAEPP/GINA):

  • Step 1 (intermittent): SABA (albuterol) PRN; ICS-formoterol as PRN reliever per GINA
  • Step 2 (mild persistent): Low-dose ICS daily + SABA PRN
  • Step 3: Low-dose ICS + LABA, or medium-dose ICS
  • Step 4: Medium-dose ICS + LABA
  • Step 5: High-dose ICS + LABA; consider biologics (omalizumab, mepolizumab) for severe
  • Step 6: + oral corticosteroids
  • Leukotriene modifiers (montelukast) — alternative or add-on

Acute exacerbation:

  • SABA via nebulizer or MDI with spacer (albuterol)
  • Ipratropium (anticholinergic) in moderate-severe
  • Systemic corticosteroids (prednisone, methylprednisolone)
  • Oxygen to maintain SpO2 ≥ 90–94%
  • IV magnesium for severe
  • Heliox, ICU/intubation for refractory severe

Non-pharm:

  • Trigger avoidance: HEPA filters, dust-mite covers, smoking cessation
  • Influenza and pneumococcal vaccines
  • Asthma Action Plan with green/yellow/red zones
  • Pulmonary rehabilitation for severe cases

Client Education

  • Distinguish reliever (rescue) vs controller medications — rescue (SABA) for symptoms; controllers (ICS) DAILY even when feeling well
  • Use of MDI/DPI with proper technique; spacer with MDI improves delivery
  • Rinse mouth after ICS to prevent thrush
  • Peak flow monitoring: know personal best; act on zones (green/yellow/red)
  • Asthma Action Plan: when to take rescue, when to add steroids, when to seek emergency care
  • Identify and avoid personal triggers
  • Cold air: cover mouth with scarf; exercise: pre-treat with SABA 15–30 min before
  • Vaccinations: annual flu shot, pneumococcal series
  • NEVER use only SABA as monotherapy in chronic asthma (linked to mortality)
  • Seek emergency care for: severe shortness of breath unrelieved by rescue, peak flow < 50% personal best, cannot speak in full sentences, cyanosis
  • Regular follow-up with provider; PFTs annually
Worked Example Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) Ch 17 — Airflow Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
COPD
Review Module Chapter
Ch 17 — Airflow Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) — preventable and treatable disease characterized by persistent airflow limitation that is usually progressive, associated with enhanced chronic inflammatory response.

  • Includes emphysema (alveolar destruction; loss of elastic recoil) and chronic bronchitis (chronic productive cough ≥ 3 months in 2 consecutive years)
  • Primary cause: cigarette smoking (85–90%); also environmental pollutants, occupational dusts, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
  • 3rd leading cause of death in US
  • GOLD staging based on FEV1 % predicted:
    • GOLD 1 (mild): FEV1 ≥ 80%
    • GOLD 2 (moderate): 50–80%
    • GOLD 3 (severe): 30–50%
    • GOLD 4 (very severe): < 30%

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Chronic inflammation from noxious particles/gases (tobacco smoke)
  • Emphysema: destruction of alveolar walls → loss of elasticity → air trapping; barrel chest from hyperinflation
  • Chronic bronchitis: goblet cell hyperplasia → mucus hypersecretion → chronic productive cough
  • Small airway disease: peripheral airway narrowing from inflammation and fibrosis
  • V/Q mismatch: impaired gas exchange → hypoxemia, hypercapnia (later stages)
  • Pulmonary hypertension → cor pulmonale (right heart failure)
  • Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in some clients

Expected Findings

Symptoms (progressive over years):

  • Dyspnea on exertion (early), then at rest (late)
  • Chronic productive cough (often clear/white sputum)
  • Wheezing, prolonged expiration
  • Pursed-lip breathing (compensatory)
  • Fatigue, decreased exercise tolerance
  • Weight loss, cachexia (late)

Physical exam:

  • Barrel chest (increased AP diameter)
  • Use of accessory muscles, tripod position
  • Decreased breath sounds, hyperresonance on percussion
  • Wheezing, rhonchi, prolonged expiratory phase
  • Clubbing (chronic hypoxia)
  • Cyanosis (late)
  • Edema (cor pulmonale)

Diagnostic:

  • Spirometry: FEV1/FVC ratio < 0.70 (post-bronchodilator) — CONFIRMS COPD
  • Chest X-ray: hyperinflation, flattened diaphragm
  • ABG: hypoxemia, hypercapnia (later stages)
  • CBC: polycythemia (chronic hypoxia)
  • Alpha-1 antitrypsin level (especially < 45 yo or non-smoker COPD)

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy (stepwise per GOLD):

  • SABA (albuterol) for acute symptoms; PRN
  • LAMA (tiotropium, umeclidinium) — first-line maintenance; long-acting bronchodilator
  • LABA (salmeterol, formoterol) — long-acting bronchodilator
  • LAMA/LABA combinations (umeclidinium/vilanterol)
  • ICS add-on for frequent exacerbations or with asthma overlap
  • Triple therapy (ICS/LAMA/LABA) for severe with frequent exacerbations
  • Phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor (roflumilast) for severe chronic bronchitis with exacerbations
  • Oral steroids for acute exacerbations (5–7 days)
  • Antibiotics for infectious exacerbations (azithromycin sometimes used preventively)

Oxygen therapy:

  • Indicated when PaO2 ≤ 55 mmHg or SpO2 ≤ 88%
  • Target SpO2 88–92% (avoid over-oxygenation — can suppress hypoxic drive)
  • Long-term home oxygen if criteria met (improves survival)

Non-pharm:

  • Smoking cessation — the single most important intervention
  • Pulmonary rehabilitation — improves QOL, exercise tolerance
  • Vaccines: influenza annually, pneumococcal, COVID-19, Tdap, RSV (older adults)
  • Nutrition: high-protein, smaller frequent meals (large meals worsen dyspnea)
  • Breathing techniques: pursed-lip, diaphragmatic breathing
  • End-stage: palliative care discussion, lung transplant for select patients

Client Education

  • Stop smoking — this is the most important step for slowing disease progression
  • Use inhalers with proper technique; demonstrate at every visit
  • Rinse mouth after ICS (oral candidiasis prevention)
  • Recognize exacerbation signs: increased dyspnea, sputum color change, increased volume; contact provider promptly
  • Pulmonary rehabilitation participation improves quality of life
  • Annual flu shot; one-time pneumococcal vaccines
  • Pursed-lip breathing during dyspnea episodes; tripod position to ease breathing
  • Activity pacing; energy conservation strategies
  • Adequate hydration to thin secretions
  • Cor pulmonale signs: peripheral edema, weight gain, JVD — report
  • Home oxygen safety: no smoking, no open flames, keep away from heat
  • Avoid people with respiratory infections; hand hygiene
  • Advance directives and end-of-life planning conversations EARLY
Worked Example Inhaler & Spacer Administration Technique Ch 17 — Airflow Disorders · Antiinflammatory section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill
Inhaler / Spacer / Nebulizer Use
Review Module Chapter
Ch 17 — Airflow Disorders

Description of Skill

Proper technique for inhaled medications via metered-dose inhalers (MDIs), dry powder inhalers (DPIs), soft mist inhalers (SMIs), and nebulizers. Up to 50–70% of clients use inhalers incorrectly — impacting drug delivery and disease control.

Choice depends on client’s coordination, age, severity, and inspiratory effort.

Indications

  • Asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis
  • Croup, RSV (nebulizers in pediatrics)
  • Pulmonary hypertension (some agents)
  • Acute pulmonary edema (some nebulized agents)

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre:

  • Verify order: medication, dose, device, frequency
  • Assess client’s ability to coordinate inhalation with actuation (determines need for spacer)
  • Inspect device: full canister, mouthpiece clean, expiration date
  • Position client upright (sitting or high Fowler’s)

Intra (MDI without spacer):

  1. Shake the inhaler
  2. Prime if first use or unused ≥ 2 weeks
  3. Exhale completely
  4. Hold mouthpiece 1–2 inches from open mouth OR seal lips around mouthpiece (per device instructions)
  5. Begin SLOW deep inhalation; press canister at start of inhalation
  6. Continue inhaling deeply for 3–5 sec
  7. Hold breath for 10 seconds (or as long as comfortable)
  8. Exhale slowly through pursed lips
  9. Wait 30–60 sec between puffs of same medication; 1–5 min between different medications

MDI WITH spacer (preferred for most clients):

  1. Shake inhaler; attach to spacer
  2. Exhale completely; seal lips around spacer mouthpiece
  3. Press canister ONE time; breathe in slowly and deeply
  4. Hold breath 10 sec
  5. Exhale; wait 30–60 sec; repeat for additional puffs

DPI (e.g., Diskus, Flexhaler):

  1. Load the dose per device-specific instructions
  2. Exhale FULLY away from device (moisture deactivates)
  3. Seal lips; inhale RAPIDLY and deeply (different from MDI)
  4. Hold breath 10 sec
  5. Exhale slowly away from device

Nebulizer:

  1. Assemble per kit instructions; add medication to chamber
  2. Connect to oxygen source (6–8 L/min) or compressor
  3. Client sits upright; uses mouthpiece (preferred) or mask
  4. Slow normal breaths with occasional deep breaths
  5. Treatment continues 8–15 min until medication is fully nebulized

Post:

  • RINSE MOUTH with water after inhaled corticosteroids (prevents oral candidiasis and dysphonia)
  • Clean mouthpiece weekly with warm water; allow to air-dry
  • Track doses remaining (some devices have counters)
  • Document medication, dose, response, peak flow if applicable
  • Reassess technique at every visit (≥ 70% have errors)

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Client demonstrates correct technique on return-demonstration
  • Improvement in pulmonary symptoms (decreased wheeze, dyspnea)
  • Improvement in peak flow or FEV1
  • Reduced need for rescue inhaler
  • No oral side effects (thrush, hoarseness) from ICS — indicates good rinse habit
  • Adherence to controller medications evident in refill patterns

Potential Complications

  • Sub-therapeutic delivery from poor technique (~50–70% of clients)
  • Oropharyngeal candidiasis (thrush) and dysphonia from ICS without rinsing
  • Systemic absorption with high-dose ICS: adrenal suppression, growth suppression in children, cataracts/glaucoma, osteoporosis
  • Paradoxical bronchospasm (rare; with first dose or new device)
  • Tachycardia, tremor from SABAs (especially with overuse)
  • Pneumonia risk with high-dose ICS in COPD (numerically increased)
  • Device-specific issues: empty canister not detected (older devices), DPI moisture damage
  • Confusion between rescue and controller inhaler → missed control, overuse of rescue
Worked Example Diphenhydramine Ch 18 — Upper Respiratory Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Diphenhydramine
Review Module Chapter
Ch 18 — Upper Respiratory Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • First-generation antihistamine (H1 blocker) with strong anticholinergic and sedative effects; blocks histamine to relieve allergy symptoms

Therapeutic Use

  • Allergic rhinitis, urticaria, and allergic reactions/anaphylaxis adjunct
  • Motion sickness, insomnia, and as an antiemetic; mild parkinsonism/EPS

Complications

  • Sedation, drowsiness
  • Anticholinergic effects: dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention
  • Dizziness, paradoxical excitation in children; confusion/falls in older adults

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Acute narrow-angle glaucoma, BPH/urinary retention
  • Newborns/breastfeeding
  • Beers — avoid in older adults (anticholinergic, falls)

Interactions

  • Alcohol and other CNS depressants → additive sedation
  • Other anticholinergics → additive effects
  • MAOIs → intensified anticholinergic effects

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Relief of allergic symptoms or target symptom (sleep, nausea, dystonia)
  • No excessive sedation or anticholinergic toxicity

Medication Administration

  • Routes: PO, IM, IV
  • Caution with driving/sedation; give with food if GI upset
  • Use cautiously and at lower doses in older adults

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor sedation, fall risk, and anticholinergic effects
  • Caution in older adults and those with glaucoma/BPH
  • Assess effectiveness for the intended use

Client Education

  • Causes drowsiness — avoid driving/hazardous tasks and alcohol
  • Relieve dry mouth with sugar-free gum; increase fluids/fiber for constipation
  • Report difficulty urinating or confusion
  • Use cautiously in older adults
Worked Example Loratadine (Claritin) Ch 18 — Upper Respiratory Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Loratadine (Claritin)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 18 — Upper Respiratory Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Second-generation H1 antihistamine — selectively blocks peripheral H1 receptors
  • Minimal CNS penetration (does NOT cross BBB significantly) → non-sedating at recommended doses
  • Minimal anticholinergic effects (vs first-gen like diphenhydramine)
  • OTC and prescription availability
  • Onset 1–3 hr; duration 24 hr

Therapeutic Use

  • Allergic rhinitis (seasonal and perennial)
  • Chronic idiopathic urticaria (hives)
  • Allergic conjunctivitis
  • Mild allergic reactions
  • Preferred in older adults due to less sedation and fewer anticholinergic effects

Complications

  • Mild headache, dry mouth, fatigue (usually well tolerated)
  • Minimal sedation at standard doses (slight increase at high doses)
  • Tachycardia, palpitations (rare)
  • Hepatotoxicity (rare; monitor LFTs if pre-existing hepatic disease)
  • QT prolongation at very high doses (much less than older antihistamines like terfenadine)
  • GI upset

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to loratadine
  • Hepatic impairment — dose reduction
  • Renal impairment — dose adjustment
  • Pregnancy — Category B (no evidence of harm; preferred antihistamine in pregnancy along with cetirizine)
  • Lactation — small amounts in breast milk; generally considered safe
  • Children < 2 yr (separate dosing for ages 2–5)

Interactions

  • Most clinically significant interactions minimal at standard doses
  • CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, erythromycin, ritonavir) — mild increase in loratadine levels
  • Concurrent use with first-gen antihistamines — additive (but redundant)
  • Alcohol — minimal interaction (much less than diphenhydramine)
  • Antihistamines + decongestant combination products: monitor BP

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Relief of allergy symptoms: less sneezing, rhinorrhea, itchy/watery eyes, nasal congestion
  • Resolution of urticaria (hives)
  • No undue sedation or impairment
  • Improved quality of life during allergy season
  • Tolerable side effect profile

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (tablet, ODT, syrup)
  • Adult/> 6 yr dose: 10 mg PO once daily
  • Children 2–5 yr: 5 mg PO once daily
  • Hepatic/severe renal impairment: every other day
  • Take with or without food (food slightly delays absorption but not extent)
  • ODT (RediTabs): place on tongue; will dissolve quickly

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess allergy symptoms, severity, triggers
  • Verify diagnosis is consistent with histamine-mediated symptoms
  • Educate about non-pharmacologic strategies: allergen avoidance, nasal saline, environmental control
  • For severe allergies: ensure client has epinephrine auto-injector available
  • Consider intranasal corticosteroids (more effective for chronic allergic rhinitis)
  • Monitor for response after 1–2 weeks; if inadequate, consider alternative or add-on

Client Education

  • Take once daily at the same time
  • Less drowsiness than first-generation antihistamines (diphenhydramine) — generally safe for driving
  • May take a few days to reach full effect
  • Combine with allergen avoidance, nasal saline, and HEPA filters
  • For seasonal allergies: start BEFORE peak season (1–2 weeks)
  • Drink adequate fluids if dry mouth
  • Carry epinephrine auto-injector if known severe allergies (anaphylaxis)
  • OTC: choose loratadine OR cetirizine OR fexofenadine; not multiple antihistamines at once
  • Pregnancy/lactation: loratadine is among the preferred antihistamines — discuss with provider
Worked Example Allergic Rhinitis Ch 18 — Upper Respiratory Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Allergic Rhinitis
Review Module Chapter
Ch 18 — Upper Respiratory Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Allergic Rhinitis — IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction of the nasal mucosa to environmental allergens, characterized by sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, and itching.

  • Seasonal (hay fever): triggered by pollens (trees in spring, grasses in summer, weeds in fall, ragweed)
  • Perennial: year-round; triggered by dust mites, pet dander, mold, cockroaches
  • Affects ~15–30% of population; often onset in childhood/adolescence
  • Strong association with asthma, eczema (atopic march); ~30% of allergic rhinitis clients develop asthma
  • Family history of atopy is a major risk factor

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Sensitization phase: initial allergen exposure → IgE production by B-cells → IgE binds to mast cells
  • Early-phase reaction (within minutes): allergen re-exposure crosslinks IgE on mast cells → histamine release + other mediators (leukotrienes, prostaglandins, tryptase) → vasodilation, edema, mucus, itching, sneezing
  • Late-phase reaction (4–8 hr later): eosinophils, neutrophils, T-cells infiltrate → sustained nasal congestion, hyperresponsiveness
  • Chronic exposure → mucosal hypertrophy, polyp formation

Expected Findings

Classic symptoms:

  • Sneezing (often paroxysmal)
  • Rhinorrhea (clear, watery)
  • Nasal congestion
  • Nasal itching
  • Itchy/watery eyes (allergic conjunctivitis)
  • Postnasal drip, throat clearing, cough
  • Mild fatigue, headache
  • Decreased sense of smell

Physical signs:

  • Allergic shiners — dark periorbital circles (venous congestion)
  • Allergic salute — transverse nasal crease from rubbing
  • Pale, boggy, blue-gray nasal mucosa with clear discharge
  • Cobblestone appearance of posterior pharynx
  • Mouth breathing in children — can cause dental malocclusion

Diagnostic:

  • Clinical history (often sufficient)
  • Skin prick testing — gold standard for specific allergen identification
  • Serum-specific IgE testing (RAST or ImmunoCAP) — alternative if skin testing contraindicated
  • Nasal smear (eosinophils > 10%)

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy (stepwise):

  • Intranasal corticosteroids (fluticasone, mometasone, budesonide) — MOST EFFECTIVE for moderate-severe; daily use; takes days for full effect
  • Second-generation antihistamines (loratadine, cetirizine, fexofenadine) — first-line for mild-moderate; less sedating
  • Intranasal antihistamines (azelastine) — alternative or add-on
  • Leukotriene receptor antagonists (montelukast) — if asthma + allergic rhinitis
  • Nasal decongestants (pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine, oxymetazoline spray) — SHORT-TERM only; rhinitis medicamentosa risk with topical > 3–5 days
  • Saline nasal irrigation (neti pot, NeilMed) — mechanical removal of allergens
  • Allergen immunotherapy (subcutaneous or sublingual) — for severe persistent symptoms; modifies underlying immune response
  • First-gen antihistamines (diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine) — very sedating; avoid in older adults (Beers list)

Non-pharm:

  • Allergen avoidance/reduction (HEPA filters, dust mite covers, hardwood floors, no carpets)
  • Shower after outdoor activity during pollen season
  • Keep windows closed during high pollen days
  • Wear sunglasses outdoors (reduces ocular exposure)
  • Vacuum with HEPA filter
  • Remove pets from bedroom if pet allergy

Client Education

  • Allergic rhinitis is not infectious; family/coworkers cannot catch it
  • Most effective treatment: intranasal corticosteroids — daily, takes days for full effect
  • Combine medication with allergen avoidance for best results
  • Start medications BEFORE peak season (1–2 weeks); continue throughout
  • Proper nasal spray technique: tilt head slightly forward, spray AWAY from septum (lateral) to avoid epistaxis
  • Identify and avoid your specific allergens
  • Monitor for asthma symptoms (often co-occurs); use rescue inhaler if prescribed
  • Decongestants only short-term (≤ 3 days for nasal sprays to avoid rebound)
  • Consider allergist referral for severe symptoms or immunotherapy
  • Track symptoms in a diary; identify patterns
  • For children: discuss with school nurse for medication during school hours
Worked Example Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) Ch 18 — Upper Respiratory Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 18 — Upper Respiratory Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Alpha-1 adrenergic agonist — vasoconstricts mucosal blood vessels in nasal passages
  • Reduces nasal edema and congestion
  • Also has some beta-adrenergic activity (cardiac, bronchodilatory)
  • Behind-the-counter (BTC) in US — restricted purchase due to methamphetamine precursor status (Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act)
  • Onset 30 min; duration 4–6 hr (IR); 12 hr (ER)

Therapeutic Use

  • Nasal congestion from allergic rhinitis
  • Sinusitis with congestion
  • Common cold / upper respiratory infection
  • Eustachian tube congestion (ear)
  • Adjunct in allergic rhinitis combined with antihistamine

Complications

  • Hypertension — vasoconstriction; especially risky in HTN clients
  • Tachycardia, palpitations, arrhythmias
  • CNS stimulation: nervousness, insomnia, anxiety, tremor, headache
  • Dry mouth
  • Urinary retention — especially BPH
  • Rebound congestion with prolonged use (less than topical decongestants)
  • Rare: stroke, MI, hypertensive crisis (with MAOI or in vulnerable clients)
  • Hallucinations, paranoia at high doses

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Severe hypertension or coronary artery disease
  • Hyperthyroidism, diabetes (caution — can affect BP and glucose)
  • Closed-angle glaucoma
  • BPH or urinary retention
  • Concurrent or recent (14 days) MAOI use — hypertensive crisis
  • Pregnancy — avoid in 1st trimester (some risk of birth defects)
  • Lactation — may decrease milk supply
  • Children < 4 yr — avoid (overdose risk; OTC cough/cold meds not recommended)

Interactions

  • MAOIs (within 14 days) — hypertensive crisis (CONTRAINDICATED)
  • Other sympathomimetics (stimulants, ADHD meds) — additive cardiovascular effects
  • Beta blockers — unopposed alpha effects can cause hypertension
  • TCAs — potentiate cardiovascular effects
  • Methyldopa, reserpine — decreased antihypertensive effect
  • Caffeine — additive stimulant effects (avoid in product combinations)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Relief of nasal congestion
  • Improved breathing through nose
  • Stable blood pressure and heart rate
  • No insomnia, anxiety, or jitteriness
  • Resolution of symptoms within expected timeframe (typically 7–10 days for acute)

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (tablet, ER tablet, liquid)
  • Adult dose: 60 mg PO every 4–6 hr (IR); 120 mg every 12 hr (12-hr ER); 240 mg once daily (24-hr ER); max 240 mg/day
  • Take last dose several hours before bedtime to avoid insomnia
  • Take with or without food
  • BTC: must show ID; sales limits per federal law
  • Children: dose by age per product (avoid in < 4 yr)

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline BP, HR, history of CV disease, urinary symptoms, mental health
  • Verify no MAOI use in past 14 days
  • Check medication list for sympathomimetics, stimulants, beta blockers, TCAs
  • Monitor BP especially in older adults and HTN clients
  • Assess insomnia, anxiety, palpitations at follow-up
  • Educate about combination products (cold/sinus formulations often contain pseudoephedrine + others)
  • Document BTC purchase per state requirements

Client Education

  • Take in morning/early afternoon; avoid evening (insomnia)
  • Stay hydrated (vasoconstriction can dry mucous membranes)
  • Limit to a few days for self-treatment; longer use should be discussed with provider
  • Do NOT combine with other decongestants or stimulants
  • Avoid if you have high blood pressure, heart disease, glaucoma, BPH, or hyperthyroidism (consult provider)
  • Do NOT take if you have used an MAOI in the last 2 weeks
  • Report: chest pain, palpitations, severe headache, vision changes (signs of hypertensive event)
  • Discontinue and seek care if symptoms worsen or last > 7 days
  • Pregnancy: discuss with provider before use, especially 1st trimester
  • BTC restrictions: show ID at pharmacy; tracked purchase
  • Use saline nasal sprays as alternative or adjunct (no systemic effects)
Worked Example Spironolactone Ch 19 — Medications Affecting Urinary Output · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Spironolactone
Review Module Chapter
Ch 19 — Medications Affecting Urinary Output
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Potassium-sparing diuretic (aldosterone antagonist) — blocks aldosterone in the distal nephron → excretes sodium/water while retaining potassium

Therapeutic Use

  • Heart failure, hypertension, edema
  • Hyperaldosteronism, ascites (cirrhosis); off-label for acne/hirsutism

Complications

  • Hyperkalemia (most serious)
  • Gynecomastia, menstrual irregularities (endocrine effects)
  • Dizziness, GI upset

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hyperkalemia, severe renal impairment, Addison disease
  • Concurrent potassium supplements/salt substitutes
  • Caution: diabetes, other potassium-raising drugs

Interactions

  • ACE inhibitors/ARBs, potassium supplements, salt substitutes → hyperkalemia
  • NSAIDs → ↓ effect and ↑ renal risk
  • Lithium → ↑ lithium level

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ edema, controlled BP, improved HF symptoms
  • Potassium within normal range

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, with food; give in the morning to limit nocturia
  • Monitor potassium and renal function
  • Effect on potassium is the key monitoring point

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor potassium and renal function; report K > 5.0
  • Assess edema, daily weights, BP
  • Educate to avoid potassium supplements/salt substitutes

Client Education

  • Avoid potassium supplements, salt substitutes, and high-potassium foods in excess
  • Report muscle weakness, palpitations (hyperkalemia)
  • Gynecomastia/menstrual changes are possible — discuss with provider
  • Take in the morning; rise slowly
Worked Example Hydrochlorothiazide Ch 19 — Medications Affecting Urinary Output · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Hydrochlorothiazide
Review Module Chapter
Ch 19 — Medications Affecting Urinary Output
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Thiazide diuretic — blocks sodium reabsorption in the distal tubule → diuresis and lowered blood pressure

Therapeutic Use

  • Hypertension (first-line)
  • Mild edema/heart failure; reduces calcium-based kidney stones

Complications

  • Hypokalemia, hyponatremia, dehydration
  • Hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia (gout), hyperlipidemia, hypercalcemia
  • Orthostatic hypotension; photosensitivity; sulfa cross-sensitivity

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Anuria, severe renal impairment (ineffective)
  • Sulfonamide allergy (cross-sensitivity)
  • Caution: gout, diabetes, electrolyte imbalance

Interactions

  • Digoxin → hypokalemia ↑ digoxin toxicity
  • Lithium → ↑ lithium level
  • NSAIDs → ↓ effect; antihypertensives → ↑ hypotension

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • BP at target; ↓ edema
  • Electrolytes (especially potassium) within normal limits

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, in the morning (avoid nocturia)
  • Monitor electrolytes, glucose, uric acid, and renal function
  • Less effective in significant renal impairment (use a loop diuretic)

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor potassium/sodium, glucose, uric acid, and BP
  • Encourage potassium-rich foods; daily weights
  • Assess for orthostatic hypotension/fall risk

Client Education

  • Take in the morning; rise slowly
  • Eat potassium-rich foods (bananas, oranges) unless told otherwise
  • Use sunscreen (photosensitivity); report muscle cramps/weakness
  • Diabetics: monitor glucose; report gout symptoms
Worked Example Mannitol (Osmotic Diuretic) Ch 19 — Medications Affecting Urinary Output · Other section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Mannitol (Osmitrol)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 19 — Medications Affecting Urinary Output
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Osmotic diuretic — freely filtered at glomerulus but not reabsorbed; increases osmolarity of filtrate → draws water into the tubule → diuresis
  • Also increases plasma osmolarity → pulls fluid from tissues (brain, eye) into vascular space
  • Onset 1–3 hr (diuresis); 15 min for reducing ICP

Therapeutic Use

  • Increased intracranial pressure (ICP) — reduces cerebral edema
  • Increased intraocular pressure (IOP) — acute glaucoma
  • Acute kidney injury prevention — maintains urine flow (oliguria from low perfusion)
  • Promote excretion of toxins (rhabdomyolysis, certain overdoses)

Complications

  • Fluid and electrolyte imbalances — dehydration, hypo/hypernatremia, hypokalemia
  • Pulmonary edema / fluid overload — initial intravascular volume expansion (DANGEROUS in heart failure)
  • Rebound increased ICP if mannitol crosses damaged BBB
  • Headache, nausea, vomiting
  • Crystallization of solution at low temperatures (must use filter needle/in-line filter)
  • Acute kidney injury at high cumulative doses
  • Hypotension from rapid diuresis

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Anuria (no urine output) — cannot excrete; causes fluid overload
