  • Severe heart failure / pulmonary edema — volume expansion worsens
  • Severe dehydration
  • Active intracranial bleeding (except during craniotomy)
  • Severe renal impairment without proven response
  • Hypersensitivity to mannitol

Interactions

  • Other diuretics — additive electrolyte depletion
  • Nephrotoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, NSAIDs) — increased renal injury risk
  • Digoxin — hypokalemia increases digoxin toxicity risk
  • Lithium — increased renal clearance → reduced lithium levels

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Increased urine output
  • Reduced ICP (improved neuro status, ICP monitor reading)
  • Reduced IOP
  • Maintained urine flow in AKI prevention
  • Stable or improved electrolytes and fluid balance
  • No signs of fluid overload

Medication Administration

  • Route: IV ONLY
  • ICP dose: 0.25–1 g/kg IV over 30–60 min
  • USE AN IN-LINE FILTER — mannitol can crystallize
  • If crystals present: warm the solution (warm water bath), then re-inspect before use
  • Test dose for oliguria (assess for response before full dosing)
  • Continuous monitoring during administration
  • Indwelling catheter for accurate output measurement

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline: renal function, electrolytes, vital signs, neuro status, weight, I&O
  • Use in-line filter; inspect for crystals before administration
  • Insert indwelling catheter; monitor hourly urine output
  • Monitor for fluid overload: lung sounds, JVD, edema, SpO2 (especially first hour)
  • Frequent electrolyte and serum osmolality monitoring
  • Neuro checks for ICP indication (LOC, pupils, GCS)
  • Strict I&O and daily weights
  • Have emergency equipment ready (pulmonary edema risk)

Client Education

  • (Often given in acute/critical settings; education to family) Mannitol reduces brain or eye swelling and increases urine output
  • Frequent monitoring of urine output, labs, and vital signs is necessary
  • Indwelling catheter is needed to measure response accurately
  • Report headache, nausea, shortness of breath, swelling, or chest tightness
  • Expect frequent neuro checks (for brain swelling indication)
  • Position: head of bed elevated 30 degrees for ICP management
Worked Example Heart Failure Ch 19 — Medications Affecting Urinary Output · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Heart Failure
Review Module Chapter
Ch 19 — Medications Affecting Urinary Output

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Heart Failure (HF) — clinical syndrome in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body’s metabolic demands, resulting in fluid congestion and/or inadequate tissue perfusion.

  • HFrEF (reduced ejection fraction, ≤ 40%) — systolic dysfunction; impaired contractility
  • HFpEF (preserved ejection fraction, ≥ 50%) — diastolic dysfunction; impaired filling
  • Left-sided HF → pulmonary congestion (most common)
  • Right-sided HF → systemic venous congestion (often from left-sided)
  • NYHA Functional Classification I–IV based on activity limitation
  • Common causes: CAD/MI, hypertension, valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, diabetes

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Decreased cardiac output → compensatory mechanisms become maladaptive over time
  • RAAS activation: low renal perfusion → renin → angiotensin II (vasoconstriction) → aldosterone (sodium/water retention) → increased preload and afterload
  • Sympathetic activation: increased HR and contractility (initially helpful, eventually harmful; increases myocardial oxygen demand)
  • Ventricular remodeling: hypertrophy and dilation → worsening function
  • Natriuretic peptides (BNP) released in response to ventricular stretch
  • Fluid backs up: left HF → lungs (pulmonary edema); right HF → periphery (edema, ascites, hepatomegaly)

Expected Findings

Left-sided HF (pulmonary congestion):

  • Dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
  • Crackles (rales), wheezing
  • Pink frothy sputum (pulmonary edema)
  • Fatigue, weakness
  • S3 gallop, tachycardia
  • Cough (especially when lying down)

Right-sided HF (systemic congestion):

  • Peripheral edema (dependent: ankles, sacrum)
  • Jugular venous distension (JVD)
  • Hepatomegaly, ascites
  • Weight gain (fluid retention)
  • Nausea, anorexia (GI congestion)

Diagnostic:

  • BNP / NT-proBNP elevated (key marker; correlates with severity)
  • Echocardiogram: ejection fraction, wall motion, valve function
  • Chest X-ray: cardiomegaly, pulmonary congestion, pleural effusion
  • EKG: arrhythmias, ischemia, hypertrophy
  • Labs: electrolytes, renal function, troponin

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy (Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy — GDMT for HFrEF):

  • ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) or ACE inhibitor/ARB — reduce afterload, block RAAS
  • Beta blockers (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol) — reduce sympathetic effects; improve survival
  • Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) — reduce mortality
  • SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) — reduce hospitalization/mortality
  • Loop diuretics (furosemide) — symptom relief (congestion); do NOT improve survival but essential for fluid control
  • Digoxin — symptom control in select cases (narrow therapeutic index)
  • Hydralazine + isosorbide dinitrate — especially in Black clients or ACE/ARB intolerant

Nursing care:

  • Daily weights (same time, same scale, same clothing) — report gain > 2–3 lb in a day or 5 lb in a week
  • Strict I&O; fluid restriction if ordered (often 2 L/day)
  • Sodium restriction (2–3 g/day)
  • Position: high Fowler’s for dyspnea
  • Oxygen as needed; monitor SpO2
  • Monitor electrolytes (especially K+ with diuretics), renal function, BNP
  • Energy conservation; gradual activity progression

Client Education

  • Daily weights — same time each morning; report gain of 2–3 lb in a day or 5 lb in a week
  • Low-sodium diet (read labels; avoid processed/canned foods, deli meats)
  • Fluid restriction if prescribed
  • Take all medications as prescribed (do not skip even when feeling well)
  • Recognize worsening HF: increased SOB, swelling, weight gain, fatigue, orthopnea — report promptly
  • Diuretics: take in the morning (avoid nocturia); monitor for dizziness; eat potassium-rich foods if on loop diuretics (unless on K-sparing)
  • Daily activity as tolerated; cardiac rehab if available
  • Smoking cessation; limit alcohol
  • Influenza and pneumococcal vaccines
  • Weigh medications’ benefits (improved survival, fewer hospitalizations)
  • Advance directives discussion as appropriate
  • Keep all follow-up appointments; lab monitoring essential
Worked Example Diuretic-Related Electrolyte Imbalances Ch 19 — Medications Affecting Urinary Output · Other section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Diuretic-Related Electrolyte Imbalances

Defining Characteristics

Diuretic-related electrolyte imbalances are disturbances in serum electrolyte concentrations caused by the renal effects of diuretic medications.

The pattern depends on the diuretic class:

  • Loop (furosemide): hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, metabolic alkalosis
  • Thiazide (HCTZ): hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, HYPERcalcemia, hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia
  • Potassium-sparing (spironolactone): HYPERkalemia (opposite!)
  • Osmotic (mannitol): variable; initial hyponatremia then hypernatremia, hypokalemia

Antecedents

  • Diuretic therapy (especially higher doses or combination therapy)
  • Underlying renal impairment
  • Concurrent medications affecting electrolytes (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium supplements, NSAIDs)
  • Older age (reduced renal reserve)
  • Inadequate or excessive dietary intake
  • Comorbidities: heart failure, cirrhosis, diabetes
  • Dehydration, vomiting, diarrhea
  • Inadequate monitoring of labs

Negative Consequences

  • Hypokalemia: cardiac arrhythmias (especially dangerous with digoxin — potentiates toxicity), muscle weakness, cramps, ileus
  • Hyperkalemia (K-sparing): peaked T-waves, widened QRS, cardiac arrest
  • Hyponatremia: confusion, seizures, falls (especially older adults), cerebral edema
  • Hypomagnesemia: arrhythmias (torsades), refractory hypokalemia
  • Hypovolemia/dehydration: hypotension, falls, AKI
  • Metabolic alkalosis (loop/thiazide) or acidosis (K-sparing/carbonic anhydrase inhibitors)
  • Increased mortality if severe or unrecognized

Related Concepts

Loop diuretics, thiazide diuretics, potassium-sparing diuretics, digoxin toxicity, RAAS, electrolyte monitoring, fluid balance, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, potassium supplementation, ECG changes, fall prevention.

Exemplars

  • Loop + digoxin: furosemide-induced hypokalemia potentiates digoxin toxicity → life-threatening arrhythmias. Monitor K+ closely; replace as needed.
  • Thiazide + lithium: reduced lithium clearance → lithium toxicity. Monitor lithium levels.
  • Spironolactone + ACE inhibitor + K supplement: dangerous hyperkalemia — combination requires close monitoring; avoid K supplements with K-sparing diuretics.
  • Loop hypokalemia management: potassium-rich diet (bananas, oranges, potatoes, spinach), oral/IV K supplements, or add K-sparing diuretic. Target K+ 3.5–5.0 mEq/L.
  • Hyponatremia from thiazides: especially in older women; presents with confusion, falls; hold diuretic and correct sodium SLOWLY (rapid correction → osmotic demyelination).
  • Monitoring schedule: baseline electrolytes, BUN/Cr; recheck within 1–2 weeks of starting/dose change, then periodically.
  • Patient teaching: report muscle cramps, weakness, palpitations, dizziness, confusion; eat appropriate diet for diuretic type; keep lab appointments.
Worked Example Amiodarone Ch 23 — Medications Affecting Cardiac Rhythm · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Amiodarone
Review Module Chapter
Ch 23 — Medications Affecting Cardiac Rhythm
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Class III antidysrhythmic — blocks potassium (and multiple other) channels to prolong repolarization and stabilize cardiac rhythm

Therapeutic Use

  • Life-threatening ventricular dysrhythmias and atrial fibrillation/flutter (rhythm control)

Complications

  • Pulmonary toxicity/fibrosis (cough, dyspnea)
  • Thyroid dysfunction (hypo- or hyper-), hepatotoxicity
  • Bradycardia, hypotension, QT prolongation, proarrhythmia
  • Blue-gray skin discoloration, corneal deposits, photosensitivity

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Severe bradycardia, heart block (without pacemaker)
  • Iodine hypersensitivity (contains iodine)
  • Caution: thyroid, hepatic, and pulmonary disease

Interactions

  • Digoxin and warfarin → amiodarone ↑ their levels (reduce doses)
  • Other QT-prolonging drugs → ↑ dysrhythmia risk
  • Grapefruit juice → ↑ amiodarone level

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Controlled/converted dysrhythmia; stable rhythm
  • No pulmonary, thyroid, hepatic, or cardiac toxicity

Medication Administration

  • Routes: PO and IV (IV via central line/filter when prolonged; continuous monitoring)
  • Baseline and periodic chest X-ray/PFTs, TFTs, LFTs, ECG, eye exams
  • Long half-life — effects persist for weeks after stopping

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor ECG, BP, heart rate, and for pulmonary/thyroid/hepatic toxicity
  • Reduce digoxin/warfarin doses and monitor levels/INR
  • Assess for vision changes and skin discoloration

Client Education

  • Report cough, shortness of breath (lung toxicity), or fatigue/weight changes (thyroid)
  • Use sunscreen; expect possible blue-gray skin tint
  • Get regular eye exams and labs; avoid grapefruit juice
  • Report palpitations or fainting
Worked Example Adenosine (Adenocard) Ch 23 — Medications Affecting Cardiac Rhythm · Classes section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Adenosine (Adenocard)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 23 — Medications Affecting Cardiac Rhythm
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Endogenous nucleoside antidysrhythmic — slows conduction through the AV node
  • Briefly interrupts AV nodal reentry pathways → terminates SVT
  • Causes transient asystole (brief pause) — this is EXPECTED as the heart “resets”
  • Extremely short half-life: ~10 seconds — must be given by rapid IV push followed by immediate flush

Therapeutic Use

  • Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT/SVT) — first-line conversion to sinus rhythm
  • Diagnostic aid in differentiating wide-complex tachycardias
  • Pharmacologic stress testing (vasodilation)
  • NOT effective for atrial fibrillation/flutter or ventricular tachycardia

Complications

  • Transient asystole / brief pause (several seconds) — expected; alarming but self-limiting
  • Sense of impending doom, chest pressure, flushing, dyspnea — very brief (seconds), due to short half-life
  • Facial flushing
  • Bronchospasm (caution in asthma/COPD)
  • Transient dysrhythmias during conversion (PVCs, bradycardia)
  • Headache, dizziness

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Second- or third-degree AV block (without pacemaker)
  • Sick sinus syndrome (without pacemaker)
  • Severe asthma/bronchospastic disease (caution — bronchospasm risk)
  • Known hypersensitivity
  • Atrial fibrillation/flutter (not effective; may worsen)
  • Caution with carbamazepine (heart block potentiation)

Interactions

  • Methylxanthines (caffeine, theophylline) — ANTAGONIZE adenosine; may need higher dose
  • Dipyridamole — POTENTIATES adenosine; reduce dose
  • Carbamazepine — increased heart block risk
  • Nicotine — may potentiate

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Conversion of SVT to normal sinus rhythm
  • Resolution of tachycardia symptoms (palpitations, dyspnea)
  • Brief pause/asystole followed by return of normal rhythm on monitor
  • Stable hemodynamics after conversion

Medication Administration

  • Route: rapid IV push ONLY
  • Dose: 6 mg rapid IV push over 1–2 seconds; if no conversion in 1–2 min, give 12 mg; may repeat 12 mg once
  • IMMEDIATELY follow with 20 mL rapid saline flush and elevate the extremity (drug has ~10 sec half-life)
  • Use the IV port CLOSEST to the patient (proximal)
  • Use a stopcock or two-syringe technique for rapid drug-then-flush
  • Continuous cardiac monitoring with rhythm strip/print during administration
  • Have emergency/resuscitation equipment available

Nursing Interventions

  • Continuous cardiac monitoring; PRINT a rhythm strip during administration to document conversion
  • Establish proximal large-bore IV; prepare flush in advance
  • Warn the client about brief but intense sensations (chest pressure, flushing, feeling of doom, brief pause) lasting only seconds
  • Have resuscitation equipment and ACLS readily available
  • Use rapid push + immediate flush technique (two-syringe or stopcock)
  • Monitor for bronchospasm in respiratory disease
  • Assess for caffeine/theophylline (may reduce effect) or dipyridamole (potentiates)
  • Reassess rhythm and vital signs after administration

Client Education

  • (Acute/emergency setting) This medication will quickly slow your heart to reset the rhythm
  • You may briefly feel chest pressure, flushing, shortness of breath, or a feeling of doom — these last only a few seconds and are expected
  • You will be on a heart monitor throughout
  • Report if symptoms persist beyond a few seconds
  • After conversion, follow-up may include evaluation for the cause of the rapid rhythm
  • Discuss avoiding triggers (excess caffeine, stimulants) for future SVT prevention
Worked Example Atrial Fibrillation Ch 23 — Medications Affecting Cardiac Rhythm · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Atrial Fibrillation
Review Module Chapter
Ch 23 — Medications Affecting Cardiac Rhythm

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Atrial Fibrillation (AFib) — the most common sustained cardiac dysrhythmia, characterized by rapid, disorganized atrial electrical activity causing an irregularly irregular ventricular response and loss of effective atrial contraction.

  • No discernible P waves on EKG; irregularly irregular rhythm
  • Classifications: paroxysmal (self-terminating < 7 days), persistent (> 7 days), long-standing persistent (> 1 yr), permanent
  • Major risk: thromboembolism / stroke (blood stasis in atria → clots)
  • Prevalence increases with age; common in HTN, HF, valvular disease, hyperthyroidism

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Multiple ectopic foci in the atria (often near pulmonary veins) fire chaotically → disorganized atrial depolarization (400–600/min)
  • AV node filters impulses → irregular ventricular response (often rapid)
  • Loss of “atrial kick” → reduced cardiac output (up to 20–30%)
  • Blood stasis in fibrillating atria (especially left atrial appendage) → thrombus formation → embolic stroke risk
  • Triggers: HTN, CAD, HF, valvular disease, hyperthyroidism, alcohol (“holiday heart”), sleep apnea, sepsis, post-cardiac surgery, pulmonary disease

Expected Findings

Symptoms (may be asymptomatic):

  • Palpitations
  • Fatigue, weakness
  • Dyspnea, reduced exercise tolerance
  • Dizziness, lightheadedness, syncope
  • Chest discomfort
  • Anxiety

Physical/diagnostic:

  • Irregularly irregular pulse; pulse deficit (apical > radial)
  • EKG: irregularly irregular R-R intervals, absent P waves, fibrillatory waves
  • Echocardiogram: assess for structural disease, atrial size, thrombus (TEE)
  • Labs: thyroid function, electrolytes, BNP
  • Holter monitor for paroxysmal AFib

Nursing Care

Three pillars of management:

1. Rate control:

  • Beta blockers (metoprolol)
  • Non-dihydropyridine CCBs (diltiazem, verapamil)
  • Digoxin (especially with HF)
  • Goal: resting HR < 110 (lenient) or < 80 (strict)

2. Rhythm control (restore sinus rhythm):

  • Antidysrhythmics: amiodarone, flecainide, propafenone, sotalol, dofetilide
  • Electrical cardioversion (anticoagulate first or TEE to rule out clot)
  • Catheter ablation (pulmonary vein isolation)

3. Anticoagulation (stroke prevention):

  • CHA2DS2-VASc score determines anticoagulation need (CHF, HTN, Age, Diabetes, Stroke, Vascular, Sex)
  • DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran) — preferred for non-valvular AFib
  • Warfarin (target INR 2–3) — for valvular AFib or mechanical valves
  • Left atrial appendage closure (Watchman) for anticoagulation-ineligible

Nursing care:

  • Continuous or intermittent cardiac monitoring
  • Assess apical-radial pulse deficit
  • Monitor for signs of stroke, HF, hemodynamic instability
  • Bleeding precautions if anticoagulated

Client Education

  • AFib increases stroke risk — anticoagulation is critical even when you feel fine
  • Anticoagulant teaching: bleeding precautions, regular INR for warfarin, consistent vitamin K intake (warfarin), do not skip doses (DOACs have short action)
  • Recognize stroke (FAST: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call 911)
  • Take rate/rhythm medications as prescribed; do not stop abruptly
  • Check pulse; report rates that are very high, very low, or with new symptoms
  • Limit alcohol and caffeine (triggers)
  • Manage underlying conditions: HTN, sleep apnea, thyroid, HF
  • Report palpitations, dizziness, chest pain, syncope, shortness of breath
  • Report bleeding: black stools, blood in urine, prolonged bleeding, severe bruising
  • Keep all follow-up and lab appointments
  • Carry medication list and anticoagulant alert ID
Worked Example Antidysrhythmic Classes (Vaughan-Williams) Ch 23 — Medications Affecting Cardiac Rhythm · Overview section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Antidysrhythmic Classes (Vaughan-Williams)

Defining Characteristics

The Vaughan-Williams classification organizes antidysrhythmic medications by their primary mechanism of action on cardiac ion channels and receptors.

  • Class I — Sodium channel blockers: slow depolarization (phase 0)
    • IA: quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide (moderate; prolong QT)
    • IB: lidocaine, mexiletine (weak; ventricular)
    • IC: flecainide, propafenone (strong; avoid in structural heart disease)
  • Class II — Beta blockers: metoprolol, esmolol, propranolol (slow SA/AV node)
  • Class III — Potassium channel blockers: amiodarone, sotalol, dofetilide (prolong repolarization/QT)
  • Class IV — Calcium channel blockers: verapamil, diltiazem (slow AV node)
  • Unclassified: adenosine, digoxin, magnesium

Antecedents

  • Presence of a cardiac dysrhythmia requiring pharmacologic management
  • Type of dysrhythmia (supraventricular vs ventricular) guides class selection
  • Underlying cardiac structure/function (structural disease limits Class IC)
  • Comorbidities: renal/hepatic function, thyroid, electrolytes
  • QT interval status
  • Concurrent medications (interaction and additive QT risk)

Negative Consequences

  • Proarrhythmia — antidysrhythmics can CAUSE new or worse dysrhythmias (the central paradox of this drug class)
  • Torsades de pointes from QT prolongation (Class IA, III)
  • Class IC danger — increased mortality in structural heart disease/post-MI (CAST trial)
  • Amiodarone multi-organ toxicity (pulmonary, hepatic, thyroid, corneal, skin)
  • Bradycardia, heart block (Class II, IV)
  • Electrolyte-related arrhythmias if hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia
  • Hemodynamic compromise (negative inotropy)

Related Concepts

Cardiac action potential, ion channels, QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, proarrhythmia, CAST trial, therapeutic drug monitoring, electrolyte balance (K+, Mg++), amiodarone toxicity, atrial fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia, SVT.

Exemplars

  • Class IB (lidocaine): ventricular dysrhythmias; monitor for CNS toxicity (confusion, seizures) at high levels
  • Class IC (flecainide): effective for AFib in structurally normal hearts; contraindicated post-MI / structural heart disease (CAST trial showed increased mortality)
  • Class II (metoprolol, esmolol): rate control in AFib/SVT; monitor for bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm
  • Class III (amiodarone): broad-spectrum but highly toxic — monitor PFTs, LFTs, TFTs, eye exams, “blue-gray” skin; long half-life (~58 days)
  • Class III (sotalol, dofetilide): require inpatient initiation with QT monitoring (torsades risk)
  • Class IV (diltiazem, verapamil): rate control; avoid in HFrEF (negative inotropy); avoid verapamil + beta blocker (severe bradycardia)
  • Universal principle: correct electrolytes (K+, Mg++) and monitor QT before/during therapy; ALL antidysrhythmics carry proarrhythmic risk
  • Monitoring: continuous telemetry during initiation; baseline and periodic ECG (QT), drug levels where applicable, organ function for amiodarone
Worked Example Famotidine Ch 28 — Peptic Ulcer Disease · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Famotidine
Review Module Chapter
Ch 28 — Peptic Ulcer Disease
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Histamine H2-receptor antagonist — blocks histamine at H2 receptors on gastric parietal cells, reducing acid secretion

Therapeutic Use

  • GERD, peptic ulcer disease, heartburn
  • Stress ulcer prophylaxis; Zollinger-Ellison syndrome

Complications

  • Generally well tolerated: headache, dizziness, constipation/diarrhea
  • Confusion in older adults or with renal impairment (high doses)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity
  • Caution: renal impairment (dose reduction), older adults

Interactions

  • Reduces absorption of drugs needing an acidic environment (some antifungals)
  • Fewer interactions than cimetidine (which inhibits CYP450)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Relief of heartburn/epigastric pain; ulcer healing
  • Reduced GI bleeding risk in prophylaxis

Medication Administration

  • Routes: PO and IV
  • May take without regard to meals; can be taken before meals to prevent symptoms
  • Reduce dose in renal impairment

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess symptom relief; monitor renal function and mental status in older adults
  • Separate from acid-dependent drugs
  • Reinforce lifestyle measures for GERD

Client Education

  • Take as directed; may use before meals to prevent heartburn
  • Report black/tarry stools or persistent pain
  • Avoid smoking, alcohol, and trigger foods
  • Report confusion (older adults) or no improvement
Worked Example Sucralfate (Carafate) Ch 28 — Peptic Ulcer Disease · Mucosal protectants section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Sucralfate (Carafate)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 28 — Peptic Ulcer Disease
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Mucosal protectant — in acidic environment, forms a thick, sticky, protective barrier (paste) that adheres to ulcerated/eroded tissue
  • Protects the ulcer from acid, pepsin, and bile
  • Acts locally; minimal systemic absorption
  • Does NOT reduce acid secretion (different from PPIs/H2 blockers)

Therapeutic Use

  • Duodenal and gastric ulcers — treatment and maintenance
  • Stress ulcer prophylaxis
  • Mucositis/stomatitis (oral form)
  • GERD-related esophagitis (adjunct)

Complications

  • Constipation (most common)
  • Dry mouth, nausea
  • Aluminum toxicity in renal impairment (contains aluminum)
  • Bezoar formation (rare)
  • Reduced absorption of many other medications (binds them)
  • Hypophosphatemia (binds phosphate)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to sucralfate
  • Chronic renal failure / dialysis (aluminum accumulation)
  • Diabetic gastroparesis (bezoar risk)
  • Dysphagia (aspiration risk with tablets)
  • Caution with concurrent medications (timing)

Interactions

  • Binds and reduces absorption of MANY drugs: fluoroquinolones, digoxin, phenytoin, levothyroxine, warfarin, tetracyclines
  • Separate other medications by ≥ 2 hours
  • Antacids — reduce sucralfate effectiveness (needs acid to activate); separate by 30 min
  • May reduce absorption of fat-soluble vitamins

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Ulcer healing (symptom relief, endoscopic confirmation)
  • Reduced epigastric pain
  • No GI bleeding (black stools, hematemesis)
  • No constipation or other intolerable effects
  • No interference with other medication effectiveness (proper timing)

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (tablet or suspension)
  • Dose: 1 g PO four times daily
  • Take on an EMPTY stomach — 1 hour before meals and at bedtime
  • Separate other medications by ≥ 2 hours
  • If also on antacids: give antacids 30 min before or after sucralfate (not together)
  • Shake suspension well

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess renal function (aluminum accumulation risk)
  • Carefully time other medications (≥ 2 hr separation) — review full med list
  • Monitor for constipation; implement prevention (fluids, fiber)
  • Assess for ongoing GI bleeding (stool color, Hgb)
  • Educate on empty-stomach timing
  • Monitor phosphate in long-term/renal patients
  • Assess swallowing ability if using tablets

Client Education

  • Take on an empty stomach — 1 hour before meals and at bedtime
  • Take other medications at least 2 hours apart from sucralfate
  • Increase fluids and fiber to prevent constipation
  • Do not take antacids within 30 minutes of sucralfate
  • Complete the full course even if feeling better
  • Report black/tarry stools, worsening pain, or no improvement
  • Avoid smoking, alcohol, NSAIDs, and trigger foods (worsen ulcers)
  • Shake liquid form well before use
Worked Example Peptic Ulcer Disease Ch 28 — Peptic Ulcer Disease · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 28 — Peptic Ulcer Disease

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD) — erosion (ulceration) of the mucosal lining of the stomach (gastric ulcer) or duodenum (duodenal ulcer) due to imbalance between protective and damaging factors.

  • Duodenal ulcers (more common): pain 2–3 hr after meals; relieved BY eating; nocturnal pain
  • Gastric ulcers: pain DURING/shortly after eating; worsened by food; weight loss
  • Two main causes: H. pylori infection and NSAID use
  • Less common: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrin-secreting tumor)

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • H. pylori: bacteria colonize gastric mucosa, produce urease (ammonia), trigger inflammation, damage protective mucus layer
  • NSAIDs: inhibit COX-1 → decreased protective prostaglandins → reduced mucus/bicarbonate, reduced mucosal blood flow
  • Imbalance: aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs) overwhelm defensive factors (mucus, bicarbonate, blood flow, prostaglandins)
  • Mucosal erosion exposes underlying tissue to acid → ulcer
  • Risk factors: H. pylori, NSAIDs, smoking, alcohol, stress, corticosteroids, family history

Expected Findings

  • Epigastric pain (burning, gnawing) — timing differs by ulcer type
  • Dyspepsia, bloating, belching
  • Nausea; with gastric ulcers, food may worsen pain
  • Early satiety, weight loss (gastric)

Complications (alarm features):

  • GI bleeding: hematemesis (coffee-ground or bright red), melena (black tarry stools), anemia
  • Perforation: sudden severe pain, rigid board-like abdomen, signs of peritonitis (emergency)
  • Obstruction: vomiting, feeling of fullness

Diagnostic:

  • Upper endoscopy (EGD) — gold standard; visualize and biopsy
  • H. pylori testing: urea breath test, stool antigen, biopsy, serology
  • CBC (anemia), stool occult blood

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy:

  • H. pylori triple therapy: PPI + two antibiotics (clarithromycin + amoxicillin or metronidazole) for 10–14 days; quadruple therapy (+ bismuth) if resistance
  • Proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole) — potent acid suppression; promote healing
  • H2-receptor antagonists (famotidine) — reduce acid
  • Mucosal protectants (sucralfate) — coat ulcer
  • Antacids — symptomatic relief
  • Discontinue NSAIDs; if needed, use COX-2 selective + PPI

Nursing care:

  • Pain assessment and management
  • Monitor for bleeding (vitals, Hgb, stool); be alert for perforation
  • Dietary counseling (avoid triggers)
  • Smoking and alcohol cessation
  • Medication adherence (especially completing H. pylori antibiotics)
  • Stress management

Client Education

  • Complete the entire H. pylori antibiotic course — stopping early causes resistance and treatment failure
  • Take medications as scheduled (PPIs before meals)
  • Avoid NSAIDs, aspirin (use acetaminophen for pain unless directed otherwise)
  • Stop smoking (delays healing, increases recurrence)
  • Limit alcohol and caffeine
  • Avoid trigger foods (individualized — spicy, acidic, fatty if they worsen symptoms)
  • Eat regular meals; avoid eating right before bed
  • Manage stress
  • Report ALARM signs immediately: black/tarry stools, vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, severe sudden abdominal pain, dizziness/fainting
  • Follow up for confirmation of H. pylori eradication if treated
  • Keep follow-up endoscopy appointments (especially gastric ulcers — rule out malignancy)
Worked Example Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) Ch 28 — Peptic Ulcer Disease · Acid suppression section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
GERD
Review Module Chapter
Ch 28 — Peptic Ulcer Disease

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — chronic condition where stomach contents reflux into the esophagus, causing symptoms and/or mucosal damage, due to incompetent lower esophageal sphincter (LES).

  • Very common; affects ~20% of adults
  • Spectrum: occasional heartburn → erosive esophagitis → Barrett’s esophagus (premalignant) → esophageal adenocarcinoma
  • Risk factors: obesity, hiatal hernia, pregnancy, smoking, certain foods, large/late meals, medications that relax LES

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Incompetent or relaxed lower esophageal sphincter (LES) → gastric acid refluxes upward
  • Esophageal mucosa lacks protection against acid → inflammation (esophagitis)
  • Delayed gastric emptying increases reflux
  • Hiatal hernia disrupts the anatomic barrier
  • Chronic acid exposure → metaplasia (Barrett’s esophagus) → increased cancer risk
  • LES-relaxing factors: fatty/spicy foods, caffeine, chocolate, peppermint, alcohol, nicotine, certain meds (CCBs, anticholinergics, nitrates)

Expected Findings

  • Heartburn (pyrosis) — burning retrosternal sensation, often after meals or lying down
  • Regurgitation of sour/bitter material
  • Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing)
  • Chest pain (can mimic cardiac — rule out)
  • Chronic cough, hoarseness, sore throat (laryngopharyngeal reflux)
  • Worsening when supine or bending over
  • Water brash (excess salivation)

Alarm features (warrant endoscopy):

  • Dysphagia, odynophagia (painful swallowing)
  • Weight loss, anemia, GI bleeding
  • Persistent symptoms despite therapy

Diagnostic:

  • Clinical diagnosis often sufficient; PPI trial
  • Upper endoscopy (esophagitis, Barrett’s, complications)
  • Ambulatory pH monitoring; esophageal manometry

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole, esomeprazole) — first-line for moderate-severe; most effective
  • H2-receptor antagonists (famotidine) — mild/intermittent symptoms
  • Antacids — rapid, short-term relief
  • Prokinetics (metoclopramide) — select cases (delayed emptying)

Lifestyle modifications (cornerstone):

  • Weight loss if overweight
  • Elevate head of bed 6–8 inches
  • Avoid eating 2–3 hours before lying down
  • Smaller, more frequent meals
  • Avoid trigger foods
  • Smoking cessation; limit alcohol

Severe/refractory: surgical fundoplication (Nissen).

Client Education

  • Lifestyle changes are essential:
  • Elevate the head of the bed 6–8 inches (blocks/wedge, not just extra pillows)
  • Do not lie down for 2–3 hours after eating
  • Eat smaller, more frequent meals; avoid large/late meals
  • Avoid trigger foods: fatty, fried, spicy, acidic, caffeine, chocolate, peppermint, alcohol, carbonated drinks
  • Lose weight if overweight
  • Stop smoking
  • Avoid tight clothing around the waist
  • Take PPIs 30–60 min before the first meal of the day
  • Report difficulty/pain swallowing, weight loss, vomiting blood, or black stools (need evaluation)
  • Long-term PPI risks (discuss with provider): B12 deficiency, fractures, C. diff, hypomagnesemia — use lowest effective dose
  • Persistent symptoms despite treatment warrant endoscopy (Barrett’s screening)
Worked Example Bupropion Ch 8 — Depressive Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Bupropion
Review Module Chapter
Ch 8 — Depressive Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Atypical antidepressant — inhibits reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine; no significant serotonergic activity

Therapeutic Use

  • Major depressive disorder, seasonal affective disorder
  • Smoking cessation (sustained-release form)
  • Often chosen to avoid SSRI sexual dysfunction/weight gain

Complications

  • Lowers seizure threshold (dose-related)
  • Insomnia, agitation, headache, dry mouth, weight loss
  • Hypertension; no sexual dysfunction (advantage)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Seizure disorder; eating disorders (bulimia/anorexia)
  • Abrupt alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal
  • Concurrent MAOIs; caution: head injury

Interactions

  • MAOIs → hypertensive crisis
  • Drugs that lower seizure threshold → ↑ seizure risk
  • Alcohol → ↑ seizure risk

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ depressive symptoms over weeks
  • Smoking cessation achieved; no seizures

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO; do not exceed recommended dose (seizure risk)
  • Give doses spaced apart; avoid bedtime dosing (insomnia)
  • For smoking cessation, start while still smoking; set a quit date ~1–2 weeks in

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess suicide risk and for seizures
  • Monitor BP, sleep, and weight
  • Reinforce not exceeding the dose; screen for eating disorder history

Client Education

  • Take as prescribed; do not double doses (seizure risk)
  • Avoid alcohol; take earlier in the day to limit insomnia
  • Report mood worsening or any seizure
  • For quitting smoking, continue smoking until the quit date as directed
Worked Example Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) Ch 8 — Depressive Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 8 — Depressive Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) — mood disorder characterized by persistent depressed mood and/or anhedonia plus additional symptoms for ≥ 2 weeks, causing significant impairment.

  • DSM-5 requires ≥ 5 of 9 symptoms (one must be depressed mood OR anhedonia): SIG E CAPS — Sleep changes, Interest loss, Guilt/worthlessness, Energy loss, Concentration impaired, Appetite changes, Psychomotor changes, Suicidality
  • Lifetime prevalence ~17%; twice as common in women
  • Subtypes: melancholic, atypical, peripartum, seasonal, with psychotic features, treatment-resistant
  • High rate of recurrence; comorbid with anxiety, substance use, medical illness

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Monoamine hypothesis: reduced serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine activity
  • HPA axis hyperactivity: elevated cortisol; impaired feedback
  • Neuroplasticity deficits: reduced BDNF; hippocampal volume loss
  • Inflammation hypothesis: elevated inflammatory cytokines
  • Genetic predisposition — heritability ~40%
  • Psychosocial: trauma, loss, chronic stress, social isolation
  • Medical contributors: hypothyroidism, vitamin D/B12 deficiency, chronic pain, neurological disease

Expected Findings

Psychological: depressed mood, anhedonia, hopelessness, worthlessness, guilt, suicidal ideation, concentration difficulty, indecisiveness.

Physical: fatigue, sleep disturbance (insomnia or hypersomnia), appetite/weight changes, psychomotor agitation or retardation, decreased libido, somatic complaints (headache, GI distress).

Severity tools:

  • PHQ-9 (Patient Health Questionnaire): ≥ 10 moderate; ≥ 20 severe
  • Beck Depression Inventory
  • Hamilton Depression Rating Scale

Always assess suicide risk — ideation, plan, intent, means, history.

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy (first-line):

  • SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine) — best tolerated
  • SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine) — effective; may help with pain
  • Atypical: bupropion (no sexual side effects; lowers seizure threshold), mirtazapine (sleep/appetite)
  • TCAs — effective but anticholinergic burden; LETHAL IN OVERDOSE
  • MAOIs — reserved; tyramine diet, drug interactions
  • Augmentation: lithium, atypical antipsychotics, T3
  • Ketamine/esketamine for treatment-resistant depression
  • ECT for severe/refractory cases

Non-pharm:

  • CBT, IPT (interpersonal therapy), behavioral activation
  • Light therapy for seasonal affective disorder
  • Exercise (as effective as medication for mild-moderate)
  • Sleep hygiene, social support

Suicide safety: assess risk every visit; safety plan; lethal-means counseling (restricting access generally, not naming methods); hospitalize if imminent risk; involve trusted support persons.

Client Education

  • Antidepressants take 4–6 weeks for full effect — do not stop early
  • Side effects often improve in 1–2 weeks
  • Do NOT stop abruptly — discontinuation syndrome; taper with provider
  • Black box warning: increased suicidal thoughts in clients < 25 yr in first weeks — closer monitoring needed
  • Avoid alcohol (worsens depression, sedating combination)
  • Engage in therapy alongside medication
  • Identify support system; attend follow-up
  • Crisis line: 988 (Suicide and Crisis Lifeline)
  • Report worsening symptoms, suicidal thoughts, unusual bleeding, or signs of serotonin syndrome
Worked Example Phenelzine (MAOI) Ch 8 — Depressive Disorders · MAOIs section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Phenelzine (Nardil)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 8 — Depressive Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) — non-selective, irreversibly inhibits MAO-A and MAO-B enzymes
  • Prevents breakdown of serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine → increased synaptic levels
  • Tyramine (from food) is normally broken down by MAO in the GI tract — MAOI blocks this, allowing tyramine accumulation → hypertensive crisis

Therapeutic Use

  • Treatment-resistant depression (third- or fourth-line; rarely first-line due to dietary/drug restrictions)
  • Atypical depression (mood reactivity, hypersomnia, weight gain, sensitivity to rejection)
  • Panic disorder, social phobia
  • Selegiline (selective MAO-B inhibitor) used for Parkinson’s disease

Complications

  • Hypertensive crisis — from tyramine-rich foods or sympathomimetic drugs (severe headache, palpitations, neck stiffness, blurred vision, chest pain, sweating, intracranial hemorrhage, death)
  • Serotonin syndrome — with serotonergic agents (SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, tramadol, triptans, meperidine, dextromethorphan, St. John’s wort)
  • Orthostatic hypotension (paradoxical — common at therapeutic doses)
  • Sexual dysfunction
  • Weight gain, insomnia, peripheral edema
  • Suicidality (FDA black box warning, especially < 25 yr)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Pheochromocytoma, severe cardiovascular disease, hepatic/renal impairment
  • Recent stroke or CHF
  • Concurrent serotonergic medications (require 2-week washout; 5 weeks for fluoxetine)
  • Sympathomimetic exposure (OTC cold meds, recreational stimulants)
  • Pregnancy — avoid; lactation — avoid
  • Inability to follow strict tyramine-restricted diet

Interactions

  • Tyramine-rich foods: aged cheeses, cured/smoked meats, fermented foods (sauerkraut, soy sauce, miso), red wine, draft/tap beer, fava beans, overripe bananas, smoked fish
  • Serotonergic drugs (any) → serotonin syndrome
  • Sympathomimetics (pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine, dopamine, epinephrine) → hypertensive crisis
  • Meperidine → severe reactions (fatal); use fentanyl or morphine instead
  • Alcohol — avoid (some beers/wines contain tyramine)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Improved mood, sleep, appetite, and energy within 2–4 weeks
  • PHQ-9 score reduction
  • Absence of hypertensive crisis or serotonin syndrome events
  • Adherence to dietary restrictions (key indicator of successful management)

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral
  • Adult dose: 15 mg PO TID, titrate to 60–90 mg/day
  • Take with food to reduce GI upset
  • Therapeutic effect: 2–4 weeks
  • Effects PERSIST 2 weeks after discontinuation (irreversible MAOI) — dietary and drug restrictions continue 2 weeks after stopping

Nursing Interventions

  • Verify dietary restrictions are understood BEFORE starting
  • Comprehensive medication reconciliation including OTC and herbal — no serotonergic or sympathomimetic agents
  • Monitor BP at baseline and regularly
  • Provide written list of foods and drugs to avoid
  • Assess suicide risk at every visit
  • Monitor for hypertensive crisis: severe headache, chest pain — emergency BP-lowering with phentolamine if confirmed
  • Have phentolamine available in inpatient settings

Client Education

  • Strict tyramine-restricted diet — continue 2 weeks AFTER discontinuation
  • Avoid: aged cheeses, cured meats, fermented foods, red wine, tap beer, soy sauce, fava beans, overripe bananas
  • Notify all healthcare providers and pharmacists about MAOI use
  • Avoid all OTC cold/cough/allergy/decongestant medications (consult pharmacist for safe alternatives like saline spray, antihistamines may be OK)
  • Carry MAOI alert card or wear medical alert ID
  • Report immediately: severe headache, chest pain, palpitations, neck stiffness, vision changes (signs of hypertensive crisis — emergency)
  • Rise slowly to prevent orthostatic dizziness
  • Do not abruptly discontinue — taper
Worked Example Suicide Risk Assessment in Depression Ch 8 — Depressive Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Suicide Risk Assessment in Depression

Defining Characteristics

Suicide risk assessment is the systematic clinical evaluation of a client’s risk for suicide attempt or death by suicide, with a focus on identifying protective factors and implementing safety interventions.

Core elements: assess ideation (thoughts), intent (commitment to act), plan (specifics), and protective factors. Direct, compassionate questioning does NOT increase risk — it opens needed conversation.

Standardized tools include Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS), PHQ-9 item 9, and SAFE-T (Suicide Assessment Five-step Evaluation and Triage).

Antecedents

  • Active depression, particularly with hopelessness, severe anhedonia, or mixed/agitated features
  • Comorbid conditions: anxiety, PTSD, substance use, chronic pain, serious medical illness
  • Previous suicide attempts (strongest single risk factor)
  • Family history of suicide
  • Recent loss (relationship, job, health, identity)
  • Social isolation, lack of support
  • Recent psychiatric hospitalization (discharge period is high risk)
  • Sleep deprivation (energy returns before mood lifts)
  • Initial weeks on antidepressant therapy (especially < 25 yo — FDA black box)

Negative Consequences

  • Death by suicide — preventable cause of death; ~700,000+ deaths globally per year
  • Long-term psychological impact on family and survivors
  • Missed opportunities for intervention when warning signs not recognized or addressed
  • Re-attempts — risk highest in first months after an attempt
  • Nurse moral distress and trauma
  • Public health burden

Related Concepts

Depression severity, hopelessness, protective factors, lethal-means counseling (general, not method-specific), safety planning, no-suicide contracts (limited evidence; safety plans preferred), suicide precautions (1:1 observation, environmental safety), crisis intervention, 988 Crisis Lifeline, postvention.

Exemplars

  • Direct questions to ask: “Sometimes when people feel this badly, they have thoughts of suicide. Have you been having any thoughts like that?” — assess ideation, intent, plan, prior attempts.
  • Protective factors to assess: reasons for living, social support, religious/cultural beliefs against suicide, responsibility to family/pets, fear of death, future-orientation, engagement in treatment.
  • Imminent risk response: do not leave client alone; remove access to harmful items from the environment; psychiatric evaluation; hospitalization if needed.
  • Safety planning (collaborative document with client):
    • Recognize warning signs
    • Identify coping strategies
    • List people and social settings that provide distraction
    • List trusted contacts to call when in crisis
    • Professional contacts and emergency resources (988)
    • Plan for restricting access to means generally (kept general, not naming methods)
  • Lethal-means counseling: work with client and family to restrict access to potentially harmful items in the environment — framed generally, not naming specific methods.
  • Avoid: dismissing statements (“you don’t mean that”), arguing with hopelessness, making promises that can’t be kept, breaking confidentiality unnecessarily (but always break confidentiality when safety requires).
  • 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline — available 24/7 by call or text. Veterans Crisis Line: 988 then press 1.
Worked Example Valproic Acid Ch 9 — Bipolar Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Valproic Acid
Review Module Chapter
Ch 9 — Bipolar Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Mood stabilizer/antiepileptic — increases GABA and stabilizes neuronal membranes

Therapeutic Use

  • Bipolar disorder (acute mania, maintenance)
  • Seizure disorders; migraine prophylaxis

Complications

  • GI upset, sedation, tremor, weight gain
  • Hepatotoxicity and pancreatitis
  • Thrombocytopenia; teratogenic (neural tube defects)
  • Hyperammonemia

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hepatic disease
  • Pregnancy (neural tube defects)
  • Urea cycle disorders; caution: bleeding/platelet issues

Interactions

  • Other hepatotoxic drugs → ↑ liver injury
  • Aspirin → ↑ free valproate level
  • Lamotrigine → ↑ rash risk; warfarin → ↑ bleeding

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Stabilized mood / seizure control
  • Therapeutic level 50–125 mcg/mL; normal LFTs and platelets

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO (do not crush ER); give with food to reduce GI upset
  • Monitor serum levels, LFTs, platelets, and ammonia
  • Baseline and periodic labs; pregnancy screening

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor LFTs, platelets, drug levels, and for pancreatitis (abdominal pain, vomiting)
  • Assess for bruising/bleeding and sedation
  • Educate on teratogenic risk and contraception

Client Education

  • Report abdominal pain, vomiting, yellowing of skin/eyes (liver/pancreas)
  • Report unusual bruising or bleeding
  • Use reliable contraception; do not stop abruptly
  • Take with food; keep all lab appointments
Worked Example Disulfiram Ch 12 — Substance Use Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Disulfiram
Review Module Chapter
Ch 12 — Substance Use Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Alcohol deterrent — inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase so that drinking alcohol causes a buildup of acetaldehyde, producing a highly unpleasant reaction

Therapeutic Use

  • Maintenance of abstinence in alcohol use disorder (adjunct to counseling/support)

Complications

  • If alcohol is consumed: flushing, throbbing headache, nausea/vomiting, tachycardia, hypotension, dyspnea (can be severe)
  • Drowsiness, metallic/garlic taste; rare hepatotoxicity, neuropathy

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Recent alcohol intake (within 12 hr); use of alcohol-containing products
  • Severe cardiac disease, psychosis
  • Pregnancy; concurrent metronidazole

Interactions

  • Any alcohol (including OTC cough syrups, mouthwash, aftershave, sauces) → disulfiram-alcohol reaction
  • Metronidazole → psychosis/confusion
  • Warfarin, phenytoin → ↑ levels

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Maintained sobriety; client engaged in a recovery program
  • No accidental disulfiram-alcohol reactions

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO once daily
  • Start only after ≥ 12 hr alcohol-free
  • Effects (with alcohol) can occur up to 2 weeks after stopping the drug
  • Most effective combined with counseling and support

Nursing Interventions

  • Confirm the client understands the reaction and is motivated/abstinent
  • Teach avoidance of all hidden alcohol sources
  • Monitor LFTs; reinforce support program participation

Client Education

  • Avoid ALL alcohol — including mouthwash, cough syrup, vinegar, aftershave, hand sanitizer
  • A reaction can occur up to 2 weeks after the last dose
  • Wear medical identification
  • Take daily as part of a recovery plan; report yellowing skin or numbness/tingling
Worked Example Naltrexone Ch 12 — Substance Use Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Naltrexone
Review Module Chapter
Ch 12 — Substance Use Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Opioid antagonist — blocks opioid receptors, reducing the rewarding effects and cravings of alcohol and opioids

Therapeutic Use

  • Alcohol use disorder and opioid use disorder (maintenance of abstinence)

Complications

  • Nausea, headache, dizziness, fatigue
  • Hepatotoxicity (high doses)
  • Precipitates withdrawal if opioids are present; loss of opioid tolerance → overdose risk if relapse

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Current opioid use / acute opioid withdrawal (must be opioid-free ~7–10 days)
  • Acute hepatitis or liver failure
  • Caution: hepatic impairment

Interactions

  • Opioids → blocked analgesia and precipitated withdrawal
  • Other hepatotoxic drugs → ↑ liver injury

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ cravings; maintained abstinence
  • Engagement in recovery program; normal LFTs

Medication Administration

  • Routes: PO daily or monthly IM depot (extended-release) for adherence
  • Confirm opioid-free status before starting
  • Monitor LFTs; combine with counseling/support

Nursing Interventions

  • Verify no recent opioid use before initiating
  • Monitor liver function and for withdrawal
  • Educate on reduced opioid tolerance and overdose risk if relapse
  • Promote adherence (consider IM form)

Client Education

  • Must be opioid-free before starting (avoids withdrawal)
  • If you relapse, your tolerance is lower — overdose risk is high
  • Carry medical identification (opioid analgesics will be blocked)
  • Report yellowing skin, dark urine, or abdominal pain; continue counseling
Worked Example Naloxone (Narcan) Ch 12 — Substance Use Disorders · Opioid section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Naloxone (Narcan, Evzio)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 12 — Substance Use Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Pure opioid receptor antagonist — competitively binds to mu, kappa, delta opioid receptors
  • Rapidly reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression, sedation, and analgesia
  • Onset: 1–3 min IV/IM/IN; duration 30–90 min (often SHORTER than the opioid causing overdose — redose required)

Therapeutic Use

  • Opioid overdose — reversal of respiratory depression (FIRST-LINE emergency)
  • Suspected opioid overdose in unresponsive client
  • Iatrogenic opioid overdose (post-op, PCA error)
  • Reversal of opioid sedation when needed (e.g., for procedure completion)
  • Available OTC for layperson use to reverse community overdose

Complications

  • Precipitated opioid withdrawal — in opioid-dependent clients: agitation, nausea/vomiting, diarrhea, sweating, tachycardia, hypertension, severe pain
  • Acute pain return in clients with chronic opioid pain management
  • Rare: pulmonary edema, ventricular arrhythmias (especially with rapid reversal in cardiac clients)
  • RE-NARCOTIZATION — opioid effects can return when naloxone wears off; client may relapse into respiratory depression

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to naloxone
  • Caution in opioid-dependent clients (precipitates withdrawal)
  • Caution in chronic pain clients (reverses analgesia)
  • Pregnancy: use if benefits outweigh risks (will precipitate withdrawal in fetus of opioid-dependent mother)
  • Cardiac disease — rapid reversal may cause hemodynamic stress

Interactions

  • All opioids — reverses effects (morphine, fentanyl, oxycodone, hydromorphone, methadone, heroin)
  • Buprenorphine — may require higher dose due to high-affinity binding
  • Mixed agonist-antagonists (pentazocine, butorphanol) — partial reversal
  • No significant CYP450 interactions; no clinically significant drug interactions otherwise

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Return of spontaneous breathing (RR ≥ 12)
  • Increased responsiveness, arousal
  • Reversal of pinpoint pupils
  • Sustained reversal — no relapse into respiratory depression
  • Continued monitoring for at least 2–4 hours after the longest-acting opioid effect would normally last

Medication Administration

  • Routes: IV (preferred in healthcare), IM, SC, intranasal (community use), sublingual
  • Adult initial dose: 0.4–2 mg IV/IM/SC; repeat every 2–3 min as needed (max 10 mg if no response — reconsider diagnosis)
  • Intranasal (Narcan): 4 mg (one spray) per nostril; alternate nostrils for repeat doses every 2–3 min
  • Pediatric: 0.1 mg/kg IV/IM; up to adult dose
  • IV infusion may be needed for long-acting opioids (methadone, sustained-release formulations)
  • Stable at room temperature; protect from light

Nursing Interventions

  • Activate emergency response immediately for suspected overdose
  • Position: lateral recovery position to prevent aspiration
  • Establish airway, provide bag-valve-mask ventilation if needed
  • Administer naloxone per protocol; redose every 2–3 min until response or max
  • Monitor closely for at least 2–4 hours — opioid effect may outlast naloxone (re-narcotization)
  • For long-acting opioids (methadone, ER formulations): admit and consider naloxone IV infusion
  • Anticipate withdrawal in dependent clients: have IV access, antiemetics, anxiolytics ready
  • Connect to substance use treatment after stabilization

Client Education

  • For families/contacts of opioid users: obtain and learn to use naloxone (OTC in most states)
  • Recognize overdose: slow/no breathing, blue/gray skin, unresponsive, pinpoint pupils
  • Call 911 IMMEDIATELY after administering naloxone — effect is temporary
  • Roll person to side after dosing (recovery position)
  • Be prepared for the person to be confused/upset on waking
  • Multiple doses may be needed for synthetic opioids (fentanyl)
  • Naloxone is safe even if opioid use is uncertain — can’t hurt; can save a life
  • Good Samaritan laws protect those who call for help
  • Discuss with provider: substance use treatment options after this crisis
Worked Example Buprenorphine / Suboxone Ch 12 — Substance Use Disorders · Opioid section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Buprenorphine (Subutex) / Buprenorphine-Naloxone (Suboxone)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 12 — Substance Use Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Partial mu-opioid receptor agonist — relieves cravings and prevents withdrawal without producing the full opioid “high”
  • Ceiling effect — respiratory depression plateaus at higher doses, making it safer than methadone
  • Suboxone combines buprenorphine + naloxone — naloxone is inactive sublingually but causes withdrawal if injected (anti-diversion)

Therapeutic Use

  • Opioid Use Disorder (OUD) — induction, stabilization, and maintenance
  • Medication-Assisted Treatment (MAT) in office-based settings
  • Withdrawal management (less intense than going cold-turkey)
  • Chronic pain (less common indication)

Complications

  • Precipitated withdrawal — if started before opioid has cleared (must wait until client is in mild-moderate withdrawal: COWS ≥ 8)
  • Respiratory depression (lower risk than full agonists due to ceiling effect; combine with benzos → danger)
  • Dependence (physical dependence develops; tapering required to stop)
  • QT prolongation (high doses, especially methadone interaction)
  • Constipation (typical opioid effect)
  • Hepatotoxicity (rare; monitor LFTs)
  • Neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS) in pregnancy — less severe than methadone NAS

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to buprenorphine or naloxone
  • Severe hepatic impairment
  • Concurrent use of full opioid agonists (may precipitate withdrawal OR additive sedation)
  • Concurrent benzodiazepines/alcohol (risk of fatal respiratory depression)
  • Pregnancy: buprenorphine alone (Subutex) preferred over Suboxone in pregnancy
  • Mental health crisis without close monitoring

Interactions

  • CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, alcohol, sedatives) — fatal respiratory depression risk
  • CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, ritonavir, clarithromycin) — raise buprenorphine levels
  • CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin) — lower levels; may precipitate withdrawal
  • Other opioids — partial agonism can displace full agonists and cause withdrawal
  • Naltrexone — will precipitate severe withdrawal

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Reduced cravings and use of illicit opioids
  • Improved functional status (work, relationships, self-care)
  • Negative urine drug screens for illicit opioids
  • Stable dose without diversion or misuse
  • Engagement in counseling and recovery support
  • Reduced overdose risk in OUD population

Medication Administration

  • Routes: sublingual (tablets, films), subdermal implant (Probuphine 6-month), monthly SC injection (Sublocade)
  • Induction: wait until COWS ≥ 8 (mild-moderate withdrawal) before first dose to avoid precipitated withdrawal; start 2–4 mg; titrate to 8–16 mg day 1
  • Maintenance: 8–24 mg sublingually once daily (typical 16 mg)
  • SL administration: place under tongue; let dissolve completely; do not chew or swallow whole; no eating/drinking for 5–10 min after
  • Schedule III — restricted prescribing; requires DEA X-waiver (recently broadened access)

Nursing Interventions

  • Verify withdrawal severity (COWS scale) before induction
  • Baseline: LFTs, HIV, hepatitis screen, pregnancy test (in childbearing age)
  • Observed dosing during induction; titrate based on COWS reduction
  • Naloxone available for emergency reversal (high dose may be needed due to high affinity)
  • Monitor for signs of diversion (asking for early refills, multiple prescribers)
  • Coordinate counseling and behavioral therapy (MAT is more than just medication)
  • Educate family on signs of overdose and naloxone use

Client Education

  • Take sublingually exactly as prescribed; do not swallow, chew, or snort/inject (precipitates withdrawal)
  • Allow tablet/film to dissolve completely; no eating/drinking for 5–10 min
  • Do NOT combine with alcohol, benzodiazepines, or other sedatives (fatal)
  • Do not stop abruptly — taper with provider to prevent withdrawal
  • Continue counseling/support groups — MAT works best with behavioral treatment
  • Naloxone access: keep available for emergency overdose reversal
  • Carry medication ID card; inform all providers about MAT
  • Pregnancy: discuss with provider; Subutex preferred
  • Recovery is a process; relapse does not mean failure; reach out for help
Worked Example Alcohol Withdrawal Management (CIWA-Ar) Ch 12 — Substance Use Disorders · Alcohol section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure
Alcohol Withdrawal Management (CIWA-Ar Protocol)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 12 — Substance Use Disorders

Description of Procedure

Management of alcohol withdrawal syndrome using the CIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, revised) protocol — a symptom-triggered or scheduled dosing approach to prevent and treat alcohol withdrawal.

CIWA-Ar is a 10-item scale (max score 67) assessing: nausea/vomiting, tremor, sweats, anxiety, agitation, tactile/auditory/visual disturbances, headache, orientation. Scores guide benzodiazepine dosing.

  • < 10: mild withdrawal — supportive care only
  • 10–19: moderate — symptom-triggered benzo dosing
  • ≥ 20: severe — aggressive treatment, ICU consideration, scheduled benzo dosing

Indications

  • Hospitalized client with history of heavy alcohol use and stopping/reducing intake
  • Last drink within ~6–48 hours (withdrawal onset)
  • Symptoms: tremor, anxiety, autonomic hyperactivity (tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis)
  • Prevention of progression to seizures, delirium tremens (DTs), Wernicke encephalopathy
  • Planned detoxification before rehabilitation

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre (assessment):

  • Alcohol use history: amount, frequency, last drink time, prior withdrawal history (seizures, DTs)
  • Baseline vital signs, mental status
  • Labs: CBC, BMP, magnesium, phosphate, LFTs, ammonia, urine drug screen
  • Assess for Wernicke risk: nystagmus, ataxia, confusion
  • Administer thiamine 100 mg IV/IM BEFORE giving any glucose (prevents Wernicke); also folate, multivitamin

Intra (treatment per CIWA-Ar):

  • Assess CIWA-Ar every 1–4 hours; more frequently if score increasing
  • Benzodiazepines first-line: chlordiazepoxide (long-acting, smooth taper) or lorazepam (preferred in liver disease — not metabolized by liver)
  • Symptom-triggered: give benzo dose when CIWA ≥ 8–10; reassess in 1 hr
  • Adjunct: alpha-2 agonist (clonidine, dexmedetomidine) for autonomic symptoms; antipsychotic (haloperidol) for hallucinations (NOT instead of benzos)
  • Hydration with IV fluids if dehydrated; correct electrolytes (especially magnesium)
  • Monitor for seizures (peak 24–48 hr); DTs (peak 48–96 hr): severe agitation, hallucinations, autonomic instability
  • Maintain quiet environment; orient frequently

Post:

  • Transition to outpatient: motivational interviewing, referral to AA/treatment program
  • Maintenance medications: naltrexone, acamprosate, disulfiram
  • Address underlying co-occurring mental health, social issues
  • Family/support involvement

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • CIWA-Ar score decreases over 48–72 hours
  • No seizures, DTs, or Wernicke encephalopathy
  • Stable vital signs return to baseline
  • Client tolerates oral intake; electrolytes normalize
  • Engagement in continued treatment plan
  • Safe transition to outpatient or rehab setting

Potential Complications

  • Withdrawal seizures — typically tonic-clonic, single or in flurries; peak 12–48 hr; require IV benzo
  • Delirium Tremens (DTs) — severe withdrawal: confusion, hallucinations, autonomic instability, fever; mortality 5–15% without treatment; peak 48–96 hr
  • Wernicke encephalopathy (thiamine deficiency) — triad: confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia; can progress to permanent Korsakoff psychosis
  • Aspiration pneumonia from altered mental status
  • Trauma from falls during agitation/confusion
  • Cardiac arrhythmias from electrolyte imbalance and autonomic surges
  • Hypoglycemia, especially if thiamine delayed
  • Over-sedation from benzodiazepines (respiratory depression)
Worked Example Metoclopramide Ch 29 — Gastrointestinal Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Metoclopramide
Review Module Chapter
Ch 29 — Gastrointestinal Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Prokinetic / antiemetic — blocks dopamine (and at higher doses serotonin) receptors; increases upper GI motility and gastric emptying

Therapeutic Use

  • Gastroparesis (especially diabetic), GERD
  • Nausea/vomiting (chemotherapy, postoperative)

Complications

  • Extrapyramidal symptoms and tardive dyskinesia (black box — limit to ≤ 12 weeks)
  • Sedation, restlessness, diarrhea
  • Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (rare)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • GI obstruction, perforation, or hemorrhage
  • Pheochromocytoma, seizure disorder
  • Parkinson disease; caution: older adults, depression

Interactions

  • Other dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics) → ↑ EPS
  • CNS depressants/alcohol → ↑ sedation
  • Affects absorption/timing of other oral drugs

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ nausea/vomiting; improved gastric emptying (less bloating, early satiety)
  • No EPS or tardive dyskinesia

Medication Administration

  • Routes: PO (before meals and at bedtime), IV, IM
  • Limit duration to ≤ 12 weeks (tardive dyskinesia risk)
  • Give 30 min before meals for gastroparesis

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess for EPS/tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements)
  • Limit treatment duration; monitor for sedation
  • Give before meals; assess GI symptom relief

Client Education

  • Take before meals as directed; limit to prescribed duration
  • Report involuntary movements (face, tongue, limbs) immediately
  • Avoid alcohol; report restlessness or muscle stiffness
  • May cause drowsiness — use caution driving
Worked Example Loperamide (Imodium) Ch 29 — Gastrointestinal Disorders · Other section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Loperamide (Imodium)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 29 — Gastrointestinal Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Antidiarrheal — opioid receptor agonist acting locally on intestinal mu-receptors
  • Slows intestinal motility → increases transit time → more water/electrolyte reabsorption → firmer stools
  • Does NOT cross blood-brain barrier at normal doses (no central opioid/analgesic effects)
  • Reduces stool frequency and volume

Therapeutic Use

  • Acute nonspecific diarrhea
  • Chronic diarrhea (IBS-D, IBD — with caution)
  • Reduce ostomy output
  • Traveler’s diarrhea (with caution)

Complications

  • Constipation (most common)
  • Toxic megacolon — in infectious/inflammatory colitis (C. diff, ulcerative colitis); slowing motility traps toxins/bacteria
  • Cardiac arrhythmias / QT prolongation at high (abuse) doses — FDA warning; torsades, cardiac arrest
  • Abdominal cramping, bloating, nausea
  • Dizziness, drowsiness
  • Paralytic ileus

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Bloody diarrhea or high fever (suspected invasive bacterial infection — do not slow clearance)
  • C. difficile or pseudomembranous colitis (toxic megacolon risk)
  • Acute ulcerative colitis flare (toxic megacolon)
  • Children < 2 years
  • Known QT prolongation
  • Do not use for abuse/euphoria (cardiotoxic at high doses)

Interactions

  • CYP3A4/CYP2C8 inhibitors (ritonavir, gemfibrozil, ketoconazole) — increase loperamide levels
  • P-glycoprotein inhibitors (quinidine) — may allow CNS penetration (opioid effects)
  • QT-prolonging drugs — additive arrhythmia risk
  • Other CNS depressants — additive drowsiness (high doses)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Reduced stool frequency and improved consistency
  • Resolution of diarrhea
  • Maintained hydration and electrolyte balance
  • No constipation, ileus, or toxic megacolon
  • No cardiac effects (used appropriately)

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (capsule, tablet, liquid)
  • Adult: 4 mg initially, then 2 mg after each loose stool; max 8 mg/day OTC (16 mg/day Rx)
  • Do not exceed recommended dose (cardiac risk)
  • Take with adequate fluids
  • OTC available; counsel on appropriate use

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess cause of diarrhea — do NOT use if infectious (bloody stool, fever) or C. diff suspected
  • Monitor stool frequency, consistency, hydration, electrolytes
  • Assess for abdominal distension (ileus, megacolon)
  • Monitor for cardiac effects if high doses suspected
  • Educate on max dose (cardiotoxicity with overuse/abuse)
  • Encourage oral rehydration
  • Reassess if diarrhea persists > 48 hr (needs evaluation)

Client Education

  • Take as directed; do NOT exceed the maximum dose — high doses can cause serious heart rhythm problems
  • Do NOT use if you have bloody stools or high fever — see a provider
  • Stay hydrated; use oral rehydration solutions
  • Stop and seek care if diarrhea lasts more than 48 hours, abdominal swelling, or no improvement
  • Report severe constipation or abdominal distension
  • Avoid alcohol
  • Keep out of reach of children
  • This medication treats symptoms, not the cause — persistent diarrhea needs evaluation
Worked Example Inflammatory Bowel Disease (Crohn’s / Ulcerative Colitis) Ch 29 — Gastrointestinal Disorders · Other section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 29 — Gastrointestinal Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) — chronic, relapsing autoimmune inflammation of the GI tract. Two main types:

  • Crohn’s disease: can affect ANY part of GI tract (mouth to anus); transmural (full-thickness); “skip lesions” (patchy); commonly terminal ileum
  • Ulcerative colitis (UC): affects ONLY the colon and rectum; continuous mucosal/submucosal inflammation starting at rectum; no skip lesions

Chronic course with flares and remissions. Onset often young adulthood. Increased colorectal cancer risk (especially UC).

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Dysregulated immune response to gut microbiota in genetically susceptible individuals
  • Chronic inflammation damages the intestinal wall
  • Crohn’s: transmural inflammation → strictures, fistulas, abscesses, “cobblestone” mucosa
  • UC: superficial continuous inflammation → ulcerations, friable mucosa, pseudopolyps
  • Contributing factors: genetics (NOD2/CARD15), environment, smoking (worsens Crohn’s, paradoxically protective in UC), altered microbiome, immune dysregulation

Expected Findings

Crohn’s disease:

  • Abdominal pain (often RLQ), often non-bloody diarrhea
  • Weight loss, malnutrition, malabsorption (B12, fat-soluble vitamins)
  • Fistulas, perianal disease, strictures, abscesses
  • Fewer bloody stools than UC

Ulcerative colitis:

  • Bloody diarrhea with mucus (hallmark)
  • Lower abdominal cramping, urgency, tenesmus
  • Frequent small-volume stools
  • Weight loss, fatigue

Both: fever, fatigue, extraintestinal manifestations (arthritis, uveitis, erythema nodosum, primary sclerosing cholangitis).

Diagnostic: colonoscopy with biopsy, CT/MR enterography (Crohn’s), labs (CRP, ESR, fecal calprotectin, anemia), stool studies to exclude infection.

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy (step-up):

  • 5-aminosalicylates (sulfasalazine, mesalamine) — mild-moderate UC; maintenance
  • Corticosteroids (prednisone, budesonide) — acute flares (short-term; not maintenance)
  • Immunomodulators (azathioprine, methotrexate) — steroid-sparing maintenance
  • Biologics (infliximab, adalimumab — anti-TNF; vedolizumab; ustekinumab) — moderate-severe
  • Antibiotics (metronidazole, ciprofloxacin) for Crohn’s complications
  • Antidiarrheals — with CAUTION (toxic megacolon risk in active UC)

Nursing care:

  • Monitor bowel pattern, hydration, electrolytes, nutrition, weight
  • Assess for complications: toxic megacolon, perforation, obstruction, hemorrhage
  • Nutritional support (may need TPN in severe Crohn’s); vitamin supplementation
  • Monitor for medication side effects (immunosuppression → infection)
  • Skin/ostomy care if surgical
  • Emotional support (chronic disease, body image)
  • Surgery: colectomy can cure UC; Crohn’s recurs

Client Education

  • IBD is a chronic, relapsing condition — adherence to maintenance therapy reduces flares
  • Do not stop medications during remission without provider guidance
  • Recognize flare symptoms; report increased pain, bleeding, fever, dehydration
  • Dietary management: identify trigger foods; low-residue diet during flares; adequate protein/calories; stay hydrated
  • Vitamin/mineral supplementation (B12 for Crohn’s ileal disease, iron, calcium/vitamin D with steroids)
  • Smoking cessation (especially Crohn’s)
  • Biologics/immunomodulators increase infection risk: report fever, signs of infection; stay current on vaccines (no live vaccines while immunosuppressed)
  • Regular colonoscopy surveillance (increased colorectal cancer risk)
  • Stress management (can trigger flares)
  • Support groups (Crohn’s & Colitis Foundation)
  • Ostomy education if surgical
Worked Example Nausea & Vomiting Management Ch 29 — Gastrointestinal Disorders · Overview section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Nausea & Vomiting Management

Defining Characteristics

Nausea and vomiting are protective reflexes coordinated by the vomiting center in the medulla, triggered by multiple pathways. Antiemetic selection targets the responsible pathway/receptor.

Major trigger pathways and receptors:

  • Chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ): dopamine (D2), serotonin (5-HT3), neurokinin (NK1) — drugs, toxins, chemo
  • GI tract: 5-HT3 (vagal) — chemo, irritants
  • Vestibular system: histamine (H1), muscarinic (ACh) — motion sickness
  • Cerebral cortex: anticipatory, anxiety

Antecedents

  • Chemotherapy and radiation
  • Post-operative state (anesthesia, opioids)
  • Pregnancy (morning sickness, hyperemesis gravidarum)
  • Motion sickness
  • GI disorders (gastroenteritis, obstruction, gastroparesis)
  • Medications (opioids, antibiotics)
  • Metabolic (uremia, DKA), increased ICP, vestibular disorders
  • Anxiety, anticipatory triggers

Negative Consequences

  • Dehydration and electrolyte imbalances (hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis from loss of gastric acid)
  • Aspiration pneumonia (especially with reduced consciousness)
  • Malnutrition, weight loss
  • Mallory-Weiss tear (esophageal) from forceful vomiting
  • Poor adherence to needed treatments (e.g., chemo) due to distress
  • Reduced quality of life
  • Wound dehiscence (post-op straining)

Related Concepts

Chemoreceptor trigger zone, 5-HT3 antagonists (ondansetron), dopamine antagonists (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine), NK1 antagonists (aprepitant), antihistamines (promethazine, meclizine), anticholinergics (scopolamine), corticosteroids (dexamethasone), cannabinoids, fluid/electrolyte balance, aspiration precautions.

Exemplars

  • 5-HT3 antagonists (ondansetron): first-line for chemo-induced and post-op N/V; watch QT prolongation, constipation, headache
  • Dopamine antagonists (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine): CTZ + prokinetic (metoclopramide); risk of EPS and tardive dyskinesia
  • NK1 antagonists (aprepitant): delayed chemo-induced N/V; combined with 5-HT3 + steroid
  • Antihistamines/anticholinergics (meclizine, scopolamine patch): motion sickness, vestibular; drowsiness, anticholinergic effects
  • Corticosteroids (dexamethasone): adjunct for chemo N/V
  • Pregnancy: pyridoxine (B6) +/- doxylamine first-line; ondansetron with caution
  • Chemo regimen: often 5-HT3 + dexamethasone + NK1 antagonist for highly emetogenic chemo
  • Nursing care: assess hydration/electrolytes, give antiemetics PROPHYLACTICALLY before known triggers (chemo, surgery), aspiration precautions (position on side if vomiting), small bland meals, oral care, quiet environment, monitor I&O
Worked Example Ferrous Sulfate Ch 30 — Vitamins and Minerals · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Ferrous Sulfate
Review Module Chapter
Ch 30 — Vitamins and Minerals
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Oral iron supplement — provides elemental iron needed for hemoglobin synthesis and oxygen transport

Therapeutic Use

  • Prevention/treatment of iron-deficiency anemia

Complications

  • GI: constipation, nausea, epigastric pain, dark/black stools (harmless)
  • Teeth staining (liquid forms)
  • Overdose is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in children

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hemochromatosis/iron overload, hemolytic anemia
  • Peptic ulcer disease, ulcerative colitis (caution)

Interactions

  • Antacids, PPIs, dairy, calcium, tea/coffee → ↓ iron absorption
  • Vitamin C → ↑ absorption
  • Reduces absorption of tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, levothyroxine

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↑ hemoglobin, hematocrit, and reticulocytes; ↑ energy
  • Resolution of anemia symptoms

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, ideally on an empty stomach (take with food if GI upset)
  • Take with vitamin C / orange juice to enhance absorption
  • Use a straw for liquid forms; separate from antacids/dairy/other drugs by ≥ 2 hr

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess hemoglobin/hematocrit response
  • Manage constipation (fluids, fiber)
  • Store safely away from children (overdose risk)

Client Education

  • Take on an empty stomach with vitamin C; expect dark stools (normal)
  • Increase fluids and fiber to prevent constipation
  • Keep away from children (poisoning danger)
  • Separate from antacids, dairy, and tea/coffee by 1–2 hr
Worked Example Potassium Chloride Supplement Ch 30 — Vitamins and Minerals · Minerals section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Potassium Chloride (KCl)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 30 — Vitamins and Minerals
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Electrolyte supplement — replaces potassium, essential for cardiac rhythm, neuromuscular function, and acid-base balance
  • Potassium is the major intracellular cation
  • Normal serum: 3.5–5.0 mEq/L
  • HIGH-ALERT MEDICATION (ISMP)

Therapeutic Use

  • Hypokalemia — from diuretics (loop/thiazide), GI losses (vomiting, diarrhea), DKA treatment
  • Prevention of hypokalemia in at-risk clients
  • Maintenance with potassium-wasting medications

Complications

  • Hyperkalemia — peaked T-waves, widened QRS, bradycardia, cardiac arrest (especially if given too fast/too much or renal impairment)
  • GI irritation — nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, GI ulceration/bleeding (oral)
  • IV: phlebitis, pain at site; FATAL ARRHYTHMIA if given IV push
