  • Cardiac arrhythmias

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hyperkalemia (existing)
  • Severe renal impairment / oliguria (cannot excrete)
  • Concurrent potassium-sparing diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs (hyperkalemia risk)
  • Addison’s disease
  • Severe dehydration
  • GI obstruction or delayed transit (oral — ulceration)

Interactions

  • Potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone), ACE inhibitors, ARBs — additive hyperkalemia
  • NSAIDs — reduce potassium excretion
  • Salt substitutes (contain potassium) — additive
  • Digoxin — both hypo- and hyperkalemia affect digoxin toxicity

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Serum potassium returns to normal (3.5–5.0 mEq/L)
  • Resolution of hypokalemia symptoms (weakness, arrhythmias, cramps)
  • Normal EKG
  • No hyperkalemia
  • No GI ulceration (oral) or phlebitis (IV)

Medication Administration

  • Oral: take WITH food and a full glass of water; do not crush ER tablets; dilute liquid/effervescent forms
  • IV: NEVER give IV push or bolus — FATAL. Always DILUTE and give as slow infusion
  • IV rate: generally ≤ 10 mEq/hr on a general floor (higher only in ICU with continuous cardiac monitoring)
  • Maximum concentration limits per policy; use infusion pump
  • NEVER concentrated KCl on floor stock (removed for safety)
  • Central line for higher concentrations (peripheral causes phlebitis)
  • High-alert: independent double-check

Nursing Interventions

  • Verify adequate urine output / renal function BEFORE administering (must be able to excrete)
  • Baseline and follow-up serum potassium, renal function, EKG
  • IV: always dilute; use pump; cardiac monitoring for higher rates; never push
  • Assess IV site for phlebitis; central line for high concentration
  • Oral: give with food/water; sit upright; don’t crush ER forms
  • Monitor for hyperkalemia: peaked T-waves, weakness, paresthesias, arrhythmias
  • High-alert medication: independent double-check; verify concentration and rate
  • Review concurrent medications (K-sparing diuretics, ACE/ARB)

Client Education

  • Take oral potassium WITH food and a full glass of water to prevent stomach upset
  • Do not crush or chew extended-release tablets; swallow whole
  • Report nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, black stools (GI irritation)
  • Report muscle weakness, irregular heartbeat, tingling (potassium imbalance)
  • Do not use salt substitutes (high in potassium) without provider approval
  • Keep all lab appointments (potassium monitoring)
  • Eat potassium-rich foods if recommended (bananas, oranges, potatoes)
  • Tell provider about all medications (some raise potassium)
  • Keep out of reach of children
Worked Example Folic Acid (Vitamin B9) Ch 30 — Vitamins and Minerals · Vitamins section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Folic Acid (Vitamin B9)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 30 — Vitamins and Minerals
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Water-soluble B vitamin — essential for DNA synthesis, RBC formation, and cell division
  • Required for normal erythropoiesis (prevents megaloblastic anemia)
  • Critical for fetal neural tube development

Therapeutic Use

  • Prevention of neural tube defects (spina bifida, anencephaly) — before conception and during pregnancy
  • Folate-deficiency (megaloblastic) anemia
  • Malabsorption states, alcoholism, pregnancy/lactation
  • Counteract folate-depleting drugs (methotrexate rescue [leucovorin], phenytoin, sulfasalazine)

Complications

  • Generally very safe (water-soluble; excess excreted)
  • CAN MASK vitamin B12 deficiency — corrects the anemia but allows neurologic damage of B12 deficiency to progress undetected
  • Rare: allergic reactions, GI upset, altered sleep, irritability (high doses)
  • May reduce phenytoin levels (lowered seizure threshold)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity
  • Undiagnosed anemia — must rule out/co-treat B12 deficiency first (folate alone masks B12 deficiency)
  • Pernicious anemia (give with B12)
  • Generally safe in pregnancy (recommended)

Interactions

  • Phenytoin — folic acid may decrease phenytoin levels (seizure risk); phenytoin lowers folate
  • Methotrexate — folate antagonist (leucovorin is the reduced form used as rescue)
  • Sulfasalazine, trimethoprim — reduce folate
  • Oral contraceptives — may lower folate

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Correction of megaloblastic anemia (Hgb, MCV normalize; reticulocytosis)
  • Adequate serum folate levels
  • Prevention of neural tube defects (pregnancy)
  • No masked B12 deficiency (B12 checked/co-treated)

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (also IM/IV/SC for severe deficiency or malabsorption)
  • Prevention in pregnancy: 400–800 mcg/day; start before conception, continue 1st trimester
  • High-risk (prior NTD pregnancy): 4 mg/day
  • Deficiency treatment: 1 mg/day
  • Take with or without food

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess for B12 deficiency BEFORE/with folate treatment in anemia (folate masks B12)
  • Baseline CBC, folate level, B12 level
  • Monitor hematologic response (reticulocytes, Hgb, MCV)
  • Counsel women of childbearing age on preconception folate
  • Monitor phenytoin levels if co-prescribed
  • Dietary counseling: leafy greens, citrus, legumes, fortified grains

Client Education

  • Women of childbearing age: take folic acid daily — neural tube forms in the first weeks, often before pregnancy is known
  • Take before conception and through early pregnancy
  • Folate-rich foods: dark leafy greens, citrus fruits, beans, fortified cereals/grains
  • If treating anemia, B12 deficiency must also be checked (folate alone can hide it)
  • Take as directed; safe vitamin but follow dosing
  • If on phenytoin, keep seizure follow-up (interaction)
  • Generally well-tolerated; report unusual symptoms
Worked Example Electrolyte Imbalances (K⁺ / Ca²⁺ / Mg²⁺) Ch 30 — Vitamins and Minerals · Minerals section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Electrolyte Imbalances (K⁺ / Ca²⁺ / Mg²⁺)

Defining Characteristics

Electrolyte imbalances are deviations from normal serum concentrations of key minerals, disrupting cardiac, neuromuscular, and metabolic function.

Normal ranges:

  • Potassium (K⁺): 3.5–5.0 mEq/L
  • Calcium (Ca²⁺): 9.0–10.5 mg/dL (total); ionized 4.5–5.6
  • Magnesium (Mg²⁺): 1.3–2.1 mEq/L
  • Sodium (Na⁺): 135–145 mEq/L

These electrolytes are interrelated — e.g., hypomagnesemia causes refractory hypokalemia and hypocalcemia.

Antecedents

  • Diuretics (loop/thiazide → lose K, Mg; K-sparing → retain K)
  • GI losses (vomiting, diarrhea, NG suction)
  • Renal impairment (retention)
  • Endocrine disorders (hyperparathyroidism → high Ca; Addison’s → high K)
  • Medications (PPIs → low Mg; digoxin interactions)
  • Inadequate or excessive intake
  • Acid-base disorders (shift K)
  • Tumor lysis, rhabdomyolysis (release K, phosphate)

Negative Consequences

  • Cardiac arrhythmias and arrest — especially K⁺ and Mg²⁺ derangements
  • Hyperkalemia: peaked T-waves, widened QRS, asystole
  • Hypokalemia: U-waves, flattened T, arrhythmias, digoxin toxicity, weakness
  • Hypercalcemia: “stones, bones, groans, psychiatric overtones”; shortened QT
  • Hypocalcemia: tetany, Chvostek/Trousseau signs, laryngospasm, prolonged QT, seizures
  • Hypomagnesemia: torsades de pointes, refractory hypokalemia
  • Neuromuscular dysfunction, seizures, death if severe

Related Concepts

Diuretics, digoxin toxicity, EKG changes, Chvostek/Trousseau signs, tetany, torsades de pointes, fluid balance, parathyroid hormone, vitamin D, acid-base balance, therapeutic drug monitoring, high-alert medications (IV KCl, IV magnesium).

Exemplars

  • Hyperkalemia treatment: calcium gluconate (cardiac membrane stabilization), insulin + glucose (shift K into cells), albuterol, sodium bicarbonate, sodium polystyrene/patiromer (removal), dialysis. EKG monitoring throughout.
  • Hypokalemia treatment: oral or IV KCl (never IV push; ≤ 10 mEq/hr on floor); correct magnesium too (low Mg causes refractory low K).
  • Hypercalcemia treatment: IV normal saline + loop diuretic (after hydration), calcitonin, bisphosphonates; identify cause (malignancy, hyperparathyroidism).
  • Hypocalcemia treatment: IV calcium gluconate (acute/tetany); oral calcium + vitamin D; check magnesium. Watch for laryngospasm (emergency).
  • Hypomagnesemia treatment: IV/oral magnesium; ESSENTIAL to correct before/with potassium and calcium (low Mg makes them refractory).
  • Chvostek sign: facial twitch when tapping cheek (hypocalcemia). Trousseau sign: carpal spasm with BP cuff inflation (hypocalcemia).
  • Nursing priority: cardiac monitoring for severe K⁺/Mg²⁺ imbalances; safe IV electrolyte administration (dilution, pump, rate limits); frequent lab monitoring; assess interrelated electrolytes.
Worked Example Acetaminophen Ch 35 — Non-Opioid Analgesics · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Acetaminophen
Review Module Chapter
Ch 35 — Non-Opioid Analgesics
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Non-opioid analgesic/antipyretic — reduces pain and fever primarily through central inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis. Little anti-inflammatory effect

Therapeutic Use

  • Mild-to-moderate pain and fever
  • Preferred when NSAIDs are contraindicated (no GI/bleeding effects)

Complications

  • Well tolerated at therapeutic doses
  • Hepatotoxicity with overdose or chronic high intake (especially with alcohol) — leading cause of acute liver failure

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Severe hepatic impairment/active liver disease
  • Chronic high alcohol use (caution)
  • Hypersensitivity

Interactions

  • Alcohol and other hepatotoxic drugs → ↑ liver injury
  • Warfarin → ↑ INR with high/prolonged doses

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Relief of pain; reduced fever
  • No signs of liver injury

Medication Administration

  • Routes: PO, rectal, IV
  • Maximum ~4 g/day for healthy adults (lower with liver disease/alcohol)
  • Beware hidden acetaminophen in many combination OTC/cold products
  • Antidote for overdose: acetylcysteine

Nursing Interventions

  • Total all acetaminophen sources to avoid exceeding the daily max
  • Monitor liver function in at-risk clients
  • Recognize overdose; have acetylcysteine available

Client Education

  • Do not exceed the maximum daily dose; check all OTC/combination products for acetaminophen
  • Limit or avoid alcohol
  • Report nausea, abdominal pain, or yellowing of skin/eyes
  • Keep out of reach of children
Worked Example Alteplase Ch 25 — Medications Affecting Coagulation · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Alteplase
Review Module Chapter
Ch 25 — Medications Affecting Coagulation
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Thrombolytic (tissue plasminogen activator) — converts plasminogen to plasmin, which dissolves existing clots (fibrinolysis)

Therapeutic Use

  • Acute ischemic stroke, STEMI, and massive pulmonary embolism
  • Clearing occluded central venous catheters (low dose)

Complications

  • Serious bleeding/hemorrhage (including intracranial) — primary risk
  • Reperfusion dysrhythmias; hypotension; angioedema

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Active internal bleeding, recent intracranial hemorrhage/surgery/trauma, history of hemorrhagic stroke
  • Severe uncontrolled hypertension, known bleeding disorder
  • Narrow time window from symptom onset

Interactions

  • Anticoagulants, antiplatelets, NSAIDs → ↑ bleeding (timing carefully managed)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Restored perfusion (e.g., neurologic improvement in stroke, reperfusion in MI)
  • No major bleeding

Medication Administration

  • Route: IV per strict protocol; give within the approved time window from symptom onset
  • Obtain baseline coagulation studies; avoid unnecessary punctures/invasive procedures
  • Continuous neuro and bleeding assessment; have it ready as a high-alert drug

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor for bleeding (neuro checks, puncture sites, GI/GU), vital signs, and dysrhythmias
  • Minimize invasive procedures; apply prolonged pressure to sites
  • Verify eligibility/time window and absence of contraindications

Client Education

  • Report any bleeding, severe headache, or weakness immediately
  • Understand the need for close monitoring during/after infusion
  • Avoid activities risking injury during the bleeding-risk period
Worked Example Warfarin (Coumadin) Ch 25 — Medications Affecting Coagulation · Warfarin section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Warfarin (Coumadin)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 25 — Medications Affecting Coagulation
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant — inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase → reduces synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) and proteins C and S
  • Delayed onset (full effect 3–5 days; existing factors must deplete)
  • Narrow therapeutic index — requires INR monitoring
  • Often bridged with heparin/LMWH initially (until INR therapeutic)

Therapeutic Use

  • Atrial fibrillation — stroke prevention (especially mechanical valves)
  • Venous thromboembolism (DVT, PE) treatment and prevention
  • Mechanical heart valves (DOACs not used here — warfarin required)
  • Post-MI in select cases
  • Antiphospholipid syndrome

Complications

  • Bleeding/hemorrhage (BLACK BOX) — major risk; GI bleed, intracranial hemorrhage, hematuria, epistaxis
  • Warfarin-induced skin necrosis (early; protein C depletion before factor depletion)
  • Purple toe syndrome
  • Teratogenic (Category X) — fetal warfarin syndrome; use heparin/LMWH in pregnancy
  • Numerous drug and food interactions affecting INR

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Pregnancy — teratogenic (use heparin/LMWH instead)
  • Active bleeding, severe thrombocytopenia
  • Recent or planned surgery/invasive procedures
  • Severe hepatic disease (impaired factor synthesis)
  • Uncontrolled hypertension
  • History of warfarin-induced skin necrosis
  • Inability to monitor INR or adhere to monitoring
  • Fall risk (caution in older adults)

Interactions

  • INCREASE INR / bleeding risk: amiodarone, fluconazole/azoles, metronidazole, SSRIs, NSAIDs, aspirin, many antibiotics, acetaminophen (high dose), cranberry juice, alcohol (acute)
  • DECREASE INR / clot risk: rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, high vitamin K foods (leafy greens — keep CONSISTENT, not avoided), St. John’s wort, chronic alcohol
  • CYP2C9 and VKORC1 genetic variants affect dosing
  • Always review interactions before starting any new medication

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • INR within target range: 2–3 for most indications; 2.5–3.5 for mechanical mitral valves
  • Prevention of thromboembolic events (no stroke, DVT, PE)
  • No bleeding complications
  • Stable, consistent INR over time
  • Adherence to monitoring schedule

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (also IV in hospital)
  • Individualized dose based on INR (typical 2–10 mg/day)
  • Take at the same time each day, usually evening
  • Antidote: vitamin K (phytonadione) for elevated INR/bleeding; fresh frozen plasma or prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) for major bleeding
  • Bridge with heparin/LMWH until INR therapeutic (overlap 4–5 days)
  • INR monitoring: frequent initially, then every 2–4 weeks when stable

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline and ongoing INR/PT; CBC; assess bleeding risk
  • Monitor for bleeding: gums, urine, stool (guaiac), bruising, neuro changes (intracranial)
  • Have vitamin K available as antidote
  • Comprehensive medication AND diet review (interactions)
  • Bleeding precautions: soft toothbrush, electric razor, fall prevention
  • Educate on consistent vitamin K intake (don’t eliminate greens — keep steady)
  • Pregnancy screening in childbearing age (teratogenic)
  • Coordinate INR monitoring and follow-up; consider anticoagulation clinic

Client Education

  • Take exactly as prescribed at the same time daily; never double up for a missed dose
  • Regular INR blood tests are essential — keep all appointments
  • Keep vitamin K intake CONSISTENT (don’t suddenly increase or eliminate leafy greens, broccoli, etc.)
  • Report bleeding: gums, nosebleeds, blood in urine/stool, excessive bruising, severe headache
  • Use soft toothbrush, electric razor; avoid injury-prone activities
  • Tell ALL providers and dentists you take warfarin; check before any new medication (including OTC and herbal)
  • Avoid alcohol excess; avoid cranberry juice and St. John’s wort
  • Carry medical alert ID
  • Do NOT take if pregnant or planning pregnancy — tell provider immediately
  • Limit aspirin/NSAIDs unless directed
Worked Example Anticoagulation Therapy & Bleeding Risk Ch 25 — Medications Affecting Coagulation · Overview section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Anticoagulation Therapy & Bleeding Risk

Defining Characteristics

Anticoagulation therapy uses medications to prevent or treat thromboembolism by interfering with the clotting cascade. The central nursing concern is balancing therapeutic anticoagulation against bleeding risk.

Major drug categories and their monitoring/antidotes:

  • Warfarin — monitor INR; antidote vitamin K
  • Unfractionated heparin — monitor aPTT (or anti-Xa); antidote protamine sulfate
  • LMWH (enoxaparin) — usually no routine monitoring; partial reversal with protamine
  • DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran) — no routine monitoring; antidotes: idarucizumab (dabigatran), andexanet alfa (factor Xa inhibitors)
  • Antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel) — no specific antidote; platelet transfusion if severe
  • Thrombolytics (alteplase) — highest bleeding risk; aminocaproic acid

Antecedents

  • Indication for anticoagulation: AFib, VTE, mechanical valve, ACS, stroke prevention
  • Patient bleeding-risk factors: age, prior bleeding, renal/hepatic impairment, concurrent antiplatelets/NSAIDs, fall risk, uncontrolled HTN
  • Drug interactions affecting anticoagulant levels
  • Procedures/surgery requiring anticoagulation interruption
  • Adherence and monitoring capability
  • Genetic factors (CYP2C9, VKORC1 for warfarin)

Negative Consequences

  • Major bleeding: intracranial hemorrhage (most feared), GI bleed, retroperitoneal bleed — can be fatal
  • Inadequate anticoagulation: thromboembolic events — stroke, PE, valve thrombosis
  • Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) — paradoxical clotting
  • Need for reversal agents and transfusions
  • Hospitalization, disability, death
  • Patient anxiety, lifestyle restrictions

Related Concepts

Coagulation cascade, INR/aPTT/anti-Xa monitoring, antidotes (vitamin K, protamine, idarucizumab, andexanet alfa), HIT, bleeding precautions, CHA₂DS₂-VASc score, HAS-BLED score, bridging therapy, drug-food interactions, fall prevention.

Exemplars

  • Bleeding precautions (all anticoagulants): soft toothbrush, electric razor, avoid IM injections, fall prevention, no contact sports, careful with sharp objects, hold pressure longer after blood draws.
  • Lab monitoring matching: warfarin → INR (target 2–3); UF heparin → aPTT (1.5–2× control) or anti-Xa; LMWH → usually none (anti-Xa in renal impairment/pregnancy/obesity); DOACs → none routine.
  • Antidote matching: warfarin → vitamin K (+ PCC/FFP for major bleed); heparin → protamine sulfate; dabigatran → idarucizumab; apixaban/rivaroxaban → andexanet alfa.
  • HIT recognition: platelet drop > 50% 5–10 days after starting heparin → STOP all heparin, use non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban), never give platelets.
  • Periprocedural management: warfarin held ~5 days before surgery; bridge with LMWH if high thrombotic risk; DOACs held 1–3 days depending on renal function and bleed risk.
  • Assessment for bleeding: monitor for hematuria, melena/hematochezia, hemoptysis, epistaxis, gingival bleeding, ecchymosis, and neuro changes (intracranial bleed — headache, confusion, focal deficits).
  • Patient teaching: recognize bleeding signs, medication adherence, consistent diet (warfarin), interaction awareness, medical alert ID, regular monitoring.
Worked Example Methotrexate Ch 33 — Connective Tissue Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Methotrexate
Review Module Chapter
Ch 33 — Connective Tissue Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) / antimetabolite — inhibits folic acid metabolism and rapidly dividing cells, suppressing inflammation and immune response

Therapeutic Use

  • Rheumatoid arthritis (first-line DMARD), psoriasis
  • Certain cancers (higher doses)

Complications

  • Bone marrow suppression (infection, bleeding, anemia)
  • Hepatotoxicity and pulmonary toxicity
  • GI ulceration/stomatitis, nausea
  • Highly teratogenic; nephrotoxicity (high dose)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Pregnancy and breastfeeding
  • Liver disease, alcohol use disorder, significant blood dyscrasias
  • Active infection; caution: renal impairment

Interactions

  • NSAIDs and salicylates → ↑ methotrexate toxicity
  • Other hepatotoxic/nephrotoxic drugs → ↑ toxicity
  • Live vaccines → infection risk

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ joint inflammation/pain and slowed joint damage (RA)
  • Normal CBC, LFTs; no infection or pulmonary symptoms

Medication Administration

  • Routes: PO, SubQ, IM (RA dosing is usually once weekly — not daily)
  • Folic acid supplementation reduces toxicity
  • Monitor CBC, LFTs, and renal function; leucovorin rescue for high-dose/overdose

Nursing Interventions

  • Confirm weekly (not daily) dosing for RA — a common, dangerous error
  • Monitor CBC, LFTs, renal function, and for infection/bleeding/cough
  • Ensure folic acid; verify contraception

Client Education

  • Take once weekly as prescribed (never daily) for arthritis
  • Avoid alcohol and NSAIDs/aspirin unless approved; take folic acid as directed
  • Report fever, sore throat, mouth sores, unusual bleeding, cough, or yellowing skin
  • Use reliable contraception (do not become pregnant)
Worked Example Allopurinol Ch 33 — Connective Tissue Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Allopurinol
Review Module Chapter
Ch 33 — Connective Tissue Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Xanthine oxidase inhibitor — reduces uric acid production, lowering serum urate

Therapeutic Use

  • Chronic gout (prevention — not for acute attacks)
  • Hyperuricemia from chemotherapy/tumor lysis; recurrent uric acid stones

Complications

  • Hypersensitivity/severe skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) — stop if rash
  • GI upset, drowsiness
  • May trigger an acute gout flare when starting

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity/prior severe reaction
  • Caution: renal impairment (dose reduction)

Interactions

  • Azathioprine, mercaptopurine → toxic accumulation (reduce their dose)
  • Warfarin → ↑ effect
  • Ampicillin → ↑ rash; thiazides → ↑ allopurinol level

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ serum uric acid; fewer gout attacks over time
  • No severe skin reaction

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, after meals to reduce GI upset
  • Not for acute attacks — continue during a flare if already taking it
  • Increase fluids; titrate to target urate; reduce dose in renal impairment

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor serum uric acid, renal/liver function, and for rash
  • Encourage fluids (2–3 L/day)
  • Explain it prevents (not treats) acute attacks

Client Education

  • Stop and report any rash immediately (serious reaction risk)
  • Take after meals; drink plenty of fluids
  • Continue daily even when feeling well; it won’t relieve an acute attack
  • Limit alcohol and purine-rich foods
Worked Example Colchicine (Acute Gout) Ch 33 — Connective Tissue Disorders · Gout/SLE section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Colchicine (Colcrys)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 33 — Connective Tissue Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Anti-inflammatory (not a uric acid drug) — inhibits microtubule polymerization, disrupting neutrophil migration and activation
  • Reduces the inflammatory response to urate crystals in joints
  • Does NOT lower uric acid levels (different from allopurinol)
  • Most effective when started early in an acute attack

Therapeutic Use

  • Acute gout flares — relieve pain/inflammation
  • Gout flare prophylaxis when starting urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol can trigger flares initially)
  • Familial Mediterranean fever
  • Pericarditis (off-label)

Complications

  • GI toxicity (most common, dose-limiting) — nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain (early sign of toxicity)
  • Bone marrow suppression (high/toxic doses) — agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia
  • Myopathy/rhabdomyolysis (especially with statins, renal impairment)
  • Narrow therapeutic index — overdose can be fatal
  • Peripheral neuropathy
  • Hepatotoxicity

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Severe renal or hepatic impairment (dose adjust; combination renal+hepatic = avoid)
  • Concurrent strong CYP3A4 or P-gp inhibitors (in renal/hepatic impairment — fatal toxicity)
  • Blood dyscrasias
  • Older adults (toxicity risk)
  • Pregnancy — weigh risk

Interactions

  • Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, ketoconazole, ritonavir) — increase colchicine to toxic/fatal levels
  • P-glycoprotein inhibitors (cyclosporine, verapamil) — increase levels
  • Statins, fibrates — additive myopathy/rhabdomyolysis
  • Grapefruit juice — increases levels
  • Avoid combinations in renal/hepatic impairment

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Relief of acute gout pain and inflammation (usually within 24–48 hr)
  • Reduced joint swelling, redness, warmth
  • Prevention of flares during urate-lowering initiation
  • No GI toxicity, myopathy, or marrow suppression

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral
  • Acute gout: 1.2 mg at first sign, then 0.6 mg 1 hr later (max 1.8 mg over 1 hr per attack)
  • Prophylaxis: 0.6 mg once or twice daily
  • Reduce dose in renal/hepatic impairment and with interacting drugs
  • Start as EARLY as possible in a flare for best effect
  • Take with food to reduce GI upset

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess renal and hepatic function (dose adjustment)
  • Review for CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors and statins (toxicity)
  • Monitor for GI symptoms — first sign of toxicity; hold and notify if severe diarrhea/vomiting
  • Periodic CBC (marrow suppression with chronic use)
  • Assess for muscle pain/weakness (myopathy)
  • Educate on early use in flares and max dosing limits
  • Distinguish from urate-lowering therapy (colchicine does not lower uric acid)

Client Education

  • Take at the FIRST sign of a gout attack for best results
  • Do NOT exceed the prescribed dose — overdose can be dangerous
  • Stop and call your provider for severe diarrhea, vomiting, or abdominal pain (early toxicity signs)
  • Report muscle pain, weakness, numbness/tingling, unusual bleeding or infection
  • Take with food
  • Avoid grapefruit juice
  • Tell providers about all medications (serious interactions, especially certain antibiotics and statins)
  • This relieves the attack but does NOT lower uric acid — continue any urate-lowering medication separately
  • Limit alcohol and purine-rich foods
Worked Example Rheumatoid Arthritis Ch 33 — Connective Tissue Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 33 — Connective Tissue Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) — chronic, systemic autoimmune disease causing symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis, primarily affecting synovial joints, with potential extra-articular involvement.

  • Autoimmune; more common in women; onset typically 30–60 yr
  • Symmetric joint involvement (both sides)
  • Affects small joints first (hands, wrists, feet), then larger joints
  • Systemic: fatigue, fever, weight loss; can affect lungs, heart, eyes, vessels
  • Progressive joint destruction and deformity if untreated

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Autoimmune attack on synovium — immune cells infiltrate the joint lining
  • Chronic inflammation → pannus formation (inflammatory granulation tissue)
  • Pannus erodes cartilage and bone → joint destruction, deformity
  • Autoantibodies: rheumatoid factor (RF), anti-CCP (more specific)
  • Cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-6) drive inflammation (targets for biologics)
  • Genetic predisposition (HLA-DR4) + environmental triggers (smoking)

Expected Findings

  • Symmetric joint pain, swelling, warmth, stiffness
  • Morning stiffness > 1 hour (hallmark; improves with activity)
  • Small joints of hands (MCP, PIP), wrists, feet
  • Joint deformities: ulnar deviation, swan-neck, boutonnière, hallux valgus
  • Rheumatoid nodules (subcutaneous)
  • Fatigue, low-grade fever, malaise, weight loss
  • Extra-articular: pleuritis, pericarditis, dry eyes (Sjogren’s), vasculitis, anemia

Diagnostic:

  • RF and anti-CCP antibodies
  • Elevated ESR, CRP (inflammation)
  • X-rays: joint space narrowing, erosions
  • CBC: anemia of chronic disease
  • Clinical criteria (ACR/EULAR)

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy (treat-to-target, early DMARDs):

  • DMARDs (disease-modifying) — methotrexate is first-line/anchor; also hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, leflunomide
  • Biologic DMARDs — TNF inhibitors (etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab), IL-6 (tocilizumab), others — for inadequate response
  • JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib)
  • Corticosteroids — bridge therapy/flares (short-term; minimize)
  • NSAIDs — symptom relief (not disease-modifying)

Nursing care:

  • Pain and inflammation management; balance rest and activity
  • Joint protection; assistive devices; OT/PT referral
  • Heat/cold therapy
  • Monitor DMARD/biologic toxicity (LFTs, CBC, infection)
  • Promote function and independence
  • Emotional support (chronic disease, body image)

Client Education

  • RA is a chronic autoimmune disease; early aggressive treatment prevents joint damage
  • Take DMARDs consistently even when feeling well (they slow disease progression)
  • Methotrexate: weekly dosing (NOT daily — fatal if daily); take folic acid; avoid alcohol; effective contraception (teratogenic); monitor labs
  • Biologics/immunosuppressants: increase infection risk — report fever/signs of infection; no live vaccines; screen for TB before starting
  • Balance activity and rest; protect joints (use larger joints, assistive devices)
  • Apply heat for stiffness, cold for acute inflammation
  • Morning stiffness routines (warm shower)
  • Regular exercise (low-impact: swimming, walking) maintains function
  • Smoking cessation (worsens RA)
  • Keep all lab/follow-up appointments for medication monitoring
  • Report increasing joint damage, new symptoms, medication side effects
Worked Example Gout Ch 33 — Connective Tissue Disorders · Gout/SLE section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Gout
Review Module Chapter
Ch 33 — Connective Tissue Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Gout — a form of inflammatory arthritis caused by deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints and tissues, due to hyperuricemia.

  • More common in men; postmenopausal women
  • Acute gout: sudden, severe monoarticular attack (often great toe — podagra)
  • Chronic gout: recurrent attacks, tophi, chronic arthropathy
  • Associated with metabolic syndrome, obesity, HTN, CKD, alcohol use

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Hyperuricemia — serum urate > 6.8 mg/dL (saturation point)
  • Causes: underexcretion (~90%, renal) or overproduction (~10%) of uric acid
  • Uric acid is the end product of purine metabolism
  • Urate crystals precipitate in cooler peripheral joints → trigger intense neutrophil-mediated inflammation
  • Chronic deposits form tophi (urate masses in tissues)
  • Triggers: purine-rich foods (red meat, organ meats, shellfish), alcohol (especially beer), fructose, dehydration, diuretics, rapid urate changes

Expected Findings

Acute attack:

  • Sudden, excruciating joint pain (often at night)
  • First MTP joint of great toe (podagra) — classic
  • Joint red, hot, swollen, exquisitely tender (even sheet touch hurts)
  • Low-grade fever possible
  • Usually monoarticular early

Chronic gout:

  • Tophi (ears, joints, tendons) — firm nodules
  • Chronic joint pain, deformity
  • Uric acid kidney stones

Diagnostic:

  • Joint aspiration (gold standard): needle-shaped, negatively birefringent urate crystals
  • Serum uric acid (may be normal during acute attack)
  • X-ray (chronic: erosions, tophi)
  • 24-hr urine uric acid (over- vs under-excretion)

Nursing Care

Acute attack treatment:

  • NSAIDs (indomethacin, naproxen) — first-line if no contraindication
  • Colchicine — especially early in attack
  • Corticosteroids (oral or intra-articular) — if NSAIDs/colchicine contraindicated
  • Rest and elevate joint; ice
  • Do NOT start or stop urate-lowering therapy during an acute attack (but continue if already on it)

Chronic/preventive (urate-lowering therapy):

  • Allopurinol or febuxostat (xanthine oxidase inhibitors) — reduce uric acid production
  • Probenecid (uricosuric) — increase excretion
  • Start prophylactic colchicine/NSAID when initiating (prevents flares)
  • Target serum urate < 6 mg/dL

Nursing care: pain management, hydration, dietary counseling, monitor renal function and uric acid.

Client Education

  • Dietary modifications: limit purine-rich foods (red/organ meats, shellfish, anchovies), limit alcohol (especially beer), avoid high-fructose drinks
  • Stay well hydrated (helps excrete uric acid, prevents stones)
  • Maintain healthy weight; gradual weight loss (rapid loss can trigger attacks)
  • Urate-lowering medications (allopurinol): take daily, long-term, even when no symptoms — they prevent future attacks but do NOT relieve an acute one
  • May initially cause more flares when starting — continue as directed; prophylaxis given
  • Report rash with allopurinol (serious hypersensitivity risk)
  • Take acute medications at the first sign of an attack
  • Rest and elevate the affected joint during attacks
  • Low-fat dairy and cherries may help
  • Keep follow-up for uric acid and renal monitoring
  • Tell providers about gout (some medications, like thiazides, raise uric acid)
Worked Example Aspirin Ch 35 — Non-Opioid Analgesics · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Aspirin
Review Module Chapter
Ch 35 — Non-Opioid Analgesics
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • NSAID/salicylate — irreversibly inhibits COX enzymes, reducing prostaglandins (anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antipyretic) and thromboxane (antiplatelet)

Therapeutic Use

  • Pain, fever, inflammation
  • Low-dose: prevention of MI/stroke (antiplatelet)

Complications

  • GI bleeding/ulceration, dyspepsia
  • Salicism/toxicity (tinnitus, hyperventilation) at high doses
  • Bleeding (prolonged); Reye syndrome in children/teens with viral illness

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Children/adolescents with viral illness (Reye syndrome)
  • Active GI bleeding/peptic ulcer, bleeding disorders
  • Third-trimester pregnancy; aspirin/NSAID allergy

Interactions

  • Anticoagulants, other NSAIDs, alcohol → ↑ bleeding
  • Ibuprofen → may blunt aspirin’s cardioprotective effect
  • ↑ effect of some hypoglycemics; ↓ effect of some antihypertensives

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Relief of pain/fever/inflammation
  • Cardioprotection (no MI/stroke) for low-dose preventive use; no bleeding

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO with food/full glass of water (enteric-coated to reduce GI effects)
  • Stop ~1 week before surgery (per provider) due to bleeding
  • Avoid in children with fever/viral illness

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor for GI bleeding (black/tarry stools), bleeding, and tinnitus (toxicity)
  • Give with food; assess for allergy/asthma sensitivity
  • Hold before procedures per orders

Client Education

  • Take with food; report black/tarry stools, ringing in the ears, or unusual bleeding
  • Do not give to children/teens with fever or viral illness
  • Avoid alcohol and other NSAIDs; tell providers before surgery/dental work
  • Low-dose daily aspirin only if prescribed
Worked Example Acetaminophen Toxicity & N-Acetylcysteine Ch 35 — Non-Opioid Analgesics · Overview section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Acetaminophen Toxicity & N-Acetylcysteine

Defining Characteristics

Acetaminophen toxicity is dose-dependent hepatotoxicity resulting from overdose (acute or chronic). Acetaminophen is the leading cause of acute liver failure in the US.

  • Maximum adult dose: 4 g/day (3 g/day or less if hepatic risk, chronic alcohol use, older adults)
  • Acute toxic dose: generally > 7.5–10 g (or > 150 mg/kg) in adults
  • Antidote: N-acetylcysteine (NAC / Acetadote, Mucomyst)
  • Toxicity often hidden — acetaminophen is in MANY combination products (cold/flu, opioid combos)

Antecedents

  • Intentional overdose (suicide attempt)
  • Unintentional overdose — stacking combination products (cold remedies, opioid-acetaminophen combos) unaware of total dose
  • Chronic alcohol use (depletes glutathione; lower safe dose)
  • Pre-existing liver disease, malnutrition
  • Exceeding recommended dose for pain/fever
  • Pediatric dosing errors

Negative Consequences

  • Hepatotoxicity / fulminant hepatic failure
  • The toxic metabolite NAPQI accumulates when glutathione is depleted → hepatocyte death
  • Four phases: (1) 0–24 hr: mild/asymptomatic, nausea; (2) 24–72 hr: RUQ pain, rising LFTs; (3) 72–96 hr: peak hepatotoxicity, jaundice, coagulopathy, encephalopathy; (4) recovery or death
  • Acute kidney injury
  • Death without treatment

Related Concepts

NAPQI metabolite, glutathione, Rumack-Matthew nomogram, N-acetylcysteine (NAC), liver function tests, INR/coagulopathy, combination products, hepatic failure, activated charcoal, maximum daily dose.

Exemplars

  • Mechanism: NAPQI (toxic metabolite) is normally neutralized by glutathione. Overdose depletes glutathione → NAPQI damages liver. NAC replenishes glutathione and binds NAPQI.
  • Rumack-Matthew nomogram: plots serum acetaminophen level vs time since ingestion (use level drawn ≥ 4 hr post-ingestion) to determine NAC need.
  • N-acetylcysteine (NAC): most effective within 8–10 hours of ingestion; still beneficial later. Oral (rotten-egg smell/taste — may cause nausea; dilute) or IV (anaphylactoid reactions possible).
  • Acute overdose management: activated charcoal if within ~1–2 hr; draw acetaminophen level at 4 hr; plot on nomogram; start NAC if indicated (do not delay if presentation late or level pending in massive ingestion).
  • Monitoring: serial LFTs, INR, renal function, mental status.
  • Prevention/teaching: never exceed 4 g/day (less with liver risk/alcohol); read labels for hidden acetaminophen in combination products; limit alcohol; report dark urine, jaundice, RUQ pain.
  • Chronic toxicity can occur from repeated supratherapeutic dosing, not just single overdose.
Worked Example NSAID Therapy & GI/Renal Risk Ch 35 — Non-Opioid Analgesics · Overview section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
NSAID Therapy & GI/Renal Risk

Defining Characteristics

NSAID therapy uses nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (ibuprofen, naproxen, ketorolac, aspirin, celecoxib) for anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antipyretic effects by inhibiting cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes.

  • COX-1: protective (gastric mucosa, platelets, renal flow)
  • COX-2: inflammation/pain
  • Nonselective NSAIDs inhibit both → efficacy + GI/renal/bleeding risks
  • COX-2 selective (celecoxib) → less GI risk but cardiovascular concerns

Antecedents

  • Pain, inflammation, fever requiring treatment
  • Chronic conditions: arthritis, musculoskeletal pain
  • Risk factors for complications: older age, history of GI ulcer/bleed, renal impairment, heart failure, dehydration, concurrent anticoagulants/corticosteroids
  • Long-term or high-dose use
  • OTC availability → unmonitored use

Negative Consequences

  • GI: dyspepsia, peptic ulcers, GI bleeding/perforation (reduced protective prostaglandins)
  • Renal: acute kidney injury, sodium/water retention, hyperkalemia (reduced renal prostaglandins, decreased perfusion); worsens HF and HTN
  • Cardiovascular: increased MI/stroke risk (BLACK BOX, especially with prolonged use; not low-dose aspirin)
  • Bleeding: platelet inhibition (aspirin irreversible; others reversible)
  • Hypersensitivity (especially aspirin — asthma/nasal polyps triad)
  • Masking of fever/infection signs

Related Concepts

COX-1/COX-2, prostaglandins, peptic ulcer disease, GI bleeding, acute kidney injury, platelet aggregation, anticoagulants, proton pump inhibitors (gastroprotection), Reye syndrome (aspirin in children), heart failure, hyperkalemia, Samter’s triad.

Exemplars

  • GI protection: high-risk clients on NSAIDs → add a PPI; take NSAIDs with food; use lowest effective dose for shortest time.
  • Renal caution: avoid NSAIDs in CKD, HF, dehydration, and with ACE inhibitors/ARBs + diuretics (“triple whammy” → AKI). Monitor renal function and BP.
  • Bleeding: hold NSAIDs before surgery; caution with warfarin/anticoagulants/corticosteroids (additive bleed risk); aspirin’s antiplatelet effect lasts the platelet lifespan (~7–10 days).
  • Ketorolac: potent; limit to ≤ 5 days (high GI/renal risk).
  • Aspirin + children: avoid with viral illness/fever (Reye syndrome).
  • Cardiovascular: NSAIDs (except aspirin) increase CV events; avoid/limit in heart disease; naproxen may have lower CV risk.
  • Patient teaching: take with food, report black/tarry stools, abdominal pain, decreased urine output, swelling, weight gain; avoid combining NSAIDs; limit alcohol; tell providers before surgery; know hidden NSAID content.
  • Monitoring: renal function, BP, signs of GI bleeding (Hgb, stool), edema.
Worked Example Fentanyl Ch 36 — Opioid Agonists and Antagonists · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Fentanyl
Review Module Chapter
Ch 36 — Opioid Agonists and Antagonists
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Potent opioid agonist (~100x morphine) — binds mu opioid receptors in the CNS to produce strong analgesia and sedation

Therapeutic Use

  • Severe pain (surgical, procedural, breakthrough cancer pain)
  • Anesthesia adjunct; transdermal patch for chronic, opioid-tolerant pain

Complications

  • Respiratory depression (most serious), sedation
  • Constipation, nausea, urinary retention, hypotension, bradycardia
  • Chest wall rigidity (rapid IV); high overdose/diversion risk

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Opioid-naïve clients (transdermal/long-acting forms)
  • Severe respiratory depression, acute/severe asthma
  • Paralytic ileus; caution: head injury, hepatic impairment

Interactions

  • Other CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, alcohol) → additive respiratory depression
  • CYP3A4 inhibitors → ↑ fentanyl level
  • Serotonergic drugs → serotonin syndrome

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Adequate pain relief with maintained respirations
  • No oversedation or respiratory compromise

Medication Administration

  • Routes: IV, transdermal patch, transmucosal; Schedule II controlled substance
  • Transdermal patch: apply to clean dry skin, rotate sites; full effect ~24 hr; avoid heat (↑ absorption)
  • Monitor respirations closely; naloxone available; dispose of patches carefully

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor respiratory rate/depth, sedation, and oxygenation
  • Keep naloxone available; assess pain
  • Educate on patch use, heat avoidance, and safe disposal; prevent/manage constipation

Client Education

  • Apply patch to clean, dry, intact skin; rotate sites; avoid heat sources (heating pads, hot baths)
  • Do not cut patches; fold used patches and dispose safely away from children/pets
  • Report slow/shallow breathing or extreme drowsiness
  • Avoid alcohol/sedatives; use a bowel regimen for constipation
Worked Example Morphine Sulfate Ch 36 — Opioid Agonists and Antagonists · Overview section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Morphine Sulfate
Review Module Chapter
Ch 36 — Opioid Agonists and Antagonists
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Pure opioid agonist — binds mu (and kappa) receptors in CNS
  • Alters perception of and response to pain; produces analgesia, sedation, euphoria
  • Also causes respiratory depression, miosis, decreased GI motility, venodilation
  • Prototype opioid; high-alert medication

Therapeutic Use

  • Moderate to severe acute pain (postoperative, trauma, MI)
  • Chronic severe pain (cancer)
  • Acute pulmonary edema / acute MI — reduces preload, anxiety, dyspnea
  • Sedation/comfort in palliative care

Complications

  • Respiratory depression (most serious — dose-dependent; potentiated by other CNS depressants)
  • Sedation, CNS depression
  • Constipation (does not develop tolerance; needs bowel regimen)
  • Hypotension, orthostasis (venodilation)
  • Nausea, vomiting; urinary retention
  • Miosis (pinpoint pupils)
  • Pruritus, histamine release
  • Physical dependence, tolerance, addiction potential

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Respiratory depression/insufficiency; severe asthma; paralytic ileus
  • Increased ICP / head injury (masks signs; CO2 retention)
  • Severe hypotension, shock
  • Concurrent CNS depressants, benzodiazepines (BLACK BOX — fatal respiratory depression)
  • Hepatic/renal impairment (accumulation of active metabolite)
  • Older adults; opioid-naive (lower doses)

Interactions

  • CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, alcohol, sedatives) — additive respiratory depression (BLACK BOX)
  • MAOIs — severe reactions
  • Other opioids — additive
  • Anticholinergics — worsen constipation/urinary retention
  • Serotonergic drugs — serotonin syndrome risk

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Pain reduced to acceptable level (pain scale)
  • Improved function and comfort
  • Adequate respiratory rate (≥ 12/min) and oxygenation
  • Reduced dyspnea (pulmonary edema/MI)
  • Manageable side effects; bowel regimen effective

Medication Administration

  • Routes: PO (IR/ER), IV, IM, SC, epidural/intrathecal, rectal; PCA pump common
  • IV: dilute and give slowly; never crush ER tablets
  • Antidote: naloxone (have available)
  • Assess pain and respiratory rate before and after
  • High-alert: independent double-check for IV/PCA
  • Individualize dose; lower in opioid-naive, older adults, renal/hepatic impairment

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess respiratory rate, depth, and sedation level before and after — hold and notify if RR < 12/min or excessive sedation
  • Monitor pain (scale), BP (orthostasis), bowel function, urinary output
  • Have naloxone and resuscitation equipment available
  • Use sedation scale (e.g., POSS) for opioid-induced sedation
  • Initiate prophylactic bowel regimen (stimulant laxative +/- stool softener)
  • Fall precautions; rise slowly
  • Screen for concurrent CNS depressants/benzodiazepines
  • PCA: educate client (only client presses button); monitor

Client Education

  • Take as prescribed; report inadequate pain control rather than self-increasing
  • Do NOT combine with alcohol, sedatives, or benzodiazepines (dangerous breathing slowdown)
  • Report slow/shallow breathing, extreme drowsiness, confusion
  • Use a bowel regimen (fluids, fiber, stimulant laxative) — constipation is expected and persistent
  • Rise slowly (dizziness/orthostasis); fall precautions
  • Do not crush/chew extended-release forms
  • Do not drive until you know how it affects you
  • Store securely away from others (misuse risk); dispose of unused properly
  • Naloxone may be prescribed for emergencies — teach family use
  • Physical dependence can develop; do not stop abruptly (taper)
Worked Example Opioid Toxicity & Reversal Ch 36 — Opioid Agonists and Antagonists · Other section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Opioid Toxicity & Reversal

Defining Characteristics

Opioid toxicity (overdose) is potentially fatal CNS and respiratory depression from excessive opioid effect.

Classic toxidrome triad:

  • Respiratory depression (the lethal feature — decreased rate/depth)
  • CNS depression / coma (decreased LOC, sedation)
  • Miosis (pinpoint pupils)

Other: hypotension, bradycardia, hypothermia, decreased bowel sounds. Antidote: naloxone (Narcan) — competitive opioid antagonist.

Antecedents

  • Accidental or intentional overdose
  • Opioid-naive patients given too high a dose
  • Combining opioids with CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, alcohol)
  • Renal/hepatic impairment (accumulation)
  • Loss of tolerance (after abstinence/incarceration/rehab) then resuming prior dose
  • Potent illicit opioids (fentanyl analogs)
  • Dosing/route errors (e.g., crushing ER for IV)

Negative Consequences

  • Respiratory arrest and death (primary cause of opioid death)
  • Hypoxic brain injury
  • Aspiration pneumonia
  • Cardiac arrest
  • If reversed too aggressively: acute withdrawal (agitation, pain, hypertension, tachycardia, vomiting) and loss of needed analgesia
  • Re-sedation when naloxone wears off (shorter half-life than many opioids)

Related Concepts

Naloxone (Narcan), mu-opioid receptor, respiratory depression, sedation scales (POSS), capnography, opioid withdrawal, half-life mismatch, harm reduction, take-home naloxone, CNS depressant interactions.

Exemplars

  • Recognition: unresponsive patient with RR < 8–10, pinpoint pupils, after opioid use → suspect overdose.
  • Immediate care: support airway/ventilation (bag-mask, oxygen), call for help, administer naloxone (IV, IM, SC, or intranasal); repeat every 2–3 min as needed.
  • Naloxone titration: in a hospitalized patient on opioids for pain, titrate carefully (dilute, small increments) to restore breathing WITHOUT precipitating severe withdrawal/pain; in pure overdose, prioritize reversing respiratory depression.
  • Re-sedation risk: naloxone’s duration (~30–90 min) is often SHORTER than the opioid → monitor closely; repeat doses or infusion may be needed (especially long-acting opioids, fentanyl).
  • Monitoring: continuous respiratory rate, SpO2, capnography, sedation level, LOC.
  • Prevention: sedation/respiratory assessment with opioids, avoid concurrent CNS depressants, use lowest effective dose, take-home naloxone for high-risk patients, patient/family education.
  • Withdrawal after reversal: manage symptoms supportively; balance is reversing toxicity vs comfort.
Worked Example Opioid-Induced Constipation Management Ch 36 — Opioid Agonists and Antagonists · Overview section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Opioid-Induced Constipation Management

Defining Characteristics

Opioid-induced constipation (OIC) is the most common and persistent opioid side effect, caused by opioid action on mu-receptors in the GI tract.

  • Reduced peristalsis, increased fluid absorption, increased sphincter tone → hard, infrequent stools
  • Tolerance does NOT develop — persists for the duration of opioid therapy (unlike sedation/respiratory depression)
  • Affects most patients on chronic opioids
  • Requires PROACTIVE (prophylactic) management, not just treatment

Antecedents

  • Any opioid therapy (acute or chronic)
  • Higher doses, longer duration
  • Reduced mobility, dehydration, low-fiber diet
  • Older age
  • Concurrent anticholinergics, other constipating drugs
  • Pre-existing constipation or GI disorders

Negative Consequences

  • Abdominal pain, bloating, distension
  • Fecal impaction
  • Bowel obstruction (severe)
  • Hemorrhoids, anal fissures (straining)
  • Nausea, decreased appetite
  • Reduced quality of life; some patients reduce/stop needed pain medication
  • Increased healthcare utilization

Related Concepts

Mu-opioid receptors, peristalsis, stimulant laxatives (senna, bisacodyl), osmotic laxatives (PEG), stool softeners (docusate), PAMORAs (methylnaltrexone, naloxegol), bowel regimen, fecal impaction, fluid/fiber intake, mobility.

Exemplars

  • Prophylactic bowel regimen (KEY): start a stimulant laxative (senna, bisacodyl) at the same time opioids begin — do not wait for constipation. A stool softener (docusate) alone is often insufficient.
  • Stepwise approach: stimulant laxative +/- osmotic (PEG/MiraLAX) → if inadequate, add/escalate → if refractory, a PAMORA (peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonist: methylnaltrexone, naloxegol) that blocks GI opioid effects without reversing analgesia.
  • Non-pharm: increase fluids, dietary fiber (if appropriate), mobility/ambulation, privacy and routine for toileting.
  • Avoid bulk-forming laxatives (psyllium) alone in OIC if fluid intake is low or motility severely reduced — can worsen impaction.
  • Assessment: establish baseline bowel pattern; monitor frequency, consistency, distension, bowel sounds; assess for impaction.
  • Patient teaching: expect constipation; take the bowel regimen proactively (not PRN only); report no bowel movement in 3 days, severe pain, or distension; maintain fluids, fiber, and activity.
  • Distinguish: OIC management differs from naloxone reversal — PAMORAs treat constipation without reversing pain relief.
Worked Example Glipizide Ch 39 — Diabetes Mellitus · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Glipizide
Review Module Chapter
Ch 39 — Diabetes Mellitus
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Sulfonylurea (oral hypoglycemic) — stimulates the pancreas to release insulin (requires functioning beta cells)

Therapeutic Use

  • Type 2 diabetes mellitus (when diet/metformin are insufficient)

Complications

  • Hypoglycemia (main risk, especially with missed meals)
  • Weight gain, GI upset
  • Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Type 1 diabetes/DKA
  • Severe renal or hepatic impairment
  • Sulfonamide allergy (caution); caution: older adults

Interactions

  • Alcohol → disulfiram-like reaction and hypoglycemia
  • Beta blockers → mask hypoglycemia
  • NSAIDs, sulfonamides → ↑ hypoglycemia; corticosteroids/thiazides → ↑ glucose

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Fasting glucose and HbA1c within target
  • No severe hypoglycemia

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, ~30 min before a meal (immediate-release)
  • Ensure the client will eat to avoid hypoglycemia
  • Monitor glucose, HbA1c

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor blood glucose and for hypoglycemia
  • Ensure meals are eaten; educate on hypoglycemia management
  • Review alcohol interaction

Client Education

  • Take before a meal and do not skip meals (hypoglycemia)
  • Recognize/treat hypoglycemia (15 g fast carb); carry a source
  • Avoid alcohol (flushing/illness, low glucose)
  • Monitor glucose; continue diet and exercise
Worked Example Diabetes Mellitus (Type 1 & Type 2) Ch 39 — Diabetes Mellitus · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Diabetes Mellitus
Review Module Chapter
Ch 39 — Diabetes Mellitus

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Diabetes Mellitus — a group of metabolic disorders characterized by chronic hyperglycemia due to defects in insulin secretion, insulin action, or both.

  • Type 1: autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells → absolute insulin deficiency; requires insulin; usually younger onset; prone to DKA
  • Type 2: insulin resistance + relative insulin deficiency; associated with obesity/metabolic syndrome; managed with lifestyle, oral agents, sometimes insulin; prone to HHS
  • Gestational diabetes (pregnancy)

Diagnostic criteria: A1c ≥ 6.5%, fasting glucose ≥ 126 mg/dL, 2-hr OGTT ≥ 200, or random ≥ 200 with symptoms.

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Insulin normally moves glucose into cells; deficiency/resistance → glucose stays in blood (hyperglycemia)
  • Cells starve despite high blood glucose → body breaks down fat/protein
  • Type 1: no insulin → lipolysis → ketones → DKA (metabolic acidosis)
  • Type 2: some insulin present (prevents ketosis usually) → severe hyperglycemia → HHS (hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state)
  • Chronic hyperglycemia → micro/macrovascular damage
  • Osmotic diuresis from glucosuria → dehydration, electrolyte loss

Expected Findings

Classic (“3 Ps”):

  • Polyuria (excessive urination)
  • Polydipsia (excessive thirst)
  • Polyphagia (excessive hunger)
  • Weight loss (especially type 1), fatigue, blurred vision
  • Slow wound healing, recurrent infections
  • Type 1: rapid onset, may present in DKA
  • Type 2: gradual; often found on screening

Chronic complications:

  • Microvascular: retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy
  • Macrovascular: CAD, stroke, PAD
  • Foot ulcers, increased infection risk

Diagnostic: A1c, fasting/random glucose, OGTT; monitor lipids, renal function, eye/foot exams.

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Type 1: insulin (basal-bolus, pump) — lifelong; match to carbs/activity
  • Type 2: metformin first-line; add sulfonylureas, DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 agonists, insulin as needed
  • GLP-1 agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors have CV/renal benefits

Nursing care:

  • Blood glucose monitoring; A1c (goal generally < 7%)
  • Recognize/treat hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia (DKA/HHS)
  • Insulin administration teaching (rotation, storage, technique)
  • Foot care, eye exams, renal monitoring
  • Sick-day management; nutrition (carb counting); exercise
  • Cardiovascular risk reduction (BP, lipids)

Client Education

  • Blood glucose self-monitoring — technique, target ranges, when to check
  • Recognize hypoglycemia (shaky, sweaty, confused) — treat with 15 g fast carbs (rule of 15); carry a source
  • Recognize hyperglycemia/DKA (thirst, frequent urination, fruity breath, nausea) — seek care
  • Sick-day rules: continue insulin (do NOT stop), monitor glucose/ketones more often, hydrate, contact provider
  • Nutrition: consistent carbohydrate intake, balanced meals
  • Regular physical activity (monitor glucose around exercise)
  • Daily foot care: inspect feet, proper footwear, no going barefoot, report wounds
  • Annual eye and regular foot/renal exams
  • Take medications/insulin as prescribed; proper insulin storage and site rotation
  • Manage BP and cholesterol; smoking cessation
  • Wear medical alert ID
Worked Example Hypoglycemia & Glucagon Ch 39 — Diabetes Mellitus · Injectable section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Hypoglycemia & Glucagon

Defining Characteristics

Hypoglycemia — abnormally low blood glucose (typically < 70 mg/dL), a common and potentially dangerous complication of diabetes treatment.

Signs (adrenergic + neuroglycopenic):

  • Early (adrenergic): shakiness, sweating, tachycardia, palpitations, hunger, anxiety, tremor
  • Neuroglycopenic: confusion, difficulty concentrating, slurred speech, irritability, blurred vision
  • Severe: seizures, loss of consciousness, coma

Hypoglycemia unawareness can occur (especially long-standing diabetes, beta blockers mask symptoms).

Antecedents

  • Too much insulin or oral hypoglycemic (especially sulfonylureas)
  • Skipped/delayed meals or inadequate carbohydrate intake
  • Increased physical activity without dose/food adjustment
  • Alcohol consumption (impairs gluconeogenesis)
  • Renal/hepatic impairment (reduced drug clearance)
  • Incorrect insulin timing or dosing error
  • Beta blockers (mask symptoms)

Negative Consequences

  • Seizures, coma
  • Falls and injury
  • Brain injury or death if severe/prolonged (brain depends on glucose)
  • Cardiac arrhythmias
  • Hypoglycemia unawareness with recurrent episodes
  • Fear of hypoglycemia → poor glycemic control (overcompensation)

Related Concepts

Rule of 15, glucagon, insulin, sulfonylureas, neuroglycopenia, hypoglycemia unawareness, dextrose (D50), counterregulatory hormones, beta blocker masking, sick-day management.

Exemplars

  • Rule of 15 (conscious, able to swallow): give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate (4 oz juice/regular soda, glucose tablets, 1 tbsp honey) → recheck glucose in 15 min → repeat if still < 70 → once normalized, give a complex carb/protein snack to prevent recurrence.
  • Severe (unconscious or cannot swallow): do NOT give oral anything (aspiration). Give glucagon (IM, SC, or intranasal) OR IV dextrose (D50) if IV access; position on side; call for help.
  • Glucagon: raises blood glucose by stimulating glycogenolysis; may cause nausea/vomiting (position on side); less effective if glycogen stores depleted (malnutrition, alcohol, prolonged fasting).
  • After glucagon: patient may vomit; give carbohydrate when alert and able to swallow; monitor (glucose may drop again).
  • Prevention: consistent meals, adjust insulin for activity, monitor glucose, limit alcohol, recognize early symptoms, carry fast carbs and glucagon, family education.
  • Hospital: IV D50 for severe hypoglycemia with IV access; recheck and treat cause.
  • Teaching: family/caregivers learn to administer glucagon; never give oral glucose to an unconscious person.
Worked Example Insulin Therapy (Onset / Peak / Duration) Ch 39 — Diabetes Mellitus · Insulin section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Insulin Therapy (Onset / Peak / Duration)

Defining Characteristics

Insulin therapy replaces or supplements insulin to control blood glucose. Insulins are classified by onset, peak, and duration — understanding the time-action profile is critical for timing, hypoglycemia prevention, and meal coordination.

  • Rapid-acting (lispro, aspart, glulisine): onset ~15 min, peak ~1 hr, duration 3–5 hr — give with meals
  • Short-acting (Regular): onset ~30 min, peak 2–3 hr, duration 5–8 hr — give 30 min before meals; ONLY insulin given IV
  • Intermediate (NPH): onset 1–2 hr, peak 4–12 hr, duration 12–18 hr; cloudy
  • Long-acting (glargine, detemir): onset ~1–2 hr, no pronounced peak, duration ~24 hr; do NOT mix

Antecedents

  • Type 1 diabetes (required)
  • Type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled by oral agents
  • Gestational diabetes
  • DKA/HHS (IV regular insulin)
  • Hyperkalemia (insulin + dextrose to shift potassium)
  • Acute illness/stress hyperglycemia

Negative Consequences

  • Hypoglycemia — especially at the insulin’s PEAK time (know when to watch)
  • Hyperglycemia/DKA if dose missed or insufficient
  • Dosing/timing errors (high-alert medication)
  • Lipohypertrophy/lipoatrophy at injection sites (poor rotation)
  • Weight gain
  • Errors from mixing incompatible insulins or wrong concentration

Related Concepts

Onset/peak/duration, basal-bolus regimen, sliding scale, insulin mixing (“clear before cloudy”), high-alert medication, site rotation, U-100/U-500 concentration, hypoglycemia, DKA, carbohydrate counting.

Exemplars

  • Peak = hypoglycemia risk window: teach patients when each insulin peaks so they can recognize/prevent lows (e.g., NPH peaks 4–12 hr → watch mid-afternoon if given at breakfast).
  • Mixing NPH + Regular: draw up clear (Regular) before cloudy (NPH) — “RN” / “clear before cloudy” — to avoid contaminating the rapid vial.
  • Do NOT mix long-acting (glargine, detemir) with other insulins.
  • Only Regular insulin is given IV (DKA, hyperkalemia).
  • Rapid-acting: give right before/with meals (onset ~15 min) — ensure food is available to avoid hypoglycemia.
  • Site rotation: rotate within and between sites (abdomen fastest absorption) to prevent lipohypertrophy.
  • High-alert safety: independent double-check for insulin doses; use insulin-specific syringes; never use “U” abbreviation (write “units”); verify concentration.
  • Storage: unopened insulin refrigerated; in-use vials/pens room temperature ~28 days; do not freeze; roll (don’t shake) cloudy insulin.
  • Nursing assessment: verify type, dose, timing relative to meals; monitor glucose; assess injection sites; educate on time-action profile.
Worked Example Methimazole Ch 40 — Endocrine Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Methimazole
Review Module Chapter
Ch 40 — Endocrine Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Antithyroid medication — inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis (blocks iodine incorporation/coupling), lowering T3 and T4

Therapeutic Use

  • Hyperthyroidism / Graves disease
  • Preparation for thyroidectomy or radioactive iodine therapy

Complications

  • Agranulocytosis (sore throat, fever — life-threatening)
  • Hepatotoxicity; rash, arthralgia
  • Hypothyroidism if over-treated; teratogenic (1st trimester)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • First trimester of pregnancy (PTU preferred then)
  • Hypersensitivity, prior agranulocytosis/severe liver injury
  • Breastfeeding (caution)

Interactions

  • Anticoagulants → effect altered as thyroid status changes
  • Digoxin, beta blockers → dose needs change as metabolism normalizes

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Normalized thyroid levels (↓ T3/T4, normalizing TSH)
  • ↓ symptoms (palpitations, heat intolerance, weight loss); no agranulocytosis/hepatotoxicity

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, taken consistently (effect over several weeks)
  • Monitor CBC and LFTs; monitor thyroid function
  • Do not stop abruptly without provider guidance

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor for infection (CBC), liver function, and thyroid levels
  • Assess for resolution of hyperthyroid symptoms and signs of hypothyroidism
  • Educate on reporting sore throat/fever immediately

Client Education

  • Report sore throat, fever, or mouth sores immediately (low white cells)
  • Report yellowing skin, dark urine, or fatigue (liver)
  • Take consistently; effects take weeks; keep lab appointments
  • Avoid pregnancy in the first trimester on this drug — discuss options
Worked Example Hypothyroidism Ch 40 — Endocrine Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Hypothyroidism
Review Module Chapter
Ch 40 — Endocrine Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Hypothyroidism — deficiency of thyroid hormone, slowing metabolic processes throughout the body.

  • Primary (most common): thyroid gland failure — Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (autoimmune) is leading cause; also post-thyroidectomy, radioactive iodine, iodine deficiency
  • Secondary: pituitary failure (low TSH)
  • Myxedema coma: severe, life-threatening decompensated hypothyroidism
  • More common in women; increases with age

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Insufficient thyroid hormone (T3, T4) → decreased metabolic rate in all tissues
  • Reduced energy production, slowed body functions
  • In primary hypothyroidism: low T4 → elevated TSH (pituitary tries to stimulate thyroid)
  • Accumulation of mucopolysaccharides → myxedema (non-pitting edema)
  • Hashimoto’s: autoimmune destruction of thyroid tissue

Expected Findings

Slowed metabolism:

  • Fatigue, lethargy, weakness
  • Cold intolerance
  • Weight gain (despite poor appetite)
  • Bradycardia
  • Constipation
  • Dry skin, brittle hair/nails, hair loss
  • Cognitive slowing, depression, memory issues
  • Menstrual irregularities
  • Periorbital edema, puffy face (myxedema)
  • Hoarseness, enlarged tongue

Myxedema coma: hypothermia, hypotension, bradycardia, respiratory depression, altered mental status (emergency).

Diagnostic:

  • Elevated TSH, low free T4 (primary)
  • Thyroid antibodies (Hashimoto’s)
  • Lipid panel (often elevated)

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Levothyroxine (synthetic T4) — lifelong replacement; titrate to TSH
  • Start low and increase slowly in older adults / cardiac disease (avoid precipitating angina/arrhythmia)
  • Myxedema coma: IV levothyroxine, supportive care (warming, ventilation, fluids, corticosteroids)

Nursing care:

  • Monitor TSH/T4 to guide dosing
  • Monitor cardiovascular response (especially when starting)
  • Warmth for cold intolerance
  • Promote bowel regularity
  • Energy conservation
  • Monitor for over-replacement (hyperthyroid symptoms)

Client Education

  • Take levothyroxine in the morning on an empty stomach, 30–60 min before breakfast, with water
  • This is lifelong therapy — do not stop even when feeling well
  • Take at the same time daily; be consistent with brand
  • Separate from calcium, iron, antacids by 4 hours (reduce absorption)
  • It may take weeks to feel full effect
  • Report symptoms of over-replacement (palpitations, weight loss, nervousness, heat intolerance, insomnia)
  • Report chest pain (especially if older/cardiac disease)
  • Keep regular lab appointments for TSH monitoring
  • Do not switch brands without provider/lab follow-up
  • Inform provider if pregnant (dose usually increases)
Worked Example Hyperthyroidism (Graves’ Disease) Ch 40 — Endocrine Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Hyperthyroidism
Review Module Chapter
Ch 40 — Endocrine Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Hyperthyroidism — excess thyroid hormone, accelerating metabolic processes.

  • Graves’ disease (most common): autoimmune; antibodies stimulate the thyroid (TSI); associated with exophthalmos and goiter
  • Toxic multinodular goiter; toxic adenoma
  • Thyroiditis (transient)
  • Excess thyroid hormone intake
  • Thyroid storm (thyrotoxic crisis): life-threatening severe hyperthyroidism

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Excess T3/T4 → increased metabolic rate in all tissues
  • Increased oxygen consumption, heat production, sympathetic activity
  • Graves’: autoantibodies (thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins) bind TSH receptors → continuous stimulation
  • Primary: low TSH, high free T4/T3
  • Exophthalmos: immune-mediated retro-orbital tissue changes

Expected Findings

Accelerated metabolism:

  • Weight loss despite increased appetite
  • Heat intolerance, sweating
  • Tachycardia, palpitations, atrial fibrillation, hypertension
  • Nervousness, anxiety, irritability, tremor
  • Insomnia
  • Diarrhea/frequent stools
  • Warm, moist skin; fine hair
  • Goiter (enlarged thyroid)
  • Graves’: exophthalmos (bulging eyes), lid lag

Thyroid storm: high fever, severe tachycardia, hypertension then hypotension, agitation/delirium, vomiting (emergency).

Diagnostic: low TSH, elevated free T4/T3; thyroid antibodies (Graves’); radioactive iodine uptake.

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Antithyroid drugs (methimazole, propylthiouracil/PTU) — block hormone synthesis; PTU preferred in 1st trimester pregnancy
  • Beta blockers (propranolol) — control symptoms (tachycardia, tremor)
  • Radioactive iodine (I-131) — destroys thyroid tissue (common definitive treatment; leads to hypothyroidism → need replacement)
  • Iodine solutions (SSKI) — before surgery / thyroid storm
  • Thyroidectomy (surgical)

Nursing care:

  • Monitor cardiac status (afib, HR), weight, temperature
  • Cool environment; promote rest; reduce stimulation
  • Adequate nutrition/calories
  • Eye care for exophthalmos (lubricants, elevate HOB)
  • Monitor for thyroid storm; agranulocytosis (antithyroid drugs)

Client Education

  • Antithyroid drugs: take consistently; effects take weeks; report sore throat, fever (agranulocytosis); report jaundice (hepatotoxicity, especially PTU)
  • Beta blockers: control symptoms; do not stop abruptly
  • Radioactive iodine: radiation precautions (limit close contact, especially children/pregnant women, for several days); will likely become hypothyroid → need lifelong levothyroxine
  • Eat a high-calorie, nutritious diet (increased metabolism)
  • Avoid caffeine and stimulants
  • Cool, calm, restful environment
  • Eye protection if exophthalmos (sunglasses, artificial tears, elevate head)
  • Report worsening symptoms: high fever, severe palpitations, agitation (thyroid storm — emergency)
  • Keep follow-up for thyroid levels
  • PTU preferred if pregnant in first trimester
Worked Example Addison’s Disease & Adrenal Crisis Ch 40 — Endocrine Disorders · Other section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Addison’s Disease (Adrenal Insufficiency)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 40 — Endocrine Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Addison’s Disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) — deficiency of adrenal cortex hormones: cortisol (glucocorticoid) and often aldosterone (mineralocorticoid).

  • Primary: adrenal gland destruction (autoimmune most common; also TB, hemorrhage)
  • Secondary: pituitary ACTH deficiency (or abrupt corticosteroid withdrawal — common iatrogenic cause)
  • Adrenal (Addisonian) crisis: acute, life-threatening insufficiency — medical emergency

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Cortisol deficiency → impaired stress response, hypoglycemia, hypotension, GI symptoms
  • Aldosterone deficiency → sodium loss, potassium retention, water loss → hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypovolemia, hypotension
  • Loss of negative feedback → high ACTH (primary) → hyperpigmentation (ACTH stimulates melanocytes)
  • Crisis triggered by stress (infection, surgery, trauma) when cortisol cannot increase, or abrupt steroid withdrawal

Expected Findings

  • Chronic fatigue, weakness, lethargy
  • Hyperpigmentation (bronze skin, especially creases, scars, mucous membranes) — primary
  • Weight loss, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain
  • Hypotension, orthostatic hypotension, salt craving
  • Hypoglycemia
  • Labs: hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia

Adrenal crisis:

  • Severe hypotension → shock
  • Severe hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia
  • Profound weakness, confusion
  • Nausea, vomiting, abdominal/flank pain, fever (emergency)

Diagnostic: low cortisol, high ACTH (primary), ACTH stimulation test, electrolytes.

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Glucocorticoid replacement (hydrocortisone, prednisone) — lifelong
  • Mineralocorticoid replacement (fludrocortisone) — if aldosterone deficient
  • Adrenal crisis: immediate IV hydrocortisone, IV fluids (NS), dextrose for hypoglycemia, correct electrolytes

Nursing care:

  • Monitor vital signs (hypotension), electrolytes, glucose, weight, I&O
  • Stress-dose steroids during illness/surgery (increased need)
  • Recognize and treat adrenal crisis promptly
  • Avoid abrupt steroid discontinuation
  • Promote rest; prevent infection

Client Education

  • Take replacement steroids every day for life — NEVER abruptly stop (can precipitate crisis)
  • “Sick-day” stress dosing: increase glucocorticoid dose during illness, fever, surgery, or major stress (per provider instructions)
  • Take glucocorticoid with food; often larger dose in morning (mimic natural rhythm)
  • Wear a medical alert bracelet (adrenal insufficiency)
  • Carry an emergency injectable hydrocortisone kit and know how to use it
  • Recognize adrenal crisis (severe weakness, dizziness, vomiting, confusion) — seek emergency care; give emergency injection if trained
  • Maintain adequate salt intake (especially if on fludrocortisone)
  • Report signs of over-replacement (Cushingoid: weight gain, moon face, swelling)
  • Keep follow-up appointments; do not run out of medication
  • Inform all providers of the condition before procedures
Worked Example Penicillin G Ch 44 — Antibiotics Affecting the Bacterial Cell Wall · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Penicillin G
Review Module Chapter
Ch 44 — Antibiotics Affecting the Bacterial Cell Wall
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Beta-lactam (penicillin) antibiotic — inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis, causing cell lysis (bactericidal)

Therapeutic Use

  • Susceptible gram-positive infections: streptococcal infections, syphilis, and others

Complications

  • Allergic reactions — including anaphylaxis (most serious)
  • GI upset, diarrhea; rash
  • Superinfection (e.g., C. difficile); high IV doses → electrolyte issues

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Penicillin or cephalosporin hypersensitivity (cross-sensitivity possible)
  • Caution: renal impairment (dose adjust)

Interactions

  • Probenecid → ↑ penicillin level (delays excretion)
  • Aminoglycosides → inactivation if mixed in same line
  • May reduce effectiveness of oral contraceptives

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Resolution of infection (↓ fever/WBC, negative cultures)
  • No allergic reaction or superinfection

Medication Administration

  • Routes: IM, IV (penicillin G); obtain allergy history before first dose
  • Observe ~30 min after administration for allergic reaction; keep emergency equipment available
  • Give around the clock to maintain levels; complete the full course

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess for penicillin/cephalosporin allergy before administering
  • Monitor for anaphylaxis (have epinephrine ready); assess for superinfection/C. difficile
  • Monitor renal function with high doses

Client Education

  • Report rash, itching, swelling, or difficulty breathing immediately (allergy)
  • Complete the entire course even if feeling better
  • Report severe/watery diarrhea (C. difficile)
  • Use a backup contraceptive method if applicable
Worked Example Ceftriaxone Ch 44 — Antibiotics Affecting the Bacterial Cell Wall · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Ceftriaxone
Review Module Chapter
Ch 44 — Antibiotics Affecting the Bacterial Cell Wall
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Third-generation cephalosporin (beta-lactam) — inhibits cell wall synthesis (bactericidal); broad spectrum with good CNS penetration

Therapeutic Use

  • Serious infections: meningitis, pneumonia, gonorrhea, sepsis, surgical prophylaxis

Complications

  • Allergic reactions (cross-sensitivity with penicillins)
  • GI upset, diarrhea; C. difficile superinfection
  • Biliary sludging; disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Cephalosporin/penicillin hypersensitivity
  • Neonates — do not combine with calcium-containing IV solutions (precipitation)
  • Caution: renal/hepatic impairment

Interactions

  • Alcohol → disulfiram-like reaction
  • Calcium-containing IV solutions (neonates) → fatal precipitates
  • Anticoagulants → ↑ bleeding risk

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Resolution of infection (↓ fever/WBC, negative cultures)
  • No allergic reaction or C. difficile infection

Medication Administration

  • Routes: IM, IV; assess penicillin/cephalosporin allergy first
  • Do not mix with calcium-containing solutions in neonates
  • Complete full course; monitor injection site

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess for beta-lactam allergy and cross-sensitivity
  • Monitor for anaphylaxis, C. difficile diarrhea, and bleeding
  • Avoid calcium co-administration in neonates

Client Education

  • Avoid alcohol during and a few days after therapy
  • Report rash/swelling/breathing trouble or severe diarrhea
  • Complete the full course
  • Report unusual bleeding/bruising
Worked Example Amoxicillin/Clavulanate (Augmentin) Ch 44 — Antibiotics Affecting the Bacterial Cell Wall · Penicillins section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Amoxicillin/Clavulanate (Augmentin)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 44 — Antibiotics Affecting the Bacterial Cell Wall
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Aminopenicillin + beta-lactamase inhibitor
  • Amoxicillin: inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis (bactericidal)
  • Clavulanate: inhibits beta-lactamase enzymes that would otherwise inactivate amoxicillin → extends spectrum to beta-lactamase-producing organisms
  • Broader spectrum than amoxicillin alone

Therapeutic Use

  • Otitis media, sinusitis
  • Respiratory infections (community-acquired pneumonia, bronchitis)
  • Skin/soft tissue infections, animal/human bites
  • Urinary tract infections
