Worked Example Safe Medication Administration and Error Reduction Ch 2 — Safe Medication Administration and Error Reduction · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill
Safe Medication Administration and Error Reduction
Review Module Chapter
Ch 2 — Safe Medication Administration and Error Reduction

Description of Skill

  • Use two unique identifiers before each medication administration
  • Acceptable identifiers: full name, date of birth, medical record number
  • Compare the medication administration record (MAR) against the client's identification armband
  • Scan the client's armband and the medication barcode when available
  • Ask the client to state their name and date of birth (when able)
  • For unconscious/non-verbal clients, verify with armband and a family member

Indications

  • Reduces wrong-patient errors
  • Required by The Joint Commission National Patient Safety Goal
  • Used at every medication administration, blood transfusion, specimen collection

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre:

  • Verify medication order against original prescription
  • Check for allergies (chart, ID band, verbal confirmation)
  • Assess client's clinical status to confirm appropriateness (e.g., HR before digoxin, BP before antihypertensive)
  • Check pertinent labs (K+ with digoxin, INR with warfarin, drug levels)
  • Verify the three checks of the medication label:
    • 1st check: when retrieving from storage
    • 2nd check: when preparing
    • 3rd check: at bedside before administering
  • Calculate doses; double-check high-alert medications (insulin, heparin, opioids, chemotherapy) with a second nurse
  • Two identifiers before administration

Intra:

  • Administer correctly per route guidelines (no IV push for oral; correct injection site, angle, technique)
  • Communicate with client about the medication
  • Stay with client until oral meds are swallowed
  • Use barcoded medication administration (BCMA) systems if available
  • Do NOT leave medications at bedside unattended

Post:

  • Document immediately after administration (never before)
  • Document any client refusal, missed dose, or adverse effect
  • Monitor for therapeutic response and adverse effects appropriate to medication
  • Report errors through institutional system (incident report); complete medication reconciliation as appropriate

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Rights of Medication Administration verified for every dose:
    • Right client (two identifiers: name + DOB or MRN)
    • Right medication (check label 3x: pulling, preparing, before giving)
    • Right dose
    • Right route
    • Right time
    • Right documentation
    • Right reason / indication
    • Right response (evaluate effect)
    • Right to refuse (educate; document)
  • Zero medication errors reaching the client
  • Errors reported through institutional error-reporting system (non-punitive culture of safety)
  • No adverse drug events from preventable errors

Potential Complications

  • Medication errors by category:
    • Prescribing errors: wrong drug, dose, route, or for wrong client
    • Transcription errors: misreading or miscommunication of order
    • Dispensing errors: pharmacy provides wrong medication or dose
    • Administration errors: omitted, wrong client, wrong time, wrong route, wrong dose
    • Monitoring errors: failure to assess response or adverse effects
  • Adverse drug events: harm caused by medication (allergic reactions, side effects, toxicity)
  • Anaphylaxis from undocumented or unrecognized allergy
  • IV line complications (infiltration, extravasation, phlebitis, infection)
  • Sound-alike / look-alike drug confusion
  • Calculation errors leading to overdose or underdose

Nursing Interventions

  • Continuously assess for complications during and after the skill
  • Maintain aseptic/sterile technique as indicated
  • Escalate per facility policy if adverse outcomes occur
  • Document findings, interventions, and patient response; notify provider of unexpected outcomes

Client Education

  • Explain each medication: name, purpose, dose, schedule, side effects, what to report
  • Reinforce "do not stop without asking" for many medications (steroids, antihypertensives, antidepressants)
  • Keep a current list of all medications (including OTC, herbals, supplements); share with all providers
  • Use one pharmacy when possible — interaction checks
  • Know what to do if a dose is missed (varies by drug — never auto-double up)
  • Use medication organizers, alarms, or other adherence aids
  • Bring all medications to every appointment ("brown bag" method) for review
  • Storage: cool, dry place; out of reach of children; check expiration dates
  • Dispose of unused/expired medications safely (drug take-back programs)
  • Never share prescription medications
  • Tell provider about any new allergies or reactions
Worked Example Six (or Eight) Rights of Medication Administration Ch 2 — Safe Medication Administration and Error Reduction · Rights section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Six (or Eight) Rights of Medication Administration

Defining Characteristics

The Rights of Medication Administration are a structured safety framework verified BEFORE every medication is given. The classic Six Rights are: Right Patient, Right Drug, Right Dose, Right Route, Right Time, and Right Documentation.

Two additional rights expand this to Eight: Right Reason/Indication and Right Response/Evaluation. Some institutions also include Right to Refuse, Right Education, and Right Assessment.

Verification occurs at three checks: (1) when retrieving from storage, (2) when preparing, (3) at the bedside immediately before administration. Use two patient identifiers (name + DOB; never the room number).

Antecedents

  • An order from a licensed provider, with all required components (drug, dose, route, frequency, indication)
  • Access to medication reconciliation and the client’s allergy history
  • Functional safety technology: BCMA (barcode med admin), eMAR (electronic MAR), smart infusion pumps
  • Nurse training and a culture of safety that supports questioning unclear orders
  • Adequate staffing and minimal distractions (the “no-interruption zone” during med prep)

Negative Consequences

  • Medication errors — wrong patient, wrong drug, wrong dose, wrong route, wrong time — are among the most common preventable healthcare errors
  • Adverse drug events (ADEs) — harm ranging from minor to fatal
  • Sentinel events with mandatory reporting and root-cause analysis
  • Legal liability for the nurse, provider, and institution
  • Loss of patient trust and damage to therapeutic relationship
  • Nurse moral distress, particularly when systemic factors (staffing, technology failures) contributed to the error

Related Concepts

Just Culture, root cause analysis, sentinel events, BCMA, two patient identifiers, medication reconciliation, ISMP Do-Not-Use abbreviations, tall-man lettering, high-alert medications, near-miss reporting, the “no-interruption zone.”

Exemplars

  • Right Patient: scan the wristband and verbally verify name and DOB; never use room number alone
  • Right Drug: read the label THREE times (when retrieving, preparing, and at bedside); check for sound-alike/look-alike drugs (LASA) using tall-man lettering (predniSONE vs prednisoLONE)
  • Right Dose: verify calculations, especially for pediatric weight-based doses and high-alert drugs (insulin, heparin, opioids); independent double-check for high-alert
  • Right Route: never assume — clarify any ambiguous order (PO vs IV; oral vs feeding tube)
  • Right Time: within 30 minutes of scheduled time for routine meds; STAT/Now/timed meds have stricter windows
  • Right Documentation: chart immediately after administration (not before — never chart what hasn’t happened); include site, response, and any client teaching provided
Worked Example High-Alert Medications (ISMP) Ch 2 — Safe Medication Administration and Error Reduction · Error Prevention section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
High-Alert Medications (ISMP)

Defining Characteristics

High-alert medications are drugs that bear a heightened risk of causing significant patient harm when used in error. The errors themselves may not be more common, but the consequences are more severe.

Identified by the Institute for Safe Medication Practices (ISMP), these drugs require additional safeguards beyond the standard Rights: independent double-checks, standardized order sets, dose limits, and barcoding. Major classes include anticoagulants, opioids, insulin, neuromuscular blockers, concentrated electrolytes, and chemotherapy.

Antecedents

  • Drug characteristics: narrow therapeutic index, look-alike/sound-alike names, complex dosing
  • Setting: acute care, ICU, OR, oncology, pediatrics — high-stakes environments
  • System factors: lack of standardization, distractions, weak forcing functions (e.g., concentrated KCl on units)
  • Human factors: fatigue, multitasking, communication failures during handoffs
  • Patient factors: extremes of age, renal/hepatic dysfunction, polypharmacy

Negative Consequences

  • Catastrophic harm or death — examples: IV KCl push → cardiac arrest; heparin overdose → fatal hemorrhage; insulin 100x overdose → severe hypoglycemia
  • Sentinel events requiring root-cause analysis and reporting
  • Increased length of stay, ICU admission, prolonged disability
  • Massive legal and financial costs
  • Loss of staff confidence and morale; burnout and second-victim phenomenon

Related Concepts

ISMP guidelines, Joint Commission patient safety goals, forcing functions, independent double-check, standardized order sets, look-alike/sound-alike (LASA), tall-man lettering, BCMA, smart pumps, medication reconciliation, sentinel events.

Exemplars

  • Anticoagulants: heparin (weight-based protocols, anti-Xa monitoring), warfarin (INR target, vitamin K antidote), DOACs (renal dose adjustment)
  • Insulin: independent double-check for IV insulin drips and pediatric doses; never use abbreviation “U” (mistaken for 0)
  • Opioids: PCA programmed by 2 nurses; naloxone available; sedation scale + respiratory rate monitoring
  • Concentrated electrolytes: KCl removed from floor stock; always diluted; never IV push (fatal)
  • Neuromuscular blockers: stored separately, labeled “WARNING: paralyzing agent”; only given to intubated/ventilated clients
  • Chemotherapy: independent double-check, certified chemotherapy nurses, vincristine NEVER given intrathecally (fatal)
Worked Example Controlled Substances and DEA Schedules Ch 2 — Safe Medication Administration and Error Reduction · Controlled section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Controlled Substances and DEA Schedules

Defining Characteristics

Controlled substances are drugs regulated under the federal Controlled Substances Act (CSA) due to their potential for abuse, dependence, and diversion. The DEA classifies them into 5 Schedules (I–V) based on abuse potential and accepted medical use.

Schedule I = highest abuse potential, no accepted medical use (heroin, LSD). Schedule II = high abuse potential, accepted medical use (morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl, methylphenidate). Schedules III–V = progressively lower abuse potential. Schedule II drugs have the strictest controls: no refills, hand-written or e-prescribed, locked storage, witnessed waste.

Antecedents

  • A licensed prescriber with DEA registration
  • A pharmacy authorized to dispense controlled substances
  • Institutional policies for storage, handling, and documentation
  • Functional secure storage (Pyxis, Omnicell, double-locked narcotic cabinet)
  • A nurse trained in proper documentation and waste procedures
  • A second licensed witness available for waste/discrepancies

Negative Consequences

  • Diversion — theft or misuse of controlled substances by staff (a major patient-safety and impaired-practice concern)
  • Inadequate pain control when fear of regulation discourages appropriate prescribing
  • Loss of nursing license, DEA registration, and employment for documentation/diversion errors
  • Criminal charges for improper handling, falsifying records, or diversion
  • Contribution to the opioid epidemic when prescribing safeguards fail
  • Impaired-nurse harm to self and patients

Related Concepts

DEA registration, opioid stewardship, diversion prevention, pain management, impaired nurse programs, naloxone access, PDMP (prescription drug monitoring program), Pyxis/Omnicell, waste documentation, end-of-shift count.

Exemplars

  • Schedule II (CII): morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl, methylphenidate (Ritalin), amphetamine (Adderall) — no refills; new prescription each time; locked storage; witnessed waste
  • Schedule III (CIII): ketamine, buprenorphine, codeine combinations (Tylenol #3); up to 5 refills within 6 months
  • Schedule IV (CIV): benzodiazepines (alprazolam, lorazepam), tramadol, zolpidem; up to 5 refills
  • Schedule V (CV): pregabalin, low-dose codeine cough preparations; least restrictive
  • Waste documentation: partial doses (e.g., draw 6 mg morphine, give 4 mg) must be witnessed by a second licensed staff member; both sign the e-MAR/waste log
  • End-of-shift count: outgoing and incoming nurses verify the count; any discrepancy is immediately reported and investigated
Worked Example Dosage Calculation Ch 3 — Dosage Calculation · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill
Dosage Calculation
Review Module Chapter
Ch 3 — Dosage Calculation

Description of Skill

  • Step 1: Convert weight — 22 lb ÷ 2.2 = 10 kg
  • Step 2: Calculate total daily dose — 8 mg/kg/day × 10 kg = 80 mg/day
  • Step 3: Divide by doses per day — 80 mg ÷ 2 doses (q12h) = 40 mg per dose
  • Step 4: Calculate volume — (40 mg ÷ 100 mg) × 5 mL = 2 mL per dose
  • Answer: 2 mL per dose

Indications

  • Every medication administration involves at minimum a confirmation that the supplied dose equals the prescribed dose
  • Calculation required when:
    • Available dose differs from prescribed dose (e.g., order 250 mg, available 500 mg tablet)
    • Weight-based dosing (most pediatric meds, chemotherapy, heparin, vancomycin)
    • Renal/hepatic dose adjustments (CrCl-based dosing)
    • IV infusion rate (mL/hr from mg/kg/min)
    • Drug conversions (mg ↔ mcg, mEq ↔ mg)
    • Pediatric dosing from adult doses (Body Surface Area)
    • Diluting concentrated drugs to safe infusion concentrations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre:

  • Confirm weight in kg (convert from lb: kg = lb / 2.2)
  • Verify the prescribed dose is within safe range (drug reference, hospital protocol)
  • Identify drug concentration available (mg/mL, units/mL)
  • Set up the calculation using a consistent method (dimensional analysis, ratio-proportion, or formula method)
  • Independent double-check by a second RN for high-alert drugs (insulin, heparin, opioids, chemotherapy, pediatric IV doses)

Intra (during preparation):

  • Use calculator for non-trivial calculations (don't rely on mental math)
  • Avoid trailing zeros (5.0 → 5); always use leading zeros (.5 → 0.5)
  • Round per hospital policy and drug type (don't round pediatric doses to 1 mg if mcg precision is required)
  • Use appropriate measurement device: oral syringe for liquid PO; tuberculin syringe for small SC volumes
  • Final check: dose calculated = dose actually drawn up?

Post:

  • Document dose given exactly
  • Document any waste (controlled substances require witnessed waste)
  • Monitor for therapeutic response and adverse effects appropriate to the drug
  • If error suspected after administration: report immediately, monitor client closely, support per protocol, complete incident report

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Correct dose delivered to client every time
  • No calculation-based medication errors
  • Therapeutic blood levels achieved (for narrow-window drugs like phenytoin, digoxin, vancomycin)
  • Independent double-check completed for high-alert medications
  • Documentation reflects accurate dose and rate

Potential Complications

  • Tenfold (decimal) errors — most common and dangerous (10x overdose or 10x underdose); especially in pediatrics and IV drugs
  • Misplaced decimal (5.0 mg vs .5 mg — use 0.5, never 5.0)
  • Unit confusion: mg vs mcg, mEq vs mg, units vs mL
  • Weight measurement errors (kg vs lb): always use kg for dose calculations
  • Incorrect drip-rate calculation → infusion too fast (toxicity, fluid overload) or too slow (subtherapeutic)
  • Heparin and insulin errors are particularly devastating (high-alert medications)
  • Chemotherapy errors can be fatal

Nursing Interventions

  • Continuously assess for complications during and after the skill
  • Maintain aseptic/sterile technique as indicated
  • Escalate per facility policy if adverse outcomes occur
  • Document findings, interventions, and patient response; notify provider of unexpected outcomes

Client Education

  • For clients managing their own medications at home:
    • Read all labels carefully every time
    • Use the measuring device provided with liquid medications (not household teaspoons — variable)
    • Tablespoons (tbsp) and teaspoons (tsp) are different — clarify with provider
    • Children's doses depend on weight; verify with pharmacist; do not estimate
    • If unsure of dose: STOP and call pharmacist or provider before giving
  • Common conversions to know:
    • 1 tsp = 5 mL
    • 1 tbsp = 15 mL
    • 1 oz = 30 mL
    • 1 lb = 0.454 kg (or kg × 2.2 = lb)
  • Never adjust dose without consulting provider
Worked Example IV Drip Rate Calculation (gtt/min) Ch 3 — Dosage Calculation · Formulas section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill
IV Drip Rate Calculation (gtt/min)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 3 — Dosage Calculation

Description of Skill

Calculating the gravity infusion drip rate in drops per minute (gtt/min) for an IV infusion administered without a pump.

Formula:

(Volume in mL / Time in min) × Drop factor (gtt/mL) = gtt/min

The drop factor is printed on the IV tubing package: macrodrip sets are typically 10, 15, or 20 gtt/mL; microdrip sets are 60 gtt/mL (used for pediatrics and slow infusions). Round to the nearest whole drop.

Example: Infuse 1,000 mL D5W over 8 hr with tubing drop factor of 15 gtt/mL.
(1,000 mL / 480 min) × 15 = 31 gtt/min.

Indications

  • Settings without infusion pumps available (some home care, field/emergency, low-resource settings)
  • Short, simple infusions where pump use is impractical
  • Verification check even WITH a pump (catches programming errors)
  • Backup if pump malfunctions or power fails

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre:

  • Verify the order: solution, volume, total time, indication
  • Identify drop factor from the IV tubing package — confirm macrodrip vs microdrip is appropriate for the rate
  • Calculate the gtt/min — double-check math; round to whole number
  • Identify client factors: age, fluid status, cardiac/renal function (limits flow rate)
  • Verify IV access patent and free of phlebitis/infiltration

Intra:

  • Open clamp and adjust roller clamp to deliver calculated gtt/min
  • Count drops in the drip chamber for a full 15 seconds × 4 (or 30 sec × 2) to confirm rate
  • Mark/label time tape on the bag to track expected level vs actual
  • Recheck rate every 30–60 min — gravity drips can drift with position changes

Post:

  • Document time started, rate, volume infused
  • Reassess IV site, vital signs, and clinical response
  • For blood transfusions: never use gravity if pump indicated; never exceed 4 hr per unit

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Infusion completes within the ordered timeframe (±5%)
  • Client maintains stable vital signs and fluid balance
  • IV site remains patent without infiltration or phlebitis
  • Therapeutic goal of the fluid/medication achieved

Potential Complications

  • Fluid overload — especially in older adults, infants, and cardiac/renal disease (rate too fast)
  • Inadequate fluid/drug delivery — subtherapeutic dose or insufficient resuscitation (rate too slow)
  • Infiltration or extravasation if line malpositioned
  • Phlebitis, infection, or air embolism (general IV risks)
  • Hypoglycemia if a dextrose infusion ends abruptly without taper
Worked Example Weight-Based Pediatric Dosing & Safe Dose Range Ch 3 — Dosage Calculation · Pediatric section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill
Weight-Based Pediatric Dosing
Review Module Chapter
Ch 3 — Dosage Calculation

Description of Skill

Calculating and verifying that a pediatric medication dose falls within the recommended safe dose range, typically expressed as mg/kg/day or mg/kg/dose.

Steps:

  1. Confirm the child’s current weight in kilograms (1 kg = 2.2 lb). Use the most recent measured weight from the chart — never an estimate.
  2. Calculate the safe dose range: minimum and maximum mg/kg from a drug reference.
  3. Compare the ordered dose to the safe range.
  4. If outside the range — hold and contact the provider. Do not administer.

Example: 18 kg child ordered acetaminophen 250 mg PO q4h PRN fever. Safe range: 10–15 mg/kg/dose. Min: 18 × 10 = 180 mg. Max: 18 × 15 = 270 mg. 250 mg is within range — safe to administer.

Indications

  • ALL pediatric medication doses (newborn through adolescent)
  • Doses in adults < 50 kg (weight-based dosing may also apply)
  • Weight-based regimens in any age (chemotherapy, heparin, vancomycin, gentamicin)
  • Verification at every dose — weights change as children grow or with illness

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre:

  • Obtain CURRENT weight in kg (not pounds; verify recent measurement; reweigh if weight is > 7 days old or clinical change)
  • Look up safe dose range in a current drug reference (Lexicomp, Micromedex, or institutional formulary)
  • Calculate min and max safe dose for THIS child
  • Compare ordered dose to calculated range
  • For high-alert medications: independent double-check with another licensed nurse

Intra:

  • If within range: administer per the Rights
  • If outside range: HOLD and contact provider; document the issue and resolution
  • For liquid medications: use an oral syringe (never household teaspoons); measure at eye level
  • For very small volumes (< 0.5 mL): use a 1-mL syringe with 0.01-mL graduations

Post:

  • Document dose, weight used, route, time, and response
  • Reassess for therapeutic effect and adverse effects (vital signs, pain score, behavior change)
  • Educate parent/caregiver on safe home dosing using the same kg-based logic

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Dose administered falls within the published safe range for the child’s weight
  • Therapeutic response achieved without adverse effects
  • No dosing errors detected on chart review or system audit
  • Family demonstrates correct measurement and dosing for home administration

Potential Complications

  • Underdose — therapeutic failure, prolonged illness
  • Overdose — toxicity (e.g., acetaminophen hepatotoxicity, opioid respiratory depression)
  • 10-fold dosing errors — classic peds error pattern (decimal point misplaced); ALWAYS use leading zero (0.5 mg) and never trailing zero (avoid 5.0 mg)
  • Wrong concentration confusion — especially for liquids that come in multiple strengths
  • Inaccurate measurement with household spoons rather than oral syringes
Worked Example Independent Double-Check (High-Alert Medications) Ch 3 — Dosage Calculation · Safety section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Independent Double-Check

Defining Characteristics

An independent double-check is a process in which two licensed clinicians separately verify a high-risk medication or process WITHOUT communicating their findings until both have completed their assessment.

The key word is INDEPENDENT — the second checker reviews the order, drug, dose, route, calculations, and pump programming WITHOUT influence from the first. A simple “Yes, that looks right” after a colleague reads it aloud is NOT an independent double-check — it is confirmation bias.

Performed for high-alert medications: heparin drips, insulin drips, chemotherapy, PCA pumps, pediatric doses, opioid infusions, IV potassium, and any concentrated electrolytes.

Antecedents

  • Institutional policy identifying which medications/situations require an independent double-check
  • Two licensed clinicians available (RN-RN, RN-pharmacist, or RN-provider per policy)
  • Access to the order, drug reference, weight, and calculations
  • A culture of safety where stopping to verify is supported, not penalized
  • Adequate staffing and time to perform the check without rushing

Negative Consequences

  • Catastrophic medication errors when the check is skipped or performed poorly — insulin overdoses, heparin overdoses, chemo errors
  • Confirmation bias when the “double-check” is just verbal agreement — both nurses agree on the same wrong answer
  • Diffusion of responsibility — each nurse relies on the other, neither fully engages
  • Sentinel events with mandatory reporting; loss of professional licensure
  • Patient harm or death

Related Concepts

High-alert medications (ISMP), forcing functions, BCMA, smart pumps, just culture, root-cause analysis, confirmation bias, sentinel events, medication reconciliation, the Six Rights, pediatric weight-based dosing.

Exemplars

  • Heparin infusion: two RNs independently verify patient weight, units/kg/hr ordered, vial concentration, pump programming, and bag label — THEN compare results. If any discrepancy: stop, recalculate, contact pharmacy/provider.
  • Insulin drip: independent check of order, drip rate, bag concentration, and pump programming at initiation and rate changes.
  • Pediatric high-alert dose: two RNs separately calculate weight-based mg/kg, compare to ordered dose, check pump programming.
  • Bad practice (NOT independent): Nurse A says “I’ve programmed 1.5 units/hr of insulin, can you check?” Nurse B looks at the pump and says “Yep, looks good” — this is verification, not independent double-check. Nurse B is influenced by Nurse A’s framing.
  • Good practice (independent): Nurse A places the order/MAR and calculation in front of Nurse B without comment. Nurse B calculates independently and programs the pump independently. They compare end results.
Worked Example Intravenous Therapy Ch 4 — Intravenous Therapy · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill
Intravenous Therapy
Review Module Chapter
Ch 4 — Intravenous Therapy

Description of Skill

Intravenous (IV) therapy delivers fluids, medications, blood, and nutrition directly into the venous circulation, providing:

  • Rapid onset — bypasses GI absorption
  • Precise dose control
  • Continuous infusion capability
  • Access for blood sampling and emergent medication delivery

Routes:

  • Peripheral IV (PIV): short-term, < 96 hours typically; hand, forearm
  • Midline catheter: 1-4 weeks; not for vesicants or TPN
  • Central venous catheter (PICC, tunneled, implanted port, non-tunneled): long-term, high-risk infusions, vesicants, TPN

Indications

  • Maintenance fluids (NPO, surgical, GI illness)
  • Fluid resuscitation (shock, hemorrhage, severe dehydration)
  • Electrolyte replacement
  • Medications that:
    • Need rapid onset (emergencies)
    • Cannot be given PO (vomiting, NPO, unconscious)
    • Are not absorbed PO (vancomycin, aminoglycosides)
    • Are irritating to GI tract or muscle (vesicants, irritants)
  • Blood and blood products
  • Total parenteral nutrition (TPN)
  • Diagnostic agents (contrast)
  • Continuous infusions (insulin, heparin, vasopressors, sedation)

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre-insertion:

  • Verify order; check fluid/medication compatibility and concentration
  • Assess client: allergies (esp. tape, latex, iodine), age, vein quality, hand dominance, AV fistula presence (avoid same arm)
  • Select appropriate gauge: 22-24 ga for routine; 18-20 ga for blood products, surgery, large-volume fluids
  • Select site: most distal first (preserves proximal sites for future use); avoid joints, areas of impaired circulation, mastectomy side
  • Hand hygiene; clean gloves; sterile technique for insertion

Insertion:

  • Apply tourniquet 5-15 cm above selected site
  • Clean with chlorhexidine (preferred) in concentric circles for 30 seconds; allow to air dry
  • Anchor vein; insert at 10-30° angle, bevel up
  • Observe flashback; advance catheter; release tourniquet
  • Connect tubing/lock; secure with transparent dressing; label with date/time/initials/gauge

During infusion:

  • Assess site q1-2h: pain, redness, swelling, warmth, drainage, infiltration
  • Verify rate per pump or count drops manually (gtt/min = mL/hr × drop factor / 60)
  • Check IV bag and tubing q1h: correct fluid, no air, no leaks, no bag empty
  • Maintain closed system; aseptic technique with any access
  • Change dressings per protocol (typically q5-7d transparent, q2d gauze, or PRN if soiled)
  • Change tubing per protocol (continuous: q96h; blood: each unit; lipids: q24h)
  • Rotate site if needed (typically PIV q72-96h or per protocol; assess routinely)

Post (discontinuation):

  • Stop infusion; remove dressing
  • Withdraw catheter parallel to skin; apply firm pressure 1-2 min (longer if anticoagulated)
  • Inspect catheter for completeness
  • Apply sterile dressing
  • Document site, condition, reason for discontinuation

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Correct fluid, medication, and rate delivered
  • Therapeutic response achieved (rehydration, ↓ symptoms, target labs)
  • IV site patent, intact, and free of complications
  • No infiltration, extravasation, phlebitis, or infection
  • Catheter removed when no longer needed
  • Client maintained at appropriate fluid status (no overload or deficit)

Potential Complications

  • Infiltration is the leakage of a non-vesicant solution into the tissue surrounding the IV catheter
  • Signs: coolness, swelling, pallor, decreased flow, possible fluid leakage
  • Caused by catheter displacement, vein wall puncture, or vein fragility

Nursing Interventions

  • Stop the IV infusion immediately
  • Remove the IV catheter
  • Elevate the extremity to promote venous return
  • Apply warm compress to most non-irritant solutions (or cool compress per specific solution protocol)
  • Restart IV in a different site, preferably proximal to or in the opposite extremity
  • Document site appearance, size, intervention, and time
  • Notify provider if significant infiltration

Client Education

  • Report immediately: pain, burning, swelling, redness, warmth, coolness, leaking around IV site; shortness of breath; chills/fever; chest pain
  • Avoid bending or twisting the affected limb
  • Avoid getting the dressing wet — cover during showering
  • Do not pull at or remove the dressing or tubing
  • You may use the hand for normal light activity unless the IV is at a joint
  • Ask for help when getting up — IV pole moves with you
  • Notify staff if the IV pump alarms, drips slow or stop, or you have any concerns
  • For central lines / PICC at home: trained on flushing, dressing changes, and signs of infection
Worked Example IV Fluid Tonicity (Isotonic / Hypotonic / Hypertonic) Ch 4 — Intravenous Therapy · Solutions section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
IV Fluid Tonicity

Defining Characteristics

Tonicity describes the osmotic pressure of an IV fluid relative to plasma, determining which way water moves between intravascular space and cells.

  • Isotonic (~285–310 mOsm/L) — same osmolarity as plasma; fluid stays in intravascular space; no shift
  • Hypotonic (< 285 mOsm/L) — lower osmolarity; water moves OUT of vessels INTO cells (cells swell)
  • Hypertonic (> 310 mOsm/L) — higher osmolarity; water moves FROM cells INTO vessels (cells shrink)

Selecting the right tonicity is essential to avoid cell injury (osmotic damage), fluid overload, or cerebral edema.

Antecedents

  • Clinical assessment of fluid status (intake/output, weight, vital signs, skin turgor, lung sounds)
  • Laboratory data (sodium, osmolality, BUN/creatinine, hematocrit)
  • Type of dehydration or imbalance (intracellular, extracellular, hypernatremic, hyponatremic)
  • Comorbidities — heart failure, kidney disease, liver disease, cerebral edema (modify fluid choice)
  • Provider order specifying solution, rate, and indication

Negative Consequences

  • Wrong isotonic (e.g., LR with hyperkalemia): precipitating cardiac arrhythmia
  • Hypotonic overuse: cellular swelling — potentially fatal cerebral edema; never give to clients with increased ICP or burns/trauma
  • Hypertonic too rapid: osmotic demyelination (central pontine myelinolysis) when correcting hyponatremia too fast
  • Fluid overload in any tonicity with cardiac/renal disease
  • Phlebitis or sclerosis from hypertonic infusions via peripheral lines (often require central access)

Related Concepts

Osmolarity, oncotic pressure, fluid balance, intracellular vs extracellular fluid, hyponatremia, hypernatremia, cerebral edema, fluid resuscitation, parenteral nutrition, central venous access.

Exemplars

  • Isotonic: 0.9% NaCl (normal saline), LR (lactated Ringer’s), D5W (initially isotonic, becomes hypotonic after dextrose metabolism). Used for: blood loss, dehydration, surgery, fluid resuscitation.
  • Hypotonic: 0.45% NaCl (1/2 NS), 0.225% NaCl (1/4 NS). Used for: cellular dehydration (DKA after initial resuscitation), maintenance fluids. AVOID with increased ICP, burns, trauma.
  • Hypertonic: 3% NaCl, D10W, D5 1/2 NS, D5 LR, D5 NS, TPN. Used for: severe hyponatremia, cerebral edema, nutrition. Requires CENTRAL line for higher concentrations; slow rate.
  • Colloids: albumin, hetastarch — large molecules that stay in vessels (oncotic pressure); used for shock, burns, hypoalbuminemia.
  • Clinical pearl: D5W is isotonic in the bag but becomes hypotonic in the body once dextrose is metabolized — equivalent to giving free water.
Worked Example Central Venous Access Device (CVAD/PICC) Management Ch 4 — Intravenous Therapy · Access section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure
CVAD/PICC Management
Review Module Chapter
Ch 4 — Intravenous Therapy

Description of Procedure

Central venous access devices (CVADs) are catheters whose tip terminates in the superior vena cava (SVC), inferior vena cava (IVC), or right atrium. Types include:

  • PICC (Peripherally Inserted Central Catheter) — inserted in upper arm, advanced to SVC; can stay weeks to months
  • Non-tunneled CVCs — subclavian, internal jugular, or femoral; short-term (days to weeks)
  • Tunneled catheters (Hickman, Broviac) — tunneled under skin to chest insertion; long-term
  • Implanted ports (Mediport, Port-a-cath) — subcutaneous reservoir accessed with Huber needle; long-term

Used for medications that are caustic to peripheral veins, long-term therapy, or rapid large-volume infusions.

Indications

  • Caustic / vesicant medications: chemotherapy, vasopressors, hypertonic fluids, TPN
  • Long-term IV therapy (> 7–10 days)
  • Frequent blood draws or hemodynamic monitoring
  • Poor peripheral access
  • Need for multiple simultaneous infusions

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre-insertion:

  • Verify informed consent and indication
  • Confirm coagulation status (PT/INR, platelets)
  • Position client (Trendelenburg for IJ/subclavian to engorge veins and prevent air embolism)

Post-insertion (most critical):

  • Verify tip placement with chest X-ray BEFORE first use — tip must be in lower SVC / cavoatrial junction
  • Sterile transparent dressing; change per protocol (typically every 7 days or when soiled/loose)
  • Scrub the hub with alcohol or CHG for 15 seconds before EVERY access (“scrub the hub”)
  • Flush with saline before and after each medication; positive-pressure technique to prevent reflux
  • Heparin lock per institutional policy (some catheters; not all)
  • Daily assessment: insertion site, dressing intact, line patency, signs of infection

Removal:

  • Position client SUPINE or Trendelenburg with Valsalva maneuver during removal
  • Apply pressure 5 min after removal; occlusive dressing
  • Inspect catheter tip for completeness

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Catheter remains patent throughout therapy without occlusion or dislodgement
  • No CLABSI (catheter-related bloodstream infection)
  • Tip placement remains correct on follow-up imaging if indicated
  • Therapy goals achieved (medication delivered, parenteral nutrition tolerated, etc.)
  • Removal without complications (intact catheter tip, no bleeding)

Potential Complications

  • Pneumothorax (subclavian/IJ insertion) — chest pain, dyspnea; chest X-ray confirms
  • Air embolism — clamp catheter, position left lateral Trendelenburg, administer O2
  • Catheter-related bloodstream infection (CLABSI) — fever, chills, positive blood cultures
  • Catheter occlusion — thrombotic (alteplase) or precipitate (specific dissolution)
  • Catheter migration / displacement — confirm with X-ray before further use
  • Pinch-off syndrome (subclavian) — catheter compressed between clavicle and first rib
  • Phlebitis at PICC insertion site; deep vein thrombosis
Worked Example Infiltration vs Extravasation Ch 4 — Intravenous Therapy · Complications section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Infiltration vs Extravasation

Defining Characteristics

Infiltration — leakage of a non-vesicant (non-irritating) IV fluid or medication into surrounding tissue.

Extravasation — leakage of a vesicant (tissue-damaging) medication into surrounding tissue. Causes tissue necrosis, potential need for surgical debridement, skin grafting, or amputation if severe.

Both present with: swelling, coolness, blanching, slowed/stopped flow, no blood return. The DISTINCTION is the drug being infused — this determines urgency and treatment.

Antecedents

  • IV catheter dislodgement, vein perforation, or venous fragility
  • Vesicant medication administered through a peripheral line that should be central (chemotherapy, vasopressors, hypertonic solutions, calcium chloride)
  • Pediatric/older adult vessels (fragile, mobile)
  • Prolonged dwell time of peripheral IV
  • Inadequate site assessment between doses
  • Inability of client to report pain (anesthesia, sedation, dementia)

Negative Consequences

  • Infiltration: tissue swelling, discomfort, delayed therapy, need to restart IV. Usually resolves with elevation and warm/cool compresses.
  • Extravasation: TISSUE NECROSIS — can require surgical debridement, skin grafting, or amputation; permanent disfigurement; nerve injury; compartment syndrome. Vesicants like doxorubicin and vincristine cause severe damage.
  • Legal liability for nursing if not detected promptly or proper protocol not followed
  • Psychological impact: pain, scarring, mistrust of healthcare

Related Concepts

Vesicant medications, central venous access, chemotherapy administration, vasopressor administration, IV site assessment, compartment syndrome, antidotes (hyaluronidase for non-chemo, dexrazoxane for anthracyclines, phentolamine for vasopressors).

Exemplars

  • Infiltration management: Stop the infusion, remove the catheter, elevate the extremity, apply warm or cool compresses (per fluid type), document. Restart IV in a different site.
  • Extravasation management: (1) STOP infusion IMMEDIATELY but LEAVE CATHETER IN PLACE; (2) aspirate residual drug through the catheter; (3) administer the drug-specific antidote (hyaluronidase, dexrazoxane, phentolamine); (4) elevate; (5) apply warm or cold compress per drug; (6) photograph and document; (7) consult plastic surgery if severe.
  • Vesicant examples: doxorubicin, daunorubicin, vincristine, vinblastine, calcium chloride, norepinephrine, dopamine, phenytoin, mannitol, hypertonic saline.
  • Vesicant prevention: Administer through CENTRAL line whenever possible. For unavoidable peripheral administration: use a large, proximal vein; assess site every 5–15 min; verify blood return throughout.
  • Antidote example: Norepinephrine extravasation → phentolamine (alpha blocker) injected subcutaneously around the area to counteract vasoconstriction and tissue ischemia.

Worked Example Individual Considerations of Medication Administration Ch 6 — Individual Considerations of Medication Administration · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Individual Considerations of Medication Administration
Review Module Chapter
Ch 6 — Individual Considerations of Medication Administration

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Individual client factors affecting medication administration, dosing, and response:

  • Age: neonates, infants, children, older adults — altered pharmacokinetics
  • Body weight and BMI: weight-based dosing; obesity affects drug distribution
  • Pregnancy and lactation: drug crosses placenta, enters breast milk; pregnancy categories
  • Renal function: dose adjustments based on CrCl/eGFR for renally cleared drugs
  • Hepatic function: dose adjustments for hepatically metabolized drugs
  • Genetic variations (pharmacogenomics): CYP2D6, CYP2C19, HLA-B variants affect metabolism and adverse reactions
  • Race, ethnicity, cultural beliefs: variable responses (ACE inhibitor sensitivity in Black clients); beliefs about medication use
  • Health literacy and language: ability to understand and adhere to regimen
  • Comorbidities, polypharmacy

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Pediatric considerations:
    • Immature liver/kidney function — slower metabolism and excretion
    • ↑ body water, ↓ body fat → altered distribution of water-soluble drugs
    • Lower albumin → ↑ free drug levels
    • Immature blood-brain barrier in neonates → ↑ CNS drug penetration
    • Doses always weight-based or BSA-based
  • Older adult considerations:
    • ↓ renal clearance (even with normal serum creatinine — use eGFR)
    • ↓ hepatic blood flow and metabolism
    • ↑ body fat, ↓ lean mass → altered distribution
    • ↓ total body water
    • ↓ plasma protein → ↑ free drug
    • ↑ sensitivity to CNS drugs, anticholinergics, opioids
    • Polypharmacy → ↑ interaction and adverse effect risk
    • Beers Criteria identifies potentially inappropriate medications
  • Pregnancy/lactation:
    • ↑ blood volume, ↑ renal clearance, ↑ hepatic metabolism
    • Drugs may cross placenta — teratogenicity (categorical risk)
    • Drugs in breast milk — infant exposure
  • Renal impairment: ↓ clearance → drug accumulation and toxicity for renally cleared drugs (digoxin, vancomycin, gabapentin, lithium, metformin)
  • Hepatic impairment: ↓ first-pass metabolism, ↓ albumin → ↑ levels of hepatically cleared drugs
ASSESSMENT

Expected Findings

  • Comprehensive medication history identifying ALL medications including OTC, supplements, herbals
  • Documented allergies and adverse drug reactions (with type of reaction)
  • Current weight (in kg) and recent labs (BUN, creatinine, GFR, LFTs, albumin)
  • Pregnancy status (if applicable)
  • Genetic testing results (when available — e.g., for warfarin, clopidogrel, abacavir)
  • Cultural and religious beliefs that may affect medication use (porcine products, alcohol-containing medications)
  • Assessment of cognition, vision, dexterity affecting self-administration
  • Identified barriers to adherence: cost, transportation, complexity of regimen
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

  • Conduct a comprehensive medication review with the provider
  • Identify potentially inappropriate medications (Beers Criteria)
  • Suggest deprescribing where appropriate
  • Check orthostatic vital signs
  • Implement fall precautions
  • Educate client and family about fall prevention
  • Consider PT consult for gait/balance

Client Education

  • Tailor education to client's literacy level and cultural background
  • Use teach-back method to verify understanding
  • Provide written materials in client's preferred language
  • Include caregivers in education for pediatric or cognitively impaired clients
  • Address common myths and concerns
  • For older adults: large-print labels, pill organizers, medication review at each visit
  • Discuss any cost concerns; explore generic substitution, patient assistance programs
  • Coordinate with social work, pharmacy for complex needs
  • For pregnant/breastfeeding clients: discuss benefits and risks of each medication
  • Encourage use of one pharmacy for interaction screening
  • Emphasize importance of consistent provider communication about all substances taken
Worked Example Bipolar Disorders Ch 9 — Bipolar Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Bipolar Disorders
Review Module Chapter
Ch 9 — Bipolar Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Bipolar Disorders — mood disorders characterized by episodes of mania (or hypomania) alternating with depressive episodes:

  • Bipolar I: ≥ 1 manic episode (with or without depression); often severe with psychotic features
  • Bipolar II: hypomanic episodes + depressive episodes; no full manic episode
  • Cyclothymic disorder: chronic (≥ 2 yr) hypomanic and depressive symptoms not meeting full criteria
  • Rapid cycling: ≥ 4 mood episodes in 12 months
  • Mixed features: depressive + manic symptoms concurrently — high suicide risk

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Multifactorial: genetic, neurochemical, and environmental factors
  • Genetics: strong heritability; first-degree relatives have ~10x risk
  • Neurotransmitter dysregulation: serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine, glutamate, GABA
  • Structural brain changes: prefrontal cortex, amygdala, hippocampus alterations on imaging
  • Circadian rhythm disruption — sleep changes both precipitate and reflect mood episodes
  • Triggers: sleep deprivation, antidepressants without mood stabilizer, substance use, major life events, postpartum period, seasonal changes
  • Onset typically late adolescence to mid-20s; chronic, episodic course
ASSESSMENT

Expected Findings

Manic episode (must last ≥ 1 week or require hospitalization):

  • Elevated, expansive, or irritable mood
  • Increased goal-directed activity or energy
  • ↓ need for sleep (feels rested after 2-3 hr)
  • Pressured speech, flight of ideas, racing thoughts
  • Grandiosity, inflated self-esteem
  • Distractibility
  • Risk-taking: excessive spending, sexual indiscretions, reckless driving, business ventures
  • Psychotic features possible (delusions, hallucinations)

Hypomanic episode: similar but ≥ 4 days, no marked impairment, no psychosis

Depressive episode: same criteria as MDD

  • Persistent sadness, anhedonia, fatigue
  • Sleep and appetite disturbances
  • Concentration impairment
  • Hopelessness, worthlessness, suicidal ideation
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

  • HOLD next lithium dose
  • Notify provider immediately
  • IV fluid replacement (NS) for hydration
  • Monitor lithium level every 6–12 hours
  • Severe toxicity (> 2.0): prepare for hemodialysis (most effective treatment)
  • Monitor vital signs, neurologic status, intake/output

Client Education

  • Maintain 2–3 L fluid intake daily
  • Maintain consistent sodium intake
  • When vomiting/diarrhea/fever/heavy sweating: hold lithium and notify provider
  • AVOID NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors
  • Carry a medical alert
  • Schedule routine lithium levels and follow up
Worked Example Lamotrigine (Lamictal) Ch 9 — Bipolar Disorders · Anticonvulsants section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Lamotrigine (Lamictal)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 9 — Bipolar Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Anticonvulsant / mood stabilizer — inhibits voltage-gated sodium channels in neurons; stabilizes neuronal membranes
  • Decreases glutamate release
  • Better tolerated than lithium for many clients; particularly effective for bipolar depression (not acute mania)

Therapeutic Use

  • Bipolar I disorder maintenance — especially preventing depressive episodes
  • Partial-onset seizures (adjunct or monotherapy)
  • Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (epilepsy)
  • Not effective for acute mania; not first-line for acute bipolar depression but excellent maintenance agent

Complications

  • Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) / Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) — BLACK BOX WARNING; potentially fatal; risk highest in first 8 weeks; higher with rapid titration or concurrent valproate
  • Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS) — multi-organ involvement; can be fatal
  • Aseptic meningitis (rare)
  • CNS: dizziness, headache, diplopia, ataxia, somnolence (typically dose-related)
  • GI upset, blurred vision
  • Pregnancy: limited risk data, generally lower teratogenic risk than valproate

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Prior hypersensitivity to lamotrigine
  • History of rash with other antiepileptics — cross-reactivity risk
  • Hepatic impairment — dose adjustment
  • Pediatrics < 2 yr (efficacy/safety not established)
  • Concurrent valproic acid — doubles lamotrigine levels; reduce lamotrigine dose by half
  • Concurrent enzyme inducers (carbamazepine, phenytoin) — reduce lamotrigine levels; may need higher dose

Interactions

  • Valproic acid — INHIBITS lamotrigine metabolism → doubles lamotrigine level; use HALF the usual lamotrigine dose
  • Carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, rifampin — INDUCE lamotrigine metabolism → reduce lamotrigine level; may need higher dose
  • Oral contraceptives — can decrease lamotrigine levels; may need higher dose during active OCP weeks
  • No significant CYP450 interactions otherwise

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Reduced frequency and severity of bipolar depressive episodes
  • Improved mood stability with maintenance dose
  • Seizure-free or reduced seizure frequency (for epilepsy)
  • No serious rash or hypersensitivity reactions
  • Tolerable side effect profile

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (tablets, chewable, ODT, XR)
  • SLOW TITRATION IS MANDATORY — 25 mg PO daily × 2 weeks, then 50 mg daily × 2 weeks, then increase by 50 mg every 1–2 weeks; target maintenance 200–400 mg/day
  • If concurrent valproate: half the dose at each titration step
  • If missed for > 5 days, MUST RESTART TITRATION from beginning
  • Take with or without food
  • Available immediate-release and extended-release

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline labs: LFTs, CBC
  • Assess and DOCUMENT any rash IMMEDIATELY — even minor rash may herald SJS; discontinue if rash develops
  • Educate on slow titration schedule; provide written titration calendar
  • Monitor mood and seizure activity
  • Assess for signs of hypersensitivity: fever, lymphadenopathy, multi-organ symptoms
  • Reinforce that missed doses for > 5 days require restart from beginning (call provider)
  • Monitor for OCP interaction in clients of childbearing age

Client Education

  • STOP and notify provider IMMEDIATELY if any rash develops — especially with fever or mucous membrane involvement (eyes, mouth, genitals)
  • Follow titration schedule EXACTLY — do not increase faster (rash risk)
  • If you miss doses for more than 5 days, call provider before restarting — you will need to restart titration
  • Do NOT abruptly discontinue (seizure risk if used for epilepsy)
  • May cause dizziness or blurred vision — avoid driving until response known
  • Birth control may be less effective — discuss alternatives with provider
  • Report sore throat, fever, mouth sores, swelling — signs of hypersensitivity
Worked Example Carbamazepine (Tegretol) Ch 9 — Bipolar Disorders · Anticonvulsants section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Carbamazepine (Tegretol)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 9 — Bipolar Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Anticonvulsant / mood stabilizer — blocks voltage-gated sodium channels; reduces high-frequency repetitive neuronal firing
  • Decreases neurotransmitter release
  • Potent CYP3A4 INDUCER — including auto-induction (induces its own metabolism in first weeks)

Therapeutic Use

  • Bipolar I disorder — acute mania, mixed episodes, and maintenance
  • Partial and tonic-clonic seizures
  • Trigeminal neuralgia — first-line
  • Diabetic neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia (off-label)

Complications

  • Bone marrow suppression (BLACK BOX) — aplastic anemia, agranulocytosis; CBC monitoring
  • Stevens-Johnson Syndrome / TEN (BLACK BOX) — especially in clients with HLA-B*1502 (mostly Asian ancestry) — screen before starting
  • Hyponatremia / SIADH — common (~5%); monitor sodium
  • Hepatotoxicity — transient mild elevation common; severe hepatitis rare
  • Hypersensitivity syndrome (DRESS) — multi-organ; can be fatal
  • CNS: drowsiness, dizziness, diplopia, ataxia, blurred vision (especially early)
  • GI: nausea, vomiting
  • Teratogenic — neural tube defects, craniofacial defects (Category D)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • History of bone marrow suppression
  • Prior hypersensitivity to TCAs (structural similarity)
  • Within 14 days of an MAOI
  • HLA-B*1502 positive (genetic test before prescribing in Asian populations)
  • Pregnancy — avoid; if essential, ensure adequate folate supplementation
  • Hepatic impairment, atrioventricular block, porphyria

Interactions

  • Carbamazepine INDUCES CYP3A4 — reduces levels of: oral contraceptives, warfarin, doxycycline, theophylline, methadone, lamotrigine, valproate, statins, HIV antiretrovirals
  • Auto-induction — carbamazepine’s OWN level drops over first 2–4 weeks; may need dose increase
  • Grapefruit juice — INHIBITS metabolism; can elevate levels to toxic range
  • Erythromycin, clarithromycin, fluoxetine, fluconazole — increase carbamazepine levels → toxicity
  • Concurrent MAOIs — contraindicated (hypertensive crisis)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Therapeutic serum level: 4–12 mcg/mL
  • Improved mood stability; reduced manic episodes
  • Seizure control
  • Pain relief in trigeminal neuralgia
  • Stable CBC, LFTs, sodium
  • No serious rash or hypersensitivity

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (tablets, chewables, suspension, XR)
  • Start 200 mg PO BID; titrate weekly; target 400–1,600 mg/day in divided doses
  • Take with food (reduces GI upset and improves absorption)
  • Avoid grapefruit juice
  • XR tablets must be swallowed whole (do not crush)
  • Serum level monitoring at steady state (~5 days after each change)

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline labs: CBC, LFTs, BUN/Cr, sodium, pregnancy test, HLA-B*1502 in Asian clients
  • Monitor CBC every 1–3 months initially; sodium periodically
  • Carbamazepine levels at trough; therapeutic 4–12 mcg/mL
  • Assess for rash at every contact — discontinue if SJS/TEN suspected
  • Monitor for signs of bone marrow suppression: fatigue, infection, bruising, bleeding
  • Comprehensive medication reconciliation due to CYP3A4 induction
  • Counsel on alternative contraception (OCPs ineffective)
  • Avoid abrupt discontinuation (seizure risk)

Client Education

  • Report any rash, fever, sore throat, mouth sores, unusual bleeding, or fatigue IMMEDIATELY
  • Use barrier contraception (carbamazepine reduces OCP effectiveness)
  • Avoid pregnancy — teratogenic; use reliable contraception; if pregnancy planned, discuss with provider
  • AVOID grapefruit juice — increases drug levels and toxicity risk
  • Take with food
  • Do NOT abruptly stop — seizure risk
  • Notify all providers and pharmacists of carbamazepine use (many drug interactions)
  • Keep follow-up appointments for blood level monitoring
  • Report dizziness, drowsiness, or vision changes — especially in first weeks
Worked Example Psychotic Disorders Ch 10 — Psychotic Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Psychotic Disorders
Review Module Chapter
Ch 10 — Psychotic Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Psychotic Disorders — characterized by loss of contact with reality:

  • Schizophrenia: chronic psychotic disorder with positive, negative, and cognitive symptoms ≥ 6 months
  • Schizophreniform disorder: schizophrenia-like symptoms 1-6 months
  • Brief psychotic disorder: < 1 month, often stress-related
  • Schizoaffective disorder: psychotic + mood disorder features
  • Delusional disorder: persistent non-bizarre delusions; otherwise functional
  • Substance/medication-induced psychotic disorder
  • Onset typically late teens to early 30s; earlier and more severe in men

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Multifactorial: genetic predisposition + environmental triggers
  • Strong genetic component: 50% concordance in identical twins; multiple genes implicated
  • Neurochemical:
    • Dopamine hyperactivity in mesolimbic pathway → positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions)
    • Dopamine hypoactivity in mesocortical pathway → negative symptoms and cognitive impairment
    • Glutamate, serotonin, and GABA also involved
  • Structural brain changes: enlarged ventricles, reduced gray matter, reduced hippocampal volume
  • Neurodevelopmental hypothesis: early disruptions in brain development with manifestation in adolescence/young adulthood
  • Environmental factors: prenatal infection or malnutrition, perinatal complications, childhood trauma, cannabis use (esp. heavy, early-life)
ASSESSMENT

Expected Findings

Positive symptoms (excesses):

  • Hallucinations — auditory most common (voices), also visual, tactile, olfactory, gustatory
  • Delusions — fixed false beliefs (persecutory, grandiose, referential, religious, somatic)
  • Disorganized speech — loose associations, tangentiality, neologisms, word salad
  • Disorganized or catatonic behavior

Negative symptoms (deficits):

  • Affective flattening — diminished emotional expression
  • Alogia — poverty of speech
  • Avolition — lack of motivation
  • Anhedonia — inability to experience pleasure
  • Asociality — lack of interest in social interactions

Cognitive symptoms: impaired attention, working memory, executive function

Functional decline in work, school, relationships, self-care

PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

  • DISCONTINUE the antipsychotic immediately
  • Notify the provider STAT — transfer to ICU
  • Cooling measures (cool blankets, IV fluids, ice packs)
  • IV fluid resuscitation
  • Continuous monitoring of vital signs, cardiac rhythm, mental status
  • Anticipate: dantrolene (muscle relaxation), bromocriptine (dopamine agonist)
  • Monitor CK (rhabdomyolysis); BUN/Cr (renal function); electrolytes

Client Education

  • This is a chronic, treatable condition — long-term management is essential
  • Take antipsychotic medications consistently as prescribed — even when feeling well
  • Non-adherence is the primary cause of relapse
  • Long-acting injectable antipsychotics may improve adherence (every 2-4 weeks or longer)
  • Recognize early warning signs of relapse (sleep changes, social withdrawal, suspicious thoughts) and have a plan
  • Avoid alcohol and recreational drugs (especially cannabis, methamphetamine — can precipitate psychosis)
  • Build daily routine and structure
  • Engage in supported employment, vocational rehabilitation, social skills training
  • Family education and involvement essential — psychoeducation reduces expressed emotion and relapse
  • Address metabolic side effects of antipsychotics: diet, exercise, regular monitoring
  • Avoid stigma — psychotic disorders are medical illnesses, not personal failings
  • Crisis plan: warning signs, who to contact, safe environment
  • Suicide risk is elevated; address openly; connect with mental health resources
  • Smoking cessation: many clients smoke heavily; affects antipsychotic levels and overall health
Worked Example Risperidone (Risperdal) Ch 10 — Psychotic Disorders · Second-generation section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Risperidone (Risperdal)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 10 — Psychotic Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Atypical (second-generation) antipsychotic
  • Blocks dopamine D2 receptors AND serotonin 5-HT2A receptors
  • 5-HT2A blockade reduces EPS risk and improves negative symptoms
  • More EPS risk than other atypicals; less than typical antipsychotics

Therapeutic Use

  • Schizophrenia (positive AND negative symptoms)
  • Bipolar I disorder — acute mania, mixed episodes, maintenance
  • Irritability in autism spectrum disorder (FDA-approved for children ≥ 5)
  • Off-label: behavioral disturbances in dementia (BLACK BOX — increased mortality in older adults)

Complications

  • EPS — dose-related; more common than other atypicals (especially > 6 mg/day)
  • Hyperprolactinemia — gynecomastia, galactorrhea, menstrual irregularities, sexual dysfunction; MORE pronounced than other atypicals
  • Metabolic syndrome — weight gain, dyslipidemia, hyperglycemia (less than olanzapine/clozapine but still significant)
  • Orthostatic hypotension — especially during titration
  • Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) — rare but life-threatening
  • Sedation, dizziness, headache
  • QT prolongation
  • Increased mortality in older adults with dementia (BLACK BOX)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to risperidone or paliperidone (active metabolite)
  • Older adults with dementia-related psychosis — black box warning
  • History of NMS, tardive dyskinesia
  • Cardiovascular disease, history of seizures
  • Diabetes, dyslipidemia (caution; monitor metabolic parameters)
  • Pregnancy — risk of withdrawal/EPS in neonate
  • Renal or hepatic impairment — dose adjustment

Interactions

  • CYP2D6 inhibitors (paroxetine, fluoxetine) — increase risperidone levels
  • CYP3A4 inducers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampin) — decrease levels
  • CNS depressants (alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines) — additive sedation
  • Levodopa, dopamine agonists — antagonistic effects (worsen psychosis vs improve parkinsonism)
  • QT-prolonging drugs (amiodarone, ondansetron, fluoroquinolones) — additive QT risk

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Reduction in positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thinking)
  • Improvement in negative symptoms (affect, motivation, social engagement)
  • Improved functioning and adherence
  • Stable mood (bipolar use)
  • Reduced irritability (autism)
  • Tolerable side-effect profile; minimal EPS; stable metabolic parameters

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (tablets, ODT, oral solution); long-acting IM injection (Risperdal Consta — every 2 weeks)
  • Schizophrenia: start 2 mg PO daily; target 4–6 mg/day; max effective < 6 mg/day (above increases EPS)
  • Bipolar mania: 2–6 mg/day
  • Autism: weight-based dosing for children
  • Take with or without food (consistent)
  • Long-acting IM: requires 3-week overlap with oral until levels established

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline: BMI/weight, BP, fasting glucose, lipid panel, EKG (if cardiac risk), AIMS for movement
  • Monitor metabolic parameters at 4 weeks, 12 weeks, then quarterly
  • Monitor for EPS (especially first weeks); use AIMS scale
  • Assess for NMS: fever, rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability — emergency
  • Monitor prolactin levels if symptomatic (gynecomastia, galactorrhea, menstrual changes)
  • Monitor orthostatic BP during titration; advise slow position changes
  • Suicide risk assessment
  • Encourage exercise, healthy diet to mitigate weight gain

Client Education

  • Therapeutic effect develops over weeks; continue even if not feeling improvement immediately
  • Take consistently; do not stop abruptly (relapse risk)
  • Report movement abnormalities (tremor, rigidity, restlessness, tongue movements)
  • Report fever, severe muscle rigidity, confusion — emergency (NMS)
  • Report breast enlargement, milk production, menstrual changes
  • Weight monitoring; diet and exercise are important to counter metabolic effects
  • Rise slowly to prevent orthostatic dizziness
  • Avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants
  • Use sunscreen (photosensitivity)
  • Pregnancy planning: discuss with provider
Worked Example Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS) Ch 10 — Psychotic Disorders · First-gen section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS)

Defining Characteristics

Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS) is a rare but life-threatening idiosyncratic reaction to antipsychotic medications (or abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic medications).

Classic tetrad:

  • Fever (hyperthermia, often > 38°C / 100.4°F — can exceed 41°C)
  • Encephalopathy / altered mental status (confusion, stupor, coma)
  • Vitals unstable / autonomic instability (BP fluctuations, tachycardia, diaphoresis)
  • Elevated enzymes / muscle rigidity (“lead pipe” rigidity, elevated CK, rhabdomyolysis)

Mnemonic: FEVER — Fever, Encephalopathy, Vitals unstable, Elevated enzymes, Rigidity.

Onset is typically within hours to days of starting or increasing antipsychotic; can occur at any point.

Antecedents

  • Initiation or dose increase of any antipsychotic (more common with typicals like haloperidol, but ALL antipsychotics can cause NMS)
  • High-potency dopamine receptor antagonists
  • Long-acting injectable antipsychotics
  • Abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic medications (levodopa, dopamine agonists in Parkinson’s)
  • Dehydration, electrolyte imbalance (hyponatremia)
  • Concurrent illness, agitation, restraint use
  • Genetic predisposition (probable)
  • Previous episode of NMS (recurrence risk)

Negative Consequences

  • Death — mortality 5–20% even with treatment
  • Rhabdomyolysis → acute kidney injury
  • Aspiration pneumonia, pulmonary embolism
  • Hyperthermia-related multi-organ damage
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
  • Permanent neurological deficits
  • Need for ICU admission, mechanical ventilation
  • Future need for non-antipsychotic alternatives to manage psychosis

Related Concepts

Serotonin syndrome (differential), malignant hyperthermia, anticholinergic toxicity, antipsychotic medications (typical and atypical), dopamine agonists, dantrolene, bromocriptine, supportive care, hyperthermia management, rhabdomyolysis.

Exemplars

  • Classic case: Client started on haloperidol IM 2 days ago presents with temp 39.5°C, BP 180/110, HR 130, lead-pipe rigidity, confusion, sweating, CK 25,000. Diagnosis: NMS.
  • Treatment:
    • (1) STOP the antipsychotic IMMEDIATELY
    • (2) Aggressive cooling (cooling blanket, ice packs, IV fluids)
    • (3) IV hydration to prevent renal failure from rhabdomyolysis
    • (4) Dantrolene — muscle relaxant (also used in malignant hyperthermia)
    • (5) Bromocriptine — dopamine agonist to counteract D2 blockade
    • (6) Benzodiazepines (lorazepam) for agitation
    • (7) ICU admission; mechanical ventilation if needed
    • (8) Monitor CK, renal function, electrolytes
  • Differential from serotonin syndrome: NMS has “lead-pipe” rigidity; serotonin syndrome has clonus and hyperreflexia. NMS onset slower (days); serotonin syndrome faster (hours). NMS — recent antipsychotic; serotonin syndrome — serotonergic drug interaction.
  • Recovery: 7–10 days typically. After recovery, consider clozapine or different drug class (NEVER restart the offending antipsychotic without specialist consultation).
Worked Example Extrapyramidal Symptoms (EPS) & Tardive Dyskinesia Ch 10 — Psychotic Disorders · First-gen section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Extrapyramidal Symptoms (EPS) & Tardive Dyskinesia

Defining Characteristics

Extrapyramidal Symptoms (EPS) are movement disorders caused by D2 receptor blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway, primarily from antipsychotics.

Four classic EPS syndromes (in order of typical onset):

  1. Acute dystonia (hours to days) — sudden muscle spasms, oculogyric crisis, torticollis, opisthotonos. Treat with IM benztropine or diphenhydramine.
  2. Akathisia (days to weeks) — subjective restlessness, inability to sit still, pacing. Treat with dose reduction, beta blockers (propranolol), or benzodiazepines.
  3. Pseudoparkinsonism (weeks) — tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, masked facies. Treat with anticholinergics (benztropine) or dose reduction.
  4. Tardive dyskinesia (TD) (months to years) — involuntary repetitive movements of face, tongue, lips, jaw, fingers. OFTEN PERMANENT; key concern.

Antecedents

  • Antipsychotic use, especially high-potency typicals (haloperidol, fluphenazine)
  • Atypicals can cause EPS but lower risk (highest risk with risperidone)
  • Higher doses, longer duration of treatment
  • Older adults (especially women) at higher risk for TD
  • Patients with mood disorders may be more susceptible
  • Other dopamine antagonists: metoclopramide, prochlorperazine

Negative Consequences

  • Tardive dyskinesia is often irreversible — even after stopping the offending drug
  • Social stigma, functional impairment, embarrassment
  • Pain and physical discomfort (dystonia can affect breathing if laryngeal)
  • Falls (from pseudoparkinsonism, akathisia)
  • Nonadherence due to side effects → relapse of psychosis
  • Acute dystonia can be life-threatening if airway involved (laryngospasm)
  • Akathisia is sometimes associated with increased suicide risk

Related Concepts

Antipsychotic medications (typical vs atypical), dopamine D2 receptor blockade, anticholinergic medications (benztropine, diphenhydramine), AIMS (Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale), VMAT-2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine for TD), neuroleptic malignant syndrome (differential).

Exemplars

  • Acute dystonia case: Young adult started on haloperidol 5 mg IM for agitation; 4 hours later develops sustained upward gaze (oculogyric crisis) and neck twisting (torticollis). Treat: IM benztropine 1–2 mg or IM/IV diphenhydramine 25–50 mg — rapid resolution.
  • Akathisia case: Client on risperidone 6 mg/day reports inability to sit still; pacing constantly; says they feel “like jumping out of their skin.” Treat: reduce dose, add propranolol 10–20 mg BID.
  • Pseudoparkinsonism case: Older adult on haloperidol develops tremor, shuffling gait, masked face. Treat: switch to atypical OR add benztropine 1–2 mg PO BID.
  • Tardive dyskinesia case: Long-term haloperidol user develops chewing-like movements of tongue and lip-smacking. Reduce/stop antipsychotic if possible; switch to clozapine (lower TD risk); consider VMAT-2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine) for TD treatment.
  • AIMS scale — performed every 3–6 months on all clients on antipsychotics to detect TD early.
  • Prevention: use atypicals when possible; lowest effective dose; periodic dose reduction trials; AIMS monitoring; switch to clozapine if TD develops.
