Worked Example Pharmacokinetics and Routes of Administration Ch 1 — Pharmacokinetics and Routes of Administration · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure
Pharmacokinetics and Routes of Administration
Review Module Chapter
Ch 1 — Pharmacokinetics and Routes of Administration

Description of Procedure

Pharmacokinetics — what the body does TO the drug — encompasses four processes (ADME):

  • Absorption: movement of drug from administration site into bloodstream
    • Influenced by: route, formulation, GI factors (pH, motility, food), first-pass metabolism
  • Distribution: movement of drug from bloodstream to tissues
    • Influenced by: blood flow, lipid solubility, protein binding, blood-brain barrier, placenta
  • Metabolism (biotransformation): chemical alteration, mostly hepatic (CYP450 enzymes)
    • Active metabolites, prodrugs, drug-drug interactions occur here
  • Excretion: removal from body, primarily renal (urine), also bile, feces, lungs, sweat, breast milk

Pharmacodynamics — what the drug does TO the body — receptor binding, signal transduction, dose-response relationships.

Indications

  • Medication absorption pattern: Rapid absorption through the alveolar capillary network. A spacer keeps the medication in the device longer, increasing the amount delivered to the lungs and decreasing the amount deposited in the oropharynx.
  • Barrier to absorption: Inadequate respiratory effort.

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre:

  • Verify ordered route is appropriate for the drug and client (e.g., morphine: PO dose >> IV dose due to first-pass)
  • Assess client factors affecting PK: age (peds/elderly altered metabolism), weight (dosing), renal function (BUN, creatinine, eGFR), hepatic function (LFTs), pregnancy, comorbidities
  • Review all medications for interactions (CYP450, protein binding, additive effects)
  • Check timing relative to food, other meds, lab draws

Intra:

  • Administer by correct route with correct technique
  • Use proper IV infusion rate, site, equipment
  • For oral: check if must be on empty stomach, with food, separated from interacting meds
  • For sublingual: must be absorbed in mouth (not swallowed) — bypasses first-pass

Post:

  • Monitor for therapeutic effect (expected onset based on route)
  • Monitor for adverse effects, especially at peak time
  • For narrow-window drugs: obtain drug levels at appropriate times (peak, trough, steady state typically after 4-5 half-lives)
  • Adjust dosing based on response and labs
  • Educate client about timing, food/drug interactions, route-specific considerations

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Therapeutic drug levels achieved without toxicity (narrow-window drugs especially)
  • Effective drug concentration at site of action
  • Predictable onset, peak, and duration based on chosen route
  • Appropriate dose adjustments made for client factors (age, weight, renal/hepatic function)
  • Drug-drug interactions identified and managed

Potential Complications

  • Subtherapeutic levels: failed treatment due to inadequate absorption, distribution, or excessive metabolism/excretion
  • Toxic levels: due to overdose, accumulation (renal/hepatic impairment), drug interactions, missed first-pass metabolism (IV vs PO)
  • First-pass effect: oral drugs metabolized extensively before reaching systemic circulation — much higher PO than IV dose needed (e.g., morphine, nitroglycerin)
  • Half-life accumulation: drugs with long half-life can accumulate to toxic levels in renal/hepatic impairment
  • CYP450 drug interactions: inducers (rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, St. John's wort) ↓ levels of substrates; inhibitors (cimetidine, fluconazole, erythromycin, grapefruit) ↑ levels
  • Protein-binding interactions: warfarin, phenytoin, valproic acid — displaced by other highly protein-bound drugs
  • Route-specific complications: IV (extravasation, infection, embolism), IM (sterile abscess, nerve injury), oral (variable absorption, GI upset)

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor vital signs and clinical status closely
  • Assess for adverse effects related to the procedure
  • Provide post-procedure care per protocol; reposition and reassess regularly
  • Document findings, interventions, and patient response; notify provider of unexpected outcomes

Client Education

  • Remove the covers from the mouthpieces of the inhaler and of the spacer
  • Insert the MDI into the end of the spacer
  • Shake the inhaler five or six times
  • Exhale completely, then close your mouth around the spacer's mouthpiece
  • Tilt your head back slightly, press the inhaler, and at the same time begin a slow, deep inhalation
  • Continue to breathe in slowly and deeply for 3 to 5 seconds to facilitate delivery to the air passages
  • Hold your breath for 10 seconds to allow the medication to deposit in your airways
  • Take the mouthpiece out of your mouth and slowly exhale through pursed lips
  • Resume normal breathing
Worked Example First-Pass Effect Ch 1 — Pharmacokinetics and Routes of Administration · Metabolism section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
First-Pass Effect

Defining Characteristics

The first-pass effect (also called first-pass metabolism or pre-systemic metabolism) is the extensive hepatic metabolism of an orally administered drug BEFORE it reaches systemic circulation.

Path: oral drug → GI absorption → portal vein → liver (CYP450 enzymes) → systemic circulation.

The result: a substantial portion of an oral dose may be metabolized to inactive compounds before reaching its target tissue — meaning the oral dose must be significantly higher than the IV dose to achieve the same therapeutic effect.

Antecedents

  • Oral route of administration (only affects drugs absorbed via the GI tract that drain to portal circulation)
  • Lipid-soluble drugs that are metabolized by hepatic CYP450 enzymes
  • Hepatic CYP450 activity — affected by age, genetics (poor vs ultra-rapid metabolizers), liver disease, drug interactions (inducers/inhibitors)
  • Drug-specific factors: extent of hepatic extraction ratio (high-extraction drugs have the most pronounced first-pass effect)

Negative Consequences

  • Reduced bioavailability — only a fraction of the oral dose reaches systemic circulation
  • Requires higher oral doses than equivalent parenteral doses (e.g., morphine: PO 30 mg ≈ IV 10 mg)
  • Variable drug levels due to inter-individual differences in CYP450 activity
  • Drug interactions — CYP450 inhibitors (e.g., grapefruit juice, erythromycin) can dramatically increase drug levels by blocking first-pass metabolism
  • Generation of active or toxic metabolites (e.g., codeine → morphine via CYP2D6)

Related Concepts

Bioavailability, hepatic extraction ratio, CYP450 metabolism, pharmacogenomics, drug interactions, prodrugs, routes that BYPASS first-pass (sublingual, buccal, rectal lower 2/3, IV, IM, SC, transdermal, inhaled).

Exemplars

  • High first-pass drugs (low oral bioavailability): morphine (~25%), lidocaine (negligible orally — must be parenteral), propranolol, nitroglycerin (~0% orally — use sublingual/transdermal), verapamil
  • Bypassing first-pass: sublingual nitroglycerin enters venous return directly without portal circulation passage — immediate systemic effect
  • Prodrug strategy: codeine is converted to morphine (active) by hepatic CYP2D6 — clients with reduced CYP2D6 activity get little pain relief
  • Drug interaction: grapefruit juice inhibits intestinal CYP3A4, blocking first-pass metabolism of calcium channel blockers and statins → elevated drug levels and toxicity risk
Worked Example Half-Life and Steady State Ch 1 — Pharmacokinetics and Routes of Administration · Half-life section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Half-Life and Steady State

Defining Characteristics

Half-life (t½) — the time required for the plasma drug concentration to decrease by 50%. Determined by the drug’s clearance and volume of distribution.

Steady state — the dynamic equilibrium reached when the amount of drug administered per dosing interval equals the amount eliminated. At steady state, peak and trough levels are predictable and stable.

Key rule: it takes approximately 4–5 half-lives to reach steady state with regular dosing, and similarly 4–5 half-lives to eliminate a drug after stopping it.

Antecedents

  • Drug-specific: intrinsic clearance, volume of distribution, protein binding
  • Hepatic function — CYP450 metabolism affects clearance of many drugs
  • Renal function — eGFR affects renally cleared drugs (digoxin, gentamicin, vancomycin, lithium)
  • Age — neonates and older adults often have reduced clearance → longer half-life
  • Drug interactions affecting metabolism or excretion
  • Dosing regimen — interval should align with half-life to maintain steady-state levels

Negative Consequences

  • Sub-therapeutic levels if dosing interval is too long relative to half-life — clinical failure
  • Toxicity / accumulation if dosing interval is too short or clearance is impaired — drug builds up beyond therapeutic range (especially for narrow-TI drugs like digoxin, lithium, warfarin, vancomycin)
  • Delayed onset of full effect — clients may stop a medication too early because they don’t feel an effect (e.g., antidepressants take weeks)
  • Delayed offset — withdrawal/effect persists after discontinuation (e.g., amiodarone t½ ~58 days)
  • Missed doses cause level drops that take time to recover at steady state

Related Concepts

Clearance, volume of distribution, therapeutic drug monitoring, peak and trough levels, loading dose, maintenance dose, therapeutic index, drug accumulation, withdrawal syndromes.

Exemplars

  • Short half-life: adenosine (~10 seconds — rapid IV push, immediate effect, brief duration); nitroglycerin SL (~1–3 min)
  • Intermediate half-life: digoxin (~36–40 hr — reaches steady state in ~5–7 days; daily dosing maintains levels)
  • Long half-life: amiodarone (~58 days — effects persist for weeks after discontinuation; loading dose used to reach therapeutic levels faster); fluoxetine (4–6 day half-life of active metabolite)
  • Loading dose rationale: for drugs with long half-lives (digoxin, amiodarone, vancomycin), a higher initial dose “loads” the drug to therapeutic range, avoiding the 5-half-life wait
  • Trough timing: draw 30 min BEFORE the next dose at steady state — this reflects the lowest concentration to avoid toxicity
Worked Example Therapeutic Index (TI) Ch 1 — Pharmacokinetics and Routes of Administration · Half-life section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Therapeutic Index (TI)

Defining Characteristics

Therapeutic Index (TI) is the safety margin of a drug — the ratio of the toxic dose to the therapeutic dose. Mathematically: TI = TD50 / ED50 (median toxic dose / median effective dose).

A wide TI = large safety margin between effective and toxic doses (forgiving). A narrow TI = small margin; small dose changes can cause toxicity. Narrow-TI drugs require therapeutic drug monitoring (peak/trough levels) and dose adjustment for organ dysfunction.

Antecedents

  • Drug-specific: pharmacokinetic properties (absorption variability, protein binding, metabolism, excretion) and pharmacodynamic dose-response curve
  • Genetic factors: CYP450 polymorphisms (poor vs ultra-rapid metabolizers)
  • Organ dysfunction: reduced renal or hepatic function narrows the effective TI for drugs cleared by those organs
  • Drug interactions: inducers/inhibitors of metabolism can push levels out of the therapeutic window
  • Comorbidities and age extremes (neonates, older adults)

Negative Consequences

  • Toxicity at therapeutic-appearing doses (especially with comorbidities or drug interactions)
  • Sub-therapeutic levels causing treatment failure
  • Required intensive monitoring (peak/trough levels, INR, drug levels, organ function tests) adds cost and complexity
  • Risk of medication errors — narrow-TI drugs are on the ISMP “high-alert medications” list
  • Patient burden from frequent labs, dose changes, and adverse effects

Related Concepts

Therapeutic drug monitoring, peak and trough levels, INR for warfarin, drug interactions, pharmacogenomics, high-alert medications, organ-function dose adjustment.

Exemplars

  • Narrow-TI drugs requiring monitoring: warfarin (INR 2–3), digoxin (level 0.5–2 ng/mL), lithium (0.6–1.2 mEq/L), phenytoin (10–20 mcg/mL), theophylline, gentamicin/vancomycin (peaks and troughs)
  • Wide-TI drugs: penicillins, most NSAIDs, most antihistamines — generally well-tolerated even with dose variability
  • Narrow-TI in renal impairment: digoxin and lithium accumulate dangerously; reduce dose or extend interval based on creatinine clearance
  • Narrow-TI in hepatic impairment: warfarin (clotting factors reduced), benzodiazepines (slower clearance), acetaminophen (depleted glutathione)
  • Drug interaction example: amiodarone raises digoxin level by ~50–100% — must reduce digoxin dose and monitor
Worked Example Blood and Blood Products Ch 27 — Blood and Blood Products · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure
Blood and Blood Products
Review Module Chapter
Ch 27 — Blood and Blood Products

Description of Procedure

Administration of blood and blood products through IV infusion for transfusion:

  • Packed Red Blood Cells (PRBCs): most common; ↑ oxygen-carrying capacity; ~250-350 mL/unit; ↑ Hgb ~1 g/dL per unit
  • Platelets: ↑ platelet count and clotting capacity
  • Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP): contains all clotting factors; for warfarin reversal, DIC, massive transfusion
  • Cryoprecipitate: fibrinogen, factors VIII, XIII, vWF, fibronectin
  • Albumin: colloid volume expander; hypoalbuminemia, burns, ascites
  • Granulocytes (rare): severe neutropenia
  • Factor concentrates: factor VIII for hemophilia A, factor IX for hemophilia B, prothrombin complex concentrate

Indications

A client who lost blood from a GI bleed can need a unit of PRBCs for a hgb level below 10 g/dL especially if demonstrating manifestations of hypovolemia (increase in pulse and respiration rate; decrease in blood pressure; low oxygen saturation; cool and pale or cyanotic; increased capillary refill time; increased urinary output). If hypoxic, the client will exhibit decreased level of consciousness and confusion. PRBCs restore red blood cells and improve oxygenation. If the client has lost a large amount of fluid volume, whole blood, rather than PRBCs, can be indicated.

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre-transfusion:

  • Verify provider order, indication, consent (informed consent required)
  • Ensure type and crossmatch completed; verify with second nurse at bedside (right product, right client, expiration, blood type compatibility — TWO RNs check)
  • Establish dedicated IV access — at least 20 ga (18 ga preferred for rapid infusion); avoid small-gauge unless necessary
  • Use Y-tubing with filter and 0.9% normal saline only (NOT D5W or lactated Ringer's — cause hemolysis or clotting)
  • Baseline vital signs (temperature, BP, HR, RR, SpO₂) immediately before starting
  • Assess for signs of fluid overload risk (CHF, renal failure, elderly)
  • Pre-medicate (acetaminophen, diphenhydramine) if ordered for clients with history of reactions

During transfusion:

  • Start slowly: 2 mL/min (~120 mL/hr) for first 15 minutes; stay with client during this critical period
  • Vital signs after 15 minutes; if stable, may increase rate
  • Complete unit within 4 hours (bacterial growth risk after); typical infusion 2-3 hr per unit
  • Monitor VS per protocol (q30 min or per institution)
  • Observe for transfusion reaction signs: fever, chills, back/flank pain, dyspnea, urticaria, hypotension, anxiety, dark urine
  • If reaction suspected:
    1. STOP transfusion immediately
    2. Keep IV line open with NS via NEW tubing
    3. Notify provider and blood bank
    4. Send blood bag and tubing to blood bank
    5. Collect blood and urine samples per protocol
    6. Treat symptoms (epinephrine for anaphylaxis, antihistamines, antipyretics, etc.)
    7. Complete transfusion reaction report

Post-transfusion:

  • Vital signs at end of transfusion and per protocol
  • Document: time started/completed, product type, amount, response, any reactions
  • Check post-transfusion CBC at appropriate interval (e.g., 1 hr post for platelets; with next AM labs for PRBCs)
  • Monitor for delayed reactions (24-48 hr; up to 10 days for delayed hemolytic)
  • Continue to assess for fluid overload

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • PRBCs: ↑ Hgb (1 g/dL per unit), ↓ symptoms of anemia (fatigue, dyspnea, tachycardia), improved tissue oxygenation
  • Platelets: ↑ platelet count, ↓ bleeding
  • FFP: normalized INR/PTT, control of bleeding
  • Cryoprecipitate: ↑ fibrinogen, control of bleeding
  • No transfusion reactions
  • No fluid overload (esp. in elderly, HF, renal failure)
  • No transmission of blood-borne infections

Potential Complications

  • Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction (AHTR) — ABO incompatibility — most dangerous:
    • Fever, chills, flank/back pain, hypotension, tachycardia, dyspnea, hemoglobinuria, DIC, renal failure
    • Onset within minutes; STOP transfusion immediately
  • Febrile non-hemolytic reaction: fever, chills (most common; pre-medicate with acetaminophen if history)
  • Allergic reaction: urticaria, itching, mild — antihistamine; if severe → anaphylaxis
  • Anaphylaxis: severe respiratory distress, shock — often IgA-deficient clients
  • TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury): acute respiratory distress within 6 hr; non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema
  • TACO (transfusion-associated circulatory overload): rapid fluid overload — dyspnea, pulmonary edema, ↑ BP
  • Bacterial contamination/sepsis: fever, hypotension, often platelet products (room temp storage)
  • Delayed hemolytic reaction: 3-10 days post-transfusion
  • Transmission of infections (HIV, hepatitis B/C, CMV) — rare with current screening
  • Iron overload with chronic transfusion (sickle cell, thalassemia)
  • Graft-versus-host disease (rare; immunocompromised)

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor vital signs and clinical status closely
  • Assess for adverse effects related to the procedure
  • Provide post-procedure care per protocol; reposition and reassess regularly
  • Document findings, interventions, and patient response; notify provider of unexpected outcomes

Client Education

  • Report immediately: back/flank pain, chest pain, shortness of breath, fever or chills, itching or rash, dizziness, dark urine, difficulty breathing
  • You may feel slightly cool — this is normal (blood products are refrigerated; warming devices used when indicated)
  • Nurse will check on you frequently, especially in the first 15 minutes
  • Stay in bed during the transfusion; call before getting up
  • Refused transfusion (e.g., Jehovah's Witness): respect; document; plan alternatives with team
  • After: report any unusual symptoms — back pain, fever, jaundice, dark urine — within several days
  • Future transfusions: tell providers about any prior reactions; ID bracelet may be needed for severe reactions
Worked Example Blood Transfusion Administration Ch 27 — Blood and Blood Products · Administration section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill
Blood Transfusion Administration
Review Module Chapter
Ch 27 — Blood and Blood Products

Description of Skill

Safe administration of blood and blood products (packed RBCs, platelets, fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate) requiring strict verification, monitoring, and reaction recognition.

Critical safety elements: two-licensed-person verification, Y-tubing with 0.9% normal saline ONLY (no dextrose — hemolysis; no LR — clotting), blood filter, and the 4-hour maximum infusion time per unit.

Indications

  • Symptomatic anemia, acute blood loss, hemorrhage
  • Packed RBCs: low hemoglobin with symptoms (often Hgb < 7–8 g/dL)
  • Platelets: thrombocytopenia with bleeding or very low counts
  • Fresh frozen plasma: coagulation factor deficiency, warfarin reversal
  • Cryoprecipitate: fibrinogen deficiency, DIC

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre:

  • Verify provider order; confirm informed consent
  • Verify type and crossmatch completed
  • Ensure large-bore IV (18–20 gauge) patent
  • Obtain baseline vital signs (temp, HR, BP, RR, SpO2) — if febrile, notify provider before starting
  • Gather Y-tubing with in-line filter and 0.9% normal saline ONLY
  • TWO licensed personnel verify at bedside: client name/DOB (two identifiers), blood type and Rh, unit number, expiration, crossmatch compatibility, product appearance
  • Have emergency equipment available

Intra:

  • Start SLOWLY (~2 mL/min / 25–50 mL over first 15 min) — stay with client the first 15 minutes (most reactions occur early)
  • Recheck vital signs at 15 min, then per policy (often every 30–60 min) and at completion
  • If no reaction after 15 min, increase to ordered rate
  • Complete infusion within 4 hours (bacterial growth risk)
  • Use only NS to prime/flush; never add medications to blood
  • Monitor continuously for reaction signs

Post:

  • Final set of vital signs
  • Document: product, volume, time, vital signs, client response
  • Dispose of bag/tubing per policy; some retained if reaction suspected
  • Continue monitoring for delayed reactions

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Transfusion completed without adverse reaction
  • Improvement in target parameter (increased Hgb/Hct, platelet count, coagulation)
  • Resolution of symptoms (reduced fatigue, dyspnea; controlled bleeding)
  • Stable vital signs throughout
  • Client understands signs to report post-transfusion

Potential Complications

  • Acute hemolytic reaction (ABO incompatibility) — most dangerous; fever, chills, flank/back pain, hypotension, hemoglobinuria, DIC
  • Febrile non-hemolytic reaction — most common; fever, chills (from donor WBCs)
  • Allergic reaction — urticaria, itching; anaphylaxis (severe)
  • TACO (transfusion-associated circulatory overload) — dyspnea, crackles, hypertension, JVD (too fast/too much)
  • TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury) — acute respiratory distress; leading cause of transfusion death
  • Bacterial contamination/sepsis — high fever, hypotension, shock
  • Delayed hemolytic reaction (days later); iron overload (chronic); disease transmission (rare)
Worked Example Acute Hemolytic Transfusion Reaction Ch 27 — Blood and Blood Products · Reactions section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure
Acute Hemolytic Transfusion Reaction Management
Review Module Chapter
Ch 27 — Blood and Blood Products

Description of Procedure

Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction (AHTR) is a life-threatening emergency caused by ABO incompatibility — recipient antibodies attack and destroy transfused donor RBCs.

Usually results from clerical/identification error (wrong blood to wrong patient). Onset is rapid — often within the first 15 minutes, which is why nurses stay with the client during the initial phase.

Can rapidly progress to shock, DIC, acute kidney injury, and death.

Indications

  • Any client receiving a blood transfusion (recognition)
  • Sudden fever, chills, flank/back pain during transfusion
  • Hypotension, tachycardia, sense of impending doom
  • Dark/red urine (hemoglobinuria)
  • Chest pain, dyspnea
  • Oozing from IV site (DIC)

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Prevention (pre):

  • Meticulous two-person bedside verification of client identity and blood compatibility
  • Use two patient identifiers
  • Stay with client during first 15 minutes; baseline and frequent vital signs

If reaction occurs (intra) — act IMMEDIATELY:

  1. STOP the transfusion immediately
  2. Keep the IV line open with 0.9% normal saline using NEW tubing (do not flush remaining blood into client)
  3. Stay with client; notify provider and blood bank STAT
  4. Recheck identification of client and blood product (verify clerical error)
  5. Monitor vital signs frequently; assess for shock
  6. Maintain airway, oxygen, prepare for emergency support
  7. Administer ordered medications: IV fluids (maintain BP/renal perfusion), diuretics (maintain urine output), vasopressors if needed
  8. Insert/monitor indwelling catheter; monitor urine output and color
  9. Send blood bag, tubing, and blood/urine samples to lab per protocol
  10. Treat DIC if it develops

Post:

  • Continuous monitoring (ICU if severe)
  • Monitor renal function (AKI from hemoglobin), coagulation (DIC)
  • Complete transfusion reaction report and incident documentation
  • Investigate root cause (clerical error)
  • Update records to prevent recurrence

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Transfusion stopped promptly at first signs
  • Hemodynamic stability restored
  • Adequate urine output maintained (renal protection)
  • No progression to DIC, renal failure, or death
  • Root cause identified; system error corrected
  • Accurate documentation and reporting completed

Potential Complications

  • Shock and cardiovascular collapse
  • Acute kidney injury — free hemoglobin damages renal tubules
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
  • Death — AHTR has significant mortality
  • Multi-organ failure
  • Hyperkalemia (from cell lysis)
  • If transfusion not stopped promptly — outcomes worsen dramatically
Worked Example Blood Typing & Compatibility Ch 27 — Blood and Blood Products · Products section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Blood Typing & Compatibility

Defining Characteristics

Blood typing and compatibility determine which blood products a recipient can safely receive, based on ABO and Rh antigen systems on RBC surfaces and corresponding antibodies in plasma.

ABO system:

  • Type A: A antigen; anti-B antibodies
  • Type B: B antigen; anti-A antibodies
  • Type AB: both antigens; NO antibodies (universal recipient)
  • Type O: no antigens; both anti-A and anti-B antibodies (universal donor)

Rh system: Rh-positive (D antigen present) or Rh-negative (absent). Rh-negative people can develop anti-D antibodies if exposed to Rh-positive blood.

Antecedents

  • Need for transfusion (anemia, bleeding, surgery)
  • Type and screen or type and crossmatch ordered
  • Pregnancy (Rh status critical for hemolytic disease of newborn)
  • History of prior transfusions or pregnancies (alloantibody formation)
  • Emergency situations (may use O-negative before full typing)

Negative Consequences

  • ABO incompatibility → acute hemolytic reaction (life-threatening)
  • Rh incompatibility: sensitization; hemolytic disease of the newborn (Rh-negative mother, Rh-positive fetus)
  • Alloimmunization from repeated exposure → harder to find compatible blood
  • Delayed hemolytic reactions
  • Death from incompatible transfusion

Related Concepts

Type and crossmatch, universal donor (O-negative), universal recipient (AB-positive), Rh factor, RhoGAM (Rh immune globulin), hemolytic disease of the newborn, acute hemolytic transfusion reaction, antibody screen, emergency transfusion.

Exemplars

  • Universal RBC donor: O-negative — no A, B, or Rh antigens; used in emergencies before typing complete
  • Universal RBC recipient: AB-positive — no anti-A or anti-B antibodies; can receive any ABO type
  • Plasma compatibility is OPPOSITE of RBC: AB plasma is the universal donor (no antibodies); O is universal recipient for plasma
  • Rh-negative recipient should receive Rh-negative blood (especially women of childbearing age) to prevent sensitization
  • RhoGAM example: Rh-negative mother carrying Rh-positive fetus receives Rh immune globulin (RhoGAM) at 28 weeks and after delivery to prevent maternal sensitization and protect future pregnancies
  • Crossmatch: donor RBCs mixed with recipient serum to confirm compatibility before transfusion (detects agglutination)
  • Type and screen: determines ABO/Rh and screens for unexpected antibodies; type and crossmatch reserves specific compatible units
  • Verification: two licensed personnel confirm blood type matches recipient before every transfusion — the critical error-prevention step

Worked Example Medication Adherence Concept spans Ch 1 (Pharmacokinetics & Routes), Ch 2 (Individual Considerations), and every drug-class chapter · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Medication Adherence

Defining Characteristics

The extent to which a person takes medication as prescribed — correct dose, correct interval, correct duration. Distinguished from the older term "compliance" — adherence emphasizes the patient as an active partner in the therapeutic plan.

Two complementary domains:

  • Initiation — filling the prescription and starting the medication
  • Persistence — continuing the medication as prescribed over time

Estimated at ~50% globally for chronic-disease medications — a major modifiable contributor to treatment failure.

Antecedents

  • Understanding of the indication and expected benefit
  • Manageable regimen — fewer pills, fewer daily doses, simpler timing
  • Affordability — cost is a major modifiable antecedent
  • Tolerable side effects
  • Trust in the prescriber and therapeutic relationship
  • Health literacy and language access
  • Social support, reminders, pill organizers
  • Stable housing, food, and routine

Negative Consequences

  • Treatment failure and disease progression
  • Antimicrobial resistance when antibiotic courses are not completed
  • Withdrawal or rebound with abrupt discontinuation (e.g., SSRIs, beta-blockers, benzodiazepines, opioids)
  • Avoidable hospitalization and mortality
  • Wasted medications and rising healthcare cost
  • "Diagnostic creep" — prescribers add more medications to address apparent treatment failure, when the underlying issue is non-adherence — masking and worsening polypharmacy

Related Concepts

Health literacy, therapeutic relationship, motivational interviewing, pill burden, polypharmacy, antimicrobial stewardship, shared decision-making, deprescribing.

Exemplars

  • Positive (system-level): client uses a 7-day pill organizer and smartphone reminder; prescriber selects an affordable generic; nurse simplifies the regimen to once-daily where pharmacokinetically possible
  • Negative (intentional non-adherence): client stops antihypertensive because "I feel fine" — leads to stroke or MI months later
  • Negative (unintentional non-adherence): client confused by a complex regimen; nurse uses motivational interviewing and adherence aids to address barriers rather than blaming the client
  • Negative (antimicrobial): client stops a 10-day antibiotic course at day 4 when feeling better — incomplete course drives antimicrobial resistance
Worked Example Polypharmacy Concept spans Ch 2 (Individual Considerations), Ch 8 (Older Adult), Ch 47 (Special Populations), and across drug-class chapters · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Polypharmacy

Defining Characteristics

Use of multiple medications by a single patient — typically defined as ≥5 routine medications (some sources use ≥10). May be:

  • Appropriate polypharmacy — necessary for multiple chronic conditions, with each medication justified and regularly reviewed
  • Inappropriate polypharmacy — drug interactions, therapeutic duplication, low-value medications, or medications continued beyond their indication

Strong correlation with age — common in older adults — and often involves multiple prescribers, OTCs, and supplements.

Antecedents

  • Multimorbidity — multiple chronic conditions, each guideline-driven to a specific medication
  • Multiple prescribers without care coordination
  • Prescribing cascade — a medication side effect is mistaken for a new condition and treated with another medication, which causes its own side effect, and so on
  • Failure to deprescribe outdated or no-longer-indicated medications
  • Patient hesitance to stop "their" medications
  • Inadequate medication reconciliation at transitions of care

Negative Consequences

  • Drug-drug interactions — risk rises exponentially with each added medication
  • Drug-disease interactions
  • Adverse drug events — especially falls, delirium, and cognitive impairment in older adults
  • Lower adherence (regimen complexity as barrier)
  • Increased hospitalization and cost
  • Reduced quality of life and functional decline
  • Beers Criteria medications (anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, some sleep aids) are particularly high-risk in older adults

Related Concepts

Pharmacokinetics in aging, drug-drug interactions, Beers criteria, prescribing cascade, deprescribing, medication reconciliation, comprehensive medication review, falls risk.

Exemplars

  • Positive (appropriate polypharmacy): a 75-year-old with heart failure, atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes, and CKD takes 9 medications, all guideline-indicated, with regular review and clear monitoring
  • Negative (prescribing cascade): client started on amlodipine for hypertension → develops ankle edema → started on furosemide → develops urinary frequency → prescribed an anticholinergic for "overactive bladder" → develops cognitive decline and falls. The cascade is the real problem.
  • Intervention exemplar: a hospital admission triggers complete medication reconciliation and a pharmacist consult — three medications are deprescribed before discharge with prescriber concurrence and clear taper schedule
Worked Example Therapeutic Drug Monitoring Concept spans Ch 1 (Pharmacokinetics), and drug-class chapters (lithium, vancomycin, gentamicin, phenytoin, digoxin) · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Therapeutic Drug Monitoring (TDM)

Defining Characteristics

The practice of measuring drug concentration in blood to optimize dosing and minimize toxicity. Applied selectively — primarily to drugs with a narrow therapeutic index (a small gap between effective and toxic concentrations) or with high inter-patient variability.

Two timing concepts:

  • Peak — highest concentration, drawn shortly after the dose (timing depends on route and drug)
  • Trough — lowest concentration, drawn immediately before the next scheduled dose

For most narrow-TI drugs, the trough is the key safety and efficacy measure. Common TDM targets: lithium, vancomycin, gentamicin, phenytoin, digoxin. For warfarin, the INR is monitored (a pharmacodynamic measure, not direct drug level).

Antecedents

  • Drug with narrow therapeutic index (e.g., lithium, vancomycin, digoxin, phenytoin)
  • High inter-patient pharmacokinetic variability
  • Steady state achieved (typically 4–5 half-lives) before reliable measurement
  • Renal or hepatic dysfunction affecting clearance
  • Drug interactions altering metabolism (e.g., CYP inducers/inhibitors)
  • Clinical concern for toxicity or therapeutic failure
  • Pediatric, geriatric, or pregnant patient — altered pharmacokinetics warrants TDM

Negative Consequences

Without TDM:

  • Subtherapeutic dosing → treatment failure (infection not eradicated, seizures continue)
  • Toxic dosing → preventable adverse events (vancomycin nephrotoxicity, lithium tremor/ataxia/seizure, digoxin arrhythmias)
  • Antimicrobial resistance emergence from subtherapeutic dosing

With improperly performed TDM:

  • Timing errors — sample drawn at the wrong moment (peak instead of trough; before steady state) → misinterpretation and inappropriate dose changes
  • Misreading peak for trough or vice versa
  • Treating the "lab number" rather than the patient — ignoring clinical context

Related Concepts

Pharmacokinetics, half-life, narrow therapeutic index, steady state, drug-drug interactions, INR (warfarin), antimicrobial stewardship, individualized dosing.

Exemplars

  • Positive (vancomycin): trough level drawn 30 minutes before the 4th dose; target 15–20 mcg/mL for severe MRSA infections; dose adjusted to target and monitored serially
  • Positive (lithium): trough drawn 12 hours after the last dose; maintenance target 0.6–1.2 mEq/L; dose carefully titrated to maintain the narrow therapeutic window
  • Positive (digoxin): level drawn at trough; target 0.5–2 ng/mL; toxicity considered at any level if symptoms present (vision changes, arrhythmias)
  • Negative (timing error): gentamicin level drawn during the infusion (not at trough) — falsely high reading triggers unnecessary dose reduction → infection undertreated → resistance emergence
